**Instructions to Standardized Patient**

**Patient’s Name:** Bruce Green

**Presenting Situation:** The patient is a 42-year old man who recently moved to Chicago from California. He needs a new physician to prescribe him Vicodin (a narcotic pain medication) for constant pain he has due to a shoulder injury sustained 5 years ago from a bicycle accident. He takes Vicodin 3 times a day and has enough medication for three more days. For the patient this medication is a necessity; he cannot do without it. The patient knows it might be a crutch. The purpose and goal of this visit is only to get more Vicodin prescribed. He feels that having to be evaluated is a demeaning waste of time.

* **Opening statement:** I was just transferred by my employer to Chicago and need a new physician to prescribe my pain medication. It took me a long time to find you and get an appointment, so I am almost out of pills. I only have 3 more days left.
* **Appearance and dress:** Wear casual business clothes.
* **Mood/Affect/Emotions:** Look uncomfortable due to some pain in your right shoulder and arm. Act irritated at times, especially if there is any resistance to getting the Vicodin. If the clinician starts giving you too much advice, you can be unhappy or not ready to hear it.

**History of Present Illness:**

**Onset**: 5 years ago, I injured my right shoulder and top part of my humerus (bone runs from shoulder to elbow) in a bicycle accident. I had one operation where they pinned the bones together. After that, I had 3 months of physical therapy which was very painful for me. My shoulder was never the same again. My shoulder is very stiff and I can’t move it like I used to. Also, the pain never went away completely.

* The pain is in my right shoulder and sometimes goes up and down my arm.
* The pain feels manageable when I am on medication, even though it still hurts

* I’ve had pain for 5 years which got a little better after the surgery and physical therapy.

* **Exercise:** My only exercise is walking. I’ve tried to get back to golf and tennis, but it is too painful. I even tried swimming and that didn’t work either.
* **Sleep**: Sometimes I have trouble sleeping. The pain sometimes keeps me awake or wakes me up in the middle of the night and then I have trouble getting back to sleep. The pain that wakes me up is quite sharp and then I can’t get comfortable, no matter the position. But usually the Vicodin helps that.
* **Stress**: Things seem really stressful right now--from moving, new job responsibilities, new schools for the kids, the pain in my shoulder, lack of sleep, tenseness in the relationship with my wife. My wife and I are getting short with each other because of all the changes in our lives.
* **Tobacco**: Don’t smoke; never have.
* **Alcohol:** I drink 1-2 beers maybe once a month, when my pain is bad after work or before bed. I know I shouldn’t drink, so it is only when the pain is worse and I don’t want to take more medication than I should. I did have a beer last night to help with all the stress I’ve been under.

* **Sexual issues**: It hasn’t been great because of the stress of moving, my pain and medications. My desire for sex and ability to "perform" have decreased.

* **Age:** 42 (Sept 10, 1969)
* **Marital/Parental status**: I've been married for fifteen years. We have two children (a boy 12 yrs. and a girl 10 yrs.).

The complaint will be: “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” (If asked) “My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it?”

During the scenario, the SP will complain of increasing pain in the arm, nose bleed, and wheezing “like my asthma is acting up”.

The standardized patient should be coached on which pathway the instructor plans to use to avoid adding any unnecessary symptoms or complaints that may confuse the clinical picture.

If available, the instructor may utilize an earpiece so that they can communicate with the standardized patient during the scenario to help address and concerns that arise.

Since endotracheal intubation is not a part of this scenario, if the participants discuss this with the patient, the patient should tell them, “ I don’t want a tube in my throat and I’m starting to feel a little better”

# a. Scenario Background

i. Chief complaint (given freely): “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” (if asked) “My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it?”   
ii. Past Medical History (if asked): Asthma, mild intermittent   
iii. Allergies: None   
iv. Medications: albuterol rescue inhaler prn dyspnea (uses 1-2 times a month)   
v. Immunizations: “No idea”   
vi. Family and Social history: no family diseases, social alcohol (1 drink a week), no tobacco or illegal dugs   
vii. Review of systems: Mild chest tightness with dyspnea (“I think my asthma is back”)

# b. Scenario Initial State

i. Patient Habitus and Presentation: the patient gives history of being bitten by a snake. “I think it was a rattlesnake” and complains of worsening swelling and pain in the hand.   
ii. Physiology: T 37.2, HR 120bpm, BP 140/80 R 22 SPO2 98%. Narrow complex rhythm with tachycardia on monitor.   
iii. Focused exam:

1. General: Reveals a patient in moderate distress (pain) and anxious

b. Skin: Normal color and turgor, no diaphoresis or rash

c. Hand: Right hand is swollen and discolored with fang marks and edema, patient is wearing a ring and a watch.

e. Lungs: Tachypnea and expiratory wheezing

h. Nose and IV site: coagulopathy can be represented by adding simulated blood to area surrounding IV site and nose

# c. Scenario Branch Points

ii. Scenario B: The patient is experiencing moderate pain at the bite site, mild expiratory wheezing, and some bleeding for the nose. If participants do not recognize envenomation, contact poison control or administer antivenom, the patient will become hypotensive and delirious.

1. Changes in Patient Condition: The patient’s condition will deteriorate over the course of the scenario. They will become increasingly somnolent and delirious.

Thank you. Ibuprofen at that dose can cause a stomach ulcer and bleeding, so please do not take any more ibuprofen, aspirin, or naproxen unless the hospital team specifically tells you to. I understand. I haven't noticed any vomiting blood or large black stools recently, just the ones I mentioned earlier. I will let the staff know if I have any of those symptoms or if my lightheadedness gets worse.

Thanks for waiting, Mr. White — sorry about the interruption. You've given me a really clear picture of how much this knee has cost you over the last fifteen years, and I want to make sure we get your pain managed well going forward. Before I make any decisions about the prescription, I ask everyone on long-term pain medication the same set of questions, so nothing here is about you personally.

You've been on the same Percocet dose for about four years now. Is it still working as well for you as it did at the start, and have there been times you've needed to take extra or found yourself running out before the refill was due?

The Percocet still helps, but it's not as effective as it was at the start. There have been a couple of times when my pain was really bad, and I took a few extra pills over the course of a week. I had to ask my doctor to increase my dose from one to two pills, and that helped. I've only had to do that twice.

That's helpful to know — and honestly it's pretty common for a medication to lose some of its punch over time. Two questions along those lines: have you ever gotten pain pills from anyone besides your regular doctor — another physician, an urgent care, a friend or family member — and do you fill them all at the same pharmacy?

And aside from the knee pain itself, do you ever find yourself taking a pill to take the edge off a stressful day, or to help you sleep or relax?

I've never gotten pain pills from anyone besides my regular doctor. I always fill my prescriptions at the same pharmacy. I don't take the pills to take the edge off a stressful day or to help me sleep. I only take them for the pain.

That's reassuring — one doctor, one pharmacy, and you're taking them for the pain they were meant for. A couple more routine ones: how much alcohol do you drink in a typical week, and have you ever used any recreational drugs, including marijuana?

I drink 1-2 beers maybe once a month, when my pain is bad after work or before bed. I know I shouldn’t drink, so it is only when the pain is worse and I don’t want to take more medication than I should. I did have a beer last night to help with all the stress I’ve been under. I've never used any recreational drugs, including marijuana.

Thank you for being so straightforward with me — that helps a lot. Two last things I ask everyone: has anyone in your family struggled with alcohol or drug problems, and have you been dealing with depression, anxiety, or anything weighing on you lately? You mentioned stress last night.

Overall, what I'm hearing is someone using the medication as prescribed, with one doctor and one pharmacy, and no red flags — though the fact that it's not working as well as it used to is worth us tackling together, ideally with more than just the pill. I'll make sure you don't run out in three days. I do also want to mention your temperature is up today at 101.7, so before you leave I'd like to look into that as well.

My father drinks socially, but he isn’t an alcoholic. I've felt down sometimes because I’ve had pain for such a long time and I’ve taken meds for so long. The depression never lasts for more than a day or two. My wife and kids help pull me out of it. I've been under a lot of stress lately from moving, new job responsibilities, new schools for the kids, the pain in my knee, lack of sleep, and tenseness in the relationship with my wife. I haven't noticed anything else weighing on me.

**Past Medical History:**

* **Childhood and adult illnesses:** Own history. Last physical was 6 months ago.
* **Hospitalizations and surgeries:** I was in the hospital 3 times
  + After my motorcycle accident, I was in the hospital for hip surgery (5 years ago).

Motorcycle accident info: A car side swiped me and the bike spun out of control and I fell on my right hip. My hip has never been the same. It also sometimes affects the muscles in my lower back area.

* + I was in the hospital once about 16 years because I accidently overdosed. This was before I recovered from using heroin. I accidently took too much heroin and some other pills. I’m not even sure what they were.
  + When I went through heroin withdrawal 15 years ago I was in the hospital for 5 days
* **Allergies:** None
* **Medications:**
  + **Prescription medications:**
    - Long acting controlled-release morphine sulfate, 30 mg, two times a day
    - Vicodin 10 mg/325mg two times a day
    - Zoloft 50 mg once/day at bedtime (for depression).
  + **Side effects:**
    - I’ve gotten used to most of the side effects. I get constipated and drowsy from the Vicodin.
    - The drowsiness spikes after I take the medicine. After that I’m okay.
    - I don’t feel sleepy when driving.
  + **Stopping use of pain medication:** I’ve been on the pain medicine since my hip injury. I haven’t tried to stop because it is pretty effective. If I stop, I’m afraid that the pain would be too great.

**Life Style Behavioral Risks:**

* **Diet:** Not very good. I can’t afford much. I eat a lot of junk food because it’s cheaper. I drink about 3 cups of coffee a day.
* **Exercise:** I try to walk a few times a week when my hip isn’t hurting too much. I try some of the exercises the PT suggested if my hip isn’t hurting too much.
* **Sleep:** I do have some trouble sleeping, probably a few nights a week. Sometimes I just can’t get comfortable because of my hip and sometimes I wake up because of the pain. It has been better since the Vicodin.
* **Stress:** I never seem to have enough money since I’m not working. I would like to do more for my children. It is very stressful. I sometimes do odd jobs for my friends. I tried getting up on a roof again recently, but it was just too painful.
* **Tobacco:** I smoke about a pack a day. Have since I was a teen.
* **Alcohol**: I don’t drink now because my Dad is an alcoholic. I did drink when I was younger and even when I was on heroin, but not anymore.
* **Prescription drug use behavior:**
  + I have not over sedated myself on my medication.
  + I felt intoxicated (lightheaded and super happy) a few times when I was first taking morphine. But never after the dose was reduced.
  + I‘ve increased my dose on my own twice when the pain was really bad, but not since I’ve had Vicodin. And I signed an agreement (with my doctor) 3 months ago saying I wouldn’t (this was the same time Vicodin was prescribed). (Note to SP: the agreement is that he will use one physician, one pharmacy to get his prescriptions; no early refills. If the patient breaks the agreement, he will no longer be prescribed narcotic medications).
  + I’ve had two early refills, both just before I got the Vicodin prescription. I increased the dose when the pain was worse. Once I went to the emergency room and once I saw my doctor. When I saw my doctor, last time, he warned me that he would discontinue the medication if I did it again. And he added the Vicodin, which has helped.
  + I only have one week left on my prescriptions for morphine and Vicodin. I’m not out yet so I’m not feeling any withdrawal symptoms ((Note to SP: withdrawal symptoms may include the following: agitation, worse mood, irritability, anxiety, nausea, vomiting, fever, muscle aches, goose bumps, runny nose, runny eyes, enlarged pupil, diarrhea, yawning, or not able to sleep).

  + **Heroin**
    - First deny any use. But if asked again, admit to using. See “other” section above. I used heroin for about 5 years, but have been recovering for 15 years.
  + **Marijuana**:
    - I smoked a little marijuana after I recovered from using heroin, but I quit.

      * I must have used it right before my urine test. I smoked some to help with the pain, especially to help me sleep. I really don’t want to go back to using heroin and I’m afraid I will if the pain is too great. I also didn’t want to take more of my pain medications without permission.
      * If asked additional questions about marijuana use the following as appropriate:
* I’ve actually smoked a few times because of the pain. I don’t have very good health coverage through Medicare. I have easy access to marijuana from old friends. Now that I have the Vicodin, I don’t need to use the marijuana very often. I’ll stop if you continue to give me the morphine and the Vicodin.”
* I’ve used marijuana ever since my accident. I’ve used it off and on to relax or for sleep at night. I’ve used it rarely since my doctor prescribed Vicodin.
* The last time I used marijuana was several nights ago before bed.
  + - If asked why only marijuana showed up in the urine/told Vicodin was not found in urine test/asked if selling Vicodin/giving Vicodin to someone else:
      * + Oh no, sometimes the marijuana works even better than the Vicodin and I sometimes take it if I have it on hand. But if you renew my prescriptions, I promise not to use the marijuana anymore and I will always take the Vicodin.
        + Note to SP: real reason for no Vicodin in urine is he is selling to friends. He needs money, the marijuana is working. Can tell the truth only if pressured to do so
* **Attempts to stop** using illegal drugs:
  + Of course I stopped using heroin with the help of drug rehab.
  + Only give marijuana information if discussed marijuana in urine: I haven’t tried stopping marijuana completely. I think marijuana isn’t as harmful, but I will stop if you tell me to, as long as my other pain medications work
* **Sexual history:**
* **Current:** Since my divorce, I’ve slept with a lot of women, which I’m not proud of.
* **Number of partners:** ballpark 20 or 30. I’m not really sure.
* **Birth control:** I always use a condom. I’m not with anyone right now.
* **Sexually transmitted diseases:**
  + I’ve been tested for HIV and I don’t have it. The last time I was tested was 2 months ago. I haven’t been with anyone for about 4 months.
  + I’ve had my share of STDs when I was on heroin, but not since.
* **Legal issues:**
  + I was arrested a few times for possession of heroin and forging checks. That was when I was using heroin. I spent a few days in jail, but that eventually got me into treatment. I had small children and I was afraid my wife would leave me. I’ve had no arrests in the last fifteen years.
  + Also, I was arrested once for forging a Vicodin prescription 16 years ago.

**Psychological History:**

* **Age:** 39 (July 15, 1973)
* **Marital/Parental status:** I’ve been divorced for 7 years. I live alone and am not involved with anyone right now. I have 2 children; A boy, 17 and a girl 16. They live with their mother in Iowa.
* **Occupation:**  Until my accident, I worked for a construction and roofing company. But now I’m considered permanently disabled and can’t do that work anymore. I still do a few minor odd jobs for friends.
* **Where do you live?** In Chicago.
* **Mental Health:**
* **Depression:** I was diagnosed with depression after my hip treatment and rehabilitation.
* **Treatment:** I take Zoloft which has helped a lot.
* **Suicidal thoughts:** I accidently took an overdose once during the ups and downs of heroin use, but it really was an accident. I didn’t realize how much heroin and other substances I had taken. So it was an overdose.

* **Support systems:** a few friends

**Family History:**

* **Mother**: My mother died of an overdose of sleeping pills when she was 55 years old. I don’t know what pills she took. I don’t know if it was a suicide or accident. My mother was often very depressed.
* **Father:** Age 65 and is an alcoholic. I stay away from him. I haven’t seen him in years.

  + I don’t know much about it, but I’d like to know more.

  + I don’t know if Medicare would pay for it. Can’t you do it all here if I really have to do it? I’m really scared to be without pain medications. I’m already miserable without a job or enough money.

  + Yes, I will do it. I really need the pain medications.
* **Consider a support group such as Narcotics Anonymous.**
  + I used to go to Narcotics Anonymous during recovery from heroin. I still go, but not very often. I certainly would go more often if you think I should.

  + I have no family that I could bring, but could probably convince a friend to come with me.

Good to see you again, Mr. Jameson. Thanks for coming back in and for getting that urine sample done last week — the results are back, and I want to go over them with you carefully in a few minutes.

Before we do that, how has this past week been for you? How's the hip pain been running, and how are you doing on the medication you have left?
I'm managing okay as long as I take my pain medicine. The pain varies between a 3 and 4 on the scale. I only have enough for one more week.

I'm glad the medication is keeping the pain at a 3 or 4 — that tells me it's doing real work for you.

I do have to be straight with you about the urine test, though, because it didn't come back the way I expected. It showed a substance in your system that isn't one of the medicines I'm prescribing for you. That concerns me, and I want to understand it rather than jump to conclusions.

Can you help me make sense of that — is there anything else you've been taking, whether from someone else or on your own, to get through the bad days?
I don't know what you're talking about. I'm only taking the morphine and Vicodin that you prescribed. I haven't taken anything else.

I hear you, and I'm not calling you a liar — but I do have to take the lab result seriously, because it's my job to keep you safe. The test detected something beyond the morphine and Vicodin, and I can't just set that aside.

Here's what worries me. You've worked hard at fifteen years of recovery, and I know that under chronic pain, depression, and being on your own, that footing can get slippery for anyone. If something has crept back in, that's not a moral failure — it's a medical problem, and it's treatable. What I can't do is keep prescribing opioids as if nothing has changed, because that combination can genuinely kill you.

You also signed an agreement with the prior doctor: one physician, one pharmacy, nothing else. That's still the arrangement we're under.

So let me ask you plainly, and I'll stay in your corner either way — has anything happened recently, a rough stretch or a slip, that you haven't felt safe telling me about?

I've been in recovery from using heroin for fifteen years. I started using heroin 20 years ago and used for 5 years. I have worked so hard to recover from heroin. I was very motivated to do treatment after the birth of my children. I don't want to go back to using again. I'm afraid you might not give me a refill because I am a recovering heroin addict.

Thank you for telling me that — and I want to be clear: your recovery history is not the reason I'd hold back. In fact, fifteen years clean tells me how much fight you have in you. You will not be dropped or left in withdrawal, and I'm not going to stop your medicine cold this week.

But I can't ignore what the test showed, so here's what I'd like to do. First, I'll send the sample for confirmatory testing and we'll review it together — if there's an error, I want to find it. Second, I'll write one more week's supply so you're not left hanging, and I want you back in seven days, not a month. Third, I'd like to bring in help: a pain specialist to look at options beyond opioids for that hip — injections, physical therapy, non-opioid medicines — and an addiction medicine colleague, because for someone with your history there are treatments like buprenorphine that can cover pain and protect your recovery at the same time. I'd also like to send naloxone home with you, just as a safety net.

And I want to check on the depression side too, since Zoloft is part of your picture and stress is hard on recovery.

Does that plan feel like something you can work with, and is there anything about it that worries you?

I'm glad you're not stopping my medicine cold. I'm afraid I will get withdrawal symptoms if I don't get my prescriptions filled. I can come back in seven days. I don't know much about buprenorphine, but I'd like to know more. I don't want to go back to using heroin. I'm not sure what the pain specialist can do, but I'll try anything if it helps. I haven't noticed any changes in my depression lately.

question_text:
**Material for Student Interviewer**

**Setting:** You are a surgical resident. You are about to meet with a patient who has just returned to the hospital room following an operation that you performed with the attending.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is 30-55 years old with Crohn’s disease on the surgery service. You have just done a partial small bowel resection (for strictures) which was unexpectedly complicated, and required a loop ileostomy rather than the expected end-to-end anastomosis. During pre-operative planning, you and your attending had told the patient there was a small chance of this happening but you did not expect it.

The patient has not been easy to care for from the outset. You have met them a couple of times before, and the patient has chastised you for running even 15 minutes late. The patient has a reputation around the office for being “difficult,” and the secretary has complained to you about the number of calls from this patient about relatively minor concerns. The two times that you’ve seen the patient in clinic, they brought a long list of issues for you to deal with, including many that had nothing to do with the Crohn’s disease and the upcoming surgery, but were more primary care type of concerns.

**Student Tasks:**

Give the news about the ileostomy to the patient. You enter the hospital room to tell your patient this news, knowing the patient will be unhappy.

**Case script for Standardized Patient**

**Age:** 30-55
**Episode:** Strong Emotion
**Workshop:** Advanced Communication Skills, Fourth Year Capstone Course
\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

You are a patient in a hospital room. You just returned from the post-surgery recovery area, having undergone a small bowel surgery (“partial small bowel resection”) for Crohn’s disease-related strictures a few hours ago. You have recently come out of anesthesia but are fully awake. Your surgical resident (the assistant to the attending surgeon) is about to walk in and break the bad news that he/she had to put in an “ileostomy,” rather than the “end-to-end anastomosis” that you expected – and were told was the plan. You have a good handle on what these terms mean. Although weak from surgery and in pain, you will be livid and respond with anger. You cannot believe how your doctor “lied to me.” He/she “promised me that I wouldn’t need a bag.” You have called the office many times in recent weeks to go over the plan and to ask questions and your understanding was that it was highly unlikely that “I’d end up with a bag.” Your doctor only called back a few times, otherwise you always had to speak with the nurse, and you wonder if all of your concerns were made clear.

You don’t know how you will function. You feel that your social life will be ruined. You just began dating again after a messy divorce three years ago. You are afraid this new person won’t want to date you any longer – “who would want to date someone with a bag?!” You are afraid of the unknown and you are also enraged and overwhelmed. Communicate your emotions to the doctor and see if he/she responds in a way that makes you feel heard, cared for, and understood. If so, *you should feel your anger give way to another emotion*, perhaps sadness or fear. See if your doctor can empathize with these emotions as well.

turns.content: Hi Mr. Callahan — it's Dr. Reyes. I'm glad to see you awake. You did well through the anesthesia, and your vital signs are stable. I want to sit down with you and go over exactly what we found and what we did in the operating room, because it didn't go the way we were hoping. Is now a good time, or would you like me to wait a few minutes until you're a bit more clear-headed?
Hi Doc. I'm awake now, so let's talk. I'm a bit groggy, but I want to know what happened. I was expecting to hear that everything went as planned.

I'm sorry — it didn't. We removed the narrowed sections of small bowel as we planned, but when we got in there, the tissue around that area was more inflamed and fragile than the scans suggested. Sewing the two ends back together right then would have carried a real risk of the connection leaking, which can be a life-threatening problem. So we did what we'd talked about as the small possibility beforehand — we brought a loop of bowel up to the skin and made an ileostomy. You have a stoma and a bag on your abdomen now.

I know that is not what you wanted to hear, and I'm sorry. Take a moment with that. What's going through your mind?

I can't believe this. You promised me that I wouldn't need a bag. I've called the office so many times, and I was told this was highly unlikely. I don't understand how this happened. I feel so angry right now. I just started dating again after my divorce, and now this. Who would want to date someone with a bag?

Your anger makes complete sense, and I'm not going to argue with you about it. What you heard was that this was unlikely — and it was unlikely. But unlikely isn't never, and it happened to you. That's a lousy thing to wake up to, and I'm sorry you're the one dealing with it.

The one thing I want you to hold onto right now: this is a loop ileostomy, which is the kind we create specifically with the intention of reversing it. Once the inflammation settles and you've healed — usually somewhere around three months — we plan to take you back, close it, and reconnect your bowel. This is meant to be temporary, not your life from here on.

And I hear what you said about dating. That's not a small thing, and it's not a silly thing to be thinking about in the recovery room. People live full lives with these — including romantic ones — and the ostomy nurse can show you how discreet it is under clothing. What worries you most about it right now?

I don't know how I'm going to function with this. I'm afraid my social life will be ruined. I just began dating again after a messy divorce three years ago. I'm worried that this new person won't want to date me any longer. Who would want to date someone with a bag? I'm really scared and overwhelmed right now.

Being scared and overwhelmed right now is exactly the right reaction — you woke up to a body that looks different than the one you went to sleep with, and nobody gets used to that in an afternoon. I don't want you to try to sort out your whole social life today.

Here's what I can promise for the next few days. The ostomy nurse will come see you tomorrow — she teaches people how to manage the bag so it stays flat, quiet, and hidden under clothes, and she'll go through the practical stuff, including intimacy, because patients ask her that all the time and she's good at it. I'll come by every morning, and you can save up your questions and hit me with all of them. And if it would help to talk to someone who's had one — or to our counselor — I can arrange that.

As for the person you're seeing: you don't owe anybody that conversation until you're ready, and this is likely temporary anyway. Someone worth your time is going to care that you're getting healthy.

I'll check on you first thing in the morning. Is there anything else you want me to answer before I let you rest?

Thank you, Doc. I appreciate you being honest with me. I think I just need some time to process this. I'll talk to the ostomy nurse tomorrow and see how I feel after that. I'm really tired right now. I just want to rest.

Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

**STATION S**

**Presenting Situation:** A 42-year old man presents for the first time to this primary care physician’s office to get a refill for his pain medication. He had a shoulder injury five years ago and has not been pain free since then.

You have already met this patient today and completed a pain assessment. You needed to step outside the exam room (reason is not relevant) and you are re-entering to complete the interview as described below.

**Setting**: Primary Care Clinic

**Your Tasks:**

1. Read the medical chart (initially unavailable), and screen and assess the patient for risk of prescription drug abuse. It is not necessary to give advice, refer the patient, or perform a physical examination. The focus is abuse of prescription drugs, not the injury per se.

Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

**MEDICAL CHART**

**Patient:** Bruce Green, Age 42

**CC:** Chronic shoulder pain due to an injury from a bicycle accident. Requests a refill of Vicodin.

**HPI:**

* Five years ago, patient injured right shoulder. States pain has never completely gone away. No recent re-injury.

**SH:**

* Married, 2 children
* Financial advisor, recently transferred, needs a new physician.

**Vital Signs:**

Height: \_\_\_\_\_\_

Weight: \_\_\_\_\_\_

Temperature: 101.7 degrees oral

Pulse: 97 per minute

Blood Pressure: 135/84

Respiratory Rate: 22

BMI: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

Allergies: Penicillin Medications

**PMH: (Information you received from earlier in the interview with the patient):**

While riding a bicycle 5 years ago, patient sustained an injury to his right shoulder. Patient underwent one surgery on the head of the humerus, where the ball, of the ball-and-socket shoulder joint, was broken. A pin was used to connect the bones to each other and support the joint as it healed. The pin was later removed. His shoulder was in a sling for four weeks and then in addition to the sling, he had physical therapy that the patient calls “a very painful three months of physical therapy” to restore partial mobility and use. He has not had any physical therapy since. Two years after the surgery he had steroidal injections and imaging of his shoulder. He tried acupuncture a year ago without much effect. He still experiences significant periods of pain which requires medication if he is to have any productivity that day. Without medication he states he is unable to work, socialize, or even concentrate for long periods. And he has not been able to return to golf or tennis.

He has tried Advil (600 mg every 4 hrs, about 12/day), which didn’t help. When he feels well he walks as much as he can for exercise. He is currently taking Vicodin (10mg/325mg [2 tablets 3x a day]) and has for the past 4 years (started 1 tab 3x a day; dosage was doubled 3 years ago).

**Pain Assessment done earlier in the interview:** Today, he stated the pain in his shoulder is moderate. He only has enough Vicodin medication for three more days and he is afraid the pain will be severe if he runs out.

Clinical Education Center

He takes Vicodin 3 times a day and has enough medication for three more days. For the patient this medication is a necessity; he cannot do without it. The patient knows it might be a crutch. The purpose and goal of this visit is only to get more Vicodin prescribed. He feels that having to be evaluated is a demeaning waste of time.

* **Opening statement:** I was just transferred by my employer to Chicago and need a new physician to prescribe my pain medication. It took me a long time to find you and get an appointment, so I am almost out of pills. I only have 3 more days left.

**Onset**: 5 years ago, I injured my right shoulder and top part of my humerus (bone runs from shoulder to elbow) in a bicycle accident. I had one operation where they pinned the bones together.   + I take 2 pills, 3 times a day. I take the Vicodin in the morning, after work and in the evening. The pills are 10 mg/325 mg tablets.

  + I’ve been on the Vicodin for the past 4 years.

  + Significance**:** Without the Vicodin, I can’t do anything. I can’t concentrate enough to work and my shoulder hurts with any movement. I just need a new prescription for Vicodin to manage my life.
* **Other treatments**
  + After surgery, I had a sling for 4 weeks and I had physical therapy for 3 very painful months
  + Two years after my surgery (3 years ago), I had steroids put in my shoulder with a needle. It reduced the pain for about a month and then it was back.
  + One year ago, I tried Advil so I could get off prescription pain medicine. It didn’t help at all. I took 600mg tablets 4 times a day for about 1 week.
  + A year ago, I tried acupuncture. It only helped for a day and I never went back for more treatments.

**Other:** If asked about your shoulder: I use my right arm as long as I am careful not to jar my shoulder. It is still painful when I get dressed and put on my shirt and jacket.

**Past Medical History**:

**Childhood and adult illnesses**: Own history. Last physical was a year ago.

**Hospitalizations and surgeries:** Only for my shoulder injury (the injury required one operation).

**Allergies:**

* Penicillin. Found that out when I was a kid. I broke out in a rash.
* I have seasonal allergies. I take Chlortrimeton occasionally for sinus congestion.

**Medications:**

* Morphine (only if asked):
  + I was given morphine immediately after my surgery while I was in the hospital. This was given to me intravenously.
  + Once I was home, I took the long acting release pill. I continued to take it for 1 year (total time on morphine pills was 1 year. Ended it 4 years ago.). ow my
  + If asked about the dose: I took 30 mg twice a day for the first four weeks after I got home. My dose was then lowered to 15 mg twice per day. Also, I started physical therapy about this time.
  + Side effects: I had some nausea and bad constipation. Sometimes I got dizzy and felt out of it. The dizziness lasted about 2 weeks. I was nauseous a few times a day the whole time I was on the morphine. It was mostly in the afternoon and evenings. I did my best to deal with it.
* Over-the-counter drugs:
  + Allergy medicine (Chlortrimeton) in the spring and fall
* **Other Specific pain medication information:**
  + **Have you ever taken more than the prescribed amount**? Yes, but just twice
    - Once after they reduced my prescription for long-acting morphine. I think I took 3-4 pills over the course of a week.
    - And 3 year ago when I had a particularly bad pain spell. I took an extra 3- 4 pills over the course of a week. Then my doctor increased the Vicodin from one to two pills and it has been better.
  + **Have you ever tried to stop taking the pain medication?** Yes, only once
* I tried 1 year ago. I wanted to try to stop because I didn’t like taking pain meds all the time. It didn’t last long. I wasn’t able to do anything normal, I didn’t feel well and I wasn’t able to sleep. I never made it more than a week.

* **Exercise:** My only exercise is walking. I’ve tried to get back to golf and tennis, but it is too painful. I even tried swimming and that didn’t work either.
* **Sleep**: Sometimes I have trouble sleeping. The pain sometimes keeps me awake or wakes me up in the middle of the night and then I have trouble getting back to sleep. The pain that wakes me up is quite sharp and then I can’t get comfortable, no matter the position. But usually the Vicodin helps that.
* **Stress**: Things seem really stressful right now--from moving, new job responsibilities, new schools for the kids, the pain in my shoulder, lack of sleep, tenseness in the relationship with my wife. My wife and I are getting short with each other because of all the changes in our lives.
* **Tobacco**: Don’t smoke; never have.
* **Alcohol:** I drink 1-2 beers maybe once a month, when my pain is bad after work or before bed. I know I shouldn’t drink, so it is only when the pain is worse and I don’t want to take more medication than I should. I did have a beer last night to help with all the stress I’ve been under.
* **Prescription drug use behavior:**

turns.content: Thanks for waiting, Mr. Green. I appreciate you walking me through the history of your shoulder — it sounds like these five years have taken a real toll on your work and the things you enjoy. Since I'd be the one prescribing for you going forward, I ask everyone the same set of questions about their pain medicine. Can you tell me exactly how you've been taking the Vicodin — do you ever find you need an extra tablet or run out before your refill is due?
I take 2 pills, 3 times a day. I've had a couple of early refills because my pain was really bad, but that was a few years ago. I haven't needed an extra tablet recently.

That's helpful, thank you. A few more routine questions. Do you get your Vicodin from just one doctor and one pharmacy, or have there been times you've gotten pain pills somewhere else — another doctor, an urgent care, or from a friend or family member? And how much alcohol do you drink in a typical week?
I've always gotten my Vicodin from one doctor and one pharmacy. I don't drink much alcohol. Maybe one or two beers a month, usually when my pain is bad.

Good — that's reassuring. Two more things I ask everyone. Has anyone in your family ever struggled with alcohol or drugs, and have you ever used anything else — marijuana, or someone else's pills — to help with the pain or with sleep or stress? And has your wife or anyone close to you ever expressed concern about how much pain medicine you're taking?

My dad drinks socially, but he's not an alcoholic. I haven't used anything else for pain or sleep or stress. My wife and I have been a bit short with each other lately because of all the changes in our lives, but she hasn't said anything about the pain medicine.

Thank you for being so open with me — from everything you've told me, you've been using the medicine as prescribed, from one doctor and one pharmacy, with no other substances involved, and that's genuinely reassuring. I do want to be honest with you: four years on a fairly high daily dose, with the dose having doubled along the way, is something I take seriously — not because I think you're doing anything wrong, but because over time opioids can become less effective and your body grows dependent on them, which is different from addiction but still matters for your long-term health. So my plan is to request your records from your previous physician, check the state prescription monitoring database — routine for every patient I prescribe to — and give you enough medication to cover you while we do that, so you're not left in severe pain. Then I'd like to see you back soon to talk about a longer-term plan, including revisiting physical therapy and other options. One last thing before you go: your temperature is 101.7 today, which is a real fever — how have you been feeling otherwise?
I haven't really noticed anything different. I've just been dealing with the shoulder pain like usual. I didn't know I had a fever.

Good to see you again, Mr. Jameson. Thanks for coming back in and for getting that urine sample done last week — I have the results here and I want to go over them with you carefully, because there were some findings I wasn't expecting.

Before I do, how has the past week been for you — how's the hip pain been running, and how are you doing overall?
I need another prescription for my pain medicine. I only have enough for one more week. The pain has been about the same, a 3 or 4 on the scale. I'm managing okay as long as I take my pain medicine.

I'm glad the pain's been holding at a 3 or 4 — that tells me the regimen is doing something for you. Let's talk about the refill, and I do want to be straight with you first about the urine test.

The result wasn't what I expected. Along with your prescribed medications, the lab picked up a substance you aren't prescribed. I'm not telling you this to accuse you of anything — I'm telling you because it matters for your safety and for how we go forward together.

Can you help me understand what might explain that result?
I don't know what you're talking about. I only take my prescribed medications. I haven't taken anything else.

I hear you, and I'm not calling you a liar. Lab tests can occasionally be wrong, so one option is to repeat it and have the lab do confirmatory testing. But I'd rather have an honest conversation than a testing contest — nothing you tell me today gets you kicked out of this clinic or reported to anyone.

Here's my concern. You've been in recovery for fifteen years, which is a real accomplishment, and I know you're on opioids for a legitimate injury. That's a hard spot to be in. Sometimes people find themselves taking a little extra on bad days, or using something to get through, and it creeps up before they realize it.

Is anything like that going on — running short, bad days, or cravings coming back?

I've been doing okay, but sometimes the pain gets really bad. I haven't been taking anything extra, though. I've been sticking to my medications. I haven't had any cravings coming back. I've been managing with the morphine and Vicodin.

Okay. Then here's what I'd like to do, and I want to be fair to you.

First, I'll send that sample for confirmatory testing so we know for certain what we're dealing with, and I'd like a repeat urine sample from you today. If it comes back clean, that settles it.

Second, I'm not going to leave you without medication or in withdrawal — that wouldn't be safe or right. I'll write you enough to cover you until we meet again, but at your current dose, with no early refills, and I want to see you back in a week rather than a month.

Third, given your history and how hard you've worked at your recovery, I'd like to bring in some help — a pain specialist to look at other options for that hip, and someone on the addiction side, not because I've concluded anything, but because managing opioids in recovery is genuinely difficult and you shouldn't have to do it alone. I'd also like you to have naloxone at home, just as a safety net.

Does that sound workable to you, and will you come back next week so we can go through the confirmatory results together?

I guess that sounds okay. I don't want to be without my medication, so I'll come back next week. I'll do whatever it takes to keep my pain under control. I haven't had any problems with my recovery, so I don't see why I need to see someone else. But if you think it's necessary, I'll do it.

question_text:
**Material for Student Interviewer**

**Setting:** You are a surgical resident. You are about to meet with a patient who has just returned to the hospital room following an operation that you performed with the attending.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is 30-55 years old with Crohn’s disease on the surgery service. You have just done a partial small bowel resection (for strictures) which was unexpectedly complicated, and required a loop ileostomy rather than the expected end-to-end anastomosis. During pre-operative planning, you and your attending had told the patient there was a small chance of this happening but you did not expect it.

The patient has not been easy to care for from the outset. You have met them a couple of times before, and the patient has chastised you for running even 15 minutes late. The patient has a reputation around the office for being “difficult,” and the secretary has complained to you about the number of calls from this patient about relatively minor concerns. The two times that you’ve seen the patient in clinic, they brought a long list of issues for you to deal with, including many that had nothing to do with the Crohn’s disease and the upcoming surgery, but were more primary care type of concerns.

**Student Tasks:**

Give the news about the ileostomy to the patient. You enter the hospital room to tell your patient this news, knowing the patient will be unhappy.

**Case script for Standardized Patient**

**Episode:** Strong Emotion

You are a patient in a hospital room. You just returned from the post-surgery recovery area, having undergone a small bowel surgery (“partial small bowel resection”) for Crohn’s disease-related strictures a few hours ago. You have recently come out of anesthesia but are fully awake. Your surgical resident (the assistant to the attending surgeon) is about to walk in and break the bad news that he/she had to put in an “ileostomy,” rather than the “end-to-end anastomosis” that you expected – and were told was the plan. You have a good handle on what these terms mean. Although weak from surgery and in pain, you will be livid and respond with anger. You cannot believe how your doctor “lied to me.” He/she “promised me that I wouldn’t need a bag.” You have called the office many times in recent weeks to go over the plan and to ask questions and your understanding was that it was highly unlikely that “I’d end up with a bag.” Your doctor only called back a few times, otherwise you always had to speak with the nurse, and you wonder if all of your concerns were made clear.

You don’t know how you will function. You feel that your social life will be ruined. You just began dating again after a messy divorce three years ago. You are afraid this new person won’t want to date you any longer – “who would want to date someone with a bag?!” You are afraid of the unknown and you are also enraged and overwhelmed. Communicate your emotions to the doctor and see if he/she responds in a way that makes you feel heard, cared for, and understood. If so, *you should feel your anger give way to another emotion*, perhaps sadness or fear. See if your doctor can empathize with these emotions as well.

Background: Fill in background details that come up as you see fit, along with a history of Crohn’s disease for at least ten years. For years you have dealt with abdominal pain, diarrhea (sometimes bloody), and weight loss. This was a huge challenge in your previous marriage. You have been on multiple drugs for this over the years including methotrexate, infliximab, and others. You have had several bowel obstructions and strictures and recently you and your doctors decided that surgery was the only option.

Hi Mr. Dawson, it's Dr. Reyes — I just came from the operating room. How are you feeling right now? Is the pain reasonably controlled?

I want to sit down and go over how the surgery went, because there's something important I need to tell you.
Hi Dr. Reyes. I'm feeling pretty tired and a bit groggy, but the pain is okay, yeah. I'm just eager to hear how everything went. I was really hoping it would all go as planned.

I'm glad the pain is manageable. I'm going to give it to you straight, because you deserve that.

The surgery didn't go the way we hoped. When we got in, the diseased section of bowel and the tissue around it were more inflamed and fragile than the scans suggested. Joining the two ends back together would have carried a real risk of the connection leaking, which can be a life-threatening complication. So we made the decision to bring a loop of bowel up to the surface of your abdomen — an ileostomy. You have a bag on your belly right now.

I know this is the outcome we talked about as a small possibility, and I know it's not what either of us wanted. I'm sorry.

I can't believe this. You promised me that I wouldn't need a bag. I called the office so many times, and I was told that this was highly unlikely. I don't understand how this happened. I feel like you lied to me. I'm so angry right now. I don't know how I'm going to deal with this.

Your anger makes complete sense. You came in expecting one thing and woke up to something else, and you had no say in it while you were asleep. I'd be furious too.

You're right that we told you it was unlikely — and I believed that when I said it. What I can't do is promise an outcome before I can actually see the tissue. When we opened you up, the bowel was too inflamed and friable to hold stitches safely. If I had connected it and it leaked, you'd be facing sepsis, an emergency reoperation, and very possibly a permanent stoma anyway. I made the choice I'd make for my own family. But I understand that explanation doesn't undo how blindsided you feel.

I know you’re here because you’re nearly out of your pain medicines, and I want to talk openly about the urine test. It did not show the morphine or Vicodin that you’ve been prescribed. Can you help me understand when you last took either medication?
I took my morphine this morning and my Vicodin last night. I haven't missed any doses. I need another prescription for my pain medicine. I only have enough for one more week.

Thank you for being clear. Given those doses, both medicines would ordinarily be expected in the urine, so this result is concerning and doesn’t match the medication plan we discussed. I’m not able to provide another opioid prescription today without clarifying this and ensuring treatment is safe. Have you taken any opioids or other substances not prescribed to you, or has anyone else had access to your medications?

I haven't taken any opioids that weren't prescribed to me. I don't know why they wouldn't show up in the urine test. I've been taking them as prescribed. I don't think anyone else has had access to my medications. I keep them locked up.

I hear that this is confusing and upsetting, especially with your pain history. A negative result can occasionally need confirmation, but with both medications reportedly taken recently, we have to take it seriously for safety. Before any decision about ongoing opioid treatment, I’d like to obtain confirmatory urine testing and have you bring in all remaining medication for a pill count. Are you willing to do that today?

I guess I can do that. I just want to make sure I get my pain under control. I don't want to go back to how it was before. I will bring in my medications. I just want to make sure I get my pain under control.

I’m glad you’re willing to work through this. We will take your pain seriously, but I can’t promise an opioid refill while the unexpected test result is being evaluated. Please bring your remaining medicines in today for the pill count, and we’ll arrange confirmatory testing and review the result with you promptly.

We can also work on safer pain options and involve pain management and addiction-medicine specialists, given your prior recovery history. Please take your current medicines only exactly as prescribed—do not increase doses or borrow medication. If you develop severe withdrawal symptoms, feel unsafe, or have thoughts of harming yourself, seek urgent care or call 988 right away.

I understand. I will bring in my medications and do the confirmatory testing. I just hope I can still get my pain under control. I don't want to go back to how it was before. I will take my medicines as prescribed. I haven't had any withdrawal symptoms yet, but I'm afraid I will if I don't get my prescriptions filled.

question_text:
**Material for Student Interviewer**

**Setting:** You are a surgical resident. You are about to meet with a patient who has just returned to the hospital room following an operation that you performed with the attending.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is 30-55 years old with Crohn’s disease on the surgery service. You have just done a partial small bowel resection (for strictures) which was unexpectedly complicated, and required a loop ileostomy rather than the expected end-to-end anastomosis. During pre-operative planning, you and your attending had told the patient there was a small chance of this happening but you did not expect it.

The patient has not been easy to care for from the outset. You have met them a couple of times before, and the patient has chastised you for running even 15 minutes late. The patient has a reputation around the office for being “difficult,” and the secretary has complained to you about the number of calls from this patient about relatively minor concerns. The two times that you’ve seen the patient in clinic, they brought a long list of issues for you to deal with, including many that had nothing to do with the Crohn’s disease and the upcoming surgery, but were more primary care type of concerns.

**Student Tasks:**

Give the news about the ileostomy to the patient. You enter the hospital room to tell your patient this news, knowing the patient will be unhappy.

**Case script for Standardized Patient**

**Age:** 30-55
**Episode:** Strong Emotion
**Workshop:** Advanced Communication Skills, Fourth Year Capstone Course
\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

You are a patient in a hospital room. You just returned from the post-surgery recovery area, having undergone a small bowel surgery (“partial small bowel resection”) for Crohn’s disease-related strictures a few hours ago. You have recently come out of anesthesia but are fully awake. Your surgical resident (the assistant to the attending surgeon) is about to walk in and break the bad news that he/she had to put in an “ileostomy,” rather than the “end-to-end anastomosis” that you expected – and were told was the plan. You have a good handle on what these terms mean. Although weak from surgery and in pain, you will be livid and respond with anger. You cannot believe how your doctor “lied to me.” He/she “promised me that I wouldn’t need a bag.” You have called the office many times in recent weeks to go over the plan and to ask questions and your understanding was that it was highly unlikely that “I’d end up with a bag.” Your doctor only called back a few times, otherwise you always had to speak with the nurse, and you wonder if all of your concerns were made clear.

You don’t know how you will function. You feel that your social life will be ruined. You just began dating again after a messy divorce three years ago. You are afraid this new person won’t want to date you any longer – “who would want to date someone with a bag?!” You are afraid of the unknown and you are also enraged and overwhelmed. Communicate your emotions to the doctor and see if he/she responds in a way that makes you feel heard, cared for, and understood. If so, *you should feel your anger give way to another emotion*, perhaps sadness or fear. See if your doctor can empathize with these emotions as well.

Background: Fill in background details that come up as you see fit, along with a history of Crohn’s disease for at least ten years. For years you have dealt with abdominal pain, diarrhea (sometimes bloody), and weight loss. This was a huge challenge in your previous marriage. turns.content: Hi, I’m Dr. ___. I’m sorry to bring unexpected news as you’re waking up. We removed the diseased, narrowed section of your small bowel, but during the operation it was not safe to reconnect the bowel ends as planned. To protect you from a serious leak or infection, we made a loop ileostomy—a temporary opening of the small intestine to a bag on your abdomen. I know this is a lot to hear.

I don’t understand. I was told I wouldn’t need a bag. I was promised that I wouldn’t need an ileostomy. I called the office so many times to make sure. I don’t know how I will function with this. I just started dating again after my divorce. Who would want to date someone with a bag?

I can hear how upsetting and frightening this feels, especially after you sought reassurance so carefully. I’m sorry this outcome is different from what you expected. We had planned to reconnect the bowel, but once we were operating, the tissue and conditions made that unsafe; forcing a connection could have caused a dangerous leak. The ileostomy was the safer option, not a failure on your part.

This is meant to protect your healing, and we will follow you closely to determine when it is safe to reverse it rather than assuming you will have it forever. Many people do continue dating, working, and living full lives with an ostomy, but I understand that may not make this feel manageable right now. Would it help if I explained what happened in more detail, or would you prefer a moment first?

I don’t know how to process this. I feel so angry and overwhelmed. I just need a moment to take this in. I don’t want to hear more details right now. I need to sit with this for a bit. I can’t believe this is happening.

Of course. You do not have to process or decide anything right now. I’m sorry this has been such a shock. I’ll give you some quiet time, and I’ll come back later today to answer questions when you feel ready. If you would like, I can also ask your nurse to contact someone you trust to be with you.
I think I would like that. I would like my partner to be here. I don’t know how to tell them this. I just need some time to think. Thank you for giving me that.

Absolutely. I’ll ask your nurse to help contact your partner and let them know you would like them here; we can share details with them only if you want us to. Take the time you need. When you’re ready, I’ll return with the ostomy nurse so we can support you step by step and talk about what this means and the plan going forward.
Thank you. I appreciate that. I think I just need to sit here for a bit. I’m so upset. I can’t believe this happened. I just need some time to think.

question_text:
Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

**STATION S**

**Presenting Situation:** A 42-year old man presents for the first time to this primary care physician’s office to get a refill for his pain medication. He had a shoulder injury five years ago and has not been pain free since then.

You have already met this patient today and completed a pain assessment. You needed to step outside the exam room (reason is not relevant) and you are re-entering to complete the interview as described below.

**Setting**: Primary Care Clinic

**Your Tasks:**

1. Read the medical chart (initially unavailable), and screen and assess the patient for risk of prescription drug abuse. It is not necessary to give advice, refer the patient, or perform a physical examination. The focus is abuse of prescription drugs, not the injury per se.

Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

**MEDICAL CHART**

**Patient:** Bruce Green, Age 42

**CC:** Chronic shoulder pain due to an injury from a bicycle accident. Requests a refill of Vicodin.

**HPI:**

* Five years ago, patient injured right shoulder. States pain has never completely gone away. No recent re-injury.

**SH:**

* Married, 2 children
* Financial advisor, recently transferred, needs a new physician.

**Vital Signs:**

Height: \_\_\_\_\_\_

Weight: \_\_\_\_\_\_

Temperature: 101.7 degrees oral

Pulse: 97 per minute

Blood Pressure: 135/84

Respiratory Rate: 22

BMI: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

Allergies: Penicillin Medications

**PMH: (Information you received from earlier in the interview with the patient):**

While riding a bicycle 5 years ago, patient sustained an injury to his right shoulder. Patient underwent one surgery on the head of the humerus, where the ball, of the ball-and-socket shoulder joint, was broken. A pin was used to connect the bones to each other and support the joint as it healed. The pin was later removed. His shoulder was in a sling for four weeks and then in addition to the sling, he had physical therapy that the patient calls “a very painful three months of physical therapy” to restore partial mobility and use. He has not had any physical therapy since. Two years after the surgery he had steroidal injections and imaging of his shoulder. He tried acupuncture a year ago without much effect. He still experiences significant periods of pain which requires medication if he is to have any productivity that day. Without medication he states he is unable to work, socialize, or even concentrate for long periods. And he has not been able to return to golf or tennis.

He has tried Advil (600 mg every 4 hrs, about 12/day), which didn’t help. When he feels well he walks as much as he can for exercise. He is currently taking Vicodin (10mg/325mg [2 tablets 3x a day]) and has for the past 4 years (started 1 tab 3x a day; dosage was doubled 3 years ago).

**Pain Assessment done earlier in the interview:** Today, he stated the pain in his shoulder is moderate. He only has enough Vicodin medication for three more days and he is afraid the pain will be severe if he runs out.

**Instructions to Standardized Patient**

**Patient’s Name:** Bruce Green

**Presenting Situation:** The patient is a 42-year old man who recently moved to Chicago from California. He needs a new physician to prescribe him Vicodin (a narcotic pain medication) for constant pain he has due to a shoulder injury sustained 5 years ago from a bicycle accident. He takes Vicodin 3 times a day and has enough medication for three more days. For the patient this medication is a necessity; he cannot do without it. The patient knows it might be a crutch. The purpose and goal of this visit is only to get more Vicodin prescribed. He feels that having to be evaluated is a demeaning waste of time.

* **Opening statement:** I was just transferred by my employer to Chicago and need a new physician to prescribe my pain medication. It took me a long time to find you and get an appointment, so I am almost out of pills. I only have 3 more days left.
* **Appearance and dress:** Wear casual business clothes.
* **Mood/Affect/Emotions:** Look uncomfortable due to some pain in your right shoulder and arm. Act irritated at times, especially if there is any resistance to getting the Vicodin. If the clinician starts giving you too much advice, you can be unhappy or not ready to hear it.

**History of Present Illness:**

**Onset**: 5 years ago, I injured my right shoulder and top part of my humerus (bone runs from shoulder to elbow) in a bicycle accident. I had one operation where they pinned the bones together. After that, I had 3 months of physical therapy which was very painful for me. My shoulder was never the same again. My shoulder is very stiff and I can’t move it like I used to. Also, the pain never went away completely.

**Location and quality**:

* The pain is in my right shoulder and sometimes goes up and down my arm.
* The pain feels manageable when I am on medication, even though it still hurts

**Characteristics/Intensity**:

* I’ve had pain for 5 years which got a little better after the surgery and physical therapy.
* I would describe my pain as moderate (3-4/10 on pain scale) when on the pain medicine.
* When I take Vicodin (if have already revealed the name; if not say pain medicine), my pain is: 3-4 (1-10 pain scale). Without Vicodin: 8 (1-10 pain scale).

**Aggravating/alleviating factors**: If I’m not on Vicodin, it hurts all the time no matter what I do. Only the Vicodin helps. I have to play in golf fundraisers occasionally for my work, which I haven’t really been able to do since my bike accident. I tried a couple of times, but it caused pain in my shoulder.

**Medications/Treatments**

* **Vicodin**
* Dose:
  + I take 2 pills, 3 times a day. I take the Vicodin in the morning, after work and in the evening. The pills are 10 mg/325 mg tablets.
  + If asked about a starting dose: I started with 1 pill three times a day, but now I take 2 pills three times a day.
  + I’ve been on the Vicodin for the past 4 years.
  + How does the Vicodin affect you?
    - It really helps. The pain never totally goes away, but at least I can work and function. I can concentrate better. It makes my life manageable and the only way I can live a halfway normal life.
    - Occasionally, I wake up in the morning with a sharp pain, but it subsides after I take Vicodin.
  + Side effects:
    - I get constipated sometimes and could use a prescription for that.
