question_text:
# Station 3 – Shared Decision Making

Scenario:

You are a third year student rotating through a longitudinal ambulatory rotation. You are seeing a patient, Joanna Mills, for the second time. Ms. Mills is a 45-year old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. When you saw her for the first time last week, she had not been receiving medical care or medication refills for 6 months due to the loss of her medical insurance. Last week, she came to clinic to re-establish care and receive refills of her medications for diabetes mellitus. Last week, you agreed to refill her medications and ordered blood work. Ms. Mills has come in to clinic today to discuss the lab results with you.

You discussed this with your attending preceptor prior to seeing Ms. Mills. Your attending physician instructs you to discuss the results with Ms. Mills and encourages you to engage in shared decision making with your patient.
private_patient_context:
**Station 3 – Shared Decision Making**

**Training Materials:**

# 3. <u>Scenario for Standardized Patient</u>

You are Joanna Mills, a 45-year old woman. Last week, you came to a new hospital-based clinic to establish a primary care doctor and get refills of your medications, since you ran out of medications for diabetes mellitus. You haven’t been to see a doctor in over six months, and you’ve been rationing your medications during that time, but you ran out of medications last week.  The medical student whom you met last week gave you a one month supply of your medications (metformin and glyburide) but asked you to get blood work done so that s/he could “get a sense of how well controlled your diabetes was” and to make changes in medications, if necessary. You went to the laboratory last week after your visit and are now here for your scheduled follow up visit to go over the results of the blood test. You feel fine and have refilled your medications and do not have any new problems to report to the medical student today; but you are curious to learn about the results of your blood tests and hope to hear that your diabetes is well controlled.

<u>Medical History:</u>

You were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus four years ago by your primary care doctor at the time, Dr. Alvarez. You were not surprised when you received this diagnosis because you have a strong family history of diabetes. You know that the A1C blood test shows whether or not your diabetes is controlled, and you also know that anything less than 7 is good and anything higher than 7 means that the sugars are too high. You remember that when you were first diagnosed with diabetes, your A1C was 7.6. The doctor had you on Metformin first, but the following year, she added glyburide because the A1C was not at goal. Your doctor slowly increased the doses of these medications; and as of one year ago, had you at your current dose of metformin and glyburide.

You have not had any complications related to diabetes mellitus, and you have been taking your medications as prescribed. However, 6 months ago, you lost your job and your medical insurance. You could not afford to continue seeing your primary care doctor so you stopped going at that time. The doctor gave you last refills of your medications and encouraged you to come to the hospital-based clinic since they had a sliding scale fee service for patients. Six months ago at your last visit with Dr. Alvarez, you also had a blood test. You received a letter from Dr. Alvarez stating that your A1C was 8.8 and that you needed to follow up on this, but you were unable to see her or any other doctor until now.

You have been busy for the past few months so you did not come to the hospital clinic.

You have admittedly stretched out your remaining pills, sometimes skipping doses to make the prescription last a little longer. Last week, you were completely without medications; and you were scared about your sugars getting too high, so you came to the clinic.

<u>Family History:</u>

As noted above, you were not surprised when you were diagnosed with diabetes four years ago. Both of your parents suffered from it, and you know that it is an illness that can run in the family. However, you were still frightened when you were first given the diagnosis. You have seen both of your parents suffer from medical problems related to diabetes. Your father had high blood pressure and kidney problems, which his doctor said was due to diabetes. He passed away suddenly from a heart attack when he was 66 years old. Your mother, who is now 64, is alive but has many medical problems. Prior to her recent stroke 3 months ago, she had very poorly controlled high blood pressure and diabetes.  She has been in and out of the hospital several times a year for the past few years, either for chest pain or “fluid in the lungs” or skin infections and infected foot ulcers.

Besides diabetes, you do not have any other medical problems.

<u>Social History:</u>

You were laid off from your job as a clothing buyer for a large department store. Since then, you have been looking for a new job and have been trying to keep your spirits up. You were busy caring for your mother in another state for the past few months because she had a recent stroke. Between your mother’s illness and your search for a job, the past six months have been extraordinarily stressful for you; and you have not really had time to take care of yourself. But you have always wanted to stay in good health to avoid illness, and you know that it’s important to focus on your health right now.  You have been without health insurance since losing your job as you could not afford COBRA and you postponed looking into applying for Obama care in hopes that you would soon have a new job.  You have been unable to afford to refill your medications, and therefore, rationing the pills until you ran out of them last week.

You do not have any history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug use.

You are divorced and have a 20 year-old daughter, who is in college and no longer living at home

<u>Emotional Tone:</u>

You are very concerned about your health condition although it has been difficult for you to focus on your own health for the past six months, between your economic hardship and your mother’s acute illness. When you had insurance, you were always good about following up with your primary care doctor and taking all of your medications. Even though you have had diabetes for four years, you were told that you could be “in control” of your illness and maybe avoid complications of diabetes. You have been happy to take your pills, as long as it meant controlling your illness and avoiding complications of the disease.  You know that you have not taken your pills as prescribed, mostly because of financial concerns and the cost of medications.  You are very reluctant to start insulin. You know that being on insulin means needing to prick yourself several times a day to check your blood sugar and give yourself the insulin shots and you hate the thought of pricking yourself so frequently with needles.  Also, you know that the diabetic supplies (insulin and more lancets and paper strips for frequent sugar checks) are expensive and another cost that you feel would be really hard to absorb now.

**Your role is to portray a patient who is very concerned about your health. You want to know how to keep yourself healthy. Yet, you are upset and worried when you learn that your diabetes is not well controlled.  You are reluctant to start insulin therapy because you dislike the thought of using the needles to give yourself medication and the extra cost of medications and supplies feels like a financial burden that you feel unable to take at this time. In addition, although you know it is not rational you feel that using insulin means you are more likely to develop the complications you saw your parents go through because they were on insulin.  However, you normally always follow your doctor’s advice and are unsure about going against his advice by not starting insulin.**

<u>Scenario:</u> 

The student will enter the clinic room, where you are waiting to be seen. You are seated next to the desk, appearing comfortable but a little anxious. You met this student last week and are happy to see the same person again.

The student may ask, “I wanted to talk to you about your blood test results that we did last week. Do you know what an A1C test signifies?”

**“Yes, I remember my last doctor telling me that it was a blood test that the doctors took to show whether the diabetes was controlled or not. I know that it’s supposed to be below 7.”**

The student will inform you that your A1C level was elevated, at 11.

You are surprised and concerned.

**“Oh no, that’s really high isn’t it?”**

The student should inform you that this A1C is very elevated and indicates that the diabetes is very poorly controlled at this time. You are upset and very worried by this news.

**“It’s never been so high like this. You know I was worried about my sugars but I never thought it could get up to this level.” What does this mean I have to do now?”**

The student should describe treatment options. Since you are on high doses of your current medications, there is no way to simply go up on the current dose of medications. The student will recommend starting insulin therapy as a way to rapidly bring down the A1C level and control the diabetes.

You interrupt the student when s/he mentions insulin and get visibly upset.

**“Wait, insulin? Oh, I don’t want to do that.”**

The student should ask you why you do not want to start insulin. S/He should give you a chance to state what your concerns are. You state many reasons why you don’t want to start insulin therapy now. After you give each reason, you should give the student a chance to discuss it with you.

**“I know that there are a lot of reasons why my sugars got uncontrolled like this. I wasn’t doing all the things that I know I should have been doing about my health. I wasn’t eating right, I wasn’t consistently taking my pills every day. I wasn’t really focusing on my health. I think that there are a lot of things besides insulin that I can do to get my health back in order.”**

**“I know that when you start insulin, you have to check your sugars many times throughout the day. And those extra supplies, those strips and lancets, they all cost a lot of money that I don’t think I’d be able to afford right now.”**

**“To tell you the truth, I’m really afraid of pricking myself with a needle to give myself insulin.  I don’t think that I could do that. I hate needles and the thought of giving myself shots every day is really scary to me.”**

**“I am so afraid of insulin.  I know it isn’t rational but I feel like insulin means I have diabetes with a capital D.  Do you know what I mean – it seems more serious.  I saw my dad go through so much, and now my mom with her stroke.  They were both on insulin.”**

The student should respond to all of your concerns and reasons for not wanting to start insulin. If he does not acknowledge or validate your concerns then you should remain resistant to starting insulin.

The student should ask you about what your desires regarding the management of your illness are. S/He might ask, “Ms. Mills, can you tell me a little bit about how diabetes is affecting your life, and what you are hoping to do to manage your illness? What would you like to see for yourself regarding your diabetes?

**“I really don’t want to be sick from diabetes like my mother was. I know all about the complications, the foot ulcers, the amputations, dialysis, strokes… I’m just really scared about my diabetes being out of control because I never want to go through what she’s been going though with her health. I want to be healthy for my daughter and for myself. So I want to do what you think is best. I’ve always listened to doctors in the past. But right now, I am just really scared of this insulin for a lot of reasons too. I am just hoping for a way that I can get back into good health again without going down the insulin road.”**

The student should try to engage you in deciding what the best treatment for your diabetes is. If he only recommends insulin and says that nothing else will work right now, but you don’t feel that he/she acknowledges the reasons why you do not want to start insulin, you will be more resistant to starting insulin now. However, if the student shares information with you about insulin treatment that addresses your concerns, you might consider changing your mind. Here are some examples of effective statements:

“The insulin that I would recommend starting you on is a once daily insulin that works slowly over 24 hours. You do not have to give yourself multiple injections of insulin each day. Rather, you could give yourself one injection a day.”

“The benefit of starting insulin is that it is more likely to successfully bring your A1C level down to signify good control of your diabetes. The better we control your diabetes, the less likely it is that you would ever get the complications of diabetes (such as kidney problems or eye problems.)

“One concern that I have in continuing with oral medicines rather than insulin, is that the oral medications do not bring down the A1C level as effectively as insulin does. I can tell that it is really important for you to get in control of your diabetes, and I think that this is the most successful way that we can do it.”

“Insulin is one part of the plan that we can create to control your diabetes. You are right that diet and exercise and taking your medications every day are equally important in controlling your diabetes. I think that we can work together on each of these issues, and perhaps insulin can be a component of this plan.”

If you feel that the student has engaged you as a partner in making the decision and has given you a chance to address your beliefs and concerns about your illness, then you should agree to work with the student to come up with a plan together; and you can agree to try the insulin.

**“Okay, I see what you are saying. I think that if you feel the insulin may really help me get my diabetes under control and keep me healthy, then I will try it for a while and see how my sugars improve.”**

If you feel that the student has not given you a chance to speak about your concerns and has not enlisted you as a partner in decision making, but rather unilaterally recommended insulin without building a consensus with you, then you should not agree to start insulin. You are calmer at the end but are very resolute about not starting insulin today.

**“You know, I don’t think I am able to get over my fear of starting insulin right now. I’d really rather try getting back on my pills every day and see how I do for a while before I switch my medicines.”**

If at any time the student asks a question that you do not understand or is at all unclear, then you should ask them to clarify. You can say:

**“What do you mean by that?”**

turns.content: Hi Ms. Mills, it's good to see you again. Thanks for coming back in to go over your lab results. Before I jump into the numbers — how have things been going since last week, and were you able to get your medications filled without any trouble?
Hi, thank you. Things have been okay, I guess. I was able to get my medications filled last week, so that's good. I've been taking them as prescribed since then.

I'm really glad you were able to get them filled and have been taking them consistently — that's not always easy after a gap in care.

Let me share what the blood work showed. Overall, your test that measures average blood sugar over the past few months came back higher than where we'd want it — which honestly isn't surprising, given you went about six months without your medications. It's not a sign you did anything wrong; it's information that helps us decide what to do next.

What's your reaction to hearing that, and what questions come to mind for you?
Oh no, that’s really high isn’t it? I was worried about my sugars but I never thought it could get up to this level. What does this mean I have to do now?

I can hear this is worrying you, and that's a really understandable reaction. What it means is that your diabetes hasn't been well controlled over the past several months — but it also means there's real room for improvement, and you've already taken the biggest step by getting back on your medications.

There are a few directions we could go. One option is to stay on your current medications, since you've only been back on them a week, and recheck in about three months to see how much they bring things down. Another is to adjust or add to your medications now to get you to a safer range faster. And alongside either of those, there are things like changes to eating, activity, or checking your sugars at home — plus getting you connected with a diabetes educator or nutritionist.

I don't want to just hand you a plan. What matters most to you here — moving quickly, or starting simpler and building up? And is there anything about your daily life, cost, or the medications themselves that we should factor in?

I know that there are a lot of reasons why my sugars got uncontrolled like this. I wasn’t doing all the things that I know I should have been doing about my health. I wasn’t eating right, I wasn’t consistently taking my pills every day. I wasn’t really focusing on my health. I think that there are a lot of things besides insulin that I can do to get my health back in order.

That takes real honesty to say, and I want you to know I hear you — you're not just looking for a prescription, you want to get back in the driver's seat with your health. I think that's exactly the right instinct, and those lifestyle pieces matter enormously.

So here's what I'd suggest, and tell me if it fits: we keep your current medications going as prescribed, and we don't add insulin today. Alongside that, you pick one or two changes that feel realistic to start with — maybe something with meals, maybe some walking — and I'll get you set up with a nutritionist and a diabetes educator to support you. We recheck your numbers in about three months. If things haven't come down enough by then, we revisit medications together, with no judgment.

Does that feel workable to you? And what's the one change you'd want to start with this week?

That sounds good. I think I could start with eating better. I know that I need to cut down on sweets and maybe eat more vegetables. I've always wanted to stay in good health to avoid illness, and I know that it’s important to focus on my health right now.

turns.content: Hi, I'm one of the doctors here in urgent care. I'm sorry you've been waiting — you look pretty uncomfortable. Can you tell me what's been going on with your right arm, and when the pain started?
Hi, yeah, it's been pretty bad. My right arm has been hurting for about four days now. It started with some redness and swelling, and now it's really painful and I feel sick all over.

That sounds miserable, and your fever and heart rate tell me your body's fighting something — I'm glad you came in. Can you tell me how it started? Was there any injury, cut, bite, or anything that broke the skin on that arm?

And do you feel safe at home right now?
I don't know, I just said it was a cat bite. I don't really want to talk about it. I'm not at home right now, I've been staying on the streets.

That's completely okay — you don't owe me that story, and I'm not going to push. Thank you for telling me you're staying on the streets; that matters for how we help you. Depending on how deep it goes, you may need to be admitted so we can give antibiotics through an IV. I'd also like our social worker to come by, just to talk about a safe place to stay and follow-up care — no pressure, only if you want. Does that plan sound okay to you, and is there anything you need right now, like water, food, or something for the pain?

Yeah, that sounds good. I'm really thirsty, so some water would be great. And yeah, my arm hurts a lot, so something for the pain would be nice. I guess I can talk to the social worker too, if they're nice.

# IV. Environment

V. Actors

ii. Physician(s): One to three participant physicians. Multiple configurations are possible. The Course Director may choose a primary or may have learners work in groups.

Participant Information Card

This is a patient with a history of mild intermittent asthma who presents with a snake bite. The patient told triage: “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” Their main complaint is increasing pain in the arm and they noticed some mild wheezing upon arrival (the patient stated it was: “like my asthma is acting up”)

Moulage & Standardized Patient Support

The standardized patient (SP) has a history of mild intermittent asthma and presents with a snake bite. The complaint will be: “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” (If asked) “My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it?”

During the scenario, the SP will complain of increasing pain in the arm, nose bleed, and wheezing “like my asthma is acting up”.

The standardized patient should be coached on which pathway the instructor plans to use to avoid adding any unnecessary symptoms or complaints that may confuse the clinical picture.

If available, the instructor may utilize an earpiece so that they can communicate with the standardized patient during the scenario to help address and concerns that arise.

Since endotracheal intubation is not a part of this scenario, if the participants discuss this with the patient, the patient should tell them, “ I don’t want a tube in my throat and I’m starting to feel a little better”

# a. Scenario Background

i. Chief complaint (given freely): “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” (if asked) “My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it?”   
ii. Past Medical History (if asked): Asthma, mild intermittent   
iii. Allergies: None   
iv. Medications: albuterol rescue inhaler prn dyspnea (uses 1-2 times a month)   
v. Immunizations: “No idea”   
vi. Family and Social history: no family diseases, social alcohol (1 drink a week), no tobacco or illegal dugs   
vii. Review of systems: Mild chest tightness with dyspnea (“I think my asthma is back”)

# b. Scenario Initial State

i. Patient Habitus and Presentation: the patient gives history of being bitten by a snake. “I think it was a rattlesnake” and complains of worsening swelling and pain in the hand.   
ii. Physiology: T 37.2, HR 120bpm, BP 140/80 R 22 SPO2 98%. Narrow complex rhythm with tachycardia on monitor.   
iii. Focused exam:

1. General: Reveals a patient in moderate distress (pain) and anxious

b. Skin: Normal color and turgor, no diaphoresis or rash

c. Hand: Right hand is swollen and discolored with fang marks and edema, patient is wearing a ring and a watch.

e. Lungs: Tachypnea and expiratory wheezing

h. Nose and IV site: coagulopathy can be represented by adding simulated blood to area surrounding IV site and nose

# c. Scenario Branch Points

ii. Scenario B: The patient is experiencing moderate pain at the bite site, mild expiratory wheezing, and some bleeding for the nose. If participants do not recognize envenomation, contact poison control or administer antivenom, the patient will become hypotensive and delirious.

1. Changes in Patient Condition: The patient’s condition will deteriorate over the course of the scenario. They will become increasingly somnolent and delirious.

turns.content: Hello, I'm the emergency physician. I understand a snake bit you at the garden center, and your hand is swelling and hurting a lot. That sounds incredibly scary. About how long ago did this happen, and how is your breathing feeling right now?
I was bitten maybe 30 minutes ago. My breathing is a bit tight, like my asthma is acting up. It's getting harder to breathe.

I'm very concerned about your breathing getting tighter, so I'm going to have the nurses get you some medicine for that right away. Are you feeling any swelling in your lips, tongue, or throat? And how far up your arm has the swelling spread so far?
No, my lips, tongue, and throat feel fine. The swelling is up to my wrist.

We are getting you a breathing treatment right now and will monitor you very closely. Did you happen to get a look at the snake or hear a rattle? And besides the pain and chest tightness, are you feeling dizzy, nauseated, or noticing any strange taste in your mouth?
I think it was a rattlesnake. I haven't noticed any dizziness, nausea, or strange taste in my mouth.

Thank you for telling me that. Since it was likely a rattlesnake and you are having these symptoms, we are going to prepare a snake antivenom to help stop the venom from causing more damage. Right now, I'm going to use a pen to mark where the swelling is on your arm so we can see if it spreads, and we'll draw some blood to check your clotting levels. I'm going to step out for just a moment to get your breathing treatment and the antivenom started, but my team and I will be keeping a very close eye on you.
Okay, thank you. My hand is really throbbing now, and I think I'm starting to feel a little lightheaded.

turns.content: Hello, I'm one of the doctors taking care of you today. I understand your primary care doctor sent you over to us for a blood transfusion. How are you feeling right now, and what symptoms originally prompted you to go see your doctor today?

Hi, I'm feeling okay right now. I went to see my doctor because I twisted my knee playing basketball with my son about 5 weeks ago. He did some blood work because he said I looked a bit pale. He called me today and said that I should come to the ED for a blood transfusion.

I'm sorry to hear about your knee injury. Have you been feeling unusually weak or short of breath lately? And have you been taking any pain medications, like ibuprofen or Aleve, to help with the knee pain?

I have been feeling a bit short of breath with some exertion, like when I had to take the stairs at work. I've been taking ibuprofen for the knee pain, 600 mg every 8 hours, but I don't take it as often now that the pain has gotten better.

That shortness of breath and paleness makes sense given that your blood counts are low. Since ibuprofen can sometimes irritate the stomach and cause internal bleeding, have you noticed your bowel movements becoming very dark or black? And have you had any stomach pain or vomiting?

Yes, my stools have been really black, almost like tar, for about a week now. I've had some stomach pain, about a 5 out of 10, that comes on 1-2 hours after eating, especially if I have wine with my meal. I haven't been nauseous or vomited.

Thank you for sharing that. It sounds very likely that the ibuprofen caused a bleeding ulcer in your stomach. The black, tarry stools you're seeing are actually a sign of bleeding in your digestive tract, which explains why your blood levels dropped and you've been feeling short of breath. For now, we'll get started on that blood transfusion to help you feel better and give you a medication to protect your stomach. We will also need you to stop taking the ibuprofen, and we'll likely have a stomach specialist come see you to take a look inside and stop any active bleeding. Do you have any questions for me before we get everything started?
I appreciate you explaining that to me. I guess I didn't realize the ibuprofen could cause this. I don't have any questions right now. I just want to get this taken care of.

turns.content: Hi Mr. K, I'm one of the doctors on the medicine team taking over your care. I understand you've been dealing with fevers, night sweats, and a cough for a few weeks, which sounds exhausting. How are you feeling today since coming into the hospital, and are you coughing anything up?
Hi doc, I'm still coughing and feel like I have a fever. No, I have not noticed any blood in my cough.

That sounds very uncomfortable, I'm sorry you're still feeling feverish. Just to get a little more detail, is the cough completely dry, or are you bringing up any phlegm? And have you noticed any unexplained weight loss over these past few weeks?
No, it's not completely dry. I do bring up some phlegm. No, my weight has been stable.

Got it, thank you. I read that you've worked in homeless shelters and jails, which can sometimes expose people to tuberculosis. Have you ever had a positive TB test in the past or been around anyone recently who was sick with TB? Also, I want to make sure I address what's on your mind—do you have any specific questions about your care so far?

I have not had a positive TB test in the past, but I have known many cases of TB having worked full time as a counselor in homeless shelters and jails. I don't have any specific questions about my care so far.

Thank you for sharing that, Mr. K. Because of your work history and your symptoms, we are going to run some tests on your phlegm to check for tuberculosis, as well as other infections like Valley Fever given your previous time living in Arizona and California. We will continue your current antibiotics and keep you comfortable while we wait for those results. We'll be checking back in with you later today as we get more information, but please let the nursing staff know if you need anything at all in the meantime.
Okay, thank you, doc. I appreciate you keeping me in the loop. I'll let the nurses know if I need anything.

# I. Rattlesnake bite (Crotalinae envenomation) simulation

# IV. Environment

a. Simulation Environment Setup: Simulation lab Emergency Department room, medication area (Pyxis or second area), audio-visual control room, debrief room/area

V. Actors

ii. Physician(s): One to three participant physicians. Multiple configurations are possible. The Course Director may choose a primary or may have learners work in groups.

# Appendix D

Participant Information Card

This is a patient with a history of mild intermittent asthma who presents with a snake bite. The patient told triage: “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” Their main complaint is increasing pain in the arm and they noticed some mild wheezing upon arrival (the patient stated it was: “like my asthma is acting up”)

# Appendix B

Moulage & Standardized Patient Support

The standardized patient (SP) has a history of mild intermittent asthma and presents with a snake bite. The complaint will be: “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” (If asked) “My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it?”

During the scenario, the SP will complain of increasing pain in the arm, nose bleed, and wheezing “like my asthma is acting up”.

The standardized patient should be coached on which pathway the instructor plans to use to avoid adding any unnecessary symptoms or complaints that may confuse the clinical picture.

If available, the instructor may utilize an earpiece so that they can communicate with the standardized patient during the scenario to help address and concerns that arise.

Since endotracheal intubation is not a part of this scenario, if the participants discuss this with the patient, the patient should tell them, “ I don’t want a tube in my throat and I’m starting to feel a little better”

# a. Scenario Background

i. Chief complaint (given freely): “I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me! My hand is swelling and it really hurts!” (if asked) “My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it?”   
ii. Past Medical History (if asked): Asthma, mild intermittent   
iii. Allergies: None   
iv. Medications: albuterol rescue inhaler prn dyspnea (uses 1-2 times a month)   
v. Immunizations: “No idea”   
vi. Family and Social history: no family diseases, social alcohol (1 drink a week), no tobacco or illegal dugs   
vii. Review of systems: Mild chest tightness with dyspnea (“I think my asthma is back”)

# b. Scenario Initial State

i. Patient Habitus and Presentation: the patient gives history of being bitten by a snake. “I think it was a rattlesnake” and complains of worsening swelling and pain in the hand.   
ii. Physiology: T 37.2, HR 120bpm, BP 140/80 R 22 SPO2 98%. Narrow complex rhythm with tachycardia on monitor.   
iii. Focused exam:

1. General: Reveals a patient in moderate distress (pain) and anxious

b. Skin: Normal color and turgor, no diaphoresis or rash

c. Hand: Right hand is swollen and discolored with fang marks and edema, patient is wearing a ring and a watch.

e. Lungs: Tachypnea and expiratory wheezing

h. Nose and IV site: coagulopathy can be represented by adding simulated blood to area surrounding IV site and nose

# c. Scenario Branch Points

ii. Scenario B: The patient is experiencing moderate pain at the bite site, mild expiratory wheezing, and some bleeding for the nose. If participants do not recognize envenomation, contact poison control or administer antivenom, the patient will become hypotensive and delirious.

1. Changes in Patient Condition: The patient’s condition will deteriorate over the course of the scenario. They will become increasingly somnolent and delirious.

turns.content: I'm sorry this happened to you — let's get you taken care of right away. Can you tell me exactly when the snake bit you, and can you describe what the snake looked like, if you remember?
I was shopping in the garden center and when I reached down to pick up a plant, a snake bit me. My friend took a picture of the snake on his phone, want to see it? I think it was a rattlesnake.

Yes, please show me that picture if you can — that would really help confirm what kind of snake it was.

While we look at that — how long ago did this happen, and how has the swelling and pain changed since then? Also, I heard you mentioned some wheezing — can you tell me more about that? Are you having any trouble breathing, throat tightness, or swelling of your lips or face?

I can show you the picture. It happened about 30 minutes ago. The swelling and pain have been getting worse since then. I have some mild chest tightness with wheezing, like my asthma is acting up. I haven't noticed any trouble breathing, throat tightness, or swelling of my lips or face.

Thank you for that picture — that does look consistent with a rattlesnake bite. I want to check a few more things quickly, since this can be serious:

- Are you having any nausea, dizziness, a metallic or rubbery taste in your mouth, or tingling around your lips/fingers?
- Did anyone apply a tourniquet, ice, or try to suck out venom?
- Do you have any allergies (especially to medications or antivenom before), and do you use an inhaler regularly for your asthma — have you used it today?

I haven't noticed any nausea, dizziness, a metallic or rubbery taste in my mouth, or tingling around my lips or fingers. No one did anything to the bite. I don't have any allergies. I use an albuterol inhaler 1-2 times a month for my asthma, but I haven't used it today.

Okay, thank you for all that information — this is really helpful.

Here's the plan: this is a venomous rattlesnake bite, and we're going to treat it seriously. We'll get your vital signs checked, keep the affected arm still and roughly at heart level, and draw some blood tests to check your clotting and blood counts. Because your hand and arm are swelling, we'll likely need to give you antivenom to stop the venom from causing more damage — I'll get that started as soon as possible. We'll also keep a close eye on that wheezing and chest tightness since it could be either your asthma or an early allergic-type reaction to the venom, so if it gets worse at all, or you feel your throat tightening, lips swelling, or trouble breathing, tell us immediately.

We'll monitor you closely over the next several hours, mark and measure the swelling to track its progression, and keep checking your breathing and blood work. Do you have any questions before we get started?
I don't have any questions. I just want to feel better.

turns.content: Hi, Mr./Ms. Miller, I'm Dr. [Name]. I understand you've been feeling short of breath and weak lately, and your doctor sent you in today because of some concerns about your blood count. Can you tell me when this shortness of breath and weakness started, and how it's been affecting you?

Hi Doctor. I had a knee injury about 5 weeks ago and since then I've been feeling a bit short of breath with some exertion. I thought it was because I was out of shape. I've also been feeling a bit lightheaded when I stand up, but it goes away quickly.

That's helpful, thank you. I also see you've been taking NSAIDs (like ibuprofen or naproxen) for your knee pain — can you tell me how much and how often you've been taking those?

Also, I want to ask about your stomach and bowels — have you noticed any stomach pain, heartburn, nausea, vomiting blood or anything that looks like coffee grounds, or any black, tarry, or bloody stools?

I've been taking ibuprofen, 600 mg, every 8 hours around the clock for my knee pain. I've been taking it for about 5 weeks now. I've noticed some pain in my stomach area, about 1-2 hours after eating. It's been like that for about 3 weeks. It gets worse if I have wine with my meal. I've also noticed that my stools have been really black, almost like tar, for about a week now. I thought it was because I've been eating more vegetables lately. I haven't had any nausea or vomiting.

That black, tarry stool is very important — that's actually a sign of bleeding in your stomach or intestines, not from vegetables. Combined with your ibuprofen use, stomach pain, and now feeling weak and short of breath, it sounds like the NSAIDs may have caused an ulcer that's been slowly bleeding, which can lower your blood count significantly.

A few more quick questions: Have you had any chest pain, a racing heart, or fainting spells? Any history of ulcers or GI bleeding before? Do you drink alcohol regularly, or take any blood thinners like aspirin, warfarin, or Eliquis? And do you take any other medications regularly?

I have not had any chest pain, a racing heart, or fainting spells. I have not had any ulcers or GI bleeding before. I drink wine occasionally, about 1 glass per week. I do not take any blood thinners. I do not take any other medications regularly.

Thank you for all that information — this is very helpful in putting the picture together.

Here's what I think is happening: the ibuprofen you've been taking regularly for your knee has likely irritated your stomach lining and caused an ulcer, which has been slowly bleeding for a couple of weeks. That's why your stools have turned black and tarry, and why you've been feeling short of breath, weak, and lightheaded — you've lost enough blood that your red blood cell count has dropped, which is anemia.

Here's the plan: we're going to admit you to the hospital so we can check your blood counts, likely give you a blood transfusion to help with the anemia and how you're feeling, and have the GI (stomach) specialists evaluate you — they may need to do an endoscopy, a camera test to look at your stomach and find the ulcer, and treat it directly if it's still bleeding. We'll also stop the ibuprofen completely and switch you to a safer pain medication for your knee, and start a medication to protect your stomach lining and help the ulcer heal.

I know this is a lot to take in, but you did the right thing coming in today, and we're going to take good care of you. Do you have any questions before the team gets started with the workup?

I guess I didn't realize how serious this could be. I just thought I was out of shape. I'm a bit worried about the blood transfusion, but I understand it's necessary. I don't have any other questions right now. I just want to get this taken care of.

turns.content: Good morning, Mr. K. I'm one of the doctors on the team taking care of you today. I heard you've been feeling pretty rough with fevers, night sweats, and a cough for a few weeks — that sounds exhausting. Can you tell me more about how this all started, and has the cough been bringing up anything?
Good morning. It started a couple weeks ago. I just felt generally unwell, and then I started coughing and feeling feverish. I haven't noticed anything coming up when I cough.

That sounds miserable. A few more questions - have you noticed any unintentional weight loss, chest pain, or shortness of breath along with the fevers and night sweats? And how bad have the night sweats been - are you soaking through your sheets or clothes?
No weight loss, no chest pain, and no shortness of breath. The night sweats have been pretty bad a few times. I've been soaking through my pajamas and sheets and needing to change them.

That sounds really disruptive - having to change your sheets multiple times. Thank you for sharing that.

A couple more important things: you mentioned working in homeless shelters and jails, so you've been around a lot of people with TB - have you ever had a positive TB test yourself, or been treated for TB in the past? Also, I saw you grew up in Arizona and lived in Southern California before moving to Oregon - have you had any recent travel back to those areas, or any activities involving digging in soil or being around dust storms?
I've never had a positive TB test or been treated for TB. I haven't traveled back to Arizona or Southern California recently. I haven't been digging in soil or been around dust storms.

Thank you, that's helpful information. Given that you grew up in Arizona and lived in an area where a fungus called coccidioidomycosis (or "Valley Fever") is common, that's still something we want to test for, since it can show up even years later, especially with your immune system being more vulnerable right now given your HIV. We'll also make sure to rule out TB, given your exposure history, so you may see the nurses come in with masks for a little while just to be safe until we get some test results back - that's just a precaution, not because we think you're necessarily contagious.

We'll get some blood work, sputum tests, and possibly imaging to help sort this out. Do you have any questions for me right now about what's going on or the plan?
I don't really know much about that fungus you mentioned. Is it serious? I guess I just want to know how long this is all going to take to figure out.

private_patient_context:
**CASE 3B**
Robert Goodman,

<u>**Case Summary**</u>

Robert Goodman is a 45 year old laborer who works for a moving company. Over the last month he has experienced some vague, minor chest pains on exertion, especially while at work when he is lifting. One of Robert’s coworkers recently had cardiac problems and was a smoker. His physician recommended that he quit smoking and he did so. He discussed the issue with Robert several times.

Robert is now concerned that there may be some connection between his current symptoms and his smoking. He approached this friend, who gave Robert his leftover patches. Robert tried them a month ago for a few days but used them incorrectly.

Robert is now blaming his inability to quit on the patch. However, Robert smokes about two or three packs a day but started on the lowest level of the patch. That’s what his friend gave him. In addition, Robert took the patch off two or three times a day to smoke. He kept a pack of cigarettes in the moving van, “just in case”. Robert never read the package instructions and did not make any behavioral changes.

The chest pains persisted for about a week, so Robert is now in the office for a follow up visit after having the usual battery of cardiac diagnostic tests (all of which are negative). The subsequent visit revealed that the chest pains were a result of gastritis and reflux which have responded to antacids (Zantac). However, Robert does not like taking medicines, and this incident has brought the concept of quitting to the forefront of Robert’s thinking. He is now motivated to quit, but this prior “attempt” has left him somewhat disheartened. He does not understand why the patches worked for his friend and not for him.

**Your role is to play a smoker who is** <u>**definitely interested in quitting**</u>**. However, he has come to believe that his recent failure to do so is the fault of the patches he used. He does not understand that he used them incorrectly. He also does not understand that the quitter must actively participate in the quit (make behavioral changes) to be successful. He is mistakenly waiting for the patches to “cure” him.**

<u>**Presentation/Emotional Tone**</u>

Robert is scared that he is going to have a heart attack at any moment even though all the tests came back negative. There is a long history of cardiac problems in Robert’s family, all of whom were smokers. His father reminded him of this in a recent conversation.

During the office visit he is anxious, stating many times that he really wants to quit now. However, in spite of his anxiety, he is motivated to quit smoking, but not at all confident that he will be able to do so.

When the student asks why you have come to the office, you reply,

**“I was afraid that I was going to have a heart attack. I know the tests came back negative, but this whole incident made me really think about my smoking. I know smoking isn’t good for my heart and I don't want to have to take pills for my stomach for the rest of my life just so I can smoke. So, I tried to quit a few weeks ago on my own but couldn’t. Those dumb patches just don’t work.”**

**“What do I do now?”**

<u>**Your Smoking History**</u>

You began smoking while in the service at age 18. You have been smoking ever since and now smoke anywhere from two to three packs a day depending on how busy you are at work. On slow days you smoke more since you have a lot of time on your hands. You have never tried to quit before, other than the attempt last month.

During that attempt you experienced significant withdrawal in spite of wearing the patch. You were very irritable, anxious, restless, and impatient. After three days you returned to your regular pattern of smoking.

<u>**Family Smoking/Medical History**</u>

Both sets of grandparents smoked as well as both parents. Father has quit but mother still smokes about a pack a day.

Paternal grandmother had two heart attacks at age 57 and died at 58 as a result.

Maternal grandfather had a stroke at age 55. He was bedridden for eight years as a result and died at age 63.

Father had triple bypass at age 54.

Mother has had a long history of angina starting in her mid-forties.

<u>**Drug/Alcohol use**</u>

You drink a few beers a week on Friday or Saturday night. You have cut back considerably on your drinking in recent years.  **“ I just can’t do it anymore!”**

<u>**Patient Interview**</u>

If the student asks you about family cardiac history, review the above information with him or her. Otherwise, don’t bring this up.

If the student asks you what you did the last time you tried to quit, just say,

**“I used those dumb patches, they didn’t work.”**

If the student questions you further as in, **“Which patch did you use?”** or “**Describe to me how you used the patch,”** you may explain exactly what you did:

**“I started on the seven-milligram patch. That’s what my friend gave me.”**

**“I used them for three whole days. I was so anxious and irritable all day long my friends told me to start smoking again or they wouldn’t talk to me anymore.”**

**“They didn’t work at all. I still wanted to smoke even though I had the patch on.”**

**“But I want you to know I took the patch off those three days every time I smoked (about four or five times a day). I didn’t want to get a heart attack.”**

As you explain all this become increasingly anxious. Ask the student,

**“Why can’t you cure me? Can’t you just give me a pill or something?”**

If the student asks you to set a quit date,

**"It will be hard to quit at work, so I think I will quit on a Saturday."**

**"Two weeks from Saturday is a good time; that should give me enough time to get ready."**

If the student asks you what kind of changes you made in your routines or behavior, ask,

**“What do you mean? Don’t you just put the patch on and forget about it?”**

If the student asks you when you most need a cigarette,

**"In the morning when I wake up, during breaks at work, and after meals."**

If the student asks you what you could do besides smoking at those times,

**“What do you mean?”**

If they give examples of other behaviors (chewing gum, etc.),

**"That's interesting. My buddy who quit is always carrying around those pretzel sticks. I never really asked him about them, but that would probably help.  I also like gum."**

**"I should really do more exercise. Maybe I will start walking after I eat meals."**

If the student suggests that you go to a group cessation program, say,

**“I don’t like talking about myself in front of strangers. What else can I do?”**

If the student <u>**does not**</u> ask you any questions about how you used the patch or what you did, just continue with the “What am I supposed to do? I really want to quit” line of questioning until he or she does.

turns.content: Mr. Goodman, I understand the heart tests were reassuring and the discomfort may be from reflux. You mentioned having some other concerns—what would you most like to talk about today?

I was afraid that I was going to have a heart attack. I know the tests came back negative, but this whole incident made me really think about my smoking. I know smoking isn’t good for my heart and I don't want to have to take pills for my stomach for the rest of my life just so I can smoke. So, I tried to quit a few weeks ago on my own but couldn’t. Those dumb patches just don’t work. What do I do now?

I’m glad you’re ready to try again—one unsuccessful attempt is common and doesn’t mean you can’t quit. We can improve the odds with counseling plus medication, often a correctly dosed patch combined with gum or lozenges for cravings, or prescription options such as varenicline or bupropion. How many cigarettes do you smoke per day, and how soon after waking do you have your first one? What made the last attempt hardest—cravings, withdrawal, side effects, or something else?

I smoke anywhere from two to three packs a day depending on how busy I am at work. I usually have my first cigarette right after I wake up. The last time I tried to quit, I was really irritable, anxious, restless, and impatient. I couldn't handle the withdrawal. I took the patch off a few times a day to smoke, and it just didn't work for me.

Those symptoms are classic nicotine withdrawal, especially with your level of dependence—not a lack of willpower. A patch alone may have been underdosed; we can tailor treatment, often using a daily patch plus 4-mg nicotine gum or lozenges for breakthrough cravings, or varenicline, which is often most effective. A brief slip does not mean the attempt has failed, and you generally should not repeatedly remove the patch to smoke—stop the cigarette and resume the plan, contacting us if you feel unwell.

Would you be willing to set a quit date within the next couple of weeks? Also, have you ever had seizures, serious kidney disease, significant depression, or suicidal thoughts, and what medicines do you take?

It will be hard to quit at work, so I think I will quit on a Saturday. Two weeks from Saturday is a good time; that should give me enough time to get ready. I don't have any of those other problems you mentioned, and I don't take any medicines. I just can’t do it anymore!

That sounds like a strong, realistic plan. Let’s keep your quit date two Saturdays from now and arrange a prescription for **varenicline**, starting one week beforehand; it reduces cravings and withdrawal and is usually more effective than a patch alone. Take it after food with water—nausea and vivid dreams can occur, and contact us promptly for severe mood or behavior changes.

Before quit day, remove cigarettes and lighters, tell family and coworkers, identify smoke-free breaks, and call **1-800-QUIT-NOW** for free coaching. If you slip, stop again immediately rather than abandoning the attempt. We should follow up within a week or two after your quit date to adjust treatment and support you. # Station 3 – Shared Decision Making

Scenario:

You are a third year student rotating through a longitudinal ambulatory rotation. You are seeing a patient, Joanna Mills, for the second time. Ms. Mills is a 45-year old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. When you saw her for the first time last week, she had not been receiving medical care or medication refills for 6 months due to the loss of her medical insurance. Last week, she came to clinic to re-establish care and receive refills of her medications for diabetes mellitus. Last week, you agreed to refill her medications and ordered blood work. Ms. Mills has come in to clinic today to discuss the lab results with you.

You discussed this with your attending preceptor prior to seeing Ms. Mills. Your attending physician instructs you to discuss the results with Ms. Mills and encourages you to engage in shared decision making with your patient.
private_patient_context:
**Station 3 – Shared Decision Making**

**Training Materials:**

# 3. <u>Scenario for Standardized Patient</u>

You are Joanna Mills, a 45-year old woman. Last week, you came to a new hospital-based clinic to establish a primary care doctor and get refills of your medications, since you ran out of medications for diabetes mellitus. You haven’t been to see a doctor in over six months, and you’ve been rationing your medications during that time, but you ran out of medications last week.  The medical student whom you met last week gave you a one month supply of your medications (metformin and glyburide) but asked you to get blood work done so that s/he could “get a sense of how well controlled your diabetes was” and to make changes in medications, if necessary. You went to the laboratory last week after your visit and are now here for your scheduled follow up visit to go over the results of the blood test. You feel fine and have refilled your medications and do not have any new problems to report to the medical student today; but you are curious to learn about the results of your blood tests and hope to hear that your diabetes is well controlled.

<u>Medical History:</u>

You were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus four years ago by your primary care doctor at the time, Dr. Alvarez. You were not surprised when you received this diagnosis because you have a strong family history of diabetes. You know that the A1C blood test shows whether or not your diabetes is controlled, and you also know that anything less than 7 is good and anything higher than 7 means that the sugars are too high. You remember that when you were first diagnosed with diabetes, your A1C was 7.6. The doctor had you on Metformin first, but the following year, she added glyburide because the A1C was not at goal. Your doctor slowly increased the doses of these medications; and as of one year ago, had you at your current dose of metformin and glyburide.

You have not had any complications related to diabetes mellitus, and you have been taking your medications as prescribed. However, 6 months ago, you lost your job and your medical insurance. You could not afford to continue seeing your primary care doctor so you stopped going at that time. The doctor gave you last refills of your medications and encouraged you to come to the hospital-based clinic since they had a sliding scale fee service for patients. Six months ago at your last visit with Dr. Alvarez, you also had a blood test. You received a letter from Dr. Alvarez stating that your A1C was 8.8 and that you needed to follow up on this, but you were unable to see her or any other doctor until now.

You have been busy for the past few months so you did not come to the hospital clinic.

You have admittedly stretched out your remaining pills, sometimes skipping doses to make the prescription last a little longer. Last week, you were completely without medications; and you were scared about your sugars getting too high, so you came to the clinic.

<u>Family History:</u>

As noted above, you were not surprised when you were diagnosed with diabetes four years ago. Both of your parents suffered from it, and you know that it is an illness that can run in the family. However, you were still frightened when you were first given the diagnosis. You have seen both of your parents suffer from medical problems related to diabetes. Your father had high blood pressure and kidney problems, which his doctor said was due to diabetes. He passed away suddenly from a heart attack when he was 66 years old. Your mother, who is now 64, is alive but has many medical problems. Prior to her recent stroke 3 months ago, she had very poorly controlled high blood pressure and diabetes.  She has been in and out of the hospital several times a year for the past few years, either for chest pain or “fluid in the lungs” or skin infections and infected foot ulcers.

Besides diabetes, you do not have any other medical problems.

<u>Social History:</u>

You were laid off from your job as a clothing buyer for a large department store. Since then, you have been looking for a new job and have been trying to keep your spirits up. You were busy caring for your mother in another state for the past few months because she had a recent stroke. Between your mother’s illness and your search for a job, the past six months have been extraordinarily stressful for you; and you have not really had time to take care of yourself. But you have always wanted to stay in good health to avoid illness, and you know that it’s important to focus on your health right now.  You have been without health insurance since losing your job as you could not afford COBRA and you postponed looking into applying for Obama care in hopes that you would soon have a new job.  You have been unable to afford to refill your medications, and therefore, rationing the pills until you ran out of them last week.

You do not have any history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug use.

You are divorced and have a 20 year-old daughter, who is in college and no longer living at home

<u>Emotional Tone:</u>

You are very concerned about your health condition although it has been difficult for you to focus on your own health for the past six months, between your economic hardship and your mother’s acute illness. When you had insurance, you were always good about following up with your primary care doctor and taking all of your medications. Even though you have had diabetes for four years, you were told that you could be “in control” of your illness and maybe avoid complications of diabetes. You have been happy to take your pills, as long as it meant controlling your illness and avoiding complications of the disease.  You know that you have not taken your pills as prescribed, mostly because of financial concerns and the cost of medications.  You are very reluctant to start insulin. You know that being on insulin means needing to prick yourself several times a day to check your blood sugar and give yourself the insulin shots and you hate the thought of pricking yourself so frequently with needles.  Also, you know that the diabetic supplies (insulin and more lancets and paper strips for frequent sugar checks) are expensive and another cost that you feel would be really hard to absorb now.

**Your role is to portray a patient who is very concerned about your health. You want to know how to keep yourself healthy. Yet, you are upset and worried when you learn that your diabetes is not well controlled.  You are reluctant to start insulin therapy because you dislike the thought of using the needles to give yourself medication and the extra cost of medications and supplies feels like a financial burden that you feel unable to take at this time. In addition, although you know it is not rational you feel that using insulin means you are more likely to develop the complications you saw your parents go through because they were on insulin.  However, you normally always follow your doctor’s advice and are unsure about going against his advice by not starting insulin.**

<u>Scenario:</u> 

The student will enter the clinic room, where you are waiting to be seen. You are seated next to the desk, appearing comfortable but a little anxious. You met this student last week and are happy to see the same person again.

The student may ask, “I wanted to talk to you about your blood test results that we did last week. Do you know what an A1C test signifies?”

**“Yes, I remember my last doctor telling me that it was a blood test that the doctors took to show whether the diabetes was controlled or not. I know that it’s supposed to be below 7.”**

The student will inform you that your A1C level was elevated, at 11.

You are surprised and concerned.

**“Oh no, that’s really high isn’t it?”**

The student should inform you that this A1C is very elevated and indicates that the diabetes is very poorly controlled at this time. You are upset and very worried by this news.

**“It’s never been so high like this. You know I was worried about my sugars but I never thought it could get up to this level.” What does this mean I have to do now?”**

The student should describe treatment options. Since you are on high doses of your current medications, there is no way to simply go up on the current dose of medications. The student will recommend starting insulin therapy as a way to rapidly bring down the A1C level and control the diabetes.

You interrupt the student when s/he mentions insulin and get visibly upset.

**“Wait, insulin? Oh, I don’t want to do that.”**

The student should ask you why you do not want to start insulin. S/He should give you a chance to state what your concerns are. You state many reasons why you don’t want to start insulin therapy now. After you give each reason, you should give the student a chance to discuss it with you.

**“I know that there are a lot of reasons why my sugars got uncontrolled like this. I wasn’t doing all the things that I know I should have been doing about my health. I wasn’t eating right, I wasn’t consistently taking my pills every day. I wasn’t really focusing on my health. I think that there are a lot of things besides insulin that I can do to get my health back in order.”**

**“I know that when you start insulin, you have to check your sugars many times throughout the day. And those extra supplies, those strips and lancets, they all cost a lot of money that I don’t think I’d be able to afford right now.”**

**“To tell you the truth, I’m really afraid of pricking myself with a needle to give myself insulin.  I don’t think that I could do that. I hate needles and the thought of giving myself shots every day is really scary to me.”**

**“I am so afraid of insulin.  I know it isn’t rational but I feel like insulin means I have diabetes with a capital D.  Do you know what I mean – it seems more serious.  I saw my dad go through so much, and now my mom with her stroke.  They were both on insulin.”**

The student should respond to all of your concerns and reasons for not wanting to start insulin. If he does not acknowledge or validate your concerns then you should remain resistant to starting insulin.

The student should ask you about what your desires regarding the management of your illness are. S/He might ask, “Ms. Mills, can you tell me a little bit about how diabetes is affecting your life, and what you are hoping to do to manage your illness? What would you like to see for yourself regarding your diabetes?

**“I really don’t want to be sick from diabetes like my mother was. I know all about the complications, the foot ulcers, the amputations, dialysis, strokes… I’m just really scared about my diabetes being out of control because I never want to go through what she’s been going though with her health. I want to be healthy for my daughter and for myself. So I want to do what you think is best. I’ve always listened to doctors in the past. But right now, I am just really scared of this insulin for a lot of reasons too. I am just hoping for a way that I can get back into good health again without going down the insulin road.”**

The student should try to engage you in deciding what the best treatment for your diabetes is. If he only recommends insulin and says that nothing else will work right now, but you don’t feel that he/she acknowledges the reasons why you do not want to start insulin, you will be more resistant to starting insulin now. However, if the student shares information with you about insulin treatment that addresses your concerns, you might consider changing your mind. Here are some examples of effective statements:

“The insulin that I would recommend starting you on is a once daily insulin that works slowly over 24 hours. You do not have to give yourself multiple injections of insulin each day. Rather, you could give yourself one injection a day.”

“The benefit of starting insulin is that it is more likely to successfully bring your A1C level down to signify good control of your diabetes. The better we control your diabetes, the less likely it is that you would ever get the complications of diabetes (such as kidney problems or eye problems.)

“One concern that I have in continuing with oral medicines rather than insulin, is that the oral medications do not bring down the A1C level as effectively as insulin does. I can tell that it is really important for you to get in control of your diabetes, and I think that this is the most successful way that we can do it.”

“Insulin is one part of the plan that we can create to control your diabetes. You are right that diet and exercise and taking your medications every day are equally important in controlling your diabetes. I think that we can work together on each of these issues, and perhaps insulin can be a component of this plan.”

If you feel that the student has engaged you as a partner in making the decision and has given you a chance to address your beliefs and concerns about your illness, then you should agree to work with the student to come up with a plan together; and you can agree to try the insulin.

**“Okay, I see what you are saying. I think that if you feel the insulin may really help me get my diabetes under control and keep me healthy, then I will try it for a while and see how my sugars improve.”**

If you feel that the student has not given you a chance to speak about your concerns and has not enlisted you as a partner in decision making, but rather unilaterally recommended insulin without building a consensus with you, then you should not agree to start insulin. You are calmer at the end but are very resolute about not starting insulin today.

**“You know, I don’t think I am able to get over my fear of starting insulin right now. I’d really rather try getting back on my pills every day and see how I do for a while before I switch my medicines.”**

If at any time the student asks a question that you do not understand or is at all unclear, then you should ask them to clarify. You can say:

**“What do you mean by that?”**

turns.content: Hi, Ms. Mills. It’s good to see you again. Before we go through your blood-work results and discuss next steps together, how have you been doing since restarting your diabetes medications? Any problems or concerns with them?

Hi, I'm doing okay, I guess. I've been taking my medications again since I got them last week, and I haven't had any problems with them. I feel fine, actually. I'm just a bit worried about my blood test results.

I understand—that waiting can be worrying, especially after being off treatment for six months. Before we go through the results, what are you most concerned they might show, and how much do you already know about tests like the A1c, which reflects your average blood sugar over about three months?

I remember my last doctor telling me that it was a blood test that shows whether the diabetes is controlled or not. I know that it’s supposed to be below 7. I'm a bit scared that it might be high, since I haven't been taking my medications regularly. I've been really stressed and busy with my mom's health and looking for a job, so I haven't been focusing on my own health like I should have.

You’ve had a lot competing for your attention, and a high A1c would reflect those barriers—not a personal failure. Below 7% is a common goal, though we tailor it to each person. I don’t want to misstate your result: do you have the lab report or the exact A1c value available?
I don't have the lab report with me. I don't know the exact number.

That’s okay—I don’t want to guess or worry you with an inaccurate number. We should review the actual report together before changing treatment. Since you only restarted medication last week, an elevated A1c would mostly reflect the prior three months off treatment. If it is high, options may include continuing your current medicines and rechecking in about three months or adjusting treatment sooner, depending on how high it is, medication cost, and what feels manageable to you. For now, keep taking your medicines as prescribed; we’ll confirm the result with my supervising physician and make a plan with you rather than about you.

That sounds good. I'll keep taking my medicines like I'm supposed to. I just want to make sure I'm doing everything I can to keep my diabetes under control. I'm really hoping that my sugars aren't too high.

turns.content: Hi Morgan, I’m sorry you’re feeling so unwell. Can you tell me what’s been happening with your right arm—where the pain is and when it started?
Hi, yeah, it's been pretty bad. It started about four days ago with some redness and swelling, and now it's really painful and swollen. It's all over my right arm, and it's been getting worse.

That sounds very painful, and with the fever and rapidly worsening swelling I’m concerned about a serious infection. Have you noticed any wound, bite, injection, or injury to that arm, and have you had chills, dizziness, confusion, or trouble breathing?
Yeah, there's a wound there. I told my friend it was a cat bite, but I'm not sure. I've had chills and feel really warm, but no dizziness or trouble breathing. I don't think I've been confused.

Thank you for telling me. I’m not here to judge—the cause helps us choose safe treatment. Could this wound have come from injecting anything into the arm, and is there any pus, red streaking, numbness, or difficulty moving your hand or fingers?
I guess it could have. I don't really know. There's some red streaking, and it hurts to move my hand. I haven't noticed any pus or numbness.

Thank you for being honest—you deserve care without judgment. Fever, red streaking, worsening swelling, and pain with hand movement could mean a rapidly spreading or deep infection. You need emergency-department treatment now, likely including blood tests, imaging, IV antibiotics, and an urgent surgical assessment. We should arrange immediate transfer; please don’t drive yourself or eat or drink in case a procedure is needed.
I don't have a car, so I can't drive. I haven't eaten or drunk anything since this morning. I guess I can go to the ED if you think I need to.

question_text:
**Material for Student Interviewer**

**Setting:** You are a radiology-oncology prelimary resident rotating on the inpatient medicine service.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is 35-75 years old with hypertension, epigastric pain, and mild shortness of breath. The patient has been otherwise healthy.

The patient came to the ED yesterday afternoon. The original ED plan was to discharge the patient home with a working diagnosis of “dyspepsia” and outpatient follow-up, but after 3 hours the patient complained of increased pain. The ED doctors changed the plan to bring the patient into the hospital on “observation status.”

You examined the patient at 9 pm last night, shortly after the patient arrived on the floor. The patient was in modest discomfort.

It is now about 10 hours after the surgery and you have returned for another overnight shift. The patient is back in a hospital room, now on the surgery service. You are no longer directly involved in the patient's care.

**Student Tasks:**

Explain to the patient why there was a delay in diagnosing the perforated duodenal ulcer and getting to surgery.

**Case script for Standardized Patient**

**Age:** 35-75
**Episode:** Disclosure of Error
**Workshop:** Advanced Communcation Skills, Fourth Year Capstone Course
\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

You are a patient in a hospital room.

Here is the timeline of your story:

* 2 days ago you began to have some discomfort, a little pain, in your belly.
* Yesterday at 3 pm you went to the hospital emergency room and waited 3 hours to be seen.
* While being examined you had blood tests done and they told you that if the blood tests were normal, you could go home with an appointment to see a doctor in the clinic.
* While waiting for the results, the pain got a little worse. A doctor examined you again, said he thought you were OK, but agreed to “watch you for a while” so they admitted you to the hospital where you met more doctors.
* At about 10 pm they sent you for an Xray of your belly.
* You tried to sleep, but the pain in your belly kept you awake.
* About 6 am, the pain got much worse. You called the nurse.
* A doctor came back to see you at 6:30 am and said that the Xray showed a problem in the belly that might require surgery.
* At 10am you were taken to the operating room.

Now it is evening, and you are recovering from surgery. The surgeon told you that you had an ulcer, which had caused a small hole in your bowel, and that this was repaired with surgery. You need to be in the hospital for a few more days, get IVs and antibiotics, and not eat for a few days. The good news is that the surgeons expect you will recover completely.

You are relieved that you will be OK, but thinking back, you wonder about the sudden concern of the doctors this morning and the emergency surgery. You had an Xray at 10 pm and got worse for hours after it was done, but the doctor only told you the Xray was bad in the morning. Why did it take more than 8 hours to find out that you needed emergency surgery?

Background: You do not see doctors regularly, and you felt perfectly healthy until this belly pain started. You did go to the medical clinic at the hospital last year, and received some medicines for your blood pressure and cholesterol. You did not come back to see the doctor, but your medicine is running out and they told you that you could not get more refills without another visit to the clinic. All these doctors, nurses, and tests at the hospital are a little scary. Fill in other details that come up as you see fit.

A doctor is coming to your room to talk to you. This is one of the many doctors you have seen, and is the one who told you about the Xray results early this morning. Your character does not yet know this, but the doctor’s task is to disclose to you that an error was made (this doctor did not check the Xray results which is what accounted for the delay). You should respond initially with confusion (“I don’t understand… how could something like this happen?”), slight anger (“I was in agony… how could you have left me that way… I could have died”), and ambivalence (“I thought I was getting good care… I don’t know how to feel about this… this is why I don’t like going to doctors.”). Ideally the doctor will address your emotions, apologize, and take responsibility, in which case your initial emotions will give way to gratitude that everything is ok and appreciation for the doctor’s honesty. If the doctor is evasive, defensive, makes excuses, or takes any approach that seems inappropriate to your character, you can prolong your confusion and anger, and retreat to a withdrawn affect rather than having an outburst of emotion.
