| THE PATIENT STORY: The SP will be asked to tell their symptom story and the personal and emotion impact for each of their concerns. You will want to write this is the patient voice. The symptom story should be able to answer this question: “Tell me more about [chief concern/additional concern], starting at the beginning and bringing me up to now.”  The personal context should be able to answer questions concerning the broader personal/psychosocial context of symptoms, especially the patient beliefs/attributions.  The emotional context should be able to ask how are you doing with this, how does this make you feel, how has this affected you emotionally? IMPACT: How has this affected your life? How has this been for your family? | The patient is following up in the regular primary care office today but is meeting a new doctor.  You began to experience pain in your stomach and back and began to lose some weight about 8 months ago. After a couple of weeks you went to the doctor who sent you for blood work and X rays. The testing led to a diagnosis of cancer of the pancreas and you began treatment for it with chemotherapy 6 months ago. Two months into therapy, repeat scans showed that the cancer continued to grow so you were switched to another regimen. That therapy has not halted the spread of the cancer and your cancer doctor told you last week that there are no other treatments she can offer. Since the chemotherapy made you feel very sick, you are accepting of her advice. The main focus of your treatment now is on keeping you comfortable. You are fatigued, have lost your hair and 40 lbs. The oncologist sent you back to your primary care doctor to manage your symptoms and other medical problems and that is why you are here today.  At the moment you are taking lisinopril 40 mg for your high blood pressure (you have been on this medicine for over 10 years), oxycodone 5 mg as needed about twice a day for pain, and ondansetron (“Zofran") 4 mg once or twice a week for nausea. Your symptoms are well controlled and you know you could take more medicine if you were more uncomfortable. You have also begun to experience some light headedness when you stand up quickly. You sleep “okay,” but not great. You do not eat as much because your appetite has decreased.  You worked as a teacher of theater at your local college and had been able to continue with some sick days. You found it challenging to go to work and the end of the school year was a relief. You have good health insurance through work. You are happily married and you are worried about how your spouse will manage financially without the dual income. However, you know “it will be okay,” as your spouse is employed as a manager of the local grocery store and is able to take time off to care for you as needed. You have 2 adult children who are working and living independently. They know you are ill and are very sad about your declining health. Both are willing and able to help at home. You do have life insurance that will help some. Your home is paid for.  You are also pondering the question of why you are terminally ill so early in your life. You pray and meditate and that provides some comfort. On the other hand you have been doing practical things like making out a will and thinking about who will make health care decisions if you cannot. You are an active Roman Catholic who is very involved in the local church. You have also decided that you want to die a natural death when the time comes avoiding resuscitation, breathing and feeding tubes and your partner knows this.  You have used some of your family’s home remedies of taking bitter melon juice, but do not have other cultural beliefs about treating cancer. You have heard of hospice and are interested in having their support since you wish to remain at home to the extent that is possible. Your goals for the next few months are to spend time with your family and be spiritually ready for your death if there is no miracle.  You are not a smoker, do not drink alcohol, nor do you use drugs like marijuana. There is no family history of cancer.  If the student focuses too much on your cancer treatments and medical symptoms, gently redirect them and let them know that you fully understand your treatment status (“I’m done with chemo… I know there are no more options… I’m here to talk about next steps.”)  Ideally the student will provide a natural opening for you to express your emotions. Suitable windows could be inquiries about your family, mental health, or existential concerns, or more direct questions about your emotions. “Worry” about your partner’s well-being is your primary emotional concern, and thinking about this may make your character cry. If the student recognizes your emotion and demonstrates empathy, you should be able to collect yourself and move forward with the conversation. If the student is not effective in handling your emotion, the conversation will stall as you find it difficult to move beyond your worry, which could then escalate to other emotions (fear, isolation, etc.). |

turns.content: Hi, I’m glad we can talk today. I understand you’ve been through a great deal and have heard that further chemotherapy isn’t likely to help. What is your understanding of where things stand, and what has been weighing on you most?

Hi, thank you for seeing me. I know that my cancer has spread and that there are no more treatments that can cure it. The oncologist told me last week that the focus now is on keeping me comfortable. What's been weighing on me most is how my spouse will manage financially without my income. I'm just worried about what the future holds for them.

I’m really sorry—you’re carrying concern for your spouse while facing so much yourself. We can involve our social worker and palliative-care team to look at practical supports, benefits, and planning together. Have you and your spouse been able to talk about these worries, and who else is supporting you both right now?

We have talked about it some, but it's hard. My spouse is really strong, but I can see the worry in their eyes too. Our two adult children have been really supportive. They know I'm ill and they're both willing to help out at home. It means a lot to have them nearby. My spouse is a manager at the local grocery store, so they're able to take time off to care for me as needed. That's been a big help.

It sounds like you have a loving family around you, even though this is painful for everyone. I’d like to make sure we are addressing your comfort: are you having any pain, nausea, shortness of breath, or other symptoms that are troubling you most?

I've been having some pain in my stomach and back, but it's been manageable with the oxycodone. I take it about twice a day. I also get some nausea, but not too often. I take Zofran for that when I need it. I've also been feeling a bit lightheaded when I stand up quickly. Other than that, I've been sleeping okay and my appetite has decreased a bit.

I’m glad the pain and nausea are reasonably controlled, and we can have palliative care help keep adjusting medicines if they worsen. For the lightheadedness, please rise slowly and let us know if you faint or cannot keep fluids down. As we plan ahead, what matters most to you in the time ahead, and have you talked with your spouse about who you would want to make medical decisions for you if you could not speak for yourself?

What matters most to me is spending quality time with my family and being spiritually ready for whatever comes next. I've talked with my spouse about my wishes. I want to die naturally, without any resuscitation or tubes. My spouse knows that and supports my decision. I've also been thinking about making out a will and who will make health care decisions if I can't. I want to make sure everything is taken care of.

**Standardized Patient Role: Sample Patient Case 3**

**Andrea Sands**

During the practice session, students take turns playing the role of a physician who is taking a medical history of an SP.

Student should introduce himself/herself as a first-year medical student and offer to shake hands. He/she may ask how you wish to be addressed (Ms., Miss, Mrs., first name).

**Chief Complaint:** (Why you came to see the doctor today.) Feel tired and weak all the time.

**Demeanor:** Cooperative. You appear to be tired, low energy, and somewhat depressed.
private_patient_context:
**Standardized Patient Role: Sample Patient Case 3**

**Andrea Sands**

The following is the typical order for this patient encounter.

Student should introduce himself/herself as a first-year medical student and offer to shake hands. He/she may ask how you wish to be addressed (Ms., Miss, Mrs., first name).

**Chief Complaint:** (Why you came to see the doctor today.) Feel tired and weak all the time.

**History of Present Illness:** (Explanation of the chief complaint—LOCATES mnemonic. Questions in parentheses below will likely be asked. Responses for the SP are provided.)

**L**OCATION: (Where is the pain?) Low back. (Does the pain radiate [move around, do you feel it anywhere else]?) Some radiation.

**O**NSET: (When did this happen?) About 6 months ago; started feeling tired.

**C**HARACTER: (Describe the pain—dull, sharp, throbbing, etc.) Back pain is an aching pain of moderate severity. You are tired with no energy; it’s hard to get things done around the house. You want to nap or sleep several times during the day. You do not think this is just due to depression because it started before the depression, although the depression has made it worse.

**A**GGRAVATING FACTORS: (Does anything make the pain WORSE?) Nothing.

**A**LLEVIATING FACTORS: (Does anything give you relief from the pain?) Zoloft has helped with depression; take Tylenol sometimes for lower back pain, and it helps some but not completely.

**A**SSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: (Are there any other symptoms you have been experiencing?)

Starting about the same time as your tiredness, you lost interest in sex. Over the past 3 months you have been depressed, and that has gotten worse; have gotten treatment for that (taken Zoloft for past 2 months). Your menstrual periods have been irregular for the last 3 months. You notice that you bruise more easily. You have gained 15 pounds over the last 6 months. Also, for the last month, you have noticed more hair growth on your upper lip.

**T**IMING: (How often do you have the pain and how long does it last?) Feel tired almost all the

time; no part of the day is better than others.

**E**NVIRONMENT: (Is there anything that you can think of anything [new/different behavior,

something you ate, etc.] that may have caused the pain?) No. **S**EVERITY: (How bad [on a scale of 10] is the pain?) 4 or 5 on a scale of 10. **S**IMILAR PROBLEMS: (Have you ever had anything like this before?) No.

**Past Medical History:** The student will ask questions about previous hospitalizations,

surgeries, accidents or injuries, allergies, current medications, or other active medical problems.

**Prescription Medications:** (MEDICATES mnemonic—asks for every prescription medication)

**M**edication Name: Zoloft.

**E**ffectiveness: Your mood is better. Feel a little more interested in your normal hobbies, but are just too tired to do many of them.

**D**osage: 100 mg, one time a day (bedtime).

**I**ndication: Depression.

**C**linician Prescriber: Dr. Moore.

**A**dverse Effects: Some gastrointestinal upset for the first week, but nothing since.

**T**ime on Medication: 2 months.

**Over-the-Counter Medications:** Tylenol; take once or twice a day sometimes for back pain as directed on bottle.

**Herbal Medications:** Vitamins.

**Allergies:** Bacterim (antibiotic); huge hives all over your body.

**Hospitalization:**

• **What problem?** Hospitalized for tonsillectomy as a child.

• **Where hospitalized?** Altru Family Medicine.

• **Who (physician)?** Dr. Moore.

• **Complications?** None.

**Other Active Medical Problems:** None.

**Health Maintenance:**

• **Special diet?** No special diet, but you seem to be gaining weight—your clothes are getting tight—maybe 15 lbs over the last 6 months.

• **Exercise?** Usually very active and involved in regular aerobic exercise and swimming;

you have been too tired and fatigued lately to do this.

**Family History:**

- Siblings: Older brother killed in car accident 2 years ago.

**Social History:**

**Habits:**

• **Tobacco:** Not currently; used to smoke 1 pack a day from ages 21– .

• **Alcohol:** Drink occasionally, 1 or 2 drinks, usually wine with dinner, maybe 2 times per month. Most ever drank was in college, got “pretty drunk” a couple of times and had 5 or

6 drinks. Haven’t done that for years; hate hangovers.

• **Illicit drugs:** Smoked marijuana “a few times”; tried cocaine one time (“snorted”) at a party; never used meth or any other drug.

• **Prescription drug use/misuse:** Never abused prescription drugs.

• **Sexual concerns:** Right now, you have no interest in sex; this lack of interest started about the same time as your tiredness, but it has gotten worse over the last 6 to 8 weeks. You are unable to reach orgasm if you do engage in sexual activity. It is causing some problems in your relationship. Had a very good sexual relationship previously and had no concerns. No history of sexually transmitted diseases.

• **Spiritual concerns:** None.

**Demeanor:**

Cooperative. You appear to be tired, low energy, and somewhat depressed.

**\*\*\*Students may be asking some of the following questions about what you may be thinking or feeling about your current health problems. You should be able to answer these based on the details given in the case.**

How you  *FEEL* about it? (i.e., How are you feeling about…? What are your worries about…? Do you think something serious is causing it?) **Your feeling and fears:** You worry that it might be diabetes because your mother has/had diabetes.

How is it  *IMPACTING* you? (i.e., How has it affected your daily life? Have you had to stop any activities?) **The impact on you:** Impacting you a great deal because you are so tired.

Your  *IDEAS* about it? (i.e., What do think might be causing…? Do you think there is any relation between [your health problem] and what is going on in your life?) **Your idea is:** Premature menopause; diabetes.

What are your  *EXPECTATIONS* about today’s visit? (i.e., What do you think I can do to help you? Do you have any specific test or treatment in mind?) **Your expectation is:** Want blood tests to see if you are developing diabetes.

Student Pre-Encounter Instructions

You are working in a primary care clinic and are asked to see 55-year-old B. Radcliffe, who has come in complaining of cough. Please use the stethoscope provided and leave your stethoscope with the hall monitor.

Vital Signs:

HR 90

BP 130/70

RR 20

private_patient_context:
Standardized Patient Training Materials

**Standardized patient Training summary**

**First Position**: Sitting on bed in gown.

**Props**: Tissue, water bottle, glycerin and water in spray bottle for patient forehead sweat.

**Opening Statement**: "I can't seem to get rid of this cough."

**Presentation/Affect**: You are holding a tissue and cough deeply for duration of encounter.

**Current Condition**:

You are B. Radcliffe and are 55 years old. You really feel sick. You are weak. You noted a terrible shaking chill that lasted several minutes about four days ago. Since then you have felt intermittent chills but nothing like you did 4 days ago. They seem to be worse in the evenings and have been bad for the last two days. You are coughing now but this only started about 3 days ago, and seems to be getting worse. The cough is a deep, hacking cough that produces yellow phlegm but only with great effort. Your chest also hurts on the right side, down low, (on side of body, below breast) when you cough or if you take a really big breath. It feels like a deep, sharp pain when you breathe in (and has increased from a 2 to 3 out of 10 on the pain scale). You feel like you have a fever, but not checked it and your throat hurts from the coughing. Yesterday, you vomited (looked like the chicken broth soup you ate if asked) once after a coughing spell but it was mostly mucous (no nausea). You have had some shortness of breath with activity (going up the stairs), none at rest. You have not had any nasal congestion, runny nose or sinus pressure. You have not had any wheezing. At baseline you do not have a cough, sputum, shortness of breath or wheezing. You have taken Pseudoephedrine and Guaifenesin occasionally (3-4 times each day according to package directions) since it started but nothing seems to help. The coughing is waking you up at night and you have tried using extra pillows to prop yourself up.

You volunteer regularly at the Nashville Rescue Mission in downtown Nashville, TN. Even though you didn't feel well, you went in on your regularly scheduled days (three and four days ago). You have been exposed to a lot of people in the shelter and have been pushing yourself to be there helping when you really felt like being in bed. A number of people in the shelter seem to be coughing/sneezing.

**Social History:**

You are a native of Baltimore and work as an accountant for the State of Tennessee government. You have been married 28 years and have 2 children, a daughter, Amy (27), and son, David (25). David is stationed overseas in Germany and Amy lives in Nashville and has two sons, Todd (now 10) and Adam (now 7) and is currently going through a divorce. Because the divorce is not amiable, your grandsons have been staying with you for the past few months. The younger one is in the first year of grade school and the older one is in fourth grade. You live in an older frame house. You do not use drugs or tobacco currently.

You occasionally have a glass of wine in the evenings. You have environmental allergies in the spring.

**Past Medical History:**

You are generally healthy. You work at a desk five days a week. You work around the house and yard on the weekends. You have never been hospitalized nor had any surgeries. You only see a doctor when sick and you haven't seen a doctor in years (to save money). You always remember to get a flu shot every year.

You've never had the pneumococcal vaccine. No medications or medical conditions. You used to smoke about a pack of cigarettes a day (you started in high school), but quit for the third time two weeks ago because your grandchildren are living with you now. You are currently using the patch for help. Your grandson Todd has also had a sore throat last week that was diagnosed as strep throat and treated with penicillin for 7 days. His symptoms included a very sore throat and fever but no cough. He's feeling better now. If asked, "Have you ever been exposed to tuberculosis (TB)?" respond, "Not that I know of." If asked if you've had a TB test, respond, "Yes, but it has been a number of years since my last one...."

**Family History:**

* Father: had high blood pressure and smoked. Died at age 80 - 10 years ago (of old age)
* Mother: seems to be healthy but may have high cholesterol and maybe arthritis. Age 78
* Maternal grandmother: died when you were a child. Was in a nursing home and never really knew her history.
* Maternal grandfather and paternal grandparents: Died before you were born.

**Diabetic and Noncompliant with Insulin**

Information for the SP:

You are a 45-year-old patient, who has diabetes. You do not take your insulin regularly, and have had poorly controlled diabetes for years. You take your insulin only when you remember, but it is difficult to remember to take it every day since you do not feel different or badly when you do not take your insulin. You have been frustrated lately because you like to play basketball with your 10 year old son, and haven’t been able to play basketball because you have developed an ulcer on your right foot (as a result of poorly controlled diabetes).

Medical history: diabetes, diagnosed 4 years ago

Medications: Lantus insulin daily 20 units at night (you are taking this only a few times weekly) and Lisinopril 10 mg daily (blood pressure medicine you were told to take because of the diabetes)

Allergies: none

Social history: you do not smoke, drink alcohol or use any drugs

Family history: father with diabetes

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? You want to be able to play basketball with your son again, and you want to get rid of the foot ulcer. You really love your son and you love to play basketball.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? Noncompliance with insulin can lead to complications like your foot ulcer, but you will need the doctor to help you make that connection and to describe other possible complications. You cannot play basketball with your foot ulcer. You are also not taking your blood pressure medication as prescribed, and this could also result in complications.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? It is easy to “forget” to take your medications. At night you are very tired and sleepy from your day, so you tend to fall asleep while watching TV, and don’t take any medications before you fall asleep. Also, since you don’t “feel” your high sugars or blood pressure, there are no symptoms/reminders for you to take your medications. You like to think of yourself as “young and healthy,” and taking medications interferes with this way of looking at yourself.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? You are afraid you might not be able to keep playing basketball with your son. Once the doctor describes possible complications from nonadherence with diabetes, you are afraid of those.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? Your son, and ability to continue playing basketball with him; improved health.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): Maybe you could take the medication at a different time of the day, or at least before you fall asleep watching TV. Maybe you could challenge your thoughts that people who take medications are not young or healthy. You could try using reminders, pill boxes, etc. You could test your sugars regularly to remind yourself of possible complications (since you don’t “feel” the high sugar levels).
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 6/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You love your son and love to play basketball with him. You fear other complications like an amputation.
    - How could you move that number higher? Maybe put a picture of your son or a basketball on the pill bottle.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 5/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You exercise even when you are tired, so you believe you could take medications even if you are tired at night.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? Understanding the links between noncompliance and complications. Perhaps your son could help you to remember to take your medications.
* Ask for a decision: You will take your insulin and blood pressure medications.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? You will get a pill box. You will ask your son to agree not to play basketball with you unless you have taken your medications.

turns.content: Good to see you again, Mrs. Quick. I understand you've had three falls in the past six months — that must be frightening. Can you walk me through the most recent one: what you were doing right before you went down, and how you felt at that moment?
My daughter thought I should be checked because I’ve had some falls. The last fall occurred while I was in the bathtub. I think I turned too fast. I was not hurt and used my grab bars to get up.

I'm glad you weren't hurt and that those grab bars were there. You mentioned turning too fast — do you get dizzy or lightheaded when you turn your head or stand up quickly? And what were the other two falls like?

I do get dizzy sometimes. I have not noticed it when I turn my head, but I do feel a little lightheaded when I stand up quickly. The second fall involved catching my left toes in a small throw rug. I was not hurt in that fall. The third fall involved catching my hip against the counter after feeling dizzy. I had a bruise on my hip, but otherwise not hurt.

Thank you — that helps a lot. That lightheadedness on standing can come from your blood pressure pills, and the alprazolam and meclizine can add to unsteadiness too. How often are you taking the alprazolam and the meclizine, and do you use a cane or walker when you're out walking to the store?
I take one for some anxiety and one for dizziness. I do not use a cane or walker when I'm out walking to the store.

Here's what I'm thinking, Mrs. Quick. Two of your falls came with dizziness, and I suspect your medicines are a big part of that — the water pill and carvedilol can drop your blood pressure when you stand, and the alprazolam and meclizine both dull balance in someone your age. I'd like to start by checking your blood pressure sitting and standing, along with your strength, walking and balance, and some bloodwork. Then we'll work on gradually reducing the alprazolam and meclizine rather than stopping abruptly, and possibly adjusting your blood pressure pills.

In the meantime: rise slowly, sit on the edge of the bed a moment before standing, and please remove that throw rug and any others. I'd also like a physical therapist to see you for balance work and to fit you with a cane for walking to the store — not a sign of decline, just insurance so you can keep your independence. Would you be willing to bring your daughter to the next visit so we can go over all of this together?

turns.content: Hi Taylor, I'm glad to meet you — I'm one of the students working with the clinic, and I'll be seeing patients here regularly over the next year, so I hope we can get to know each other. What brings you in today, and is there anything in particular you've been hoping to get sorted out?
Hi, thanks for having me. I got a tetanus shot after I stepped on a nail. The urgent care center said I should find a primary care doctor. No current complaints.

I'm glad you got that taken care of — and I'm sorry about the nail. How's the foot doing since then, any redness, swelling, or pain that's getting worse? And other than that, have you had any ongoing medical problems or take any medications regularly?
It's all healed up now. I haven't had any issues with it since it happened. I take hormones, but no other medications.

That's good to hear it healed up cleanly. Thanks for telling me about the hormones — can you tell me more about which ones you take and who's been prescribing and monitoring them? And I want to make sure I get this right for you: what name and pronouns would you like me to use, and how do you describe your gender identity?
I take testosterone. I buy it online. I don't have a prescription. My name is Taylor, and I use he/him pronouns. I'm a transgender man.

Thank you for trusting me with that, Taylor — I'll use he/him, and I'm glad you told me, because it helps me take good care of you rather than judge you. Getting testosterone without a prescription is more common than people think, usually because access is hard, but it does mean no one's checking your levels or your blood counts. I'd like to change that: this clinic can prescribe and monitor testosterone for you, so you don't have to rely on the internet. Today I'd suggest baseline labs — a testosterone level, blood count since testosterone can thicken the blood, a metabolic panel with liver and kidney function, and lipids — plus checking whether you're due for STI screening, and if you still have a cervix, we can talk about Pap testing when you're comfortable. In the meantime, please keep taking your dose as you have been rather than stopping. Can you tell me your dose and how you inject, and would you be willing to come back with me in about two to three weeks to go over the results and get you a real prescription?

turns.content: Hello, Ms. Giancomello, I'm working with Dr. Ellis today. Before he joins us, I'd like to hear from you in your own words — what brings you in today, and how long has it been going on?
Hi, I've been having lower abdominal pain for several days now. It started off and on but has become constant.

I'm sorry you're dealing with that. Can you point to where it hurts and describe what it feels like — sharp, crampy, dull — and has anything like fever, chills, nausea, or vaginal discharge come along with it?

The pain is across my lower abdomen. It's been dull and aching lately, but it started off sharp and intermittent. I have mild nausea, but no fever, chills, or vomiting. I've had some vaginal discharge for about a week.
Thank you — the discharge is important. Can you tell me what it's like, color or smell, and whether sex or urinating has been painful? Also, when was your last period, and could you be pregnant?

The discharge is kind of yellowish and has a slight odor. I haven't noticed any pain with sex or urinating. My last period was about three weeks ago, but it was late and very light. I'm not sure if I could be pregnant.

That's all really helpful. Because your period was late and light and pregnancy is possible, the first thing we'll do is a urine pregnancy test — I want to make sure we're not missing a pregnancy in the wrong place, which can cause this kind of pain. The combination of lower belly pain with yellowish, odorous discharge also makes me think of an infection of the uterus and tubes, so Dr. Ellis and I will do a pelvic exam together and take swabs for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and other causes, plus check your urine for infection. Depending on what we find, we may start antibiotics today rather than wait for results. In the meantime, if you develop fever, worsening pain, fainting, or heavy bleeding, that's an emergency — go right in. Is there anything you're worried about or want to ask before we bring Dr. Ellis in?

**Material for Student Interviewer**

**Setting:** You are a radiology-oncology prelimary resident rotating on the inpatient medicine service.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is 35-75 years old with hypertension, epigastric pain, and mild shortness of breath. The patient has been otherwise healthy.

The patient came to the ED yesterday afternoon. The original ED plan was to discharge the patient home with a working diagnosis of “dyspepsia” and outpatient follow-up, but after 3 hours the patient complained of increased pain. The ED doctors changed the plan to bring the patient into the hospital on “observation status.”

You examined the patient at 9 pm last night, shortly after the patient arrived on the floor. The patient was in modest discomfort.

It is now about 10 hours after the surgery and you have returned for another overnight shift. The patient is back in a hospital room, now on the surgery service. You are no longer directly involved in the patient's care.

**Student Tasks:**

Explain to the patient why there was a delay in diagnosing the perforated duodenal ulcer and getting to surgery.

**Episode:** Disclosure of Error

You are a patient in a hospital room.

Here is the timeline of your story:

* 2 days ago you began to have some discomfort, a little pain, in your belly.
* Yesterday at 3 pm you went to the hospital emergency room and waited 3 hours to be seen.
* While being examined you had blood tests done and they told you that if the blood tests were normal, you could go home with an appointment to see a doctor in the clinic.
* While waiting for the results, the pain got a little worse. A doctor examined you again, said he thought you were OK, but agreed to “watch you for a while” so they admitted you to the hospital where you met more doctors.
* At about 10 pm they sent you for an Xray of your belly.
* You tried to sleep, but the pain in your belly kept you awake.
* About 6 am, the pain got much worse. You called the nurse.
* A doctor came back to see you at 6:30 am and said that the Xray showed a problem in the belly that might require surgery.
* At 10am you were taken to the operating room.

Now it is evening, and you are recovering from surgery. The surgeon told you that you had an ulcer, which had caused a small hole in your bowel, and that this was repaired with surgery. You need to be in the hospital for a few more days, get IVs and antibiotics, and not eat for a few days. The good news is that the surgeons expect you will recover completely.

You are relieved that you will be OK, but thinking back, you wonder about the sudden concern of the doctors this morning and the emergency surgery. You had an Xray at 10 pm and got worse for hours after it was done, but the doctor only told you the Xray was bad in the morning. Why did it take more than 8 hours to find out that you needed emergency surgery?

Background: You do not see doctors regularly, and you felt perfectly healthy until this belly pain started. You did go to the medical clinic at the hospital last year, and received some medicines for your blood pressure and cholesterol. You did not come back to see the doctor, but your medicine is running out and they told you that you could not get more refills without another visit to the clinic. All these doctors, nurses, and tests at the hospital are a little scary. Fill in other details that come up as you see fit.

A doctor is coming to your room to talk to you. This is one of the many doctors you have seen, and is the one who told you about the Xray results early this morning. Ideally the doctor will address your emotions, apologize, and take responsibility, in which case your initial emotions will give way to gratitude that everything is ok and appreciation for the doctor’s honesty. If the doctor is evasive, defensive, makes excuses, or takes any approach that seems inappropriate to your character, you can prolong your confusion and anger, and retreat to a withdrawn affect rather than having an outburst of emotion.

turns.content: Hi there, I'm the medicine resident who saw you when you first arrived on the floor last night. I heard that since I last saw you, things changed quickly and you had to have emergency surgery for a perforated ulcer. How are you feeling right now?

Hi doc, I'm feeling a bit tired and sore, but I'm just glad that everything is okay now. I was in a lot of pain earlier, but it's much better now. I'm just trying to rest and recover. I was wondering though, why did it take so long to find out that I needed surgery? I had that X-ray last night and then nothing happened until this morning.

I completely understand why you're asking that, and I am so sorry you had to go through all that pain and waiting. When you first came to the emergency department, your symptoms looked a lot like severe indigestion. The X-ray you had didn't clearly show the hole in your ulcer—which unfortunately can sometimes happen in the early stages of this condition. Has the surgical team gone over any of this with you yet?

No, they haven't really gone over the details with me. I just know that I had an ulcer that caused a small hole in my bowel, and that's why I needed surgery. I'm just trying to make sense of everything that happened. I was in agony last night, and I don't understand how it took so long to figure out that I needed emergency surgery. I thought I was getting good care, but now I'm not sure what to think. I was perfectly healthy until this belly pain started, and now I'm here with all these doctors and tests. It's all a bit overwhelming.

I can completely understand why you feel overwhelmed and why you are questioning the care you received. It is terrifying to be in that much pain and feel like the problem isn't being found fast enough. What happened was that early on, a very small hole sometimes doesn't leak enough air to show up on a standard X-ray. Because your initial tests were reassuring, the team thought it was severe indigestion. It wasn't until your pain got worse over those hours that the signs of the perforation finally became visible, which then triggered the emergency surgery. I am truly sorry you had to endure that agony while the clinical picture was still unfolding. Does that help explain why there was a delay, or do you have other questions about what happened?

Hi there. I'm glad we could connect virtually today since you're feeling too unwell to leave the house. I'm sorry to hear you've been dealing with a terrible cough and runny nose for the past four days. 

To help me get a better idea of what's going on, are you coughing anything up, and have you had any fevers or shortness of breath?

Hi, thanks for seeing me. I've been coughing up some clear or yellowish phlegm, but not much. I haven't had any fevers, but I've been feeling pretty achy. I haven't noticed any shortness of breath, though.

It's a good sign that you haven't had any fevers or shortness of breath, but the body aches and coughing definitely make it hard to get through the day. 

Have you noticed any sore throat or changes in your sense of taste or smell? And what, if anything, have you tried taking over-the-counter to help with these symptoms?

My throat has been a bit sore in the morning, but it gets better as the day goes on. I haven't noticed any changes in my sense of taste or smell. I've been taking some over-the-counter cold medicine, but it hasn't really helped much.

That morning sore throat is very likely from drainage from your runny nose while you sleep. Since it's been going on for a few days without much relief, it's helpful to rule a few things out. 

Have you happened to take a home COVID test, or been around anyone else who has been sick recently? Also, do you have any ongoing medical conditions like asthma or diabetes?

private_patient_context:
**CASE 3B**
Robert Goodman,

<u>**Case Summary**</u>

Robert Goodman is a 45 year old laborer who works for a moving company. Over the last month he has experienced some vague, minor chest pains on exertion, especially while at work when he is lifting. One of Robert’s coworkers recently had cardiac problems and was a smoker. His physician recommended that he quit smoking and he did so. He discussed the issue with Robert several times.

Robert is now concerned that there may be some connection between his current symptoms and his smoking. He approached this friend, who gave Robert his leftover patches. Robert tried them a month ago for a few days but used them incorrectly.

Robert is now blaming his inability to quit on the patch. However, Robert smokes about two or three packs a day but started on the lowest level of the patch. That’s what his friend gave him. In addition, Robert took the patch off two or three times a day to smoke. He kept a pack of cigarettes in the moving van, “just in case”. Robert never read the package instructions and did not make any behavioral changes.

The chest pains persisted for about a week, so Robert is now in the office for a follow up visit after having the usual battery of cardiac diagnostic tests (all of which are negative). The subsequent visit revealed that the chest pains were a result of gastritis and reflux which have responded to antacids (Zantac). However, Robert does not like taking medicines, and this incident has brought the concept of quitting to the forefront of Robert’s thinking. He is now motivated to quit, but this prior “attempt” has left him somewhat disheartened. He does not understand why the patches worked for his friend and not for him.

**Your role is to play a smoker who is** <u>**definitely interested in quitting**</u>**. However, he has come to believe that his recent failure to do so is the fault of the patches he used. He does not understand that he used them incorrectly. He also does not understand that the quitter must actively participate in the quit (make behavioral changes) to be successful. He is mistakenly waiting for the patches to “cure” him.**

<u>**Presentation/Emotional Tone**</u>

Robert is scared that he is going to have a heart attack at any moment even though all the tests came back negative. There is a long history of cardiac problems in Robert’s family, all of whom were smokers. His father reminded him of this in a recent conversation.

During the office visit he is anxious, stating many times that he really wants to quit now. However, in spite of his anxiety, he is motivated to quit smoking, but not at all confident that he will be able to do so.

When the student asks why you have come to the office, you reply,

**“I was afraid that I was going to have a heart attack. I know the tests came back negative, but this whole incident made me really think about my smoking. I know smoking isn’t good for my heart and I don't want to have to take pills for my stomach for the rest of my life just so I can smoke. So, I tried to quit a few weeks ago on my own but couldn’t. Those dumb patches just don’t work.”**

**“What do I do now?”**

<u>**Your Smoking History**</u>

You began smoking while in the service at age 18. You have been smoking ever since and now smoke anywhere from two to three packs a day depending on how busy you are at work. On slow days you smoke more since you have a lot of time on your hands. You have never tried to quit before, other than the attempt last month.

During that attempt you experienced significant withdrawal in spite of wearing the patch. You were very irritable, anxious, restless, and impatient. After three days you returned to your regular pattern of smoking.

<u>**Family Smoking/Medical History**</u>

Both sets of grandparents smoked as well as both parents. Father has quit but mother still smokes about a pack a day.

Paternal grandmother had two heart attacks at age 57 and died at 58 as a result.

Maternal grandfather had a stroke at age 55. He was bedridden for eight years as a result and died at age 63.

Father had triple bypass at age 54.

Mother has had a long history of angina starting in her mid-forties.

<u>**Drug/Alcohol use**</u>

You drink a few beers a week on Friday or Saturday night. You have cut back considerably on your drinking in recent years.  **“ I just can’t do it anymore!”**

<u>**Patient Interview**</u>

If the student asks you about family cardiac history, review the above information with him or her. Otherwise, don’t bring this up.

If the student asks you what you did the last time you tried to quit, just say,

**“I used those dumb patches, they didn’t work.”**

If the student questions you further as in, **“Which patch did you use?”** or “**Describe to me how you used the patch,”** you may explain exactly what you did:

**“I started on the seven-milligram patch. That’s what my friend gave me.”**

**“I used them for three whole days. I was so anxious and irritable all day long my friends told me to start smoking again or they wouldn’t talk to me anymore.”**

**“They didn’t work at all. I still wanted to smoke even though I had the patch on.”**

**“But I want you to know I took the patch off those three days every time I smoked (about four or five times a day). I didn’t want to get a heart attack.”**

As you explain all this become increasingly anxious. Ask the student,

**“Why can’t you cure me? Can’t you just give me a pill or something?”**

If the student asks you to set a quit date,

**"It will be hard to quit at work, so I think I will quit on a Saturday."**

**"Two weeks from Saturday is a good time; that should give me enough time to get ready."**

If the student asks you what kind of changes you made in your routines or behavior, ask,

**“What do you mean? Don’t you just put the patch on and forget about it?”**

If the student asks you when you most need a cigarette,

**"In the morning when I wake up, during breaks at work, and after meals."**

If the student asks you what you could do besides smoking at those times,

**“What do you mean?”**

If they give examples of other behaviors (chewing gum, etc.),

**"That's interesting. My buddy who quit is always carrying around those pretzel sticks. I never really asked him about them, but that would probably help.  I also like gum."**

**"I should really do more exercise. Maybe I will start walking after I eat meals."**

If the student suggests that you go to a group cessation program, say,

**“I don’t like talking about myself in front of strangers. What else can I do?”**

If the student <u>**does not**</u> ask you any questions about how you used the patch or what you did, just continue with the “What am I supposed to do? I really want to quit” line of questioning until he or she does.

turns.content: Hello Mr. Goodman, I'm glad we could sit down together today. I know you recently had tests on your heart that came back reassuring and pointed toward mild reflux, but I understand you have some other concerns you wanted to talk about. What's been on your mind?

I was afraid that I was going to have a heart attack. I know the tests came back negative, but this whole incident made me really think about my smoking. I know smoking isn’t good for my heart and I don't want to have to take pills for my stomach for the rest of my life just so I can smoke. So, I tried to quit a few weeks ago on my own but couldn’t. Those dumb patches just don’t work. What do I do now?

It is a huge positive step that you’ve made the decision to quit, and I know how frustrating it is when an attempt doesn't work out. Quitting is tough, but we have several effective options and strategies beyond just the patch alone. 

To help us find a plan that works for you, could you tell me how much you typically smoke each day, and what went wrong when you tried the patches?

I smoke anywhere from two to three packs a day depending on how busy I am at work. I used those dumb patches, they didn’t work. I started on the seven-milligram patch. That’s what my friend gave me. I used them for three whole days. I was so anxious and irritable all day long my friends told me to start smoking again or they wouldn’t talk to me anymore. I took the patch off those three days every time I smoked (about four or five times a day). I didn’t want to get a heart attack.

It completely makes sense why that attempt was so miserable for you. A 7-milligram patch is the lowest available dose, usually meant for the very end of quitting. For someone smoking two to three packs a day, that dose was far too low to prevent your nicotine withdrawal, which is why you felt so anxious and irritable.

With the right dose—or by combining a higher-strength patch with a short-acting option like nicotine gum or lozenges for sudden cravings, or even considering non-nicotine prescription pills—we can keep those withdrawal symptoms under control. How would you feel about trying a properly dosed medical plan tailored specifically to your heavy smoking level?
I don’t know much about those other options, but if they can help me quit without feeling so bad, I’m willing to try. I really want to quit this time. I just don’t want to go through that again.

I completely understand, and our main goal is to keep you comfortable so you don't have to suffer through severe withdrawal again. 

Here is what I recommend for our plan:

1. **Proper Medication:** We can start you on the full-strength 21 mg nicotine patch for steady relief throughout the day, and combine it with nicotine gum or lozenges whenever you get a sudden, strong craving. Alternatively, there are prescription non-nicotine pills like varenicline or bupropion that can reduce cravings.
2. **Choose a Quit Date:** Pick a target day within the next week or two to prepare yourself and let your coworkers and friends know so they can support you.
3. **Behavioral Support:** Changing daily routines and having a support system makes a huge difference. I also recommend utilizing the free quitline (1-800-QUIT-NOW) for extra coaching.

Let’s go ahead and prescribe the medication that fits you best today, and I’d like to see you back in two weeks so we can check on your progress and make any adjustments you need. We're going to get through this together.

I think I will quit on a Saturday. Two weeks from Saturday is a good time; that should give me enough time to get ready. I don’t like talking about myself in front of strangers. What else can I do? I like gum. I should really do more exercise. Maybe I will start walking after I eat meals.

# Station 3 – Shared Decision Making

Scenario:

You are a third year student rotating through a longitudinal ambulatory rotation. You are seeing a patient, Joanna Mills, for the second time. Ms. Mills is a 45-year old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. When you saw her for the first time last week, she had not been receiving medical care or medication refills for 6 months due to the loss of her medical insurance. Last week, she came to clinic to re-establish care and receive refills of her medications for diabetes mellitus. Last week, you agreed to refill her medications and ordered blood work. Ms. Mills has come in to clinic today to discuss the lab results with you.

You discussed this with your attending preceptor prior to seeing Ms. Mills. Your attending physician instructs you to discuss the results with Ms. Mills and encourages you to engage in shared decision making with your patient.
private_patient_context:
**Station 3 – Shared Decision Making**

**Training Materials:**

# 3. <u>Scenario for Standardized Patient</u>

You are Joanna Mills, a 45-year old woman. Last week, you came to a new hospital-based clinic to establish a primary care doctor and get refills of your medications, since you ran out of medications for diabetes mellitus. You haven’t been to see a doctor in over six months, and you’ve been rationing your medications during that time, but you ran out of medications last week.  The medical student whom you met last week gave you a one month supply of your medications (metformin and glyburide) but asked you to get blood work done so that s/he could “get a sense of how well controlled your diabetes was” and to make changes in medications, if necessary. You went to the laboratory last week after your visit and are now here for your scheduled follow up visit to go over the results of the blood test. You feel fine and have refilled your medications and do not have any new problems to report to the medical student today; but you are curious to learn about the results of your blood tests and hope to hear that your diabetes is well controlled.

<u>Medical History:</u>

You were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus four years ago by your primary care doctor at the time, Dr. Alvarez. You were not surprised when you received this diagnosis because you have a strong family history of diabetes. You know that the A1C blood test shows whether or not your diabetes is controlled, and you also know that anything less than 7 is good and anything higher than 7 means that the sugars are too high. You remember that when you were first diagnosed with diabetes, your A1C was 7.6. The doctor had you on Metformin first, but the following year, she added glyburide because the A1C was not at goal. Your doctor slowly increased the doses of these medications; and as of one year ago, had you at your current dose of metformin and glyburide.

You have not had any complications related to diabetes mellitus, and you have been taking your medications as prescribed. However, 6 months ago, you lost your job and your medical insurance. You could not afford to continue seeing your primary care doctor so you stopped going at that time. The doctor gave you last refills of your medications and encouraged you to come to the hospital-based clinic since they had a sliding scale fee service for patients. Six months ago at your last visit with Dr. Alvarez, you also had a blood test. You received a letter from Dr. Alvarez stating that your A1C was 8.8 and that you needed to follow up on this, but you were unable to see her or any other doctor until now.

You have been busy for the past few months so you did not come to the hospital clinic.

You have admittedly stretched out your remaining pills, sometimes skipping doses to make the prescription last a little longer. Last week, you were completely without medications; and you were scared about your sugars getting too high, so you came to the clinic.

<u>Family History:</u>

As noted above, you were not surprised when you were diagnosed with diabetes four years ago. Both of your parents suffered from it, and you know that it is an illness that can run in the family. However, you were still frightened when you were first given the diagnosis. You have seen both of your parents suffer from medical problems related to diabetes. Your father had high blood pressure and kidney problems, which his doctor said was due to diabetes. He passed away suddenly from a heart attack when he was 66 years old. Your mother, who is now 64, is alive but has many medical problems. Prior to her recent stroke 3 months ago, she had very poorly controlled high blood pressure and diabetes.  She has been in and out of the hospital several times a year for the past few years, either for chest pain or “fluid in the lungs” or skin infections and infected foot ulcers.

Besides diabetes, you do not have any other medical problems.

<u>Social History:</u>

You were laid off from your job as a clothing buyer for a large department store. Since then, you have been looking for a new job and have been trying to keep your spirits up. You were busy caring for your mother in another state for the past few months because she had a recent stroke. Between your mother’s illness and your search for a job, the past six months have been extraordinarily stressful for you; and you have not really had time to take care of yourself. But you have always wanted to stay in good health to avoid illness, and you know that it’s important to focus on your health right now.  You have been without health insurance since losing your job as you could not afford COBRA and you postponed looking into applying for Obama care in hopes that you would soon have a new job.  You have been unable to afford to refill your medications, and therefore, rationing the pills until you ran out of them last week.

You do not have any history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug use.

You are divorced and have a 20 year-old daughter, who is in college and no longer living at home

<u>Emotional Tone:</u>

You are very concerned about your health condition although it has been difficult for you to focus on your own health for the past six months, between your economic hardship and your mother’s acute illness. When you had insurance, you were always good about following up with your primary care doctor and taking all of your medications. Even though you have had diabetes for four years, you were told that you could be “in control” of your illness and maybe avoid complications of diabetes. You have been happy to take your pills, as long as it meant controlling your illness and avoiding complications of the disease.  You know that you have not taken your pills as prescribed, mostly because of financial concerns and the cost of medications.  You are very reluctant to start insulin. You know that being on insulin means needing to prick yourself several times a day to check your blood sugar and give yourself the insulin shots and you hate the thought of pricking yourself so frequently with needles.  Also, you know that the diabetic supplies (insulin and more lancets and paper strips for frequent sugar checks) are expensive and another cost that you feel would be really hard to absorb now.

**Your role is to portray a patient who is very concerned about your health. You want to know how to keep yourself healthy. Yet, you are upset and worried when you learn that your diabetes is not well controlled.  You are reluctant to start insulin therapy because you dislike the thought of using the needles to give yourself medication and the extra cost of medications and supplies feels like a financial burden that you feel unable to take at this time. In addition, although you know it is not rational you feel that using insulin means you are more likely to develop the complications you saw your parents go through because they were on insulin.  However, you normally always follow your doctor’s advice and are unsure about going against his advice by not starting insulin.**

<u>Scenario:</u> 

The student will enter the clinic room, where you are waiting to be seen. You are seated next to the desk, appearing comfortable but a little anxious. You met this student last week and are happy to see the same person again.

The student may ask, “I wanted to talk to you about your blood test results that we did last week. Do you know what an A1C test signifies?”

**“Yes, I remember my last doctor telling me that it was a blood test that the doctors took to show whether the diabetes was controlled or not. I know that it’s supposed to be below 7.”**

The student will inform you that your A1C level was elevated, at 11.

You are surprised and concerned.

**“Oh no, that’s really high isn’t it?”**

The student should inform you that this A1C is very elevated and indicates that the diabetes is very poorly controlled at this time. You are upset and very worried by this news.

**“It’s never been so high like this. You know I was worried about my sugars but I never thought it could get up to this level.” What does this mean I have to do now?”**

The student should describe treatment options. Since you are on high doses of your current medications, there is no way to simply go up on the current dose of medications. The student will recommend starting insulin therapy as a way to rapidly bring down the A1C level and control the diabetes.

You interrupt the student when s/he mentions insulin and get visibly upset.

**“Wait, insulin? Oh, I don’t want to do that.”**

The student should ask you why you do not want to start insulin. S/He should give you a chance to state what your concerns are. You state many reasons why you don’t want to start insulin therapy now. After you give each reason, you should give the student a chance to discuss it with you.

**“I know that there are a lot of reasons why my sugars got uncontrolled like this. I wasn’t doing all the things that I know I should have been doing about my health. I wasn’t eating right, I wasn’t consistently taking my pills every day. I wasn’t really focusing on my health. I think that there are a lot of things besides insulin that I can do to get my health back in order.”**

**“I know that when you start insulin, you have to check your sugars many times throughout the day. And those extra supplies, those strips and lancets, they all cost a lot of money that I don’t think I’d be able to afford right now.”**

**“To tell you the truth, I’m really afraid of pricking myself with a needle to give myself insulin.  I don’t think that I could do that. I hate needles and the thought of giving myself shots every day is really scary to me.”**

**“I am so afraid of insulin.  I know it isn’t rational but I feel like insulin means I have diabetes with a capital D.  Do you know what I mean – it seems more serious.  I saw my dad go through so much, and now my mom with her stroke.  They were both on insulin.”**

The student should respond to all of your concerns and reasons for not wanting to start insulin. If he does not acknowledge or validate your concerns then you should remain resistant to starting insulin.

The student should ask you about what your desires regarding the management of your illness are. S/He might ask, “Ms. Mills, can you tell me a little bit about how diabetes is affecting your life, and what you are hoping to do to manage your illness? What would you like to see for yourself regarding your diabetes?

**“I really don’t want to be sick from diabetes like my mother was. I know all about the complications, the foot ulcers, the amputations, dialysis, strokes… I’m just really scared about my diabetes being out of control because I never want to go through what she’s been going though with her health. I want to be healthy for my daughter and for myself. So I want to do what you think is best. I’ve always listened to doctors in the past. But right now, I am just really scared of this insulin for a lot of reasons too. I am just hoping for a way that I can get back into good health again without going down the insulin road.”**

The student should try to engage you in deciding what the best treatment for your diabetes is. If he only recommends insulin and says that nothing else will work right now, but you don’t feel that he/she acknowledges the reasons why you do not want to start insulin, you will be more resistant to starting insulin now. However, if the student shares information with you about insulin treatment that addresses your concerns, you might consider changing your mind. Here are some examples of effective statements:

“The insulin that I would recommend starting you on is a once daily insulin that works slowly over 24 hours. You do not have to give yourself multiple injections of insulin each day. Rather, you could give yourself one injection a day.”

“The benefit of starting insulin is that it is more likely to successfully bring your A1C level down to signify good control of your diabetes. The better we control your diabetes, the less likely it is that you would ever get the complications of diabetes (such as kidney problems or eye problems.)

“One concern that I have in continuing with oral medicines rather than insulin, is that the oral medications do not bring down the A1C level as effectively as insulin does. I can tell that it is really important for you to get in control of your diabetes, and I think that this is the most successful way that we can do it.”

“Insulin is one part of the plan that we can create to control your diabetes. You are right that diet and exercise and taking your medications every day are equally important in controlling your diabetes. I think that we can work together on each of these issues, and perhaps insulin can be a component of this plan.”

If you feel that the student has engaged you as a partner in making the decision and has given you a chance to address your beliefs and concerns about your illness, then you should agree to work with the student to come up with a plan together; and you can agree to try the insulin.

**“Okay, I see what you are saying. I think that if you feel the insulin may really help me get my diabetes under control and keep me healthy, then I will try it for a while and see how my sugars improve.”**

If you feel that the student has not given you a chance to speak about your concerns and has not enlisted you as a partner in decision making, but rather unilaterally recommended insulin without building a consensus with you, then you should not agree to start insulin. You are calmer at the end but are very resolute about not starting insulin today.

**“You know, I don’t think I am able to get over my fear of starting insulin right now. I’d really rather try getting back on my pills every day and see how I do for a while before I switch my medicines.”**

If at any time the student asks a question that you do not understand or is at all unclear, then you should ask them to clarify. You can say:

**“What do you mean by that?”**

Hello Ms. Mills, it is good to see you again. Thank you for coming back in today to go over your lab results and discuss how your diabetes management is going. 

Before we dive into the numbers, how have you been feeling since we restarted your medications last week?
Hello, I'm feeling fine, thank you. I've been taking my medications as prescribed since I got the refill last week. I haven't noticed any new problems.

I’m really glad to hear that you're back on your routine without any issues. 

Looking at your lab results, your hemoglobin A1c—which shows your average blood sugar over the past three months—came back elevated. That is completely understandable given that you had to go without your medications for six months. 

How familiar are you with the A1c test, and what are your main goals or concerns as we think about managing your blood sugar moving forward?

Yes, I remember my last doctor telling me that it was a blood test that the doctors took to show whether the diabetes was controlled or not. I know that it’s supposed to be below 7. I really don’t want to be sick from diabetes like my mother was. I know all about the complications, the foot ulcers, the amputations, dialysis, strokes… I’m just really scared about my diabetes being out of control because I never want to go through what she’s been going though with her health. I want to be healthy for my daughter and for myself.

Thank you for sharing that with me, Ms. Mills. It is completely understandable that you feel scared after watching what your mother went through, and wanting to stay healthy for your daughter is a wonderful and powerful motivation.

Because you were without medication for six months, this current A1c mostly reflects that gap. Now that you are back on your medications, we have a great opportunity to get those numbers down and protect your long-term health. 

One strong option is to keep you on your current medication regimen and work on healthy lifestyle habits, then recheck your A1c in about 3 months to see your true progress before making any major medication changes. How does that approach sound to you?

That sounds good to me. I think that there are a lot of things besides insulin that I can do to get my health back in order. I know that when you start insulin, you have to check your sugars many times throughout the day. And those extra supplies, those strips and lancets, they all cost a lot of money that I don’t think I’d be able to afford right now.

I completely understand. Medication and supply costs are a major factor, and avoiding insulin while focusing on your current oral medications and healthy lifestyle habits makes complete sense. 

Our plan moving forward is to keep you on your current prescriptions, focus on balanced nutrition and regular physical activity, and give your body time to respond to being back on treatment. We will see you back in three months to recheck your A1c and review your progress together. If you run into any issues or financial hurdles before then, please reach out to us right away.

How does that feel as a plan for you, and are there any other questions I can answer today?
That sounds like a good plan. I feel better knowing that we have a way to keep track of how I'm doing. I don't have any other questions right now. Thank you for your help.

turns.content: Hello Mrs. Quick. I’d like to understand your falls so we can help prevent another one. Could you describe what happened with your most recent fall, including where you were and what you were doing? Did you feel dizzy, faint, or otherwise unwell beforehand?
My daughter thought I should be checked because I’ve had some falls. The last fall occurred while I was in the bathtub. I think I turned too fast. I did not feel dizzy or faint beforehand.

I’m glad your daughter encouraged you to come in. Were you injured or unable to get up after the bathtub fall? What happened with the other two falls—where were you, and did you trip, lose your balance, or have any warning symptoms?

I was not hurt and used my grab bars to get up. The second fall involved catching my left toes in a small throw rug. The third fall involved catching my hip against the counter after feeling "dizzy". I have not noticed any warning symptoms before the falls.

It’s reassuring you weren’t injured, though the dizziness with the third fall is important. When you say “dizzy,” did you feel the room spinning, lightheaded as if you might faint, or simply off-balance—and had you just stood up or turned? How often does this happen, and when do you take the alprazolam and meclizine?
I felt lightheaded. I do not know how often it happens. I take a medicine for dizziness. I do not know when I take it.

Thank you—that lightheadedness could relate to a drop in blood pressure or medication effects. Several of your medicines, especially alprazolam and meclizine, can worsen balance or drowsiness, while hydrochlorothiazide and carvedilol can lower blood pressure. Please don’t stop them suddenly, but bring all medication bottles—with your daughter if possible—for a prompt review. We should also check your blood pressure lying and standing, vision, strength, walking, and balance.

Meanwhile, remove throw rugs, use the grab bars and a nonslip bath mat, rise and turn slowly, and keep a phone with you; consider having someone nearby when bathing. If you faint, develop chest pain, palpitations, new weakness, trouble speaking, or sustain a head injury, seek urgent help.
I will try to do that. I have not noticed any new weakness or trouble speaking.

turns.content: I’m sorry you’re feeling short of breath and tight in your chest. When did this begin, and did it come on suddenly or build gradually?
It started about 2 weeks ago and it’s been getting worse since then. It came on gradually.

Because chest tightness can sometimes be heart- or lung-related, I want to clarify: does it get worse with walking or other activity and improve with rest? Have you had cough, wheezing, fever, or swelling in your legs?
It gets worse when I’m outdoors and doing things like gardening. It does get better when I rest indoors. I have been having a dry cough and wheezing, but no fever or swelling in my legs.

The outdoor trigger, dry cough, and wheezing make airway irritation or asthma—often worsened by smoke, pollen, or heat—more likely, though we still need to rule out heart and other lung causes. Have you ever had asthma, allergies, or a similar episode, and do you use any inhalers or other breathing medicines?
I have had asthma since I was a child. I use an albuterol inhaler. I have been using it more often lately, about 6 times a day. I am allergic to cats and sensitive to air pollution.

This sounds most consistent with an asthma flare, likely triggered by Sacramento’s summer air pollution/smoke and outdoor exposure. Needing albuterol about six times a day means it is not adequately controlled and needs urgent treatment and reassessment today; chest tightness also means we should check for heart and other lung causes, not assume it is only asthma.

For now, stay indoors with windows closed and filtered air if possible, avoid gardening and smoke, and use an N95 mask if you must go outside. Continue your albuterol only as directed in your asthma plan, but don’t rely on it repeatedly without treatment adjustment—you may need a breathing treatment, a short course of steroid medicine, and a daily controller inhaler.

Tell staff immediately or call 911 if you become short of breath at rest, cannot speak full sentences, develop severe or persistent chest pain, fainting, blue/gray lips, or your inhaler is not helping.

I will stay indoors and avoid gardening. I have an N95 mask that I can use if I need to go outside. I will use my inhaler as directed in my asthma plan. I will let staff know if I become short of breath at rest or have severe chest pain.

**Standardized Patient Role: Sample Patient Case 1**

**J.J. Wilkins**

The following is the typical order for this patient encounter.

Student should introduce himself/herself as a first-year medical student and offer to shake hands. He/she may ask how you wish to be addressed (Mr., first name).

**Identifying Information:**

Marital status: Separated. Your wife kicked you out because of your drinking. Employment: Laid off now—usually work seasonal construction jobs.

Where do you live? Grand Forks—moved here from Minneapolis in 1998.

Children? None.

Primary physician? Dr. Deere at Altru Family Medicine Residency.

**Chief Complaint:** (Why you came to see the doctor today.) “My big toe hurts like hell.”

**History of Present Illness:** (Explanation of the chief complaint—LOCATES mnemonic. Questions in parentheses below will likely be asked. Responses for the SP are provided.)

**L**OCATION: (Where is the pain?) Left toe. (Does the pain radiate [move around, do you feel it anywhere else]?) No.

**O**NSET: (When did this happen?) It came on suddenly 2 days ago.

**C**HARACTER: (Describe the pain—dull, sharp, throbbing, etc.) Sore; it feels like it’s on fire. **A**GGRAVATING FACTORS: (Does anything make the pain WORSE?) Walking; wearing a tight shoe.

**A**LLEVIATING FACTORS: (Does anything give you relief from the pain?) Not walking; putting your foot up. You have taken ibuprofen for the last couple of days. It helps the pain somewhat, but does not make it go away entirely.

**A**SSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: (Are there any other symptoms you have been experiencing?) The

toe is red and swollen. You think you might have a fever, but you haven’t taken your temperature. You don’t have any other type of symptoms.

**T**IMING: (How often do you have the pain and how long does it last?) Constant and getting

worse.

**E**NVIRONMENT: (Is there anything that you can think of anything [new/different behavior,

something you ate, etc.] that may have caused the pain?) No.

**S**EVERITY: (How bad [on a scale of 10] is the pain?) 7 or 8 on a scale of 10.

**S**IMILAR PROBLEMS: (Have you ever had anything like this before?) You were at the clinic 6 months ago because your feet were swollen; but it was nothing like this.

**Past Medical History:** The student will ask questions about previous hospitalizations,

surgeries, accidents or injuries, allergies, current medications, or other active medical problems.

**Prescription Medications:** (MEDICATES mnemonic—asks for every prescription medication)

**M**edication name: HCTZ (hydrochlorothiazide).

**E**ffectiveness: You don’t know, you did not go back for a follow-up appointment.

**D**osage: 50 mg a day.

**C**linician prescriber: Dr. Deere.

**A**dverse effects: None that you know of.

**Over-the-Counter Medications:** Just the recent ibuprofen.

• **Where?** Minneapolis.

• **When?** 1998.

• **Physician?** Don’t remember.

• **Complications?** You were in the hospital for about a week, but it healed fine.

**Trauma/Accidents:** The above mugging is also your traumatic event.

**Other active or ongoing medical problems or conditions?** Just the high blood pressure.

**Immunizations:**

• **Tetanus booster?** Three years ago, when you went to the ER for stitches when you cut your hand on the job.

• **Pneumovax?** No.

• **Flu?** No.

• **Hepatitis?** No.

• **Tuberculosis?** No.

**Health Maintenance:**

• **Blood sugar?** Don’t know.

• **Testicular and prostate exam?** No.

• **Colonoscopy?** No.

• **Eye exam?** Five years ago.

• **Dental exam?** Ten years ago.

• **Special diet?** None.

• **Exercise?** None.

**Family History:**

| --- | --- | --- |

**Social History:**

• **Illicit drug use:** None.

**Upbringing:** Your father was an alcoholic who was physically and emotionally abusive when he was drunk. You left home at an early age.

**Education:** You never finished high school—11th grade.

**Marriages/Divorces:** Married 38 years.

**Relationship concerns:** Your wife kicked you out 3 months ago because of your drinking. The truth is you lost your construction job for not showing up at work on time.

**Sexual concerns:** If asked specifically, you don’t have any interest in it right now.

**Spiritual concerns:** If asked specifically, you don’t go to church and don’t believe in God.

\*\*After your response about drinking students may ask you the following questions: CAGE questions:

• Have you ever felt you ought to  **C**ut down on your drinking?

• Have people  **A**nnoyed you by criticizing your drinking?

• Have you ever felt bad or **G**uilty about your drinking?

• Have you ever had a drink first thing in the morning (**E**ye-opener) to steady your nerves or to get rid of a hangover?

Your answers to the above:

**C**—Your wife has criticized you many times.

**A**—You get very annoyed with her, even very angry and abusive.

**G**—You don’t feel guilty. You don’t feel you have a problem. You’ve quit many times before and will again as soon as you get through this “rough patch.”

Good morning, doctor. The pain started 2 days ago. It's on my left side, in my lower back, and it doesn't radiate to my buttock or leg.

Thanks. Did anything trigger it, such as lifting, twisting, a fall, or unusual activity? And do you have any leg weakness or numbness, trouble controlling urine or bowel movements, or numbness around the groin?

I don't think anything triggered it. I haven't done any heavy lifting or unusual activities. I don't have any leg weakness or numbness, and I'm not having any trouble controlling my urine or bowel movements. I haven't noticed any numbness around the groin.

Thank you—that’s reassuring. Do you have fever or chills, burning or blood with urination, nausea/vomiting, or new abdominal pain? And how severe is the pain from 0 to 10, and what makes it better or worse?

I've had some chills, but no fever. I've had to go to the bathroom more frequently over the past 3 days and there has been some mild irritation when I urinate. I don't have any nausea, vomiting, or new abdominal pain. The pain is a dull, constant ache, about a 4 out of 10. Nothing seems to make it better or worse.

Your left-sided back pain along with chills, frequent urination, and burning could be a urinary tract infection that may be affecting the kidney. **Setting:** You are a medicine intern in the primary care clinic. This patient has been coming to the clinic for 5 years for treatment of their hypertension, but you have not personally met the patient before.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is 50-60 years old and was diagnosed with pancreatic carcinoma 7 months ago. The patient has received 2 different chemotherapy drugs over 6 months and neither worked. The patient received the most recent chemotherapy 3 weeks ago, but the cancer has continued to spread. The patient's oncologist has said there are no other treatment options for the cancer. You have read a report from the oncologist that states the patient knows the full extent of the disease and that no further cancer specific treatment is available.

Take a palliative care history from a patient who has been told there are no more cancer treatments available.
