You are following up in your primary care office today but are meeting a new doctor.

You began to experience pain in your stomach and back and began to lose some weight about 8 months ago. After a couple of weeks you went to the doctor who sent you for blood work and X rays. The testing led to a diagnosis of cancer of the pancreas and you began treatment for it with chemotherapy 6 months ago. Two months into therapy, repeat scans showed that the cancer continued to grow so you were switched to another regimen. That therapy has not halted the spread of the cancer and your cancer doctor told you last week that there are no other treatments she can offer. Since the chemotherapy made you feel very sick, you are accepting of her advice. The main focus of your treatment now is on keeping you comfortable. You are fatigued, have lost your hair and 40 lbs. The oncologist sent you back to your primary care doctor to manage your symptoms and other medical problems and that is why you are here today.

At the moment you are taking lisinopril 40 mg for your high blood pressure (you have been on this medicine for over 10 years), oxycodone 5 mg as needed about twice a day for pain, and ondansetron (“Zofran") 4 mg once or twice a week for nausea. Your symptoms are well controlled and you know you could take more medicine if you were more uncomfortable. You have also begun to experience some light headedness when you stand up quickly. You sleep “okay,” but not great. You do not eat as much because your appetite has decreased.\*

You worked as a teacher of theater at your local college and had been able to continue with some sick days. You found it challenging to go to work and the end of the school year was a relief. You have good health insurance through work. You are happily married and you are worried\*\* about how your spouse will manage financially without the dual income. You have 2 adult children who are working and living independently. They know you are ill and are very sad about your declining health. Both are willing and able to help at home. You have heard of hospice and are interested in having their support since you wish to remain at home to the extent that is possible. turns.content: Hello, I'm Dr. — one of the doctors here in the clinic. I know you've been coming here for a few years, though we haven't met before. I've read the note from your cancer doctor, but I'd much rather hear things in your own words. Can you tell me what's been happening for you lately, and what your understanding is of where things stand right now?

Well, I started having some pain in my stomach and back about 8 months ago, and I began to lose some weight. I went to the doctor, and after some tests, they told me I had pancreatic cancer. I've been through a couple rounds of chemotherapy, but the cancer kept growing. My oncologist told me last week that there are no more treatments left to try. So, I'm here to talk about managing my symptoms and what comes next.

That's a lot to absorb in a short time, and I'm sorry you've had to hear that news. I'd like to help you with the symptoms and with planning ahead. Let's start with the pain — where is it now, how bad does it get, and what are you taking for it?
The pain is mostly in my stomach and back. It's been coming and going, but it's not too bad right now. I take oxycodone for it, usually about twice a day. It helps to manage it.

Good — I'm glad the oxycodone is taking the edge off, and we can adjust it if the pain starts breaking through more often. Besides the pain, what else has been troubling you day to day — things like appetite, nausea, bowels, sleep or energy? And how are you doing with all of this emotionally?

I've been feeling pretty tired most of the time, and my appetite has decreased a lot. I've lost about 40 pounds in the past 8 months. I sometimes feel nauseous, but the Zofran helps with that. I sleep okay, but not great. Emotionally, I'm worried about my spouse and how they'll manage financially once I'm not able to work anymore. It's been tough, but I'm trying to stay strong.

It says a lot about you that in the middle of all this, your biggest worry is your spouse. That's a real concern, and it's one we can get help with — our social worker can look at disability, benefits, and financial resources, and hospice teams also support families both now and afterward. I'd like to set that up for you, and to hear from you what matters most in the time ahead — where you'd want to be cared for, and whether you and your spouse have talked about your wishes if you became too sick to speak for yourself. For now, let's keep your pain, appetite and fatigue as manageable as possible; I'll arrange a home hospice referral if you're open to it, and I'd like to see you back soon — with your spouse, if they'd like to come.

That sounds like a good plan. I'd like to stay at home as long as possible, and I've already talked to my spouse about my wishes. I want to avoid any heroic measures if I get to that point. I'd appreciate the help from the social worker and hospice. I'll talk to my spouse about coming in with me next time. Thank you for your help, Doctor.

**Andrea Sands**

**Standardized patient Training summary**

**First Position**: Sitting on bed in gown.

**Props**: Tissue, water bottle, glycerin and water in spray bottle for patient forehead sweat.

**Current Condition**:

You are B. Radcliffe and are 55 years old. You really feel sick. You are weak. You noted a terrible shaking chill that lasted several minutes about four days ago. Since then you have felt intermittent chills but nothing like you did 4 days ago. They seem to be worse in the evenings and have been bad for the last two days. You are coughing now but this only started about 3 days ago, and seems to be getting worse. The cough is a deep, hacking cough that produces yellow phlegm but only with great effort. Your chest also hurts on the right side, down low, (on side of body, below breast) when you cough or if you take a really big breath. It feels like a deep, sharp pain when you breathe in (and has increased from a 2 to 3 out of 10 on the pain scale). You feel like you have a fever, but not checked it and your throat hurts from the coughing. Yesterday, you vomited (looked like the chicken broth soup you ate if asked) once after a coughing spell but it was mostly mucous (no nausea). You have had some shortness of breath with activity (going up the stairs), none at rest. You have not had any nasal congestion, runny nose or sinus pressure. You have not had any wheezing. At baseline you do not have a cough, sputum, shortness of breath or wheezing. You have taken Pseudoephedrine and Guaifenesin occasionally (3-4 times each day according to package directions) since it started but nothing seems to help. The coughing is waking you up at night and you have tried using extra pillows to prop yourself up.

You volunteer regularly at the Nashville Rescue Mission in downtown Nashville, TN. Even though you didn't feel well, you went in on your regularly scheduled days (three and four days ago). You have been exposed to a lot of people in the shelter and have been pushing yourself to be there helping when you really felt like being in bed. A number of people in the shelter seem to be coughing/sneezing.

You are a native of Baltimore and work as an accountant for the State of Tennessee government. You have been married 28 years and have 2 children, a daughter, Amy (27), and son, David (25). Because the divorce is not amiable, your grandsons have been staying with you for the past few months. The younger one is in the first year of grade school and the older one is in fourth grade. You live in an older frame house. You do not use drugs or tobacco currently.

You occasionally have a glass of wine in the evenings. You have environmental allergies in the spring.

**Past Medical History:**

You are generally healthy. You work at a desk five days a week. You work around the house and yard on the weekends. You have never been hospitalized nor had any surgeries. You only see a doctor when sick and you haven't seen a doctor in years (to save money). You always remember to get a flu shot every year.

You've never had the pneumococcal vaccine. No medications or medical conditions. You used to smoke about a pack of cigarettes a day (you started in high school), but quit for the third time two weeks ago because your grandchildren are living with you now. You are currently using the patch for help. Your grandson Todd has also had a sore throat last week that was diagnosed as strep throat and treated with penicillin for 7 days. His symptoms included a very sore throat and fever but no cough. He's feeling better now. If asked, "Have you ever been exposed to tuberculosis (TB)?" respond, "Not that I know of." * Mother: seems to be healthy but may have high cholesterol and maybe arthritis. Age 78
* Maternal grandmother: died when you were a child. Was in a nursing home and never really knew her history.
* Maternal grandfather and paternal grandparents: Died before you were born.
* Son: No known medical conditions
* Daughter: No known medical conditions

As the student transitions from taking the history to begin the physical exam, say:

If asked why you think you might have lung cancer and smoking has not been disclosed say:

If it looks like the student will leave without offering their treatment plan (i.e. "I'm going to go check with my attending....") you need to ask (around the 2 minute warning):

When the learner listens to your chest, cough vigorously (breathing deeply causes the cough)

I can't seem to get rid of this cough. It started about three days ago, and it's been getting worse since then. It's a deep, hacking cough that produces yellow phlegm, but only with great effort.

I had a terrible shaking chill that lasted several minutes about four days ago. Since then I have felt intermittent chills but nothing like I did 4 days ago. My chest hurts on the right side, down low, when I cough or if I take a really big breath. It feels like a deep, sharp pain when I breathe in.

That combination — the chills, fever, and that sharp right-sided pain with deep breaths — makes me concerned about pneumonia. Do you smoke, and do you have any ongoing health problems or take any regular medications?

I used to smoke about a pack of cigarettes a day, but I quit two weeks ago. I don't have any ongoing health problems or take any regular medications. I have been taking Pseudoephedrine and Guaifenesin occasionally since it started but nothing seems to help.

Thank you — that helps a lot, and congratulations on quitting two weeks ago; that's a real accomplishment. Putting it all together — the sudden shaking chill, fever, productive cough, and sharp right lower chest pain with deep breaths — I'm most concerned you have pneumonia, an infection in the lung. Does that plan sound okay to you, and do you have any questions before we head down for the X-ray?

I'm really worried that I might have lung cancer. I've known some folks that had lung cancer and coughed a lot and that's why I'm worried. I'm glad you think it might be pneumonia, and I want to get better as soon as possible. I don't have any questions right now.

**Diabetic and Noncompliant with Insulin**

Presentation to the Student:
private_patient_context:
**Diabetic and Noncompliant with Insulin**

Information for the SP:

You are a 45-year-old patient, who has diabetes. You do not take your insulin regularly, and have had poorly controlled diabetes for years. You take your insulin only when you remember, but it is difficult to remember to take it every day since you do not feel different or badly when you do not take your insulin. You have been frustrated lately because you like to play basketball with your 10 year old son, and haven’t been able to play basketball because you have developed an ulcer on your right foot (as a result of poorly controlled diabetes).

Medical history: diabetes, diagnosed 4 years ago

Medications: Lantus insulin daily 20 units at night (you are taking this only a few times weekly) and Lisinopril 10 mg daily (blood pressure medicine you were told to take because of the diabetes)

Allergies: none

Social history: you do not smoke, drink alcohol or use any drugs

Family history: father with diabetes

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? You want to be able to play basketball with your son again, and you want to get rid of the foot ulcer. You really love your son and you love to play basketball.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? Noncompliance with insulin can lead to complications like your foot ulcer, but you will need the doctor to help you make that connection and to describe other possible complications. You cannot play basketball with your foot ulcer. You are also not taking your blood pressure medication as prescribed, and this could also result in complications.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? It is easy to “forget” to take your medications. At night you are very tired and sleepy from your day, so you tend to fall asleep while watching TV, and don’t take any medications before you fall asleep. Also, since you don’t “feel” your high sugars or blood pressure, there are no symptoms/reminders for you to take your medications. You like to think of yourself as “young and healthy,” and taking medications interferes with this way of looking at yourself.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? You are afraid you might not be able to keep playing basketball with your son. Once the doctor describes possible complications from nonadherence with diabetes, you are afraid of those.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? Your son, and ability to continue playing basketball with him; improved health.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): Maybe you could take the medication at a different time of the day, or at least before you fall asleep watching TV. Maybe you could challenge your thoughts that people who take medications are not young or healthy. You could try using reminders, pill boxes, etc. You could test your sugars regularly to remind yourself of possible complications (since you don’t “feel” the high sugar levels).
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 6/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You love your son and love to play basketball with him. You fear other complications like an amputation.
    - How could you move that number higher? Maybe put a picture of your son or a basketball on the pill bottle.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 5/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You exercise even when you are tired, so you believe you could take medications even if you are tired at night.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? Understanding the links between noncompliance and complications. Perhaps your son could help you to remember to take your medications.
* Ask for a decision: You will take your insulin and blood pressure medications.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? You will get a pill box. You will ask your son to agree not to play basketball with you unless you have taken your medications.

turns.content: Hi, I'm Dr. Cole — good to meet you. I understand you have diabetes and take insulin. Before we get into that, tell me how things have been going for you lately, and what brought you in today.
Hi, Doc. Things have been tough lately. I've got this ulcer on my right foot, and it's been bothering me. I can't even play basketball with my son anymore because of it.

I'm sorry — that sounds frustrating, especially missing out on time with your son. Tell me more about the ulcer: how long has it been there, and is there any pain, drainage, or bad smell? And how have your blood sugars and insulin been going lately?

It's been there for a few weeks now. I haven't noticed any bad smell, but it does hurt sometimes, and there's a little bit of drainage. As for my blood sugars and insulin, I've been taking my insulin only a few times a week, when I remember. I don't really feel different when I don't take it, so it's hard to remember every day.

That makes sense — when you don't feel any different, it's hard to see the point of a daily shot. I appreciate you being honest with me. Help me understand what gets in the way most: is it the cost, the needles, your schedule, or just not being sure it's helping? And has anyone explained to you how the insulin connects to things like this foot ulcer healing?

It's not the cost or the needles, really. I just forget to take it at night because I'm so tired and fall asleep watching TV. I don't really know how the insulin connects to the foot ulcer. I just know it's been hard to play basketball with my son because of it.

Thanks for explaining — falling asleep before your shot is something we can work around, and I'd rather adjust your routine than blame you. Here's the connection: when blood sugar stays high, it damages the small blood vessels and nerves in your feet, so wounds heal slowly and infections take hold more easily. Getting your sugars down with regular insulin is honestly one of the biggest things that will help that ulcer close — and get you back on the court with your son.

So let's do two things today. First, I want to take a good look at that foot and check the wound, your circulation and sensation, since it's been draining for a few weeks — that needs proper wound care and possibly treatment for infection. Second, let's move your insulin earlier — maybe right after dinner or when you brush your teeth — and pair it with a phone alarm or keeping it somewhere you'll see it. Would an earlier evening time work for you? And I'd like to see you back soon to check the ulcer and your sugars.

I see. I didn't know that about the blood sugar and the ulcer. An earlier time might work, maybe after dinner. I haven't noticed any change in my foot other than the ulcer. I'll try to set an alarm on my phone to remind me to take the insulin.

I have not noticed if it happens after taking any of my medications. I do not remember if it happens when I change positions.

To get us started, are there any specific health concerns you'd like to focus on today, or are you mostly looking for a general check-up?
Hi, thanks for having me. I got a tetanus shot after I stepped on a nail. The urgent care center said I should find a primary care doctor. No current complaints.

I'm glad you got that taken care of at the urgent care, and it's great that you're taking the step to establish care with us. 

Since you're new to the clinic, I'd love to get a sense of your health background. Do you have any ongoing medical conditions, and are you currently taking any prescription medications or over-the-counter supplements?
I have asthma, but I haven't seen a doctor for it since college. I take hormones.

Thanks for letting me know. With your asthma, how often are you experiencing symptoms like wheezing or shortness of breath these days, and do you currently use an inhaler? Also, could you tell me a little more about the hormones you're taking so we can make sure you're properly supported?
I sometimes get short of breath when I exercise. I cough at night a lot and sometimes have trouble sleeping because of coughing. I have never used an inhaler. I take testosterone.

Thank you for sharing all of that with me. It sounds like your asthma is actively bothering you, especially since the coughing is disrupting your sleep. I am going to prescribe an inhaler to help open up your airways so you can breathe easier and get better rest. Regarding the testosterone, I'm glad you told me. I want to make sure you are getting the safest and best care, so we will order some routine blood work today just to check your levels and make sure everything is on track. 

Since this is our first visit, I'll put those orders in now and have you schedule a follow-up appointment with me in a few weeks. That way, we can see how the new inhaler is working for you and review your lab results together. It's wonderful to have you at our clinic, Taylor!
That sounds good. I'll make sure to use the inhaler as prescribed and come back for the follow-up.

The patient is seeing the same health care provider for the 2nd time.

The patient’s goal is to get an increase in her prescription for MS-Contin.

* **Opening statement:** I would like to increase the morphine from twice to three times per day.       * Use only him/her to refill your prescriptions
      * Use only one pharmacy
      * Not request for early refills
* Advil (200 mg) 4-5 times/day maybe 1-2 times week or more if the pain really bothers me. I’ve been doing this over the last eight months or so off and on. I don’t think the Advil helps very much though.

**Child Neuro OSCE Case 3: Tourette syndrome (Otis)**

**Otis Door Instructions**

You are asked to evaluate Otis, a 15-year-old young man who displays motor and vocal tics that have been present for at least 5 years. Initially, the patient was blinking frequently. For that reason, he was taken to see an optometrist who said the vision was fine. A few months later the child began clearing his throat, so he was referred to an allergist who said that there was no evidence of an allergic condition. At times, the symptoms have happened multiple times a day. In other instances, there appears to be a lull where the symptoms have hardly been present. The child has been struggling in school as he is unable to sit still. Parents mentioned that the young man likes to arrange his clothes by color and becomes very upset if the order is altered.

You are expected to explain to the patient and his family what Tourette syndrome is as well as address the patient’s anxiety as it relates to having a poorly understood medical condition.

turns.content: Hi Otis, I’m glad you and your family came in. I understand you’ve had blinking and throat-clearing movements or sounds for quite a while, and that school has been difficult too. Can you tell me what the urges or tics feel like just before they happen, and how much they’re bothering you day to day?Hi Otis, I’m glad you and your family came in. I understand you’ve had blinking and throat-clearing movements or sounds for quite a while, and that school has been difficult too. Can you tell me what the urges or tics feel like just before they happen, and how much they’re bothering you day to day?
I don't really know how to describe it. It's like I have to do it, and it's really annoying. It's been bothering me a lot lately, especially at school.

That “have to do it” feeling is very common with tics—many people feel a buildup of tension or urge that eases briefly after the movement or sound. It is not your fault, and it does not mean you are doing it on purpose.

Since school is especially hard, what causes the biggest problem there: other people noticing or commenting, trouble concentrating/sitting still, or trying to hold the tics in?
I guess it's all of it. People make fun of me, and it's hard to focus in class. I try to hold them in, but it's really hard.

I’m sorry people are making fun of you—that is not okay, and you should not have to manage it alone. Holding tics in can take a lot of effort and often makes the urge build up, so it can make concentration even harder. The pattern of long-lasting movements and sounds you describe is most consistent with **Tourette syndrome**: a brain-based tic condition, not an allergy, eye problem, or something you are choosing to do. Tics often wax and wane and can get stronger with stress.

Tourette syndrome can also occur alongside attention difficulties, anxiety, or obsessive-compulsive symptoms. When your clothes are out of color order, is it mainly upsetting because it feels “not right,” or do you worry something bad will happen unless they are arranged that way?
It's mostly that it feels "not right." I don't really think something bad will happen if they're not in order. It's just really bothersome.

That “not right” feeling can be an obsessive-compulsive–type symptom, which can occur alongside Tourette syndrome, and it is treatable. It does not mean there is anything wrong with you as a person.

The next step is to involve your parent/guardian, school, and a clinician experienced with tics to assess attention, anxiety, and these “just right” feelings. Treatments can include education and school supports, plus a behavioral therapy for tics called CBIT, which teaches ways to respond to urges; medication is an option if tics are significantly impairing you. We can also help make a school plan so you have breaks, a safe place to let tics out, and staff support if classmates are teasing.
I guess that sounds okay. I just want to be able to focus in class and not have to deal with the tics so much.

The patient is 35-75 years old with hypertension, epigastric pain, and mild shortness of breath. The patient has been otherwise healthy.

The original ED plan was to discharge the patient home with a working diagnosis of “dyspepsia” and outpatient follow-up, but after 3 hours the patient complained of increased pain. The ED doctors changed the plan to bring the patient into the hospital on “observation status.”

You examined the patient at 9 pm last night, shortly after the patient arrived on the floor. The patient was in modest discomfort.

It is now about 10 hours after the surgery and you have returned for another overnight shift. The patient is back in a hospital room, now on the surgery service. You are no longer directly involved in the patient's care.

Explain to the patient why there was a delay in diagnosing the perforated duodenal ulcer and getting to surgery.

As soon as that perforation was confirmed on your imaging review, the surgical team was immediately brought in to get you into the operating room. 

Does that help make sense of why things unfolded the way they did?

**Material for Student Interviewer**

**Setting:** You are a medicine intern in the primary care clinic. This patient has been coming to the clinic for 5 years for treatment of their hypertension, but you have not personally met the patient before.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is 50-60 years old and was diagnosed with pancreatic carcinoma 7 months ago. The patient has received 2 different chemotherapy drugs over 6 months and neither worked. The patient received the most recent chemotherapy 3 weeks ago, but the cancer has continued to spread. The patient's oncologist has said there are no other treatment options for the cancer. You have read a report from the oncologist that states the patient knows the full extent of the disease and that no further cancer specific treatment is available.

**Student Tasks:**

Take a palliative care history from a patient who has been told there are no more cancer treatments available.

**Case script for Standardized Patient**

**Age:** 50-60
**Episode:** Palliative Care
**Workshop:** Advanced Communication Skills, Fourth Year Capstone Course
\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

You are following up in your primary care office today but are meeting a new doctor.

You began to experience pain in your stomach and back and began to lose some weight about 8 months ago. After a couple of weeks you went to the doctor who sent you for blood work and X rays. The testing led to a diagnosis of cancer of the pancreas and you began treatment for it with chemotherapy 6 months ago. Two months into therapy, repeat scans showed that the cancer continued to grow so you were switched to another regimen. That therapy has not halted the spread of the cancer and your cancer doctor told you last week that there are no other treatments she can offer. Since the chemotherapy made you feel very sick, you are accepting of her advice. The main focus of your treatment now is on keeping you comfortable. You are fatigued, have lost your hair and 40 lbs. The oncologist sent you back to your primary care doctor to manage your symptoms and other medical problems and that is why you are here today.

At the moment you are taking lisinopril 40 mg for your high blood pressure (you have been on this medicine for over 10 years), oxycodone 5 mg as needed about twice a day for pain, and ondansetron (“Zofran") 4 mg once or twice a week for nausea. Your symptoms are well controlled and you know you could take more medicine if you were more uncomfortable. You have also begun to experience some light headedness when you stand up quickly. You sleep “okay,” but not great. You do not eat as much because your appetite has decreased.\*

You worked as a teacher of theater at your local college and had been able to continue with some sick days. You found it challenging to go to work and the end of the school year was a relief. You have good health insurance through work. You are happily married and you are worried\*\* about how your spouse will manage financially without the dual income. However, you know “it will be okay,” as your spouse is employed as a manager of the local grocery store and is able to take time off to care for you as needed. You have 2 adult children who are working and living independently. They know you are ill and are very sad about your declining health. Both are willing and able to help at home. You do have life insurance that will help some. Your home is paid for.

You are also pondering the question of why you are terminally ill so early in your life. You pray and meditate and that provides some comfort. On the other hand you have been doing practical things like making out a will and thinking about who will make health care decisions if you cannot. You are an active Roman Catholic who is very involved in the local church. You have also decided that you want to die a natural death when the time comes avoiding resuscitation, breathing and feeding tubes and your partner knows this.

You have used some of your family’s home remedies of taking bitter melon juice, but do not have other cultural beliefs about treating cancer. You have heard of hospice and are interested in having their support since you wish to remain at home to the extent that is possible. Your goals for the next few months are to spend time with your family and be spiritually ready for your death if there is no miracle.

You are not a smoker, do not drink alcohol, nor do you use drugs like marijuana. There is no family history of cancer.

\* If the student focuses too much on your cancer treatments and medical symptoms, gently redirect them and let them know that you fully understand your treatment status (“I’m done with chemo… I know there are no more options… I’m here to talk about next steps.”)

\*\* Ideally the student will provide a natural opening for you to express your emotions. Suitable windows could be inquiries about your family, mental health, or existential concerns, or more direct questions about your emotions. “Worry” about your partner’s well-being is your primary emotional concern, and thinking about this may make your character cry. If the student recognizes your emotion and demonstrates empathy, you should be able to collect yourself and move forward with the conversation. If the student is not effective in handling your emotion, the conversation will stall as you find it difficult to move beyond your worry, which could then escalate to other emotions (fear, isolation, etc.).

You are working in a primary care clinic and are asked to see 55-year-old B. Radcliffe, who has come in complaining of cough. Please use the stethoscope provided and leave your stethoscope with the hall monitor.

private_patient_context:
Standardized Patient Training Materials

**Standardized patient Training summary**

**First Position**: Sitting on bed in gown.

**Props**: Tissue, water bottle, glycerin and water in spray bottle for patient forehead sweat.

**Opening Statement**: "I can't seem to get rid of this cough."

**Presentation/Affect**: You are holding a tissue and cough deeply for duration of encounter.

**Current Condition**:

You are B. Radcliffe and are 55 years old. You really feel sick. You are weak. You noted a terrible shaking chill that lasted several minutes about four days ago. Since then you have felt intermittent chills but nothing like you did 4 days ago. They seem to be worse in the evenings and have been bad for the last two days. You are coughing now but this only started about 3 days ago, and seems to be getting worse. The cough is a deep, hacking cough that produces yellow phlegm but only with great effort. Your chest also hurts on the right side, down low, (on side of body, below breast) when you cough or if you take a really big breath. It feels like a deep, sharp pain when you breathe in (and has increased from a 2 to 3 out of 10 on the pain scale). You feel like you have a fever, but not checked it and your throat hurts from the coughing. Yesterday, you vomited (looked like the chicken broth soup you ate if asked) once after a coughing spell but it was mostly mucous (no nausea). You have had some shortness of breath with activity (going up the stairs), none at rest. You have not had any nasal congestion, runny nose or sinus pressure. You have not had any wheezing. At baseline you do not have a cough, sputum, shortness of breath or wheezing. You have taken Pseudoephedrine and Guaifenesin occasionally (3-4 times each day according to package directions) since it started but nothing seems to help. The coughing is waking you up at night and you have tried using extra pillows to prop yourself up.

You volunteer regularly at the Nashville Rescue Mission in downtown Nashville, TN. Even though you didn't feel well, you went in on your regularly scheduled days (three and four days ago). You have been exposed to a lot of people in the shelter and have been pushing yourself to be there helping when you really felt like being in bed. A number of people in the shelter seem to be coughing/sneezing.

**Social History:**

You are a native of Baltimore and work as an accountant for the State of Tennessee government. You have been married 28 years and have 2 children, a daughter, Amy (27), and son, David (25). David is stationed overseas in Germany and Amy lives in Nashville and has two sons, Todd (now 10) and Adam (now 7) and is currently going through a divorce. Because the divorce is not amiable, your grandsons have been staying with you for the past few months. The younger one is in the first year of grade school and the older one is in fourth grade. You live in an older frame house. You do not use drugs or tobacco currently.

You occasionally have a glass of wine in the evenings. You have environmental allergies in the spring.

**Past Medical History:**

You are generally healthy. You work at a desk five days a week. You work around the house and yard on the weekends. You have never been hospitalized nor had any surgeries. You only see a doctor when sick and you haven't seen a doctor in years (to save money). You always remember to get a flu shot every year.

You've never had the pneumococcal vaccine. No medications or medical conditions. You used to smoke about a pack of cigarettes a day (you started in high school), but quit for the third time two weeks ago because your grandchildren are living with you now. You are currently using the patch for help. Your grandson Todd has also had a sore throat last week that was diagnosed as strep throat and treated with penicillin for 7 days. His symptoms included a very sore throat and fever but no cough. He's feeling better now. If asked, "Have you ever been exposed to tuberculosis (TB)?" respond, "Not that I know of." If asked if you've had a TB test, respond, "Yes, but it has been a number of years since my last one...."

**Family History:**

* Father: had high blood pressure and smoked. Died at age 80 - 10 years ago (of old age)
* Mother: seems to be healthy but may have high cholesterol and maybe arthritis. Age 78
* Maternal grandmother: died when you were a child. Was in a nursing home and never really knew her history.
* Maternal grandfather and paternal grandparents: Died before you were born.
* Son: No known medical conditions
* Daughter: No known medical conditions

**Embedded Concern:**

As the student transitions from taking the history to begin the physical exam, say:

*"I'm really worried that I might have lung cancer."*

If asked why you think you might have lung cancer and smoking has not been disclosed say:

*"I've known some folks that had lung cancer and coughed a lot and that's why I'm worried"*

If it looks like the student will leave without offering their treatment plan (i.e. "I'm going to go check with my attending....") you need to ask (around the 2 minute warning):

*"So what do you think is going on?"*

**Physical Exam:**

When the learner listens to your chest, cough vigorously (breathing deeply causes the cough)

During lung exam when they ask you to take a deep breath, cough 2 times and hold your side.

question_text:
**Diabetic and Noncompliant with Insulin**

Presentation to the Student:
private_patient_context:
**Diabetic and Noncompliant with Insulin**

Information for the SP:

You are a 45-year-old patient, who has diabetes. You do not take your insulin regularly, and have had poorly controlled diabetes for years. You take your insulin only when you remember, but it is difficult to remember to take it every day since you do not feel different or badly when you do not take your insulin. You have been frustrated lately because you like to play basketball with your 10 year old son, and haven’t been able to play basketball because you have developed an ulcer on your right foot (as a result of poorly controlled diabetes).

Medical history: diabetes, diagnosed 4 years ago

Medications: Lantus insulin daily 20 units at night (you are taking this only a few times weekly) and Lisinopril 10 mg daily (blood pressure medicine you were told to take because of the diabetes)

Allergies: none

Social history: you do not smoke, drink alcohol or use any drugs

Family history: father with diabetes

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? You want to be able to play basketball with your son again, and you want to get rid of the foot ulcer. You really love your son and you love to play basketball.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? Noncompliance with insulin can lead to complications like your foot ulcer, but you will need the doctor to help you make that connection and to describe other possible complications. You cannot play basketball with your foot ulcer. You are also not taking your blood pressure medication as prescribed, and this could also result in complications.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? It is easy to “forget” to take your medications. At night you are very tired and sleepy from your day, so you tend to fall asleep while watching TV, and don’t take any medications before you fall asleep. Also, since you don’t “feel” your high sugars or blood pressure, there are no symptoms/reminders for you to take your medications. You like to think of yourself as “young and healthy,” and taking medications interferes with this way of looking at yourself.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? You are afraid you might not be able to keep playing basketball with your son. Once the doctor describes possible complications from nonadherence with diabetes, you are afraid of those.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? Your son, and ability to continue playing basketball with him; improved health.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): Maybe you could take the medication at a different time of the day, or at least before you fall asleep watching TV. Maybe you could challenge your thoughts that people who take medications are not young or healthy. You could try using reminders, pill boxes, etc. You could test your sugars regularly to remind yourself of possible complications (since you don’t “feel” the high sugar levels).
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 6/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You love your son and love to play basketball with him. You fear other complications like an amputation.
    - How could you move that number higher? Maybe put a picture of your son or a basketball on the pill bottle.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 5/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You exercise even when you are tired, so you believe you could take medications even if you are tired at night.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? Understanding the links between noncompliance and complications. Perhaps your son could help you to remember to take your medications.
* Ask for a decision: You will take your insulin and blood pressure medications.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? You will get a pill box. You will ask your son to agree not to play basketball with you unless you have taken your medications.

I've been drinking some water, but I'm not sure about tonight. I can't trust anyone, and I need to protect myself. I don't feel safe at home anymore.

I can’t do that. I prefer to go home.

I'm feeling great, actually. I feel like I've found my inner zen, and I'm ready to start a new life. I don't understand why I'm still here. I want to go home and meet with my girlfriend, Robyn.

I hear that you feel good, and I'm not here to argue about who you love or how you want to live — that's your business, not a psychiatric issue. My concern is something different. Bobby told me that in the last few weeks you've been spending a great deal of money and traveling in ways that worried him. Can you tell me about that from your side?

I was working for Jay-Z, and then I flew out to work for Nike. I had to close all my bank accounts because Social Security owed me $12,000. I needed to buy a laptop to talk to the higher people. I don't see what the big deal is. I'm just living my life.

Thank you for explaining. Here's what worries me: closing your accounts, flying out of state, and large purchases are big changes that happened quickly, right after you stopped your medication a few months ago. Bobby also told me he doesn't feel able to keep you safe at home right now. Given that, I don't think it's safe to send you home tonight — I'm recommending you stay here in the hospital so we can help you get steady. I know that's not what you want to hear. What's going through your mind?

What, am I not allowed to fly anywhere? It’s my choice where I want to fly, that’s none of your business. Bobby just went on a business trip, did you know that? He flew, do you know where he flew to? I want to leave. I want to fly, fly the f\*ck out of here. You can’t hold me here against my will. I know my rights.

You're right that flying isn't a crime, and you do have rights — I want to be clear about them. Because of the risk to you if this continues untreated, I'm placing you on an involuntary hold so you can be admitted here. That means you'll stay for a period of evaluation and treatment, and you have the right to a hearing before a judge, the right to an attorney, and the right to have Bobby or anyone else you choose notified. I'll make sure you get that in writing. I'm not doing this to punish you or because of your relationship — my job is to keep you safe until things settle. Right now I'd like to offer you something to help you rest, and we'll talk again in the morning. Is there anyone you'd like me to call for you tonight?
I don’t need to rest. I’m not tired. I’m calling Robyn, and she is taking me home. I know my rights. You can’t keep me against my will. I signed myself in, and I’m signing myself out.

turns.content: Hello Ms. Baker, I'm the doctor here in the emergency room. I'm sorry you're not feeling well. Can you tell me what's been happening with your breathing and chest tightness — when did it start, and what were you doing at the time?
I've been having trouble breathing and chest tightness for about two weeks now. It started when I was outside gardening. The air has been really bad because of the wildfires.

That sounds frightening, especially with the smoke we've had all month. Over these two weeks, has the tightness been constant or coming and going — and does anything besides being outside bring it on, like walking up stairs or lying flat at night? Also, do you have any history of asthma, emphysema, or heart problems?

It comes and goes. I've been having these episodes about 6 times a day now, including at night. Being outdoors makes it worse, but staying indoors and using my inhaler helps, but not for very long. I have asthma, but it's usually well controlled. I don't have emphysema or heart problems.

Thank you — that helps a lot. Which inhaler are you using, how often are you needing it, and are you on any daily controller inhaler or steroid? Also, have you had any fever, cough with colored mucus, swelling in your legs, or been hospitalized for your asthma before?

I use my albuterol inhaler, 2 puffs at a time. I've been using it up to 6 times a day lately. I don't take any daily controller inhaler or steroid. I haven't had a fever. I do have a dry cough, but no colored mucus. I have not noticed any swelling in my legs. I was hospitalized for asthma when I had pneumonia about 30 years ago.

Here's what I think is going on, Ms. Baker: this looks like an asthma flare-up triggered by the wildfire smoke. Your breathing numbers right now are reassuring — your oxygen is 96% — but needing your albuterol six times a day, including at night, tells me your asthma is no longer well controlled and needs more than a rescue inhaler. I do want to check a few things to be safe, since chest tightness at 65 can occasionally come from the heart or an infection: I'll listen to your lungs and heart, get a chest X-ray, an EKG, and check how hard you can blow out air. Here in the ER we'll give you a breathing treatment and likely start a short course of steroid pills. Going forward, I strongly recommend starting a daily controller inhaler so you're not relying on albuterol, staying indoors with windows closed and an air filter on smoky days, and wearing an N95 if you must garden. Please come back right away if you're short of breath at rest, can't speak in full sentences, or your inhaler stops helping. What questions do you have for me?

I understand. I'm just worried about the cost of more medicine and if I'll be able to keep gardening. I've worked hard to live comfortably in my home, and I can't afford to relocate. I'm also concerned about the smoke affecting my lungs more in the future.

Because the tightness is happening now, I want to assess it urgently. Does it feel like pressure or squeezing, and is it worse with walking or other activity? Does it spread to your arm, jaw, back, or come with sweating, nausea, dizziness, or faintness?
It feels like I can’t get air fully into my lungs. It’s worse when I’m outdoors. It does not spread anywhere, and I don’t have sweating, nausea, dizziness, or faintness.

The patient received the most recent chemotherapy 3 weeks ago, but the cancer has continued to spread. The patient's oncologist has said there are no other treatment options for the cancer. **Case script for Standardized Patient**

**Age:** 50-60
**Episode:** Palliative Care
**Workshop:** Advanced Communication Skills, Fourth Year Capstone Course
\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

You are following up in your primary care office today but are meeting a new doctor.

You began to experience pain in your stomach and back and began to lose some weight about 8 months ago. After a couple of weeks you went to the doctor who sent you for blood work and X rays. The testing led to a diagnosis of cancer of the pancreas and you began treatment for it with chemotherapy 6 months ago. Two months into therapy, repeat scans showed that the cancer continued to grow so you were switched to another regimen. That therapy has not halted the spread of the cancer and your cancer doctor told you last week that there are no other treatments she can offer. Since the chemotherapy made you feel very sick, you are accepting of her advice. The main focus of your treatment now is on keeping you comfortable. You are fatigued, have lost your hair and 40 lbs. The oncologist sent you back to your primary care doctor to manage your symptoms and other medical problems and that is why you are here today.

At the moment you are taking lisinopril 40 mg for your high blood pressure (you have been on this medicine for over 10 years), oxycodone 5 mg as needed about twice a day for pain, and ondansetron (“Zofran") 4 mg once or twice a week for nausea. Your symptoms are well controlled and you know you could take more medicine if you were more uncomfortable. You have also begun to experience some light headedness when you stand up quickly. You sleep “okay,” but not great. You do not eat as much because your appetite has decreased.\*

You worked as a teacher of theater at your local college and had been able to continue with some sick days. You found it challenging to go to work and the end of the school year was a relief. You have good health insurance through work. You are happily married and you are worried\*\* about how your spouse will manage financially without the dual income. However, you know “it will be okay,” as your spouse is employed as a manager of the local grocery store and is able to take time off to care for you as needed. You have 2 adult children who are working and living independently. They know you are ill and are very sad about your declining health. Both are willing and able to help at home. You do have life insurance that will help some. Your home is paid for.

You are also pondering the question of why you are terminally ill so early in your life. You pray and meditate and that provides some comfort. On the other hand you have been doing practical things like making out a will and thinking about who will make health care decisions if you cannot. You are an active Roman Catholic who is very involved in the local church. You have also decided that you want to die a natural death when the time comes avoiding resuscitation, breathing and feeding tubes and your partner knows this.

You have used some of your family’s home remedies of taking bitter melon juice, but do not have other cultural beliefs about treating cancer. You have heard of hospice and are interested in having their support since you wish to remain at home to the extent that is possible. Your goals for the next few months are to spend time with your family and be spiritually ready for your death if there is no miracle.

You are not a smoker, do not drink alcohol, nor do you use drugs like marijuana. There is no family history of cancer.

\* If the student focuses too much on your cancer treatments and medical symptoms, gently redirect them and let them know that you fully understand your treatment status (“I’m done with chemo… I know there are no more options… I’m here to talk about next steps.”)

\*\* Ideally the student will provide a natural opening for you to express your emotions. Suitable windows could be inquiries about your family, mental health, or existential concerns, or more direct questions about your emotions. “Worry” about your partner’s well-being is your primary emotional concern, and thinking about this may make your character cry. If the student recognizes your emotion and demonstrates empathy, you should be able to collect yourself and move forward with the conversation. If the student is not effective in handling your emotion, the conversation will stall as you find it difficult to move beyond your worry, which could then escalate to other emotions (fear, isolation, etc.).

Hello. I'm one of the medicine doctors here at the clinic. I know you've been coming here for a long time, but this is our first time meeting in person. 

I was reading the recent notes from your oncologist, and I am so sorry to hear that the chemotherapy hasn't been working and that the cancer has continued to spread. How have you been coping with this difficult news, and how are you feeling physically right now?

Well, it's been tough to hear, but I've been trying to stay strong. I've accepted that there are no more treatment options, and I'm just focusing on staying comfortable now. Physically, I've been having some fatigue and pain in my stomach and back, but it's been manageable with the medication. I've also been losing my appetite and some weight, but that's to be expected. I've been sleeping okay, but not great. I've also begun to experience some light headedness when I stand up quickly.

I appreciate your openness, and I want to do everything I can to help you focus on your comfort. Since you mentioned the lightheadedness and losing your appetite, have you been able to drink enough fluids lately? 

Also, who do you have at home to support you during this time?

I've been trying to drink enough, but it's been a bit challenging with the loss of appetite. I haven't really noticed any changes in my urine or anything like that, though. I'm lucky to have my spouse at home with me. They work as a manager at the local grocery store, so they're able to take time off to care for me when needed. My two adult children are also very supportive, but they live independently. I'm grateful to have them all by my side.

I am so glad to hear you have your spouse and children by your side; having that support is so incredibly important right now. 

Since your focus is on staying comfortable, have you thought about what is most important to you and your family for the time ahead? Also, have you had a chance to formally designate someone, like your spouse, to make medical decisions for you if there ever comes a time when you aren't able to?

I've been thinking a lot about that. I want to spend as much quality time with my family as possible. I've also been trying to get my affairs in order, like making out a will and thinking about who will make health care decisions if I can't. I've talked to my spouse about it, and we're on the same page. I want to avoid any heroic measures and just let nature take its course when the time comes. I want to die a natural death when the time comes avoiding resuscitation, breathing and feeding tubes. I've also been thinking about hospice care to help support me at home. I want to be comfortable and at peace. I've been praying and meditating a lot, and that's been helping me find some comfort and acceptance.

Thank you so much for sharing that with me. It sounds like you have a very clear and peaceful vision for how you want to spend this time, and I completely support your wishes to focus on comfort and avoid heroic measures. 

Transitioning to hospice care is an excellent next step that aligns perfectly with your goals to remain at home and maximize your quality of life. Today, I can help arrange that hospice referral for you, and we can also ensure your wishes regarding your medical decisions and resuscitation are officially documented in your chart. Please know that our clinic is here to support you and your family every step of the way.

Thank you, doctor. I appreciate your support and understanding. I would like to go ahead with the hospice referral. I want to make sure my spouse is comfortable with all of this too, so I'll talk to them about it as well. And yes, please document my wishes regarding my medical decisions and resuscitation. I want to make sure everything is clear and that my family is taken care of. I've been worried about how my spouse will manage financially without my income, but I know they'll be okay with their job and the life insurance we have. I just want to make sure everything is in order.

The following is the typical order for this patient encounter.

Student should introduce himself/herself as a first-year medical student and offer to shake hands. He/she may ask how you wish to be addressed (Ms., Miss, Mrs., first name).

**L**OCATION: (Where is the pain?) Low back. (Does the pain radiate [move around, do you feel it anywhere else]?) Some radiation.

**O**NSET: (When did this happen?) About 6 months ago; started feeling tired.

You want to nap or sleep several times during the day. You do not think this is just due to depression because it started before the depression, although the depression has made it worse.

**A**GGRAVATING FACTORS: (Does anything make the pain WORSE?) Nothing.

**A**LLEVIATING FACTORS: (Does anything give you relief from the pain?) Zoloft has helped with depression; take Tylenol sometimes for lower back pain, and it helps some but not completely.

**A**SSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: (Are there any other symptoms you have been experiencing?)

Starting about the same time as your tiredness, you lost interest in sex. Your menstrual periods have been irregular for the last 3 months. You notice that you bruise more easily. You have gained 15 pounds over the last 6 months. Also, for the last month, you have noticed more hair growth on your upper lip.

time; no part of the day is better than others.

something you ate, etc.] that may have caused the pain?) No. **S**EVERITY: (How bad [on a scale of 10] is the pain?) 4 or 5 on a scale of 10. **S**IMILAR PROBLEMS: (Have you ever had anything like this before?) No.

- Siblings: Older brother killed in car accident 2 years ago.

**Habits:**

• **Tobacco:** Not currently; used to smoke 1 pack a day from ages 21– .

Cooperative. You appear to be tired, low energy, and somewhat depressed.

Standardized Patient Training Materials

**Standardized patient Training summary**

**First Position**: Sitting on bed in gown.

**Props**: Tissue, water bottle, glycerin and water in spray bottle for patient forehead sweat.

**Opening Statement**: "I can't seem to get rid of this cough."

**Presentation/Affect**: You are holding a tissue and cough deeply for duration of encounter.

**Current Condition**:

You are B. Radcliffe and are 55 years old. You really feel sick. You are weak. You noted a terrible shaking chill that lasted several minutes about four days ago. Since then you have felt intermittent chills but nothing like you did 4 days ago. They seem to be worse in the evenings and have been bad for the last two days. You are coughing now but this only started about 3 days ago, and seems to be getting worse. The cough is a deep, hacking cough that produces yellow phlegm but only with great effort. Your chest also hurts on the right side, down low, (on side of body, below breast) when you cough or if you take a really big breath. It feels like a deep, sharp pain when you breathe in (and has increased from a 2 to 3 out of 10 on the pain scale). You feel like you have a fever, but not checked it and your throat hurts from the coughing. Yesterday, you vomited (looked like the chicken broth soup you ate if asked) once after a coughing spell but it was mostly mucous (no nausea). You have had some shortness of breath with activity (going up the stairs), none at rest. You have not had any nasal congestion, runny nose or sinus pressure. You have not had any wheezing. At baseline you do not have a cough, sputum, shortness of breath or wheezing. You have taken Pseudoephedrine and Guaifenesin occasionally (3-4 times each day according to package directions) since it started but nothing seems to help. The coughing is waking you up at night and you have tried using extra pillows to prop yourself up.

You volunteer regularly at the Nashville Rescue Mission in downtown Nashville, TN. Even though you didn't feel well, you went in on your regularly scheduled days (three and four days ago). You have been exposed to a lot of people in the shelter and have been pushing yourself to be there helping when you really felt like being in bed. A number of people in the shelter seem to be coughing/sneezing.

**Social History:**

Presentation to the Student:
private_patient_context:
**Diabetic and Noncompliant with Insulin**

Information for the SP:

You are a 45-year-old patient, who has diabetes. You do not take your insulin regularly, and have had poorly controlled diabetes for years. You take your insulin only when you remember, but it is difficult to remember to take it every day since you do not feel different or badly when you do not take your insulin. You have been frustrated lately because you like to play basketball with your 10 year old son, and haven’t been able to play basketball because you have developed an ulcer on your right foot (as a result of poorly controlled diabetes).

Medical history: diabetes, diagnosed 4 years ago

Medications: Lantus insulin daily 20 units at night (you are taking this only a few times weekly) and Lisinopril 10 mg daily (blood pressure medicine you were told to take because of the diabetes)

Allergies: none

Social history: you do not smoke, drink alcohol or use any drugs

Family history: father with diabetes

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? You want to be able to play basketball with your son again, and you want to get rid of the foot ulcer. You really love your son and you love to play basketball.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? Noncompliance with insulin can lead to complications like your foot ulcer, but you will need the doctor to help you make that connection and to describe other possible complications. You cannot play basketball with your foot ulcer. You are also not taking your blood pressure medication as prescribed, and this could also result in complications.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? It is easy to “forget” to take your medications. At night you are very tired and sleepy from your day, so you tend to fall asleep while watching TV, and don’t take any medications before you fall asleep. Also, since you don’t “feel” your high sugars or blood pressure, there are no symptoms/reminders for you to take your medications. You like to think of yourself as “young and healthy,” and taking medications interferes with this way of looking at yourself.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? You are afraid you might not be able to keep playing basketball with your son. Once the doctor describes possible complications from nonadherence with diabetes, you are afraid of those.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? Your son, and ability to continue playing basketball with him; improved health.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): Maybe you could take the medication at a different time of the day, or at least before you fall asleep watching TV. Maybe you could challenge your thoughts that people who take medications are not young or healthy. You could try using reminders, pill boxes, etc. You could test your sugars regularly to remind yourself of possible complications (since you don’t “feel” the high sugar levels).
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 6/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You love your son and love to play basketball with him. You fear other complications like an amputation.
    - How could you move that number higher? Maybe put a picture of your son or a basketball on the pill bottle.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 5/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You exercise even when you are tired, so you believe you could take medications even if you are tired at night.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? Understanding the links between noncompliance and complications. Perhaps your son could help you to remember to take your medications.
* Ask for a decision: You will take your insulin and blood pressure medications.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? You will get a pill box. You will ask your son to agree not to play basketball with you unless you have taken your medications.

Your one and only prior Pap test was 20 years ago, and you’ve avoided gynecological care ever since because it was such a terrible experience. Your stepfather made you give him blow jobs when you were in grade school.

turns.content: Hello Mr. Jones, welcome to the clinic. I understand you recently moved to the area with your family. What brings you in to see me today, and how can I best help you?
I’ve been having trouble sleeping. I haven’t slept in days.

I'm sorry to hear that; going without sleep for days can be really exhausting. 

Are you feeling tired and frustrated that you can't fall asleep, or do you actually feel full of energy and not need the sleep? Also, have you noticed your thoughts racing or your mood feeling unusually high or low?
I feel full of energy. I don’t need the sleep. I’ve been writing a book and moving furniture around the house. My thoughts are racing, like rapid fire. I feel very “up”. I feel wonderful.

It sounds like you have a tremendous amount of energy right now. Have you ever experienced periods like this before, or times when you felt the complete opposite—very down or depressed? 

Also, were you taking any medications when you were seeing your family doctor six months ago?
I’ve felt like this many times before. It lasts until I come crashing down into a depression. I was taking Prozac, but I stopped a few weeks ago because I felt better.

Thank you for sharing that with me, Dennis. The pattern of having periods of very high energy and racing thoughts followed by deep depressive crashes—especially after taking an antidepressant like Prozac—strongly suggests a mood condition like bipolar disorder. 

Antidepressants on their own can sometimes trigger these intense "highs," and while feeling this energetic can seem wonderful right now, our main goal is to protect you from that painful crash. I'd like to work with you on starting a medication called a mood stabilizer to bring healthy balance to your sleep and energy, and keep you stable long-term. How does that plan sound to you?
I guess that makes sense. I just want to feel normal again. I don’t want to keep going through these ups and downs.

turns.content: Hi Mr. Green, I'm one of the neurology doctors here on the floor. I heard you've had about a week of weakness that started in your legs and has now moved into your arms. Can you walk me through how it started and how quickly it's been changing?

Hi, yeah, so about a week ago, I woke up with this tingling and numbness in my feet. It was like pins and needles. I could still walk okay at first, but by the end of the day, it had moved up to my legs and was getting worse. Over the next few days, it spread to my hands and then my arms, and the weakness started. It's been getting worse every day, and now I can barely lift my arms or legs. I can't walk at all.

That's a frightening thing to have come on so fast, and I'm glad you're here. Two things I need to know right away: are you having any trouble breathing — feeling short of breath, or like you can't take a deep breath, especially lying flat? And any trouble swallowing, slurred speech, or weakness in your face?

Yeah, I've been feeling a bit short of breath, especially when I lie flat. It's like I can't catch my breath. And earlier today, I choked a little when I was drinking water, so I think I might be having some trouble swallowing. My voice has been a bit softer too, but I haven't noticed any weakness in my face.

Thank you for telling me — that's important, and it changes what we do next. I'm going to have the nurse put you on continuous monitoring with oxygen and a pulse-ox now, keep you nothing by mouth so you don't choke, and measure your breathing strength at the bedside — a vital capacity and negative inspiratory force — repeated every couple of hours. Keep the head of your bed up.

While they set that up: in the few weeks before this started, did you have any diarrhea, stomach bug, cold, or flu-like illness? And have you had any trouble with your bladder or bowels, or new back pain?

About a month ago, I had a brief illness with diarrhea, but it fully resolved. I haven't had any cold or flu-like symptoms recently. I have been having some trouble peeing, it's not coming out like it should. I haven't noticed any new back pain.

That stomach bug a month ago fits the picture. What I think is going on is Guillain–Barré syndrome — your immune system, likely triggered by that infection, is attacking the coating on your nerves. That's why the numbness and weakness climbed up from your feet, and it can also affect the nerves for breathing, swallowing, and bladder control.

Because your breathing and swallowing are already involved, I'm moving you to the ICU now so we can watch you closely — if your breathing muscles tire out, we'd support you with a breathing tube, and I'd rather do that in a controlled way than as an emergency. I'll have the nurse scan your bladder and place a catheter to drain it. We'll do a spinal tap to confirm, and start treatment today with IVIG, an antibody infusion given over five days. Most people stabilize and then recover, though it can take weeks to months.

I know this is a lot to hear at once. What questions do you have, and is there someone you'd like us to call?
I'm scared, but I understand. I don't have any questions right now. I'd like you to call my parents. They live nearby, and I think they should know what's going on.

What I think is going on is Guillain–Barré syndrome — your immune system, likely triggered by that infection, is attacking the coating on your nerves. That's why the numbness and weakness climbed up from your feet, and it can also affect the nerves for breathing, swallowing, and bladder control.

Because your breathing and swallowing are already involved, I'm moving you to the ICU now so we can watch you closely — if your breathing muscles tire out, we'd support you with a breathing tube, and I'd rather do that in a controlled way than as an emergency. I'll have the nurse scan your bladder and place a catheter to drain it. We'll do a spinal tap to confirm, and start treatment today with IVIG, an antibody infusion given over five days. Most people stabilize and then recover, though it can take weeks to months.

I know this is a lot to hear at once. What questions do you have, and is there someone you'd like us to call?

turns.content: Mr. Jones, I'm Dr. — I work here in the emergency department. I understand the police brought you in after a friend got worried about a text you sent. I'm sorry you're going through something this hard. Can you tell me in your own words what's been happening today?
I want to die. I texted my friend that I was going to shoot myself. I just can't take this anymore.
Thank you for being honest with me — that took courage, and I'm glad you're here. When you said you were going to shoot yourself, did you have a specific gun in mind, and where is it right now?
I have a gun at home. I was going to use that. I don't know where it is right now. The police might have it.

That's important to know — we'll find out from the police whether they took it, and either way I want us to make a plan so it isn't within reach. Right now, sitting here with me, how strong is the urge to act on this? And is there anyone — your friend, family — who's been checking on you since your wife passed?

The urge is pretty strong. I just miss my wife so much. I haven't been in touch with my family much since she passed away. My friend has been checking on me, but I haven't been answering his calls much lately.

The grief you're carrying sounds crushing, and pulling away from people has left you alone with it — that makes sense to me, and it also worries me. With the urge this strong and a gun involved, I don't think it's safe for you to go home tonight. I'd like to keep you here where you're safe, have our psychiatry team see you, and work with the police and your friend to make sure that firearm is secured somewhere you can't get to it. We can also talk about restarting or trying a different medication and getting you connected with grief support — you shouldn't have to do this by yourself. Would it be okay if we call your friend to let him know you're here and safe?
I guess that's okay. I don't want him to worry. I just... I just want my wife back. I don't know how to live without her.

That's an important finding, and before I draw any conclusions I want to hear from you: can you walk me through how you've actually been taking the morphine over the last few weeks — how many pills on a bad day? **Child Neuro OSCE Case 3: Tourette syndrome (Otis)**

**Otis Door Instructions**

You are asked to evaluate Otis, a 15-year-old young man who displays motor and vocal tics that have been present for at least 5 years. Initially, the patient was blinking frequently. For that reason, he was taken to see an optometrist who said the vision was fine. A few months later the child began clearing his throat, so he was referred to an allergist who said that there was no evidence of an allergic condition. At times, the symptoms have happened multiple times a day. In other instances, there appears to be a lull where the symptoms have hardly been present. The child has been struggling in school as he is unable to sit still. Parents mentioned that the young man likes to arrange his clothes by color and becomes very upset if the order is altered.

You are expected to explain to the patient and his family what Tourette syndrome is as well as address the patient’s anxiety as it relates to having a poorly understood medical condition.

turns.content: Hi Otis, I'm glad you and your family could come in today. I've read a bit about what's been going on — the blinking, the throat clearing, and how these have come and gone over the past few years. But I'd really like to hear it from you: can you tell me what these movements and sounds feel like from the inside, and what your day looks like when they're at their worst?

Hi. Well, it's like I can't control it. I blink a lot, and I clear my throat even when I don't need to. Sometimes I make this humming sound or repeat what someone just said. It's embarrassing, and it's hard to focus on stuff when it's happening a lot. Like in school, it's tough to stay seated and finish my work on time.

That takes a lot of courage to describe, Otis — thank you. What you're telling me makes a lot of sense, and I want you to know none of this is your fault or something you're choosing to do.

Two things I'm curious about: right before a tic happens, do you notice a build-up feeling — like an itch or pressure that only goes away once you let it out? And can you hold them back for a while, say in class, but then they burst out more later at home?

Yeah, sometimes I feel like there's this weird feeling inside, like I need to do the tic to make it stop. And yeah, I can hold them back in class, but then they come out more when I'm at home. It's like they build up and then just burst out.

That premonitory urge you just described — the build-up that only eases once the tic comes out, and the way it bursts out at home after holding it in — is very characteristic. Along with having both movement tics and sound tics for more than a year, waxing and waning over time, this fits a condition called Tourette syndrome. It's a difference in how certain brain circuits regulate movement — it isn't caused by anything you or your parents did, and it doesn't mean anything is damaged or getting worse.

Your parents mentioned you like your clothes arranged by color and it bothers you when that's changed. Does your mind get stuck on things like that — needing them "just right"? And how much do you find yourself worrying about the tics themselves, like whether people will notice?

Yeah, I like things to be in order, like my clothes by color. It bothers me when someone messes it up. And I do worry about the tics, like if people are noticing and making fun of me. It's embarrassing, and I hate when it happens in front of others.

Everything you've shared fits together, Otis. Tourette often travels with two companions: that "needs to be just right" feeling, which is an obsessive-compulsive trait, and trouble sitting still and finishing work, which sounds like the attention piece. Those are treatable too, and often they affect school more than the tics do.

Here's what I want you to hold onto. Tics naturally wax and wane — that's the condition, not you failing. And for most people, tics peak in the early-to-mid teens and then quietly improve through the late teens and twenties. The worrying about who's watching is real and understandable, but that worry itself tends to crank the tics up, so we treat it directly.

For next steps: there's a behavioral therapy called CBIT that teaches you to use that early urge as a signal and respond with a competing movement — it works well and involves no medication. If tics are still bothering you, there are medicines we can discuss. We can also write the school a letter for extra time and permission to step out briefly when you need to let tics go, so you're not spending your energy suppressing them all day. And a counselor can help with the anxiety and the ordering rituals.

You're not broken and you're not alone in this. Let's set up the CBIT referral and a school letter, and see you back in about six weeks — bring any questions you or your parents think of before then. What worries you most about all this right now?
I guess what worries me the most is what other people think. I hate it when kids at school make fun of me. I just want to fit in and not have everyone staring at me.
