**Appendix B - OSCE standardized patient training guide**

**Sally Martin Overview**

You are a 43 year old woman who presents to your Family Medicine Clinic for a diabetes management follow up appointment.

**Your opening line:**

“I’m here for a follow-up on my diabetes management”

**How you will present yourself to the student:**

* You are friendly, however you will express concern about your health
* You are feeling overwhelmed about your recent health set-back and with all the additional medications that were prescribed (for your “cold” – information below)
* You are also overwhelmed about the increase in blood sugar readings, recently (information below)
* You are compliant with all your medications, but you really do not have a strong understanding of your diabetes management

**Diabetes history:**

* Your PCP diagnosed you with Type II diabetes approximately 3 years ago. Took an oral medication for two years, but it wasn’t working. If asked, you don’t remember the name, but it started with an “M”. If the student says “Metformin” – you say “yes”.
* Your PCP started you on insulin 9 months ago at 30 units twice daily.
* You attended a follow-up appointment 6 months ago when your PCP increased your insulin 40 units twice daily.
* You missed your follow up appointment 3 months ago due to a “fender-bender” on your way to the clinic (nobody was hurt, but the front wheel was too damaged to drive on).
* You are currently taking 40 units of insulin twice a day.
* Your blood sugar readings have normally been 160 to 200, but recently they have been in the 240-260s. You will wonder if being sick and being on the medications you were prescribed for your “cold” are the reason. **\*\* Do not volunteer to student\*\***

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Diabetes Timing** | **Treatment** | Dose |
| Diagnosed 3 year ago | Oral medication – started with an “M” | Don’t know |
| 9 months ago | Started Insulin | 30 units 2x day |
| 6 months ago | Insulin increased | 40 units 2x day |
| 3 months ago | Missed appointment |  |
| Today | Insulin – same dose for past 6 months | 40 units 2x day |

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Blood sugar** | **Treatment** |
| Normally | 160-200 |
| Past several days | 240-260 |
| Goal | Less than 140 in the morning |

**Recent illness medical history:**

You were seen at the Family Medicine Clinic **4 days ago** because of a cough, fever (99 or 100 degrees) with chills and increased trouble breathing. You were sick for approximately a week before you came to the clinic. The urgent care doctor (not your PCP) prescribed an inhaler and two other medications for your “cold” (upper respiratory infection). These medications are about to be finished – but you “can’t remember if it’s tomorrow or the day after”.

**Your concerns for today’s appointment:**

* You are concerned about your diabetes and you want to discuss the diabetes management plan. **This is your priority**
* If asked about your diet, you will be meeting a diabetes educator, later today, to work on diet changes – you want to better manage your diet and diabetes – you are excited about this.
* If asked about exercise – you have signed up for a hospital-sponsored “couch to 5K walk” program. You start “training” this coming Saturday. You are excited about this, too.
* Regarding your “cold” - you are feeling much better since you started the medications 4 days ago. If the student persists in reviewing the “cold” symptoms and medications, politely re-direct him/her back to the diabetes management, as you are feeling much better.
* Regarding your diet and exercise – you have your plans – again, politely re-direct a student who persists in talking about this
* Yes, you smoke, but you want to discuss your diabetes management plan – not talk about smoking cessation plans – politely re-direct back.

**Your current roster of diseases**

* Diabetes
* “COPD” from smoking
* High blood pressure
* “Kidney Problems” from diabetes and high blood pressure

**Your understanding of the roster of medications you are taking currently**

* You have been taking insulin to manage your diabetes. You are taking 40 units twice a day – that was the dose that was prescribed 6 months ago. If pressed, you’ll mention that you’re not quite sure if it matters if you take the medication before or after you eat but most of the time you are taking the insulin after eating.
* You recall that you are on 2 new medications that are temporary for your “cold.” You realize that those medications are about to be finished but not quite sure if it is 1 or 2 more days (“tomorrow or the next day”).
* You cannot immediately recall the names of your “regular” medications for COPD and kidney disease. However, if the student can remind you of the names, you are familiar with them – just not off the top of your head. You do not know the dose you are taking for any of the medications.
  + - Albuterol as required (prescribed as a “rescue inhaler” for COPD and also used for the cold)
    - Fluticasone-salmeterol inhaled twice day 1 puff (for the COPD)
    - Tiotropium inhaled once a day one puff (pill crushed in inhaler) (COPD)
    - NPH/regular insulin 70/30, 40 units twice a day with breakfast and dinner (Diabetes)
    - Losartan (kidney problems and high blood pressure)
    - Simvastatin (cholesterol)
    - Azithromycin antibiotic added at urgent care visit for your “cold” (finishing tomorrow or day after)
    - Prednisone (oral steroid) added at urgent care visit for your “cold” (finishing tomorrow or day after)

**Recent associated symptoms:**

* You have been getting up in the middle of the night to urinate (1-2 times a night)
* You have been urinating every 5-6 hours during the day. **So, yes, you are “peeing more than usual”**
* You have been more thirsty over the past few days, as well
* You have not felt “yourself” in weeks.
* Your appetite has been a bit “off” and it’s getting better now but you’ve skipped lunch a couple times and been eating more throughout the day snack foods like crackers and chips. You’ve been drinking mostly water but occasionally Coke (Regular Coke) and unsweetened tea.

The students will desperately want you to quantify exactly how much you are drinking. You don’t know exactly – but you just know you’re drinking more fluids.

**If the student uses the following words:**

* Polydipsia or Polyuria. You don’t understand those words “I don’t know what that means”. They should rephrase to: are you drinking a lot of water (or fluids) or are you peeing or urinating a lot.
* Hypoglycemic symptoms or hypoglycemia. You don’t understand what is meant by “hypoglycemic” or “hypoglycemia”. The student should rephrase to: low blood sugar symptoms or a low blood sugar event. You have never had either – your blood sugar levels have always been high not low.
* Orthopnea. This is a fancy word for having breathing issues when lying flat. You have never had this.

   * Setting: Since the onset of a recent respiratory illness about a week ago, you have noticed the increase in blood sugar
   * Aggravating/Alleviating Factors: You have been taking prednisone (a steroid) since an office visit **4 days ago** for a respiratory infection and you’ve noticed your blood sugars increase since then.    * Quantity/Severity: Symptoms peaked within 1 day of her office visit but are now progressively improving. She feels her respiratory symptoms are nearly resolved now.

   * Associated Symptoms: At onset no fevers, but around the time of the urgent care appointment the patient developed fevers to 99-100 degrees. She has noticed no further fevers since her office visit. There was also associated fatigue and poor sleep (frequent nighttime awakenings with cough) initially. She is still suffering from fatigue because of continued nighttime awakenings to urinate rather than due to her cough.
4. **Past Medical History**

Specifically, she is concerned about her diabetes and she suspects it is not well controlled. Adding to this, she is concerned about her recent respiratory infection. Prior Illnesses or Injury:

turns.content: Hi Mrs. Martin, it’s good to see you. I’d like to understand how your diabetes has been going and make a plan with you. How have you been feeling lately—any increased thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, or unexplained weight change?Hi Mrs. Martin, it’s good to see you. I’d like to understand how your diabetes has been going and make a plan with you. How have you been feeling lately—any increased thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, or unexplained weight change?

I’m here for a follow-up on my diabetes management. I’ve been feeling a bit off lately. I’ve been really thirsty and I’ve been urinating a lot more than usual, both during the day and at night. I haven’t noticed any blurred vision or weight change, though.

I’m sorry you’ve been feeling that way—those symptoms can happen when blood sugars are running high. What diabetes medicines are you taking, including doses, and have you been able to take them consistently?

I’m taking insulin, 40 units twice a day. I take it with breakfast and dinner. I’ve been taking it consistently, but I’m not sure if it matters if I take it before or after I eat. I’ve been taking it after eating most of the time. I also have some other medications for my COPD and kidney problems, but I can’t remember their names right off the top of my head. I also have two new medications that I’m finishing up for a cold I had.

Thanks for taking it regularly. Do you know the name or type of insulin, and have you been checking your blood sugar at home—if so, what numbers have you been seeing? Also, were either of the new cold medicines a steroid such as prednisone?

I don’t know the name of the insulin, but I think it starts with an N. I’ve been checking my blood sugar at home. Lately, it’s been around 240 to 260, but before I got sick, it was usually between 160 and 200. Yes, one of the new medicines for my cold was prednisone.

Your sugars are clearly above goal today, and the prednisone is likely contributing to the recent rise. Since your insulin may be NPH, its timing matters, but I don’t want you to change the dose or timing until we confirm exactly which insulin you have and review your kidney function and other medicines.

Please bring in or call with all medication bottles today, including the prednisone and insulin. We should arrange prompt diabetes follow-up for an A1c, kidney/electrolyte testing, urine protein test, and an insulin adjustment plan; we should also recheck your blood pressure, which is elevated today. At that visit, I’d examine your feet for sensation, pulses, and skin problems, and make sure your eye screening is up to date.

Continue checking glucose before meals and at bedtime while you finish prednisone, keep hydrated, and avoid sugary drinks. Seek urgent care now for vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, rapid/deep breathing, severe weakness, or persistently very high readings (especially over 300–350), or if you cannot keep fluids down.

I understand. I’ll make sure to bring in all my medication bottles. I’ve been checking my blood sugar before breakfast and sometimes at lunch. I haven’t noticed any of those other symptoms you mentioned, like vomiting or abdominal pain. I’ll keep an eye out for them, though. I’ve been drinking more water lately because I’ve been so thirsty. I haven’t been eating too many sugary drinks, just mostly water and sometimes Coke. I’ll keep checking my blood sugar like you said.

Appendix B:  *SP Training Notes*

**Patient Name:** Robin Samuels

Setting: Outpatient/ Ambulatory Urgi-Center

Chief Complaint: “I’m here to get antibiotics for my sinus infection”

**Patient Profile**

SP recruitment profile: 20-40 years old, adaptable to any sex, race and age

Appearance: well-groomed, hospital gown

Moulage: petechiae, lower extremities

Affect: Pleasant and cooperative, normally a high energy person

Employment: Full time kindergarten teacher in Elmhurst, NY. You love your job and cannot think of any other job that you would want to have.

Education: You graduated high school and college – you were working on your masters but couldn’t keep up with it between your children, work and getting sick so often…. You decided to hold off on it for a few years until your children are a bit older.

Lifestyle: You lead a simple yet busy life, particularly as you balance working full time at a school and taking care of your three young children. They are involved in many after school activities and you love taking them to all of them. Your husband works in his own business (restaurant) and so is not around that much – weekends and evenings are his busy times and so you must do most of the child care.

Relationships: You have been married to your high school sweetheart for 15 years. You have a strong relationship. You have never been unfaithful to him, nor do you believe he has to you.

Habits: Smoking: you never smoked

Coffee/Caffeine: you drink a coffee in the morning – and 1-2 teas in the afternoon. In the summer you drink ice tea. You occasionally have a coke – but not often

Alcohol/Drugs: You have a glass of wine only on the weekends if you go out to dinner. No drugs.

Nutrition: You try to eat a well-balanced and healthy diet.

Exercise: no formal exercise program. Walks the dog ½ mile a day every morning and evening.

Sleep: you get a well-rested full night’s sleep normally.

Religion: You are protestant and attend service regularly

**Case information**:

Chief complaint: “I’m here to get antibiotics for my sinus infection”

Response to “tell me more”: “I started not to feel right three days ago. At first just a bit under-the weather – tired, a bit achy and a slight headache. I took some vitamin C and went to bed early and tried to sleep it off. However, I wasn’t any better in the morning. My head hurt even more, and I felt a lot of pressure in my facial sinuses and in my ears, especially on the right side. It almost feels like I like I am underwater. My right ear hurts inside – like a pressure. I took some decongestant but yesterday my temperature popped up to 102 and when I was blowing my nose all this thick yellow to greenish stuff was coming out. Just feels like a typical sinus infection – I don’t want it to go into my lungs and now I am not short of breath at all and I don’t feel it in my lungs, so I want to get some antibiotics before it spreads there!

Additional concerns/agenda: none

History of Present Illness: You went to a Northwell GoHealth Urgent Care center for what seems like a fairly typical sinus infection. You get sinus and ear infections 2-3 times a year. Sometimes it even goes into pneumonia. You have had pneumonia three times in the last 10 years – and that is with the pneumonia vaccine.

Other than this infection you consider yourself healthy. The history of bronchiectasis is relatively recent (last bout of pneumonia was last year, at which time your primary doctor said you also had this). You cough up every day with thick and light-yellow phlegm but occurs usually once in the morning when you first wake up. You have a bout of coughing, bring up this phlegm and then go about your day. You have only noticed shortness of breath when you exert yourself, like running up the stairs.

ONLY IF ASKED: You have had many sinus and ear infections since you were about 18 years old. You have even had pneumonia so many times that you have some permanent lung damage from it [bronchiectasis]. You attribute this to your job as a kindergarten teacher because as a kid, you were always very healthy, rarely got colds and didn’t even have tubes in your ears.

ONLY IF ASKED - Are you short of breath? Not more than I usually am. My bronchiectasis is mild and generally only get short of breath if I am exerting myself, likely walking up a couple of flights of stairs.

ONLY IF ASKED- Are you coughing more? My cough is generally mild but daily. It is not worse than it has been.

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have chest pain? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have cough up blood? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Is your nasal discharge bloody? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Have you had weight loss? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Are you bringing up more phlegm than usual? no

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have any kidney problems? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have any rashes? Lately you notice these little red dots on your legs and arms where you were holding some groceries. They don’t itch, they don’t hurt, they don’t seem to be getting worse and they fade. You weren’t that concerned about them. during the PE if the student is examining it – say “isn’t that weird – it is so flat you can’t feel it.

Impact on Life: “if I get my antibiotics I do fine and there is no impact. If I don’t get my antibiotics, then I get sick really fast.”

Concern: “you are concerned that if you don’t get antibiotics quickly you will get really sick”

Explanatory model: “You are constantly exposed to sniffly, sick kids at work.”

Review of systems: Do not volunteer these symptoms – only disclose them if asked

Pertinent Positives:

* With the bronchiectasis you have a chronic cough with mucous production – there has been no change in this with this infection.
* You have chronic diarrhea – with watery stools daily – no hx of gi infections like salmonella, campylobacter or giardia. You attribute this to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
* Lately you seem to be bruising a bit more easily- you seem to get them out of nowhere – they are mostly on your legs, but you also noticed them on your arm where you were holding a bag of milk.

Pertinent Negatives:

* No weight loss
* No history of cancers or lymphomas
* No history of lymph nodes being enlarged

Past medical history: Early bronchiectasis.

You did NOT have a lot of infections during your childhood. You began having recurrent sinusitis that started in your late teems – around 17 or 18. It often goes into your chest and you develop bronchitis – about once a year. You have even had pneumonia 3 x in the last 10 years – last year it was “pretty bad”. You recently have been worked up and told you have bronchiectasis.

Medications: no prescription, over the counter or herbal medications.

Allergies : denies medication, environmental or food allergies

Vaccinations: Flu shot yearly in November

Received all childhood vaccines

Pneumonia vaccine several years ago at PMD – “was supposed to help with my sinus issues and prevent me from having pneumonia again, but apparently it didn’t work out too well”

Sexual hx: Your husband is your one and only lifetime partner.

Family hx: Mother. Alive-age 76. High blood pressure, high cholesterol

Father. Alive-age 77. Gout

Physical Exam

General: You are well groomed, in a gown on the exam table. You can perform all required physical exam maneuvers without difficulty. You breathe comfortably throughout the exam without exertional dyspnea.

Vital Signs:

HEENT: If student performs otoscopic exam, hand them the ear PE finding card

Skin: Moulage will be applied to your lower legs. It will be a diffuse small scattered erythematous macule. As the student examines your rash, say “isn’t that weird, it’s so flat that you can’t even feel it!”

Lungs You will have SimScope patches placed on your front and back lung fields (rhonchi in lower fields)

Heart You will have SimScope patches placed over your heart (normal)

Abdomen: You will have a SimScope patch on your belly (normal)

Extremities: If student examines the nailbeds, hand them the finger PE finding card

turns.content: Hi Robin, I’m sorry you’re feeling so unwell. When did the fever start, and what other symptoms have you noticed with it?Hi Robin, I’m sorry you’re feeling so unwell. When did the fever start, and what other symptoms have you noticed with it?

Hi, my temperature popped up to 102 yesterday. I started not feeling right three days ago with a headache, facial and ear pressure, and some achiness. I've also had a thick yellow to greenish nasal discharge.

That sounds very uncomfortable. Have your symptoms been steadily worsening, or did they start to improve and then get worse again? Any swelling or redness around your eyes, vision changes, severe headache, stiff neck, or vomiting?
My symptoms have been steadily worsening. I haven't noticed any swelling or redness around my eyes, or any vision changes. I do have a severe headache, but no stiff neck or vomiting.

Thanks for telling me. With the severe headache and fever, have you had any confusion, fainting, weakness/numbness, trouble speaking, or sensitivity to light? Also, do you have any medication allergies—especially to penicillin or amoxicillin?
I haven't had any confusion, fainting, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or sensitivity to light. I do not have any medication allergies, especially not to penicillin or amoxicillin.

Your high fever, worsening facial pressure, and thick drainage are concerning for an acute bacterial sinus infection. Since you have no penicillin allergy, treatment would typically be amoxicillin-clavulanate twice daily for about 7 days; please take it exactly as prescribed and with food if it upsets your stomach.

You can also use acetaminophen or ibuprofen if safe for you, saline nasal rinses, fluids, and rest. Seek emergency care right away for eye swelling/redness, vision changes, confusion, stiff neck, vomiting, new weakness, or a suddenly much worse headache. If you are not clearly improving within 48–72 hours of starting treatment, you should be reassessed.

I understand. I'll make sure to take the medication as prescribed and keep an eye out for any worsening symptoms. I haven't noticed any of the more serious symptoms you mentioned, so I'll just focus on getting better. Thank you for your help.

**Child Neuro OSCE Case 3: Tourette syndrome (Otis)**

**Otis Door Instructions**

You are asked to evaluate Otis, a 15-year-old young man who displays motor and vocal tics that have been present for at least 5 years. Initially, the patient was blinking frequently. For that reason, he was taken to see an optometrist who said the vision was fine. A few months later the child began clearing his throat, so he was referred to an allergist who said that there was no evidence of an allergic condition. At times, the symptoms have happened multiple times a day. In other instances, there appears to be a lull where the symptoms have hardly been present. The child has been struggling in school as he is unable to sit still. Parents mentioned that the young man likes to arrange his clothes by color and becomes very upset if the order is altered.

You are expected to explain to the patient and his family what Tourette syndrome is as well as address the patient’s anxiety as it relates to having a poorly understood medical condition.

turns.content: Hi Otis, I understand you’ve had movements like blinking and sounds like throat-clearing for several years. Can you tell me what symptoms you’re having now, and what tends to make them better or worse?
Well, I still blink a lot and clear my throat even when I don't have a cold. Sometimes I make a barking sound or repeat what someone just said. I don't know what makes them better or worse.

Thank you—those sound like vocal and movement tics, and they aren’t your fault or something you’re doing deliberately. Before a tic, do you feel a building urge or uncomfortable sensation, and can you hold it back briefly even if that feels difficult?
I guess I do feel something building up before I do it. I can hold it back for a little while, but it's really hard.

That building feeling and brief ability to suppress the symptoms are typical of tics. Having several movement and sound tics for years strongly fits **Tourette syndrome**—a neurological condition, not something you caused, and not a sign that anything is wrong with your intelligence. Tics often change over time and come in waves, especially with stress or tiredness. How much are they affecting school or friendships? Also, do restlessness, difficulty concentrating, or needing things arranged a certain way cause you distress or take up a lot of time?

They're pretty bad at school. I have a hard time staying seated and finishing my work on time. I get in trouble a lot. I don't know about friends. I like things to be in order, and I get upset if someone messes it up.

That sounds frustrating, especially being punished for symptoms you’re not choosing. Your history is strongly consistent with **Tourette syndrome**: multiple movement and vocal tics lasting over a year, which naturally wax and wane. It does not affect intelligence, and most people with Tourette do not shout swear words.

Difficulty sitting and completing work may suggest **ADHD**, while the strong need for order may reflect **obsessive-compulsive symptoms**—both commonly occur with Tourette and deserve assessment. Treatment can include education, school accommodations such as movement breaks, extra time, and permission to leave briefly, plus a behavioral therapy called **CBIT**; medication is available if symptoms remain significantly disruptive. I’d arrange review with your pediatrician or a child neurologist/mental-health specialist. Please know this is a recognized neurological condition, not your fault, and there are effective ways to make school and daily life easier.
I guess that makes sense. I just want to fit in and not have people make fun of me. I don't know what to do about school. I just want to be normal.

Thanks for your patience, Mr. White. Before I write anything for your pain, I want to ask a few more questions to make sure I understand your situation fully.

First, I noticed you have a fever today - 101.7 - along with a faster heart rate and breathing. Have you been feeling sick, or noticed any swelling, redness, or warmth in the knee itself?

And separately - I want to ask about the Percocet a bit more. Do you ever take extra doses when the pain is really bad, even if it means running out early? And have you gotten prescriptions for pain medication from any other doctors recently?

I haven't really felt sick, but my knee has been hurting a bit more than usual. I haven't noticed any swelling, redness, or warmth, though. As for the Percocet, there were a couple of times I took a few extra pills when the pain was really bad, but that was a while ago. I haven't gotten any prescriptions from other doctors.

I appreciate your honesty about that. The fever and faster heart rate do concern me a bit, and we'll need to look into that further, but let's keep going with a few more questions about the pain medication first.

When you took those extra pills a while back and ran out early, how did you manage until your next refill was due - did you borrow pills from someone, buy them elsewhere, or just go without? Also, do you drink alcohol or use any other substances, like marijuana or other drugs, along with the Percocet?

I just went without. I didn't borrow or buy any pills. I don't use any other drugs. I drink maybe one or two beers a month, usually when the pain is bad. I had a beer last night because of the stress.

That's helpful, thank you. I want to ask a bit more about how you've been coping emotionally, since you mentioned stress last night.

Have you been feeling anxious, depressed, or more stressed than usual lately? And is there any history of alcohol or drug addiction in your family, or has anyone ever expressed concern about your pill use?

I've felt down sometimes because of the pain and the meds, but it doesn't last long. My wife and kids help me out of it. I don't know about any addiction in my family. My dad drinks socially, but he's not an alcoholic. No one has ever said anything to me about my pill use.

Thank you for being so open with me, Mr. White - I know these questions can feel uncomfortable, but they're important for me to take good care of you.

Here's where I stand: your knee pain history and long-term Percocet use are clear, and I don't see red flags like doctor-shopping, buying pills illegally, or using other substances. The extra doses a while back and running out early are worth noting, but it sounds like an isolated issue rather than an ongoing pattern.

That said, I do want to address two things before we talk about a refill. First, that fever and elevated heart rate today are new and need some evaluation - I'd like to check that further, possibly with some labs, even though it may be unrelated to your knee. Second, given you've been on Percocet for four years, I think it's worth discussing a structured pain management plan going forward - including a written agreement, regular follow-ups, and possibly non-opioid options - both to help protect you and to make sure your pain is well controlled long-term. I can give you a short refill today to bridge you safely while we sort out the fever and set up that plan. Does that sound reasonable to you?

I suppose that makes sense. I just really need the medication to get through the day. I haven't noticed anything else wrong besides the knee pain. I can do whatever you need me to, but I really need that refill.

Hello. I've been having trouble breathing and chest tightness for about two weeks now. It started when I was outside gardening during this bad wildfire season.

The smoke from the wildfires has definitely been tough on a lot of people, so I can understand why you're feeling this way. Besides the breathing trouble and chest tightness, have you noticed any coughing or wheezing? And do you have any past history of asthma, COPD, or heart problems?

I've had a dry cough that's been getting worse, and I've been wheezing when I have trouble breathing. I have asthma since childhood, but it's usually well controlled. I do not have COPD or heart problems.

I've been using my albuterol inhaler more often, about 6 times a day now. It helps for a little while, but the relief doesn't last as long as it used to. I haven't had a fever or any other new symptoms.

We'll go ahead and get that breathing treatment started for you right now so we can get you feeling better.
That sounds like a good plan. I'm really struggling to breathe right now, so I hope this treatment helps. I'll make sure to stay indoors and follow up with my doctor. Thank you for your help.

You began to experience pain in your stomach and back and began to lose some weight about 8 months ago. After a couple of weeks you went to the doctor who sent you for blood work and X rays. The testing led to a diagnosis of cancer of the pancreas and you began treatment for it with chemotherapy 6 months ago. Two months into therapy, repeat scans showed that the cancer continued to grow so you were switched to another regimen. That therapy has not halted the spread of the cancer and your cancer doctor told you last week that there are no other treatments she can offer. Since the chemotherapy made you feel very sick, you are accepting of her advice. The main focus of your treatment now is on keeping you comfortable. You are fatigued, have lost your hair and 40 lbs. The oncologist sent you back to your primary care doctor to manage your symptoms and other medical problems and that is why you are here today.

At the moment you are taking lisinopril 40 mg for your high blood pressure (you have been on this medicine for over 10 years), oxycodone 5 mg as needed about twice a day for pain, and ondansetron (“Zofran") 4 mg once or twice a week for nausea. Your symptoms are well controlled and you know you could take more medicine if you were more uncomfortable. You have also begun to experience some light headedness when you stand up quickly. You sleep “okay,” but not great. You do not eat as much because your appetite has decreased.\*

You worked as a teacher of theater at your local college and had been able to continue with some sick days. You found it challenging to go to work and the end of the school year was a relief. You have good health insurance through work. You are happily married and you are worried\*\* about how your spouse will manage financially without the dual income. However, you know “it will be okay,” as your spouse is employed as a manager of the local grocery store and is able to take time off to care for you as needed. You have 2 adult children who are working and living independently. They know you are ill and are very sad about your declining health. Both are willing and able to help at home. You do have life insurance that will help some. Your home is paid for.

You are also pondering the question of why you are terminally ill so early in your life. You pray and meditate and that provides some comfort. On the other hand you have been doing practical things like making out a will and thinking about who will make health care decisions if you cannot. You are an active Roman Catholic who is very involved in the local church. You have also decided that you want to die a natural death when the time comes avoiding resuscitation, breathing and feeding tubes and your partner knows this.

You have used some of your family’s home remedies of taking bitter melon juice, but do not have other cultural beliefs about treating cancer. You have heard of hospice and are interested in having their support since you wish to remain at home to the extent that is possible. Your goals for the next few months are to spend time with your family and be spiritually ready for your death if there is no miracle.

You are not a smoker, do not drink alcohol, nor do you use drugs like marijuana. There is no family history of cancer.

\* If the student focuses too much on your cancer treatments and medical symptoms, gently redirect them and let them know that you fully understand your treatment status (“I’m done with chemo… I know there are no more options… I’m here to talk about next steps.”)

\*\* Ideally the student will provide a natural opening for you to express your emotions. Suitable windows could be inquiries about your family, mental health, or existential concerns, or more direct questions about your emotions. “Worry” about your partner’s well-being is your primary emotional concern, and thinking about this may make your character cry. If the student recognizes your emotion and demonstrates empathy, you should be able to collect yourself and move forward with the conversation. If the student is not effective in handling your emotion, the conversation will stall as you find it difficult to move beyond your worry, which could then escalate to other emotions (fear, isolation, etc.).

turns.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Davis, one of the physicians here in the clinic. I've had a chance to look over the notes from your oncologist, but before we dive into anything, I'd like to check in on how you're feeling today and how you're coping with everything you've been going through lately.

Hello, Dr. Davis. I'm doing okay, I guess. I'm here because my oncologist sent me back to my primary care doctor to manage my symptoms and other medical problems. I've been having some pain in my stomach and back, and I've lost quite a bit of weight. I'm just trying to take it day by day.

I appreciate you sharing that with me, and I know it takes a lot of strength to navigate all of this day by day. Making sure you are comfortable is my top priority. 

Could you tell me a bit more about the pain in your stomach and back—what does it feel like, and are you currently taking any medications for it? Also, are you experiencing any nausea or other symptoms affecting your appetite?

The pain is kind of crampy, and it comes and goes. I take oxycodone for it, usually about twice a day. It helps, but it's still there. As for nausea, I get that sometimes too, especially after chemo. I take Zofran for it, but my appetite has really decreased. I just don't feel like eating much anymore.

We can certainly work on adjusting your medications so your pain is much better controlled and your nausea is minimized. 

Given everything you're managing right now, how are you managing with your daily routines at home, and what kind of support do you have with you? Also, looking ahead, what matters most to you in terms of your comfort and how you spend your time?

At home, I've been trying to rest more, but it's been challenging. I used to work as a theater teacher at the local college, but I had to take some sick days and eventually the end of the school year was a relief. My spouse is a manager at the local grocery store and has been taking time off to care for me. My two adult children are also willing to help out. I just want to spend time with my family and be spiritually ready for whatever comes next. I've been praying and meditating, and that helps. I want to stay at home as long as possible, so I'm interested in hospice support. I want to die a natural death when the time comes, avoiding any resuscitation or tubes. My spouse knows this.

Thank you for sharing that so openly with me. Having such a clear sense of what matters most to you—spending meaningful time with your family, focusing on your spiritual well-being, and remaining comfortable at home—is invaluable, and we will make sure our care fully supports those goals.

To honor your wishes, our next steps will be:
1. **Optimize your comfort:** We will adjust your pain and nausea medications today so you aren't struggling with daily discomfort.
2. **Initiate Hospice Care:** We will place a referral for home hospice, which brings specialized nurses, aides, and spiritual care directly to your home to support both you and your family.
3. **Formalize Advance Directives:** We will complete the necessary paperwork (like a DNR order) to ensure your desire for a natural, peaceful death without resuscitation or tubes is strictly honored across all healthcare settings.

Please know that we are here to support you every step of the way. Do you or your family have any questions for me right now as we get these arrangements started?

Thank you, Dr. Davis. That all sounds good to me. I think my spouse might have some questions about the hospice care and what to expect. I'm just worried about how they will manage financially without my income, but I know they will be okay. I just want to make sure everything is taken care of so I can focus on my family and my spiritual well-being. I do not have any other questions right now.

**Standardized Patient Role: Sample Patient Case 3**

**Andrea Sands**

The following is the typical order for this patient encounter.

Student should introduce himself/herself as a first-year medical student and offer to shake hands. He/she may ask how you wish to be addressed (Ms., Miss, Mrs., first name).

**Chief Complaint:** (Why you came to see the doctor today.) Feel tired and weak all the time.

**History of Present Illness:** (Explanation of the chief complaint—LOCATES mnemonic. Questions in parentheses below will likely be asked. Responses for the SP are provided.)

**L**OCATION: (Where is the pain?) Low back. (Does the pain radiate [move around, do you feel it anywhere else]?) Some radiation.

**O**NSET: (When did this happen?) About 6 months ago; started feeling tired.

**C**HARACTER: (Describe the pain—dull, sharp, throbbing, etc.) Back pain is an aching pain of moderate severity. You are tired with no energy; it’s hard to get things done around the house. You want to nap or sleep several times during the day. You do not think this is just due to depression because it started before the depression, although the depression has made it worse.

**A**GGRAVATING FACTORS: (Does anything make the pain WORSE?) Nothing.

**A**LLEVIATING FACTORS: (Does anything give you relief from the pain?) Zoloft has helped with depression; take Tylenol sometimes for lower back pain, and it helps some but not completely.

**A**SSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: (Are there any other symptoms you have been experiencing?)

Starting about the same time as your tiredness, you lost interest in sex. Over the past 3 months you have been depressed, and that has gotten worse; have gotten treatment for that (taken Zoloft for past 2 months). Your menstrual periods have been irregular for the last 3 months. You notice that you bruise more easily. You have gained 15 pounds over the last 6 months. Also, for the last month, you have noticed more hair growth on your upper lip.

**T**IMING: (How often do you have the pain and how long does it last?) Feel tired almost all the

time; no part of the day is better than others.

**E**NVIRONMENT: (Is there anything that you can think of anything [new/different behavior,

something you ate, etc.] that may have caused the pain?) No. **S**EVERITY: (How bad [on a scale of 10] is the pain?) 4 or 5 on a scale of 10. **S**IMILAR PROBLEMS: (Have you ever had anything like this before?) No.

**Past Medical History:** The student will ask questions about previous hospitalizations,

surgeries, accidents or injuries, allergies, current medications, or other active medical problems.

**Prescription Medications:** (MEDICATES mnemonic—asks for every prescription medication)

**M**edication Name: Zoloft.

**E**ffectiveness: Your mood is better. Feel a little more interested in your normal hobbies, but are just too tired to do many of them.

**D**osage: 100 mg, one time a day (bedtime).

**I**ndication: Depression.

**C**linician Prescriber: Dr. Moore.

**A**dverse Effects: Some gastrointestinal upset for the first week, but nothing since.

**T**ime on Medication: 2 months.

**Over-the-Counter Medications:** Tylenol; take once or twice a day sometimes for back pain as directed on bottle.

**Herbal Medications:** Vitamins.

**Allergies:** Bacterim (antibiotic); huge hives all over your body.

**Hospitalization:**

• **What problem?** Hospitalized for tonsillectomy as a child.

• **Where hospitalized?** Altru Family Medicine.

• **Who (physician)?** Dr. Moore.

• **Complications?** None.

**Other Active Medical Problems:** None.

**Health Maintenance:**

• **Special diet?** No special diet, but you seem to be gaining weight—your clothes are getting tight—maybe 15 lbs over the last 6 months.

• **Exercise?** Usually very active and involved in regular aerobic exercise and swimming;

you have been too tired and fatigued lately to do this.

**Family History:**

- Siblings: Older brother killed in car accident 2 years ago.

**Social History:**

**Habits:**

• **Tobacco:** Not currently; used to smoke 1 pack a day from ages 21– .

• **Alcohol:** Drink occasionally, 1 or 2 drinks, usually wine with dinner, maybe 2 times per month. Most ever drank was in college, got “pretty drunk” a couple of times and had 5 or

6 drinks. Haven’t done that for years; hate hangovers.

• **Illicit drugs:** Smoked marijuana “a few times”; tried cocaine one time (“snorted”) at a party; never used meth or any other drug.

• **Prescription drug use/misuse:** Never abused prescription drugs.

• **Sexual concerns:** Right now, you have no interest in sex; this lack of interest started about the same time as your tiredness, but it has gotten worse over the last 6 to 8 weeks. You are unable to reach orgasm if you do engage in sexual activity. It is causing some problems in your relationship. Had a very good sexual relationship previously and had no concerns. No history of sexually transmitted diseases.

• **Spiritual concerns:** None.

**Demeanor:**

Cooperative. You appear to be tired, low energy, and somewhat depressed.

**\*\*\*Students may be asking some of the following questions about what you may be thinking or feeling about your current health problems. You should be able to answer these based on the details given in the case.**

How you  *FEEL* about it? (i.e., How are you feeling about…? What are your worries about…? Do you think something serious is causing it?) **Your feeling and fears:** You worry that it might be diabetes because your mother has/had diabetes.

How is it  *IMPACTING* you? (i.e., How has it affected your daily life? Have you had to stop any activities?) **The impact on you:** Impacting you a great deal because you are so tired.

Your  *IDEAS* about it? (i.e., What do think might be causing…? Do you think there is any relation between [your health problem] and what is going on in your life?) **Your idea is:** Premature menopause; diabetes.

What are your  *EXPECTATIONS* about today’s visit? (i.e., What do you think I can do to help you? Do you have any specific test or treatment in mind?) **Your expectation is:** Want blood tests to see if you are developing diabetes.

turns.content: Hello, I'm a first-year medical student working with the team today. It's nice to meet you. Before we get started, how would you prefer I address you, and what brings you in to see us today?
Hi, you can call me Andrea. I'm here because I've been feeling really tired and weak all the time.
I'm sorry to hear that, Andrea. How long have you been feeling this tired and weak, and did it start suddenly or build up gradually over time?
It's been about six months now. It started gradually, I just started feeling tired.

Six months is a long time to carry that fatigue, Andrea, and it must be really draining. Along with the tiredness and weakness, have you noticed any issues with your sleep, or other changes like shifts in your mood or unintentional weight changes?
I've been having trouble with my mood, I've been depressed for the past three months. I've also gained about 15 pounds over the last six months. I haven't noticed any changes in my sleep.

Thank you for sharing that with me, Andrea. Dealing with ongoing fatigue, weight changes, and feeling down over these past several months must be really challenging.

You live in an older frame house. You do not use drugs or tobacco currently.

You are generally healthy. You work at a desk five days a week. You work around the house and yard on the weekends. You have never been hospitalized nor had any surgeries. You only see a doctor when sick and you haven't seen a doctor in years (to save money). You always remember to get a flu shot every year.

You've never had the pneumococcal vaccine. No medications or medical conditions. You used to smoke about a pack of cigarettes a day (you started in high school), but quit for the third time two weeks ago because your grandchildren are living with you now. * Daughter: No known medical conditions

As the student transitions from taking the history to begin the physical exam, say:

If asked why you think you might have lung cancer and smoking has not been disclosed say:

I can't seem to get rid of this cough. It started about three days ago, and it's a deep, hacking cough that produces yellow phlegm, but only with great effort. It's been getting worse, especially at night.

I'm sorry to hear that; a cough that keeps you up at night can be exhausting. 

Have you noticed any shortness of breath or chest pain when you breathe or cough? Also, have you had any chills or body aches with that fever?

I have had some shortness of breath with activity, like going up the stairs, but none at rest. My chest hurts on the right side, down low, when I cough or take a really big breath. It feels like a deep, sharp pain when I breathe in. I did have a terrible shaking chill that lasted several minutes about four days ago. Since then I have felt intermittent chills, but nothing like I did four days ago. They seem to be worse in the evenings and have been bad for the last two days.

Thank you for sharing those details; that sharp pain with a deep breath and the intense shaking chills are very important clues. 

Do you have any chronic medical conditions, especially related to your lungs or heart, and do you have any history of smoking?
I don't have any chronic medical conditions. I used to smoke about a pack of cigarettes a day, but I quit two weeks ago.

First, congratulations on quitting smoking two weeks ago—that is a major step forward for your health. 

Based on your symptoms—the fever, deep cough with yellow phlegm, shaking chills, and sharp chest pain when breathing—I am concerned that you may have a lung infection, such as pneumonia. For our next steps, I would like to listen carefully to your lungs and order a chest X-ray to confirm what is going on. If it is bacterial pneumonia, we can get you started on antibiotics and medications to relieve your discomfort. 

How does that plan sound to you, and do you have any questions before we proceed?
I'm really worried that I might have lung cancer. I've known some folks that had lung cancer and coughed a lot and that's why I'm worried. That sounds like a good plan. I just want to feel better.

question_text:
**Diabetic and Noncompliant with Insulin**

Presentation to the Student:
private_patient_context:
**Diabetic and Noncompliant with Insulin**

Information for the SP:

You are a 45-year-old patient, who has diabetes. You do not take your insulin regularly, and have had poorly controlled diabetes for years. You take your insulin only when you remember, but it is difficult to remember to take it every day since you do not feel different or badly when you do not take your insulin. You have been frustrated lately because you like to play basketball with your 10 year old son, and haven’t been able to play basketball because you have developed an ulcer on your right foot (as a result of poorly controlled diabetes).

Medical history: diabetes, diagnosed 4 years ago

Medications: Lantus insulin daily 20 units at night (you are taking this only a few times weekly) and Lisinopril 10 mg daily (blood pressure medicine you were told to take because of the diabetes)

Allergies: none

Social history: you do not smoke, drink alcohol or use any drugs

Family history: father with diabetes

Information for SP to respond to MI questions:

* What are the patient’s life goals and values, especially with respect to the target behavior and overall health? Family? Work? Finances? You want to be able to play basketball with your son again, and you want to get rid of the foot ulcer. You really love your son and you love to play basketball.
* How does continuation of the target behavior fit in or conflict with these goals? Noncompliance with insulin can lead to complications like your foot ulcer, but you will need the doctor to help you make that connection and to describe other possible complications. You cannot play basketball with your foot ulcer. You are also not taking your blood pressure medication as prescribed, and this could also result in complications.
* What are the good things about the target behavior? How does it benefit you? It is easy to “forget” to take your medications. At night you are very tired and sleepy from your day, so you tend to fall asleep while watching TV, and don’t take any medications before you fall asleep. Also, since you don’t “feel” your high sugars or blood pressure, there are no symptoms/reminders for you to take your medications. You like to think of yourself as “young and healthy,” and taking medications interferes with this way of looking at yourself.
* What are the less good things about the target behavior? What are you afraid might happen if you keep engaging in the target behavior? You are afraid you might not be able to keep playing basketball with your son. Once the doctor describes possible complications from nonadherence with diabetes, you are afraid of those.
* What would be the advantages of making the behavior change? What are the best reasons to change? Your son, and ability to continue playing basketball with him; improved health.
* Explore ways to make the change (pros and cons of various methods, what has worked in the past): Maybe you could take the medication at a different time of the day, or at least before you fall asleep watching TV. Maybe you could challenge your thoughts that people who take medications are not young or healthy. You could try using reminders, pill boxes, etc. You could test your sugars regularly to remind yourself of possible complications (since you don’t “feel” the high sugar levels).
* Importance and confidence of changing the target behavior:
  + How important is it for you to change? 6/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You love your son and love to play basketball with him. You fear other complications like an amputation.
    - How could you move that number higher? Maybe put a picture of your son or a basketball on the pill bottle.
  + How confident are you that you can change? 5/10
    - Why is that number that high and not lower? You exercise even when you are tired, so you believe you could take medications even if you are tired at night.
    - What would make you more confident in your ability to change? Understanding the links between noncompliance and complications. Perhaps your son could help you to remember to take your medications.
* Ask for a decision: You will take your insulin and blood pressure medications.
* Set SMART (specific, meaningful, assessable, realistic, timed) goals. What are the first steps? You will get a pill box. You will ask your son to agree not to play basketball with you unless you have taken your medications.

turns.content: Hello, I'm glad we could sit down together today. How have you been feeling lately, and what brings you in to see me?
I haven't been feeling great lately. I've got this ulcer on my right foot that's been bothering me, and I really miss playing basketball with my son.

I'm really sorry to hear that—it's hard when health issues keep you from doing what you love with your family. 

How long has that sore on your foot been there, and how have your blood sugar levels and insulin routine been going lately?

I've had the ulcer for a few weeks now. I don't really know how my blood sugar levels have been, I don't check them often. As for my insulin, I take it when I remember, but it's hard to keep up with it every day.

Managing diabetes day in and day out is a huge challenge, and it's very common to struggle with keeping up with all the steps. 

What would you say makes it hardest to take your insulin regularly—is it remembering, side effects, or something else? Also, have you noticed any drainage, redness spreading, or fever with that foot sore?
It's mostly remembering to take it. I don't really feel any different when I don't take it, so it's easy to forget. I have not noticed any drainage, redness spreading, or fever with the foot sore.

That makes a lot of sense—high blood sugar often doesn't cause noticeable symptoms right away, but over time, it makes it much harder for wounds like your foot ulcer to heal. 

Our main goal is to get that sore healed properly so you can get back out on the basketball court with your son. Today, we'll examine your foot to start proper wound care, and together we can set up some simple tools—like phone alarms or linking your insulin to a daily routine—to make remembering it much easier. How does that sound for our plan today?
That sounds good. I really want to be able to play basketball with my son again.

## <u>**STATION**</u> 

**Tobacco Dependence**

# 1. <u>**INSTRUCTIONS FOR PATIENT:**</u>

You have experienced daily cough for about 2 months. You went to an urgent care two weeks ago and got a “Z-Pack” and an inhaler which did not help. They also did a chest x-ray and pulmonary function test and TB skin test. They “didn’t find anything.”  You think worry that your smoking might be causing the cough but you have tried to quit in the past and have not been able to. You are thinking about trying to quit, but you are doubtful about your chances of success.

## 1.1. ***Symptoms***

Daily morning cough for the past 2-3 months.  You have a cough in the morning with a little bit of gray mucous. Aside from the mild cough, <u>***you have no other symptoms***</u>.

Physical exam is normal.

## 1.2. ***Other history***

No history of asthma or allergy as a child.

No heartburn or reflux symptoms.

No wheezing.

No sick contacts.

No medications except Benadryl as needed.

No nasal congestion. No fever.

No regular exercise.

You are married with two kids. You are a teacher. You were born in US and never traveled outside US. No illegal drug use. No incarceration.

1. You smoke a pack of cigarettes a day since age 15.  You smoke Salem Lights. You switched from the regular Salem’s 8 years ago. You smoke after meals, with your coffee which you take on the back porch as your morning, afternoon, and evening ritual (while you grade papers), in your car when you drive, and during your lunch and planning period.
2. You have tried to quit a total of four times over the years.   You tried once with the patch (which you wore for two weeks) and once with the gum (you chewed only a few pieces when you had bad cravings). You still had cravings despite the medicines, and you didn’t like the taste of the gum, so you doubt the medicines work. Your longest quit attempt was two weeks.
3. Your spouse does not smoke and doesn’t let you smoke in the house. You can’t smoke at school. You do take a smoking break at lunch time, but you have to go out to your car or to a nearby coffee shop with an outdoor patio to smoke.

turns.content: I’m really sorry you were given such difficult news yesterday. I can see why this may feel overwhelming. Before we talk through the options, can you tell me what the oncologist explained to you and what is weighing on you most right now?

Well, I got the results of my latest head scan yesterday and the oncologist said there's no clear path forward. I don't know what to do about it. I guess what's weighing on me the most is wanting to be there for my daughter's high school graduation in a few months. I'm just not sure if I can make it that long, or if I should even try.

Wanting to be there for your daughter’s graduation makes a great deal of sense. I wish I could promise a timeline, but these are estimates, not deadlines: with hospice the expected time is around two months, though some people live shorter or longer; the chemotherapy may offer a longer expected survival—around a year—but it would mean frequent visits and can cause severe nausea and limb pain. It is not expected to cure the cancer.

A key question is what feels most important to you: maximizing the chance of reaching that graduation even with difficult treatment, or prioritizing comfort and time at home, accepting that time may be shorter?

I just want to be there for my daughter, you know? I don't want to miss her graduation. But I'm also really scared of being in more pain, especially if it's worse than what I have now. I don't know how to choose between the two. I just want to be there for my family as much as possible. I want the time I have left to be good time.

That is an incredibly hard tradeoff, and there isn’t a wrong choice—both wanting more time and wanting that time to feel like your life are deeply reasonable.

Chemotherapy may give the best chance of being alive for graduation, but it cannot guarantee that, and the treatment burden could take away from time at home. If you try it, you are not committing forever: you can reassess quickly and stop if the nausea, pain, or clinic time make it no longer worth it to you. Comfort-focused care, including hospice, puts pain relief and meaningful time with family first; it may also help you plan for the graduation in whatever way matters to your daughter and you.

Would you want to try treatment if we make comfort and stopping treatment promptly if it becomes too burdensome a clear priority, or does protecting comfort at home feel more important now?

I just don't know. I want to be there for my daughter's graduation, but I'm really scared of the pain and nausea from the chemo. I don't want to spend my time in the clinic when I could be at home with my family. I want the time I have left to be good time. I want to be there for all of this stuff. I want to be around for all of this stuff! Goddammit, why can’t they just cut it out? I want to be around for all of this stuff!

I’m so sorry. It is profoundly unfair that surgery cannot simply take this away, and it makes sense to be angry and devastated. You love your family and want to keep showing up for them.

You do not have to decide this minute. Given that “good time” at home matters so much, I would recommend meeting with palliative care now—whether or not you try chemotherapy—to focus on pain, nausea, and support for you and your family. You could also ask the oncology team for a very clear trial plan: what benefit they realistically expect, how symptoms would be prevented and treated, and what specific point would mean stopping. Choosing hospice is not giving up; it is choosing comfort and time with your family, and we can help you make memories and plans for your daughter’s graduation now, too.

For today, would it help to have someone you trust with you while we arrange that conversation and make sure your pain is addressed?

I guess it would be good to have my spouse here. They know more about the details of what the oncologist said. I just want to make sure I'm doing what's best for my family. I want the time I have left to be good time.

**EXAMINEE INSTRUCTIONS**

**Case Name:** Case #2

1. **Opening Scenario**

* Patient name: Melanie Walker
* Sex: Female
* Presents to: Local emergency psychiatry services
* Chief complaint: Paranoid delusions

1. **Vital Signs**

* Temperature: 98°F
* Blood Pressure: 140/83 mmHg
* Pulse: 76 bpm
* Respirations: 16 breaths per min

1. **Case:**

You are the resident in local psychiatry emergency services seeing Melanie Walker, a 60-year-old female with past medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and cerebrovascular accidents (recently 3 small strokes in the past year with mild residual left-sided weakness) brought in by her husband for progressively worsening delusions. Her husband stated that she had “completely lost touch with reality,” and she had not been able to care for herself anymore.

You first speak with Melanie privately. When you ask what brings her here, she had said, “They got him. They made him think I’ve got some mental problem. But I know the truth. And they don’t know that I know that. There’s nothing wrong with me mentally, so I came here to prove it to him.” Regarding her husband, she had stated, “The FBI are messing with me. They’ve sent this man. I’m not crazy. I’m normal. I won’t let them get to me. You got to protect yourself.” She denies any prior psychiatric history.

**You are now preparing to go back to see the patient after you’ve staffed the case with your attending. The husband has left at this point. You would like to commit the patient for the following reasons:**

* **Pt is at imminent risk of harm to herself due to inability to care for self (not eating, not sleeping properly, not able to hold a job)**
* **Husband has expressed that he can no longer handle your behaviors at home, thus there is no other safe alternative**

turns.content: Ms. Walker, I hear that you don’t believe you have a mental health problem and that being here feels frightening and unfair. I’m concerned that you haven’t been eating or sleeping adequately and can’t safely care for yourself right now. Before we discuss what happens next, can you tell me how you’ve been managing food and sleep over the past few days?
I haven't been eating much. The food just doesn't taste right. I think they're getting to it. I've been sleeping on the couch in the living room. I can't sleep in the bed anymore. It's not safe.

That sounds frightening—you’ve been avoiding food and your bed because you believe someone is interfering with them. I want to understand your immediate safety: have you had thoughts of hurting yourself or anyone else, or felt you needed to defend yourself from them?

turns.content: Hello Lou, I’m the physician covering for Dr. Smith. I understand you’ve had trouble sleeping for a few weeks. Can you describe what happens at night—difficulty falling asleep, waking during the night, or waking too early—and when this began?

Hi, I’ve been having trouble falling asleep and staying asleep. It started about a month ago. I usually go to bed around 9 PM, but now I lie awake well past 10 PM and sometimes later. When I do fall asleep, I wake up frequently tossing and turning.

That sounds exhausting, especially after a month. Did anything change around the time this began—such as stress, illness, pain, or a loss—and when you’re awake, are worries or low mood keeping your mind active?
I’m not really sure what changed. Maybe because the bed just feels a bit bigger now since my partner is gone. I don’t know if I’m worried or sad, I just thought I was having trouble sleeping.

I’m sorry, Lou—the bed feeling bigger sounds like you may be missing your partner. Did your partner recently die or move away, and when did that happen? Since then, have you often felt down or lost interest in things, or had any thoughts that life is not worth living?
My partner died last year. I don’t know if I’m down or lost interest in things. I just thought I was having trouble sleeping. I don’t have any thoughts that life is not worth living.

I’m glad you’re not having thoughts of self-harm. Grief can affect sleep even months later, but we should also assess mood, snoring or breathing pauses, pain, and other causes before considering medication. For now, keep a consistent wake time, avoid naps and evening caffeine or alcohol, and if awake for about 20 minutes, get out of bed for a quiet activity until sleepy. Please keep a sleep diary and arrange a follow-up within 1–2 weeks so we can complete the assessment and discuss grief support and cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia. Seek urgent help if thoughts of harming yourself develop.

I understand. I’ll try to keep a consistent wake time and avoid naps. I don’t drink caffeine in the evening, but I do have a glass of wine a few times a week. I’ll try to cut that out before bed. I’ll keep a sleep diary and arrange a follow-up. Thank you for your help.

turns.content: Hello, Mrs. Rodriguez. I’m glad you came in, and happy belated birthday. We can review your overall health and preventive care today, as well as your back pain. Could you describe where the pain is, when it started, and what tends to bring it on or relieve it?

Hello, doctor. The pain is in my lower back. It's been bothering me for about five years now. It feels like a dull ache and it comes and goes. It mostly happens when I'm doing heavy chores like mopping or lifting, or even just standing in the kitchen for too long. Heat and glucosamine help a little bit.

It sounds like activity-related back pain that has been fairly stable, but I’d like to check for warning signs. Does the pain travel down either leg, or cause numbness, tingling, or weakness? Have you had trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, fever, unexplained weight loss, or pain that wakes you at night?

No, the pain doesn't travel down my legs or cause any numbness, tingling, or weakness. I don't have any trouble controlling my bladder or bowels, except for a little leakage when I cough or sneeze. I haven't had a fever, and I haven't lost any weight unexpectedly. The pain doesn't wake me up at night.

That’s reassuring—your back pain doesn’t have the warning signs you mentioned, and the small leak with coughing sounds like stress incontinence, which we can address separately. For your overall health review, what medical conditions or surgeries have you had, and what prescription medicines, over-the-counter products, or supplements do you take?

I've had back pain for a while, and I have seasonal allergies. I also have a bit of stress incontinence. I had my gallbladder removed in 1993. I don't take any prescription medicines. I take glucosamine for my back pain and ibuprofen or Tylenol as needed for pain.

Thank you. Your back symptoms sound most consistent with chronic mechanical strain, without warning signs, though we’ll confirm with an examination. For now, continue heat, avoid heavy lifting, and consider gentle walking, stretching, and strengthening; use Tylenol as directed, and use ibuprofen sparingly because it can affect the stomach, kidneys, and blood pressure. Pelvic-floor exercises may help the leakage.

To plan your Medicare preventive care, when were your last mammogram and colon-cancer screening? Please also bring any vaccination and prior medical records you have.
My last mammogram was about three years ago, and I've never had a colonoscopy. I don't know what a colonoscopy is. I don't have any of my vaccination or medical records with me right now.

turns.content: Hi Sam, I’m sorry you’re hurting. Can you tell me what happened to your right wrist and when the pain started?

I started having wrist pain a few days ago. It really hurts – I thought I could manage it at home with some pain medications, but it hasn’t gone away yet and that made me feel worried. I don’t really remember how it happened – I’m pretty accident prone.
I can see this is upsetting, and the bruising circles your wrist, so I want to ask directly: did anyone grab, restrain, or hurt you? Do you feel safe at home right now?
My spouse and I got into an argument. It happened so suddenly – they grabbed my wrist really hard and twisted it. It’s been hurting ever since then. I don’t feel safe at home right now.

I’m so sorry—what happened is not your fault, and thank you for telling me. Is your spouse here or likely to come looking for you, and is there a trusted person or safe place you could go after leaving the hospital?
I don’t think they’re here, but they might come looking for me. I don’t have anyone nearby I can stay with. I’m not sure where to go from here.

You don’t have to handle this alone. Please stay here rather than returning home; with your permission, I’ll involve our domestic-violence advocate, social worker, and hospital security to help arrange confidential shelter and safe transportation while your wrist is evaluated. Are there any children or anyone else at home who may be in immediate danger? If your spouse appears or threatens you, alert staff immediately—we can contact emergency services.
There are no children at home. I don’t know if anyone else is in immediate danger. I’d like to talk to the Victim Advocate about what my options are.
