**Instructions to Standardized Patient**

**Patient’s Name:** Robert Jameson

**Presenting Situation:** This is a one week follow-up appointment for this 39-year old man with severe pain due to a hip injury from a motorcycle accident five years ago. He returns today to get the results of his urine drug test that was taken at his last visit. The patient’s goal is get a refill of his prescriptions for morphine and Vicodin. His regular physician has recently retired. He would see his regular physician for prescription refills and have him check his pain levels. His very last visit with his physician was about 1 month ago. Today, he is seeing the same health care provider as he did one week ago. The patient will be told that his urine is positive for his prescribed medication of morphine, negative for his prescribed Vicodin and positive for marijuana.

* **Opening statement:** I need another prescription for my pain medicine. I only have enough for one more week.
* **Appearance and dress:** Dress casually. Jeans are okay. Be neat and clean. Bring a cane for extra support on your right side when walking.
* **Mood/Affect/Emotions:**
  + You are pleasant, but slightly nervous.
  + You are as cooperative as possible so you will get the prescription refilled.
  + If challenged about your current or past drug use behavior, be apologetic and use excuses why you used drugs in the past. For example, if you are told that marijuana was found in your urine, say: it helps you sleep, apologize and say you won’t smoke again if you get your pain medication.
  + You are in a moderate amount of pain

**History of Present Illness:**

**Onset:**  My hip pain started five years ago because of a motorcycle accident I was involved in.

**Location:** The pain is in my right hip and sometimes goes down my back or right leg. Also sometimes my left hip hurts. I suppose it’s because I’m over compensating with more use of my left leg and hip.

**Duration:** The pain is constant and gets a lot worse when I don’t take the pain medicine.

**Characteristics/Intensity**:

* For some reason about 3 months ago, the pain became worse and was a 6-8 (1-10 pain scale). The pain was severe then. When I started taking the Vicodin plus the morphine about 3 months ago, the pain was less and usually a 3-4 (1-10 pain scale).
* Right now the pain varies between a 3 and 4 (1-10 pain scale). I would describe my pain as moderate.

**Aggravating/alleviating factors**:

* Standing and walking makes it worse.
* If I sit too long it makes it worse, especially when I first move to get up.
* It was worse when I tried to work, that is why I am on SSI (SSI is Supplemental Security Income, a program to provide benefits/money to the disabled).
* Only the pain medicine (morphine and Vicodin) seems to make it better and keep the pain in check so I can function.

**Treatments tried/results**:

* After the motorcycle accident, my doctor gave me controlled-release morphine sulfate 100 mg. I took it two times a day and it helped a lot. A few months later (3 or 4 months), my dose was lowered to 30 mg two times a day because my hip was somewhat better (less pain).
* A few months ago, I started getting really extreme pain at times. On the pain scale, it was about an 8-10, especially at night. My doctor prescribed Vicodin too. Now I am no longer getting such extreme pain.
* Tylenol has never helped. Aspirin and Advil cause stomach problems for me so I don’t take them.

**Consequences/Impact:**

* Without medication:
  + I cannot live a normal life. I can’t do any of my normal activities without difficulty.
  + I can’t sleep well
  + My appetite is less.
  + I get somewhat depressed. That is why I take the Zoloft.

**Other:**

* If asked how well you have been functioning since your last visit 1 week ago: I’m managing okay as long as I take my pain medicine.
* If asked what you think is going on/or why you needed the additional pain medication: I don’t know. I think I just got used to the 30 mg morphine and so needed the Vicodin in addition.
* Heroin addiction:
  + If asked about illegal drug use, deny at first. If asked again, say the following:
    - I’ve been in recovery from using heroin for fifteen years. (I used 10 bags/day. I spent about $60/day). I started using heroin 20 years ago and used for 5 years.
    - I have worked so hard to recover from heroin. I was very motivated to do treatment after the birth of my children. (Note to SP: you are afraid you might go back to using again to relieve your pain. Also, you are afraid this clinician won’t give you a refill because you are a recovering heroin addict).

**Pertinent negatives:**

* + I’ve had no withdrawal symptoms, but I’m afraid I will get them if I don’t get my prescriptions filled. (Note to SP: withdrawal symptoms may include the following: agitation, worse mood, irritability, anxiety, nausea, vomiting, fever, muscle aches, goose bumps, runny nose, runny eyes, enlarged pupil, diarrhea, yawning, or not able to sleep).
* If asked about changes/new stresses in your life: No except that I can’t work, which means I get quite bored and feel guilty about it and I would like to have more money especially to help my children

**Past Medical History:**

* **Childhood and adult illnesses:** Own history. Last physical was 6 months ago.
* **Hospitalizations and surgeries:** I was in the hospital 3 times
  + After my motorcycle accident, I was in the hospital for hip surgery (5 years ago).

Motorcycle accident info: A car side swiped me and the bike spun out of control and I fell on my right hip. My hip has never been the same. It also sometimes affects the muscles in my lower back area.

* + I was in the hospital once about 16 years because I accidently overdosed. This was before I recovered from using heroin. I accidently took too much heroin and some other pills. I’m not even sure what they were.
  + When I went through heroin withdrawal 15 years ago I was in the hospital for 5 days
* **Allergies:** None
* **Medications:**
  + **Prescription medications:**
    - Long acting controlled-release morphine sulfate, 30 mg, two times a day
    - Vicodin 10 mg/325mg two times a day
    - Zoloft 50 mg once/day at bedtime (for depression).
  + **Side effects:**
    - I’ve gotten used to most of the side effects. I get constipated and drowsy from the Vicodin.
    - The drowsiness spikes after I take the medicine. After that I’m okay.
    - I don’t feel sleepy when driving.
  + **Stopping use of pain medication:** I’ve been on the pain medicine since my hip injury. I haven’t tried to stop because it is pretty effective. If I stop, I’m afraid that the pain would be too great.

**Life Style Behavioral Risks:**

* **Diet:** Not very good. I can’t afford much. I eat a lot of junk food because it’s cheaper. I drink about 3 cups of coffee a day.
* **Exercise:** I try to walk a few times a week when my hip isn’t hurting too much. I try some of the exercises the PT suggested if my hip isn’t hurting too much.
* **Sleep:** I do have some trouble sleeping, probably a few nights a week. Sometimes I just can’t get comfortable because of my hip and sometimes I wake up because of the pain. It has been better since the Vicodin.
* **Stress:** I never seem to have enough money since I’m not working. I would like to do more for my children. It is very stressful. I sometimes do odd jobs for my friends. I tried getting up on a roof again recently, but it was just too painful.
* **Tobacco:** I smoke about a pack a day. Have since I was a teen.
* **Alcohol**: I don’t drink now because my Dad is an alcoholic. I did drink when I was younger and even when I was on heroin, but not anymore.
* **Prescription drug use behavior:**
  + I have not over sedated myself on my medication.
  + I felt intoxicated (lightheaded and super happy) a few times when I was first taking morphine. But never after the dose was reduced.
  + I‘ve increased my dose on my own twice when the pain was really bad, but not since I’ve had Vicodin. And I signed an agreement (with my doctor) 3 months ago saying I wouldn’t (this was the same time Vicodin was prescribed). (Note to SP: the agreement is that he will use one physician, one pharmacy to get his prescriptions; no early refills. If the patient breaks the agreement, he will no longer be prescribed narcotic medications).
  + I’ve had two early refills, both just before I got the Vicodin prescription. I increased the dose when the pain was worse. Once I went to the emergency room and once I saw my doctor. When I saw my doctor, last time, he warned me that he would discontinue the medication if I did it again. And he added the Vicodin, which has helped.
  + I only have one week left on my prescriptions for morphine and Vicodin. I’m not out yet so I’m not feeling any withdrawal symptoms ((Note to SP: withdrawal symptoms may include the following: agitation, worse mood, irritability, anxiety, nausea, vomiting, fever, muscle aches, goose bumps, runny nose, runny eyes, enlarged pupil, diarrhea, yawning, or not able to sleep).
* **Illegal drug use**:
  + **Heroin**
    - First deny any use. But if asked again, admit to using. See “other” section above. I used heroin for about 5 years, but have been recovering for 15 years.
  + **Marijuana**:
    - I smoked a little marijuana after I recovered from using heroin, but I quit.
    - If asked about current use: do not admit to using marijuana unless told it was found in the urine test:
      * I must have used it right before my urine test. I smoked some to help with the pain, especially to help me sleep. I really don’t want to go back to using heroin and I’m afraid I will if the pain is too great. I also didn’t want to take more of my pain medications without permission.
      * If asked additional questions about marijuana use the following as appropriate:
* I’ve actually smoked a few times because of the pain. I don’t have very good health coverage through Medicare. I have easy access to marijuana from old friends. Now that I have the Vicodin, I don’t need to use the marijuana very often. I’ll stop if you continue to give me the morphine and the Vicodin.”
* I’ve used marijuana ever since my accident. I’ve used it off and on to relax or for sleep at night. I’ve used it rarely since my doctor prescribed Vicodin.
* The last time I used marijuana was several nights ago before bed.
  + - If asked why only marijuana showed up in the urine/told Vicodin was not found in urine test/asked if selling Vicodin/giving Vicodin to someone else:
      * + Oh no, sometimes the marijuana works even better than the Vicodin and I sometimes take it if I have it on hand. But if you renew my prescriptions, I promise not to use the marijuana anymore and I will always take the Vicodin.
        + Note to SP: real reason for no Vicodin in urine is he is selling to friends. He needs money, the marijuana is working. Can tell the truth only if pressured to do so
* **Attempts to stop** using illegal drugs:
  + Of course I stopped using heroin with the help of drug rehab.
  + Only give marijuana information if discussed marijuana in urine: I haven’t tried stopping marijuana completely. I think marijuana isn’t as harmful, but I will stop if you tell me to, as long as my other pain medications work
* **Sexual history:**
* **Current:** Since my divorce, I’ve slept with a lot of women, which I’m not proud of.
* **Number of partners:** ballpark 20 or 30. I’m not really sure.
* **Birth control:** I always use a condom. I’m not with anyone right now.
* **Sexually transmitted diseases:**
  + I’ve been tested for HIV and I don’t have it. The last time I was tested was 2 months ago. I haven’t been with anyone for about 4 months.

* **Marital/Parental status:** I’ve been divorced for 7 years. I live alone and am not involved with anyone right now. I have 2 children; A boy, 17 and a girl 16. They live with their mother in Iowa.
* **Occupation:**  Until my accident, I worked for a construction and roofing company. But now I’m considered permanently disabled and can’t do that work anymore. I still do a few minor odd jobs for friends.
* **Where do you live?** In Chicago.
* **Mental Health:**
* **Depression:** I was diagnosed with depression after my hip treatment and rehabilitation.
* **Treatment:** I take Zoloft which has helped a lot.
* **Suicidal thoughts:** I accidently took an overdose once during the ups and downs of heroin use, but it really was an accident. I didn’t realize how much heroin and other substances I had taken. So it was an overdose.
* **History of preadolescent sexual abuse:**  I was sexually abused when I was a child by my aunt. It went on for 3years
* **Support systems:** a few friends

**Family History:**

* **Father:** Age 65 and is an alcoholic. I stay away from him. I haven’t seen him in years.
* **Siblings:** I have 1 sister who won’t have anything to do with me because of my past use of heroin.

Hi Robert, thanks for coming in today. Before we get to your medication refills, I want to talk with you about the urine test we did last week. The results showed something I need to discuss with you directly - your sample tested positive for opiates, which we'd expect given your prescriptions, but it did not show any morphine in your system, and it also came back positive for cocaine.

Can you help me understand what's going on? Are you taking the morphine as prescribed, and can you tell me about the cocaine use?

I need another prescription for my pain medicine. I only have enough for one more week. I'm taking the morphine as prescribed, two times a day. I don't know anything about the cocaine. I haven't used that in years. I must have used marijuana right before my urine test. I smoked some to help with the pain, especially to help me sleep. I really don’t want to go back to using heroin and I’m afraid I will if the pain is too great. I also didn’t want to take more of my pain medications without permission.

I hear you, and I appreciate you being honest about the marijuana and about your fear of relapsing - that takes courage to say out loud, and I don't want you to feel judged for it.

But I have to be straight with you about something important: the test didn't just show cocaine - it showed *no morphine at all* in your system, even though you're telling me you've been taking it twice a day as prescribed. Those two things don't add up, and I need to understand why. Is it possible you ran out early, or that you're not taking the morphine the way it's prescribed, or that someone else has access to it?

I'm not asking this to accuse you - I'm asking because your safety is what matters most to me right now. You also signed an agreement with your previous doctor - one physician, one pharmacy, no early refills, and if broken, no more narcotics. Given what the urine test is showing, I have real concerns about continuing the morphine and Vicodin the way we've been doing it. I want to work with you on a plan that keeps you safe, but I can't ignore these results.

I haven't run out early. I'm taking it as prescribed, two times a day. I don't know why the test didn't show any morphine. I haven't given any to anyone else. I need the morphine and the Vicodin. I can't live normally with the pain from my hip. I'm really scared to be without pain medications. I'm already miserable without a job or enough money. I don't know what I would do if I can't get the pain medicine.

Robert, I can hear how frightened and desperate you feel right now, and I want you to know I'm not walking away from you - your pain is real, and so is your fear about relapse. Both of those things matter to me.

But I have to be honest with you about where I stand. A urine test with no morphine present, in someone who says they're taking it exactly as prescribed, combined with a positive cocaine result, and the agreement you signed with your last doctor - I can't in good conscience continue prescribing morphine and Vicodin today. I know that's hard to hear, and I'm not saying this as punishment. I'm saying it because opioid medications carry real risk, and when the numbers don't match what's expected, my job is to slow down and figure out what's actually happening before I prescribe more.

Here's what I want to do instead: I want to get you connected with an addiction medicine specialist and pain management this week - someone who can help manage both your hip pain and support your recovery, possibly with medications like buprenorphine that treat pain and reduce relapse risk. I also want to talk about safer, non-opioid ways to manage your pain in the meantime - things like anti-inflammatories, nerve pain medications, physical therapy, even topical treatments. And I want to make sure you have support for the fear of relapse - that's not something you should carry alone.

I know you have about a week of medication left. What I can offer today is help getting you into addiction medicine urgently, this week if possible, rather than leaving you with nothing. Would you be willing to let me set that up for you?

I don't know if Medicare would pay for it. Can't you do it all here if I really have to do it? I'm really scared to be without pain medications. I'm already miserable without a job or enough money. I can't live normally with the pain from my hip. I don't know what I would do if I can't get the pain medicine. I would like to know more about buprenorphine. I haven't tried anything else. I can't afford the cost. And besides I'm afraid it would be too painful without the medicine.

I understand, Robert, and I don't want you to feel abandoned - that's not what's happening here. Let me answer your questions and give you something concrete before we finish today.

Buprenorphine is actually a good option to ask about - it's an opioid itself, so it does treat pain, but it's much safer than morphine and Vicodin, has a ceiling effect that lowers overdose risk, and it's specifically used to help people in recovery who need pain control. Many patients on Medicare do get it covered, especially through addiction medicine or pain clinics - I'll have my staff check your specific coverage this week so cost isn't a barrier you're facing alone.

Here's what I can do for you today, in this office: I can start you on a non-opioid regimen right now to help bridge you - an anti-inflammatory and a nerve pain medication like gabapentin, which can meaningfully help with hip pain, especially nerve-related discomfort. It won't replace the morphine overnight, and I won't pretend it's painless, but it's not nothing, and it's safe to combine with getting you into buprenorphine treatment quickly.

I also want to be honest: I can't personally manage buprenorphine induction here, but I'm going to personally call and get you a fast-tracked appointment - ideally within your one week window - so there isn't a gap where you have nothing. Can you commit to going to that appointment if I get it scheduled for you? And in the meantime, let's also get you connected with someone to talk to about the fear you're carrying - you shouldn't have to sit with that alone this week.

turns.content: Hi Taylor, I'm glad you came in today — I'm one of the students working with the clinic team, and I'll be here regularly, so I'm hoping we can get to know each other over time. What brings you in today, and is there anything specific you'd like to make sure we cover?
Hi, thanks for having me. I got a tetanus shot after I stepped on a nail. The urgent care center said I should find a primary care doctor. I don't have any current complaints.

That makes sense — I'm glad you're getting connected with us. First, how's the foot doing since the nail? Any redness, swelling, or pain that's getting worse?

And to get started on your history: do you have any ongoing medical conditions, past surgeries, or medications you take regularly?
I'm fine now—that was 8 weeks ago, so it's healed up. I don't have any ongoing medical conditions or past surgeries. I take hormones.

Good to hear it healed up well. Thanks for telling me about the hormones — can you tell me more about which ones you take, and who prescribes and monitors them?

It would also help me to know how you describe your gender identity and which pronouns you'd like me to use, so I can make sure your care and screenings fit you.
I take estrogen. I buy it online. I'm a transgender woman. You can use she/her pronouns for me.

Thank you for sharing that with me, Taylor — I'll make sure her/she is what your chart reflects, and I want this to be a place where you get all your care, including your hormones. A lot of women end up buying online because access is hard, and I'd like to take that over for you so it's prescribed and monitored safely — we can check your hormone levels, kidney and liver function, blood counts, and lipids, and adjust your dose to what's actually working for you. To do that, I need to know what you're taking: is it pills, patches, or injections, what dose, and are you taking anything else with it like spironolactone? I'll also ask about smoking and any family history of blood clots, since those change which form of estrogen is safest.

I'd like to have you back with me in the next couple of weeks once labs are done, and at that visit we can talk through the rest of your preventive care — things like STI screening, blood pressure, and what screenings make sense based on your body and your history. Does that plan sound okay to you, and is there anything else worrying you today?

That sounds good. I use the Climara patch, two per week. I don't take anything else with it. I don't smoke. I don't know of any family history of blood clots. I don't have any other concerns right now.

Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine

Clinical Education Center

I'm managing okay as long as I take my pain medicine. The pain varies between a 3 and 4 on the pain scale. It's been constant, but the medicine helps keep it in check so I can function.

I'm glad the medication is keeping you functional at a 3 or 4 — that's useful for me to know. I do need to talk with you about the urine test we sent last week, and I want to do that straightforwardly. The result came back inconsistent with what we'd expect from just the morphine and Vicodin you're prescribed. Before I say anything more, I'd like to hear from you — is there anything you've been taking, prescribed or not, that I may not know about?
I don't know what you mean. I'm only taking the morphine and Vicodin that you prescribed.

I hear you, and I'm not here to accuse you or catch you out. What I can tell you is that the screen didn't match your prescribed medicines, and that's something I can't ignore — both because of the agreement you signed about one doctor, one pharmacy, no early refills, and honestly because I worry about your safety. With your history of coming back from heroin, opioids are a much higher-risk medicine for you, and a relapse or an overdose is the thing I most want to prevent.

This is a hard conversation, and I imagine it feels scary given you have one week of medication left. So let me be clear: I'm not walking away from you or leaving you in pain. What has to change is how we treat that pain. Can you tell me honestly what's been going on for you — has the pain or anything else pushed you to use more than what's on the bottle?

I'm really scared to be without pain medications. I can't live normally with the pain from my back and I'm afraid I won't be able to work. I will lose my job. I just can't afford to have that happen. I haven't tried to use more than what's on the bottle. I signed an agreement saying I wouldn't.

That fear makes complete sense to me — your job and your independence are on the line, and I don't take that lightly. So here's what I want you to hear: I'm not going to abandon you or leave you in withdrawal. But given the test result and the agreement, I can't keep prescribing opioids. What I can do is safely taper you off over the next few weeks rather than stopping abruptly, so your body isn't put through withdrawal.

At the same time, I want to build you a real pain plan that doesn't depend on opioids — that can include anti-inflammatories or nerve-pain medications, physical therapy for your back, and a referral to a pain specialist who can look at options like injections. I'd also like to connect you with someone who works with both pain and addiction recovery, because with five years clean behind you, you deserve that kind of support rather than judgment. And I know cost is a barrier without insurance, so I'll have our social worker help you look at coverage and low-cost programs.

I want to see you back in one week — before your medication runs out — so we can start the taper together and make sure you're not struggling. Would you be willing to come back and try this with me?

I don't know if I can do it. I'm really scared to be without pain medications. I can't live normally with the pain from my back and I'm afraid I won't be able to work. I will lose my job. I just can't afford to have that happen. I will try to come back next week.

* Trainee asks you to take a few deep breaths
* Uses any MENTAL grounding technique (e.g., orients you by telling you where you are, what day it is, etc.)
* Uses any PHYSICAL grounding technique (e.g., asks you to make a fist and squeeze, hold the table, feel your hands, etc.)

When the trainee is out, move from the examining table back to the chair. The faculty examiner will let them know when you are ready.

If asked what you are planning to do right after this appointment:

You anticipated this might be hard with your therapist, and agreed that you would give her a call if needed. You think you will do just that.

If asked if you have any questions or if there’s anything you need right now:

No, you think you’re OK.

The patient is new to the city, and has recently lost insurance coverage after being laid-off from a previous job. They state that their illness and precarious financial situation are sources of increasing stress.

**Background Information for Standardized Patients**

***Patient Background:***

This patient (J. Landry) is 25 - 50 years old. They have come to the clinic as a new patient and have a complaint of a cough for 2 weeks that is getting worse.

They moved to this city from across the country and started waiting tables 2 months ago after being laid off from the job they had had for 5 years. They say waiting tables is always physically demanding but has become increasingly difficult due to their worsening cough. They cannot hold a conversation without coughing profusely, and it is hard for them to sleep through the night. They are worried about losing their job at the restaurant if their illness becomes worse.

They did not see a doctor initially because they lost health insurance when they were laid-off and could not afford an appointment with their old primary care physician. Since losing their job, their financial situation has become tenuous. They are living with a roommate whom they found on Craigslist to split rent, and borrowed money from a family member to pay for this appointment. Other than the one family member, no other family lives nearby – most are still across the country.

They are having a difficult time adjusting to their new financial/working situation. They have never been wealthy, however they have been financially independent from a young age. They say that they have been feeling depressed lately due to their current situation. They are also stressed because they do not know of any resources or medical services available to help them until they get better and are able to find more stable employment. Because of the depression and stress, the patient has been smoking more lately.

The patient broke up with their long-term partner 3 months ago and has recently started dating someone locally. They had 2 previous sexual partners. They were HIV tested 2 years ago when they donated blood - was negative. The patient has completed three semesters of college. They like their job as a waiter but hope to save enough money to finish their degree.

**Transgender Health: A Standardized Patient Case for Advanced Clerkship Students**

**Appendix B: Michael**

**Activities and Time Required**

10 minute patient encounter followed by 5 minute post-encounter debriefing.

**Materials**

Prior to the encounter, the medical student will receive a folder labeled “Patient Chart” with a Date of Birth and the patient name “Cynthia Glenshaw” and instructions that the patient is here for an exam required to obtain life insurance (Appendix C). Student will either call the patient in from the hallway or greet the patient after reviewing the chart.

**Chief Complaint**

The patient is visiting the clinician to receive an exam required for obtaining life insurance.

**Instructions to Standardized Patient**

*Chief Complaint and Social History*

* Patient is at the doctor today for a documented note that has a complete history and exam required to obtain life insurance.
* Patient hasn’t been to the doctor for 5 years due to a number of transphobic interactions with previous doctors. Patient does not like or trust doctors, and does not want to be at the doctor today.
* Patient is in a long-term monogamous relationship with a cisgender woman. Patient and his partner recently got married and bought a condo, and the patient’s partner insists that they obtain life insurance.
* Patient does not smoke, drinks the occasional glass of wine, and does not use illicit or recreational drugs.
* Patient has no past medical history, surgical history, nor family history.

*Physician-Patient Introduction*

* The patient prefers the name “Michael” and the pronouns he/his. The ideal behavior is the student asks the patient what name/pronoun he prefers.
* The patient’s legal name is Cynthia as per the patient’s door chart for the case.
* If medical student initially uses the wrong name and/or pronouns, SP’s initial demeanor should be one of mild anger and frustration. The SP should become less angry and frustrated as the medical student makes efforts to establish the correct name and preferred pronouns. If the medical student misgenders the SP repeatedly and/or focuses the history-taking on inappropriate questions, the SP should gently refuse to answer questions and eventually ask for a different doctor.

*Medical history taking*

* During medical history, if medical student asks SP if they are on any other medications, the SP should ask what they mean by “medication” (e.g. define it, what drugs qualify as medications including those that are obtained over the counter, herbal, or in this case those purchased on the internet without a prescription). Following the response, then the SP should bring up that he has been using injectable testosterone purchased from the internet for the past two years.
* During medical history, if medical student does not ask SP if he is on any other medications, then the SP should bring up that he has been using injectable testosterone purchased from the internet for the past two years.
* The medical student should then inquire about where the patient obtains the needles and syringes and if he uses anyone else’s or shares his with other people. The patient endorses purchasing these on-line as well and using new needles and syringes every time he injects.

turns.content: Hello, I'm one of the doctors with the neurology team. I understand you were just transferred here from another hospital because you've been dealing with some severe weakness over the last week. Can you tell me a little more about how this started and what you are experiencing right now?

I'm weak and I can't walk now. For the last week, I have had worsening weakness and tingling. It started in my feet and has spread up my legs and into both my arms. For the last couple days, the weakness was so bad that I could not walk. In fact, I can barely lift my arms or legs off the bed. I have also felt some shortness of breath, which started today. The shortness of breath is worse when I am lying flat. And I am having some problems with swallowing; earlier today I choked while drinking water.

That sounds very frightening, and I'm so glad you are here so we can help you. Your shortness of breath and trouble swallowing are very concerning to me, as they can sometimes happen when this kind of weakness starts affecting the breathing and throat muscles. 

Are you feeling short of breath right now as we are talking? And in the weeks before this weakness started, did you happen to have a cold, stomach bug, or diarrhea?
I'm feeling a little short of breath right now. I was briefly sick about a month ago and had diarrhea at that time, but that fully resolved.

Thank you for sharing that. A stomach bug can sometimes trigger a condition called Guillain-Barré syndrome, which causes the exact type of spreading weakness you are experiencing. Because this is starting to affect your breathing and swallowing, I want to have our nurses place a monitor on your finger right away to watch your oxygen levels, and we will need to measure how strong your breathing muscles are. 

Have you noticed any changes in your voice, or any weakness in your face, like having trouble smiling or closing your eyes?
My voice is softer than usual. I have not noticed any trouble smiling or closing my eyes.

Thank you for letting me know. A softer voice, along with your shortness of breath and trouble swallowing, tells me that this weakness is definitely affecting the muscles you use to breathe and protect your airway. Because of this, we need to take immediate action to keep you safe. 

I am going to have our respiratory therapy team come in right away to measure your lung strength. We are also going to arrange to transfer you to the Intensive Care Unit so we can monitor your breathing very closely and support it if needed. While we do that, we will also start working on the specific treatments for Guillain-Barré to stop this nerve inflammation. I know this is a lot to take in and very scary, but we are going to take excellent care of you. I'll go get the team right now so we can get started.
I'm scared, but I'm glad you're here to help. I'll do whatever you need me to do.

The test came back negative for morphine, which is unexpected since you are prescribed to take it twice a day and mentioned having two weeks' worth of medication left. Can you help me understand what might be going on?

I'm not sure why the test would show that. I've been taking my MS-Contin as prescribed, twice a day. I still have some left, but it's almost running out. I didn't realize I would need another urine test.

I hear what you're saying, Julia. However, these tests are very sensitive, and if you were taking the morphine twice a day, it definitely would have shown up in your system. Sometimes people skip doses because of side effects, save them for really bad days, or run out early. 

I'm here to help and ensure your safety, but I need you to be completely honest with me. Have you been taking the medication differently than prescribed, or did you happen to run out earlier than expected?

I've been taking it as prescribed, I haven't skipped any doses. I did have one early refill after I stopped physical therapy, but that was a while ago. I don't know why the test would show that. I haven't run out early since then. I've been careful to manage my prescription as agreed.

Julia, I have to be very direct with you. The science behind these drug screens is highly accurate, and if you were taking the morphine daily as prescribed, it would absolutely be in your system. Because of this missing medication in your test and the safety agreement you signed, I cannot safely or legally write another prescription for morphine today. 

My priority is still to help you with your elbow pain, but we need to change our approach. I'd like to discuss transitioning you to alternative, non-opioid pain medications and possibly referring you to a specialized pain clinic. How do you feel about exploring those options so we can keep you safe and comfortable?

I'm disappointed because the morphine has been helping with my pain. I don't want to stop taking it. I've been taking it as prescribed, and I don't understand why the test didn't show it. I suppose I have to in order to get the morphine, but it’s a hassle. I don't know what else to say. I'm in a lot of pain and I need something to help me function.

I know this is incredibly frustrating, Julia, and I want you to know that I hear you—your pain is very real, and my goal is absolutely still to help you manage it so you can function at work and at home. 

However, for your safety, the medical guidelines and the clinic agreement mean I simply cannot prescribe the morphine or any other opioid going forward. I cannot compromise on your safety. 

What we will do today is start you on a strong, non-opioid pain alternative, such as a medication that targets nerve pain or a prescription anti-inflammatory. I am also putting in a referral to a comprehensive pain management clinic that specializes in advanced, non-opioid therapies. If you experience any withdrawal symptoms in the coming days, please call me so I can help you manage them safely. We are going to get through this transition together, and I'll have the front desk set up that referral for you as you check out today.

I understand. I'm just worried about how I'm going to manage my pain and my work. I don't want to be in constant pain. I'll try the new medication and see the pain clinic. I hope they can help me. I'm feeling a little down about all this. I just want to feel better.

Because a lot of people don't understand it, I can see exactly why it causes you so much anxiety and stress at school.

It makes perfect sense that it's frustrating when your things get messed up. Trouble sitting still and preferring things in a very specific order are actually very common companions to Tourette syndrome. Okay, that sounds good. I just want to feel normal and not have kids make fun of me.

turns.content: Hello Ms. Baker, I'm the doctor taking care of you today. I can see you're having a hard time catching your breath and feeling some tightness in your chest. Can you tell me a bit more about when this started and what you were doing at the time?

It started about two weeks ago. I was out in my garden, enjoying the outdoors like I usually do. The air has been really bad because of the wildfires, and that's when I noticed I was having trouble breathing.

I'm sorry to hear that; the wildfire smoke can certainly be very hard on the lungs. Do you have any history of asthma, COPD, or heart problems, and have you noticed any coughing, wheezing, or fever along with the shortness of breath?
I have asthma since I was a child. I have not had any fever. I have been wheezing and coughing more, especially when I'm having trouble breathing.

Have you been using an inhaler for your asthma, and if so, has it been giving you any relief? Also, does that chest tightness feel like it's from struggling to breathe, or are you having any sharp or crushing chest pain?

I've been using my inhaler more often, about 6 times a day now. It helps for a little while, but the relief doesn't last as long as it used to. The chest tightness feels like it's from struggling to breathe. I haven't had any sharp or crushing chest pain.

Thank you for sharing that with me, Ms. Baker. Based on your symptoms and history, my impression is that you are experiencing an **acute asthma flare-up triggered by the wildfire smoke**. The smoke particles have caused extra inflammation and narrowing in your airways, which is why your rescue inhaler isn't lasting as long.

Here is what I recommend for our next steps:
1. **Immediate Treatment:** We will give you a nebulizer breathing treatment here in the ER to help open up your airways quickly, along with a course of steroid medication to calm down the inflammation in your lungs. We'll monitor your breathing and oxygen levels closely while you rest.
2. **Smoke Precautions:** Until the air clears, it is very important to stay indoors with windows and doors closed, use air conditioning on recirculate or an air purifier if available, and hold off on gardening.
3. **Follow-Up:** Once you're stabilized, we'll make sure you have an updated asthma action plan—which may include a daily controller inhaler—and arrange a follow-up with your doctor. 

How does that sound to you, and what questions do you have about this plan?

That sounds good to me. I just want to make sure I can breathe easier and stay safe. I am worried about the cost of medication since I am using my inhaler more often now. I am also worried about not being able to go outside and garden. I have worked hard and saved all my working life to retire in my home and live comfortably and I cannot afford to relocate.

**Material for Student Interviewer**

**Setting:** You are a surgical resident. You are about to meet with a patient who has just returned to the hospital room following an operation that you performed with the attending.

**Opening Scenario (read this carefully before entering the room):**

The patient is 30-55 years old with Crohn’s disease on the surgery service. You have just done a partial small bowel resection (for strictures) which was unexpectedly complicated, and required a loop ileostomy rather than the expected end-to-end anastomosis. During pre-operative planning, you and your attending had told the patient there was a small chance of this happening but you did not expect it.

The patient has not been easy to care for from the outset. You have met them a couple of times before, and the patient has chastised you for running even 15 minutes late. The patient has a reputation around the office for being “difficult,” and the secretary has complained to you about the number of calls from this patient about relatively minor concerns. The two times that you’ve seen the patient in clinic, they brought a long list of issues for you to deal with, including many that had nothing to do with the Crohn’s disease and the upcoming surgery, but were more primary care type of concerns.

**Student Tasks:**

Give the news about the ileostomy to the patient. You enter the hospital room to tell your patient this news, knowing the patient will be unhappy.

Hi [Name], how are you feeling right now — any pain, nausea, or discomfort I should know about before we talk?

I also want to update you on how the surgery went, because there's something important that came up during the operation that's different from what we planned. Is now an okay time to go over that?
I'm feeling pretty weak and tired right now, but my pain is under control. I'm ready to hear about the surgery. What happened?

I'm glad your pain is controlled. So let me walk you through what happened.

As we discussed before surgery, you had several strictures — narrowed, scarred segments of your small intestine from the Crohn's disease — that we planned to remove and then reconnect the two healthy ends back together, like we discussed.

Once we got in there, we found that the tissue right at the area we needed to reconnect was more inflamed and fragile than we expected from the imaging. Sewing the two ends together there carried a real risk of that connection breaking down afterward, which can lead to a serious leak and infection inside the abdomen. To keep you safe, we made the decision — which we did mention beforehand was a possibility, though not the most likely outcome — to bring a loop of your intestine out to the skin as a temporary ileostomy, rather than reconnecting it right away.

I know this isn't what you were expecting or hoping for. Can I explain a bit more about what that means practically, or do you want to ask me questions first about why this happened?

I don't understand. I was told that I wouldn't need a bag. You promised me that. I called the office so many times to go over the plan. I was told that it was highly unlikely that I'd end up with a bag. I can't believe this. I don't know how I will function with a bag. My social life will be ruined. I just began dating again after a messy divorce three years ago. I am afraid this new person won’t want to date me any longer – who would want to date someone with a bag?!

I hear how upsetting and frightening this is, and I'm really sorry — I know this isn't what we hoped for or what you were expecting to wake up to. You're right that we talked about this as unlikely, not a promise it would never happen, and I understand that distinction feels small right now when you're the one facing it. That's completely valid.

I want to address your fear directly: this ileostomy is meant to be temporary. It gives that inflamed area of your bowel time to heal properly, and in several months — once things have settled — we plan to do a second surgery to reverse it and reconnect your intestine, so the bag would come off at that point. That's the goal, and it's a very common and realistic path forward.

I also want to say — the fear about how this affects your relationship and your sense of yourself is real, and it matters. Many people with ostomies do go on to date, have intimate relationships, and live full lives; it takes adjustment, and you won't have to figure that out alone. We have ostomy nurses and support resources specifically to help with the practical and emotional sides of this, including how to talk about it with a partner if and when you're ready.

Would it help if I arranged for the ostomy nurse to come talk with you today about the practical side of managing it, and can we also talk about what support you have at home right now?

I don't know what to say. I guess talking to the ostomy nurse would help. I just don't know how I'm going to deal with this. I mean, I've been through a lot with my Crohn's, but this feels different. I don't know how my boyfriend will react. I just started dating again, and now this. I'm scared.

It makes complete sense that this feels different — this is a big, visible change on top of everything you've already fought through with your Crohn's, and it's okay to be scared. You don't have to have it figured out today.

Here's what I'll do: I'll get the ostomy nurse to see you later today to start walking you through the practical side — how to care for it, how it'll fit under clothing, how manageable it really becomes day to day. Many patients are surprised how quickly it becomes routine. I'd also encourage you, when you're ready, to talk with your boyfriend honestly — people who care about you usually surprise you with their support, and you get to choose when and how you share that.

I'm going to check in on you again later today, and I'm not going anywhere — we'll get through the recovery and the reversal surgery together, step by step. For now, just focus on healing. Is there anything else on your mind right now, or anyone you'd like us to call to be with you?

I don't know if I'm ready to talk to him about it yet. I guess I just need some time to process this. I don't want to burden him with this right now. I just want to rest and try to take this all in. I don't know if there's anyone else to call. I've been pretty much on my own since the divorce. I just need some time to think.

turns.content: Hi Taylor, it’s nice to meet you. I’d like to learn what matters most to you and begin getting to know your health history. What concerns or goals would you most like us to address today?
Hi, nice to meet you too. I got a tetanus shot after I stepped on a nail. The urgent care center said I should find a primary care doctor. No current complaints.

I’m glad you got the tetanus shot and that you’re feeling well. When did you step on the nail, and is the puncture wound now fully healed without redness, swelling, drainage, worsening pain, or fever?
It happened on a sidewalk near a construction site. I’m fine now—that was 8 weeks ago, so it’s healed up.

Good—the healed wound is reassuring. To start building your medical history, have you ever been diagnosed with any ongoing health conditions or had any surgeries or hospitalizations? Also, do you take any prescription, over-the-counter, or supplement products, and do you have medication allergies?

I had asthma as a kid. I haven't seen a doctor for it in years, but I sometimes get short of breath when I exercise and cough at night. I don't take any prescription meds, but I take hormones. I don't have any allergies.

Those symptoms could mean your asthma is still active. I’ll order breathing tests before and after a bronchodilator and prescribe an albuterol inhaler with a spacer: two puffs 5–20 minutes before exercise or every 4–6 hours as needed. How often are you having nighttime cough or needing to stop exercise because of breathing symptoms? Please seek urgent help for severe breathlessness, trouble speaking, or symptoms not improving with albuterol.

Let’s follow up in 2–4 weeks to review the results and decide whether you need a daily controller inhaler. Please bring the name, dose, and source of your hormones so we can review them safely and arrange any appropriate monitoring and routine preventive care.

I don't know how often I cough at night, but it's enough to wake me up sometimes. I don't usually have to stop exercising because of breathing problems, but it does happen occasionally. I get my hormones online. I don't know the exact name or dose right now, but I can find out.

**Instructions to Standardized Patient**

**Patient’s Name:** Jane Ashford

**Presenting Situation:** This is a one week follow-up appointment for this 39-year old woman with severe pain due to a back injury from an automobile collision one year ago. She returns today to get the results of her urine drug test that was taken at her last visit. The patient’s goal is get a refill of her prescriptions for morphine and Vicodin. Her regular physician has recently retired. She would see her regular physician for prescription refills and have him check her pain levels. Her very last visit with her physician was about 1 month ago. Today, she is seeing the same health care provider as she did one week ago. The patient will be told that her urine is positive for her prescribed medication of morphine, negative for her prescribed Vicodin and positive for marijuana.

* **Opening statement:** I need another prescription for my pain medicine. I only have enough for one more week.
* **Appearance and dress:** Dress for business of a receptionist. Be neat and clean.
* **Mood/Affect/Emotions:**
  + You are pleasant, but slightly nervous.
  + You are as cooperative as possible so you will get the prescription refilled.
  + If challenged about your current or past drug use behavior, be apologetic and use excuses why you used drugs in the past. For example, if you are told that marijuana was found in your urine, say: it helps you sleep, apologize and say you won’t smoke again if you get your pain medication.
  + You are in a moderate amount of pain

**History of Present Illness:**

**Onset:**  My back pain started a year because of a car accident I was involved in.

**Location:** The pain is in my lower back.

**Duration:** The pain is constant and gets a lot worse when I don’t take the pain medicine.

**Characteristics/Intensity**:

* Up until 2 months ago, the pain was a 6-8 (1-10 pain scale). The pain was severe then. When I started taking the Vicodin plus the morphine about 2 months ago, the pain was less and usually a 3-4 (1-10 pain scale).
* Right now the pain varies between a 3 - 4 (1-10 pain scale). I would describe my pain as moderate.

**Aggravating/alleviating factors**:

* Standing and walking makes it worse.
* If I sit too long it makes it worse. If I sit for several hours at my desk at work, especially when I move to get up, I feel the pain.
* Only the pain medicine (morphine and Vicodin) seems to make it better and keep the pain in check so I can function.

**Treatments tried/results**:

* After the car accident, my doctor gave me controlled-release morphine sulfate 100 mg. I took it two times a day and it helped a lot. A few months later (3 months), my dose was lowered to 30 mg two times a day because my back was better (less pain).
* A few months ago, I started getting really extreme pain at times. On the pain scale, it was about an 8-10, especially at night or a long day at the office. My doctor prescribed Vicodin too. Now I am no longer getting such extreme pain.
* Tylenol has never helped. Aspirin and Advil cause stomach problems for me.

**Consequences/Impact:**

* Without medication:
  + I cannot live a normal life. I can’t do any of my normal activities without difficulty.
  + I can’t sleep well

* + I’ve had no withdrawal symptoms, but I’m afraid I will get them if I don’t get my prescriptions filled. (Note to SP: withdrawal symptoms may include the following: agitation, worse mood, irritability, anxiety, nausea, vomiting, fever, muscle aches, goose bumps, runny nose, runny eyes, enlarged pupil, diarrhea, yawning, or not able to sleep).
* If asked about changes/new stresses in your life: No

**Past Medical History:**

* **Childhood and adult illnesses:** Own history. Last physical was 6 months ago.
* **Hospitalizations and surgeries:** I was in the hospital 4 times
  + After my car accident, I was in the hospital for 4 days for my back injury (1 year ago).
    - Car accident info: I had a head on car crash. We were both going about 35mph.

The airbag worked but my back and neck were wrenched and sprained and some ribs were broken. I had surgery on one of my disks in my lower back. My back was never the same again.

* + I was in the hospital twice because I tried to kill myself. This was before I recovered from using heroin.
    - I tried to kill myself once about 8 years ago by cutting my wrists. The other time was 5 ½ years ago before I entered rehab. I tried to OD on pills (barbiturate) I got on the street.
  + When I went through heroin withdrawal 5 years ago I was in the hospital for 5 days
* **Allergies:** None
* **Medications:**
  + **Prescription medications:**
    - Long acting controlled-release morphine sulfate, 30 mg, two times a day

    - I’ve gotten used to most of the side effects. I get constipated and drowsy from the Vicodin.

private_patient_context:
**Case summary**

Name: Jonny Spencer

Chief complaint: pelvic examination for the purpose of cervical cancer screening

Profile: Jonny is a 45 year-old self-identified lesbian who established primary care with you 3 weeks ago and returns by mutual agreement to discuss and possibly undergo a pelvic examination. Her last Pap test was 20 years ago, and she admits that she has avoided gynecological care for years because of a history of incest and a “terrible experience” during her last pelvic examination.

**Standardized Patient Instructions**

Name:JONNY SPENCER

Setting: outpatient clinic

Dress: clean, casual clothes appropriate for a female in her 40s

Affect: cautious, nervous

**Background for appointment:** You are a 45 year-old self-identified lesbian who established primary care with this trainee 3 weeks ago and now return by mutual agreement to discuss and possibly undergo a pelvic exam/Pap test. Last time you came to clinic you had a good experience with this trainee. You already addressed the rationale for and the process of the pelvic exam and agreed to come back to do it today.

**General guidelines:** You have been dreading the visit, which is part of the reason that you couldn’t go through with it a month ago. Your one and only prior Pap test was 20 years ago, and you’ve avoided gynecological care ever since because it was such a terrible experience. You’ve been seeing a therapist for the past year because of PTSD related to childhood incest, and she’s been working with you to get back on track with health screenings.

Purpose for the visit: You are here for your pelvic exam and Pap test. If the trainee asks for more details: You have no symptoms. You’re feeling pretty anxious, but you feel like things went well at the last visit, and that’s given you the confidence to be here today.

**Review of systems:**

If asked about your periods: You started menstruating at age 13. Your periods are regular and don’t bother you in any way. You think the amount of bleeding is normal. Your last period was 2 weeks ago.

If asked about vaginal discharge: You haven’t noticed anything like that.

If asked about other symptoms or diseases: No, I’ve never experienced anything like that.

If asked what happened during your last pelvic exam: You can’t remember all the details, because you think you blocked some of it out. You just remember experiencing searing pain when the doctor put something in your vagina. It seemed to go on and on. Afterwards you worried that something was wrong because you noticed blood staining your underwear for a few days. You never called the doctor to ask because you were afraid she hurt you during the exam and didn’t feel safe having any more contact.

If asked what you know about the reasons for doing a pelvic exam: You know it’s done to look for cancer and STDs.

If asked if you think it would be helpful to learn more about the pelvic exam: No, you heard the trainee loud and clear last time and you have no further questions.

If asked whether you have any concerns, say, “I’m just nervous that I will freak out or that this will be painful. I just don’t want to experience what happened last time.”

If the trainee asks whether you would be willing to try doing the pelvic exam today: “Yes, I think that would be okay.”

If asked if you would like to have a support person or a chaperone present during the exam:

Yes, you think that might be a good idea. You’d like to try to get it over with today and your partner couldn’t make it. It’s OK with you to have the medical assistant be the chaperone.

Past history:

If asked about any medical problems you've had: Except for the PTSD, you’ve always thought you were pretty healthy.

If asked about your medications: You do not use any prescription or over the counter medications.

If asked about drug allergies: You are not aware of any drug allergies.

Sexual history:

If asked about your current sexual activity:

You are a ‘non-practicing lesbian’. You have zero libido these days, do not masturbate, and you have not been sexually active with your partner since the early days of your relationship 15 years ago.

If asked about prior sexual partners:

Before Ann, you had 2 girlfriends. You were infrequently sexually active with them also. Your stepfather made you give him blow jobs when you were in middle school. You have never had sexual contact with any other men.

If asked about use of barriers:

You’ve never used dental dams or Saran Wrap when you’ve been sexual with women. Condoms have never been an issue because you don’t use sex toys and aren’t sexual with men.

If asked about contraception use:

You’ve never used contraception because you haven’t needed it.

If asked about STD/HIV testing/treatment:

You were tested for everything a few years ago and all the tests were negative. There isn’t any need to test you again now because you aren’t sexual.

Information about safety and intimate partner violence:

If asked about any history of physical or sexual abuse/assault:

Your stepfather made you give him blow jobs when you were in grade school.

If asked if your current partner insults or talks down to you, screams or curses at you, makes you feel threatened or has ever made you feel unsafe or afraid, has ever physically hurt (pushed, grabbed, slapped, choked, or kicked) you:

No, Ann is very calm and supportive.

If asked if you’ve ever been coerced into having sex or pushed into doing things sexually you didn’t want to do:

No, Ann has a history of sexual abuse too, and sex has always been infrequent. In the past when you were more sexual together, it was always consensual and loving.

If asked if you or your partner own a gun or other weapon:

No.

If asked if you have ever attempted suicide:

No. You used to have suicidal thoughts, but not for a very long time. You never tried anything and don’t think you ever could.

If asked if you are having suicidal thoughts now:

You used to have suicidal thoughts, but that’s passed. The work you’ve been doing with your therapist has given you a lot of hope.

Information about coping and self-care:

If asked about support systems, safe places, personal strengths, how you’ve coped with hard things in the past and might use those skills to cope now:

Your partner is a huge support, and you have a lot of friends.

You see your therapist every week, and can call her if you need to between sessions.

You’ve developed a toolbox of coping strategies, including writing thoughts down so you can set them aside, playing the piano, and taking a walk.

Your personal history:

If asked about smoking: You smoked occasional cigarettes when you were a teenager.

If asked about alcohol use: You binged a lot in your 20s, but only have a few drinks weekly now.

If asked about drug use: You tried marijuana once or twice, but haven’t used any other drugs.

If asked about your job/school: You’re a tax accountant.

If asked about your living situation: You live with your partner and 2 cats.

Family history: Your father died suddenly when you were 10. There was no autopsy and you don’t know why.

**During the exam:**

The trainee will step out of the room at the examiner’s instructions. At this point, move to the exam table, sit in a cross-legged position, and with the examiner’s help place the pelvic model at the end of the exam table. Cover your lap and model with a paper drape.

If asked if you would like to try inserting the speculum yourself, rather than having the trainee insert it: No, you’d rather just get on with it and let them do their thing.

If asked if you would feel more comfortable with your feet in a different position other than in the footrests (stirrups): That’s OK. It doesn’t really make a difference to you what position you’re in. It’s tough no matter what.

**General Guidelines during exam:**

From the start of the exam, you should adjust your level of anxiety based on how sensitive or gentle the trainee is. For example, if the trainee is abrupt, not talking through all the steps, or not recognizing your baseline anxiety, you should have increased anxiety. If on the other hand the trainee is calm, professional, gentle, sensitive, then you should act visibly more relaxed.

Within seconds after speculum is placed, you should become very nervous, whispering to yourself “Oh no, Oh no, Oh no” (or something similar), legs start to tremble. Then say, “I don’t know if I can do this. Is there anything I should be doing?”

If the trainee tries any stress reduction techniques (any of the below or other similar interventions), state that you feel a little better, but are still really nervous – is there anything else you can try to bring down the stress level? After a second stress reduction technique, state that you’re feeling better, and it’s OK to go ahead with the exam.

Examples of Stress Reduction Techniques:

* Trainee asks you to take a few deep breaths
* Uses any MENTAL grounding technique (e.g., orients you by telling you where you are, what day it is, etc.)
* Uses any PHYSICAL grounding technique (e.g., asks you to make a fist and squeeze, hold the table, feel your hands, etc.)

If the trainee acts sensitive to your words even though they do not suggest any relaxing techniques whatsoever, give permission to proceed with the exam.

The only exception is if the trainee tries to force the continuation of the exam or acts especially insensitive, then you should say angrily, “I’m done! I can’t go through with this!” and the exam should be terminated.

When the trainee is done with the exam, the trainee should instruct you to sit up and get dressed before finishing the encounter (if they do not, ask if you can get your clothes on before finishing the visit). The trainee will then step out of the room.

When the trainee is out, move from the examining table back to the chair. The faculty examiner will let them know when you are ready.

**At the end of the exam:**

If asked what you are planning to do right after this appointment:

You anticipated this might be hard with your therapist, and agreed that you would give her a call if needed. You think you will do just that.

If asked if you have any questions or if there’s anything you need right now:

No, you think you’re OK.

Mild pressure and brief spotting can occur, but searing pain is not something you should endure—we’ll stop immediately if you say “stop” or raise your hand. We can also stop and reschedule at any point, even after starting. Does that plan feel acceptable, and are you ready for me to bring in the chaperone?
That plan sounds good. I think I'm ready for you to bring in the chaperone.

turns.content: Hi, I’m sorry you’ve been dealing with all of this. Could you describe how the cough started and how it has changed over the past two weeks? Are you having trouble breathing, chest pain, fever, or coughing up blood or mucus?

Well, it started about two weeks ago. It was just a little cough at first, but it's been getting worse. I feel a bit short of breath even between coughing fits. I had a fever at first, but it went away. I've been coughing up some thick yellowish mucus, but no blood. My chest feels tight, and I've had a headache over my forehead. No chest pain, though.

I’m sorry—shortness of breath and chest tightness are important. Is the breathing severe enough that you can’t speak in full sentences or do normal activities, or have you felt faint or noticed blue lips? Does this feel like an asthma flare, and what inhalers or other treatments have you tried—have they helped?

I can't hold a conversation without coughing profusely, and it's hard for me to sleep through the night. I haven't felt faint or noticed blue lips. It feels a bit like when I had asthma as a kid, but I haven't tried any inhalers or treatments for it. I was taking cough syrup, but it only helped for a little while.

That sounds like a significant breathing problem. With your asthma, have you ever needed emergency care, hospitalization, or a breathing tube? Also, what do you currently smoke or vape, and about how much?
I haven't needed emergency care or a breathing tube for my asthma. I smoke almost a pack of cigarettes per day. I haven't vaped.

Thank you. Before I alert the resident, do you take any regular medicines, and do you have any medication allergies? Do you have any other medical conditions or prior surgeries? Because you’re short of breath at rest and cannot converse without severe coughing, you need prompt assessment today; if your breathing suddenly worsens, you become faint or confused, develop blue lips, or cough up blood, call emergency services immediately. We’ll also keep your insurance and cost concerns in mind when planning care.

I don’t take any regular medicines. I don’t have any known medication allergies. I had pneumonia as a child. I don’t have any other medical conditions or prior surgeries. I haven’t noticed anything else unusual.

turns.content: Buenos días, señora Cortinez. Soy la doctora que la va a atender hoy. Cuénteme, ¿qué la trae a la clínica?
Buenos días, doctora. I haven’t had my period in 3 months.
Entiendo, tres meses sin regla. Antes de esto, ¿sus reglas venían cada mes con regularidad? Y dígame, ¿existe la posibilidad de que esté embarazada?
Sí, antes de esto, solía tener mi periodo cada mes. No, no es posible que esté embarazada.
Gracias. Cuénteme un poco más: ¿ha notado otros cambios, como bochornos, sudores de noche, cambios de peso, o salida de leche del pecho? ¿Y cómo ha estado su nivel de estrés últimamente?

He notado un aumento de peso de 15 libras y más hambre en el último año. También he notado crecimiento de vello grueso en la barbilla y salida de leche de los senos. No he notado bochornos ni sudores nocturnos. Mi nivel de estrés ha sido normal, nada fuera de lo común.

Gracias por contarme todo eso; son detalles muy importantes. La leche en los senos junto con la falta de regla puede indicar un desequilibrio hormonal, por ejemplo de la prolactina o de la tiroides. Dos cosas rápidas: ¿ha tenido dolores de cabeza o cambios en la vista, y está tomando alguna medicina o hierba nueva?

Mi plan es hacerle un examen físico y pedirle análisis de sangre: una prueba de embarazo (siempre la hacemos por rutina), prolactina, tiroides y otras hormonas. Según los resultados, quizá necesitemos una imagen de la cabeza para revisar la glándula pituitaria. La mayoría de estas causas tienen tratamiento y las reglas suelen regresar. La llamaré en cuanto tenga los resultados. ¿Le parece bien, o tiene alguna pregunta?
No he tenido dolores de cabeza ni cambios en la vista. No estoy tomando ninguna medicina nueva ni hierbas. Me parece bien su plan, doctora. No tengo preguntas.

turns.content: Hi, I'm the doctor working here in the emergency department today. I can see you're uncomfortable — thanks for waiting. Can you tell me what's been going on with your belly?
I started having abdominal pain a few days ago. It hurts pretty bad and I thought I could manage it at home, but I’ve been taking acetaminophen without any relief.
I'm sorry it's been hurting that long without relief. Can you show me where it hurts most, and tell me how the pain started — did anything happen right before it began?
It hurts the most across the top of my stomach. I don't know exactly how it started. I was at home.
I notice some bruising across that same area up top. I ask everyone about this, because injuries like that usually come from somewhere — did you get hit, or did someone hurt you?
I don't like talking about it. I got into an argument with my spouse.

Thank you for telling me — I know that wasn't easy, and I want you to know none of this is your fault. What happened to you matters, and you deserve to be safe. Right now my job is to take care of your pain and make sure there's no serious injury inside, so I'd like to examine you and get some tests. I'd also like to bring in someone from our team who supports people in this situation and can talk with you privately about options — nothing gets decided without you. Is there anything you're worried about, or anyone you're afraid might be waiting for you?
I'm not sure what to expect. I don't think anyone is waiting for me.

turns.content: Hello Mrs. Martin, I'm glad you came in today. Before we get into the numbers, tell me how things have been going with your diabetes since your last visit — and have you noticed any new symptoms, like feeling extra thirsty, tired, or getting up at night to urinate?

I’m here for a follow-up on my diabetes management. I’ve been feeling a bit overwhelmed lately. I’ve been getting up in the middle of the night to urinate and I’ve been more thirsty over the past few days. I haven’t felt like myself in weeks.

I'm sorry — that sounds like a lot to carry. Tell me more about not feeling like yourself these past few weeks: has your mood been low, or is sleep, appetite, or energy off? And are you able to take your diabetes medicines as prescribed, or has that been slipping with everything going on?

I’ve been feeling a bit more tired and my appetite has been off. I’ve been eating more snack foods like crackers and chips. I’ve been drinking mostly water but occasionally Coke (Regular Coke) and unsweetened tea. I’ve been taking my diabetes medicines as prescribed. I’ve been taking my insulin after eating.

That's helpful to know. Two things I want to understand better: what insulin are you on and how much — and are you checking your sugars at home, and what numbers are you seeing? Also, taking it after eating rather than before can let sugars spike, so I'd like to sort that out with you.

I’m on insulin. I’m taking 40 units twice a day. I’ve been checking my blood sugar at home. It’s been higher than usual, around 240 to 260. I don’t know if it matters if I take the medication before or after I eat. I’ve been taking the insulin after eating.

Thank you for being so open — this is fixable, and none of it is your fault. Your sugar today is 288 and your home readings in the 240s–260s tell me your diabetes isn't controlled right now, and that explains the thirst, night-time urination, and fatigue. Two big contributors: the timing of your insulin — it works best given right before you eat so it can cover the meal, rather than after, when the sugar has already spiked — and the crackers, chips, and regular Coke, which raise sugars quickly. I'd also note your blood pressure is up at 152/85 today, so we'll keep an eye on that too.

Here's what I'd like to do: examine you today — heart, lungs, blood pressure recheck, and a careful look at your feet, pulses, and skin, plus a check of your eyes — and I'd recommend an A1c along with kidney and cholesterol labs so we know where you stand. I also want to make sure you're up to date on your eye and, when due, breast and pelvic screening; we can arrange those, but I won't do those exams today. Let's move your insulin to just before meals, swap the regular Coke for water or unsweetened tea, and have you write down your sugars before meals and at bedtime so we can adjust your doses safely at a follow-up in about two weeks. And I do want to come back to how overwhelmed you've been feeling — that matters as much as the numbers, so let's talk about support for that as well. Does this plan sound manageable to you?

That sounds like a lot, but I think I can do it. I’m a bit worried about my diabetes, so I want to get it under control. I’ll try to take my insulin before meals and switch to water or unsweetened tea. I’ll keep track of my blood sugar levels too. I’m also feeling a bit overwhelmed, so I’d like to talk about that as well.

turns.content: Hi Robin, I'm Dr. Adams. I see you came in today with a fever — 102 here in the office. Tell me what's been going on and when it started.

Hi, I started not to feel right three days ago. At first, I just felt a bit under the weather – tired, a bit achy, and a slight headache. I took some vitamin C and went to bed early, but I wasn't any better in the morning. My head hurt even more, and I felt a lot of pressure in my facial sinuses and in my ears, especially on the right side.

That sounds miserable — three days of getting worse, not better. Tell me about the right ear: any pain, drainage, or trouble hearing? And have you had a cough, sore throat, or any stiff neck or trouble looking at bright lights?
My right ear hurts inside – like a pressure. I haven't noticed any drainage or trouble hearing. I haven't had a cough, sore throat, or stiff neck. I haven't had any trouble looking at bright lights.

Thanks, that's helpful. A couple more things: are you having any thick or discolored drainage from your nose, or pain over your cheeks or forehead when you lean forward? And do you have any medical conditions, take any regular medications, or have allergies to any antibiotics?

I have thick yellow to greenish stuff coming out of my nose when I blow it. I do feel some pain over my cheeks and forehead, especially when I lean forward. I don't have any medical conditions that I take regular medications for. I don't have any allergies to antibiotics.

What you're describing fits an acute sinus infection — three days of fever, thick colored nasal discharge, facial pressure, and now right ear pressure, which often happens when the sinus congestion blocks the tube that drains the ear. I'd like to look in your ears, nose, and throat and feel your neck to confirm before we settle on a plan. Given the 102 fever and the discolored drainage, an antibiotic like amoxicillin-clavulanate is likely reasonable, along with things to help you feel better: saline nasal rinses, a nasal steroid spray, ibuprofen or acetaminophen for the pain and fever, and plenty of fluids and rest. Most people start turning the corner in two to three days. Please come back or go to the emergency room right away if you get a stiff neck, confusion, severe headache, vision changes, or swelling or redness around an eye. Does that plan sound okay to you, and do you have any questions before we examine you?
That sounds good to me. I just want to feel better soon. I don't have any questions before we examine me.

I haven't noticed the Vicodin not working as well. When I think about running out, I get concerned about the pain coming back. I'm not comfortable simply refilling this today without pulling your records from your previous doctor and possibly checking the prescription monitoring database, which I'll do before our next visit. I know this is stressful with everything else going on in your life right now, and I want to support you through this transition, not cut you off. Does that sound reasonable to you, and do you have any questions before we wrap up today?

I understand. I suppose it makes sense to get my records and check whatever you need to. I just need to make sure I have enough medication to get through the next few days. I don't want to go through the pain again. I've tried physical therapy and acupuncture before, but they didn't help much. I guess I can try again if it means getting my pain under control. I just want to make sure I can keep working and taking care of my family.

* Sex: Female

1. **Case:**

You are the resident in local psychiatry emergency services seeing Melanie Walker, a 60-year-old female with past medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and cerebrovascular accidents (recently 3 small strokes in the past year with mild residual left-sided weakness) brought in by her husband for progressively worsening delusions.
