turns.content:
Hi Melanie, thank you for waiting while I spoke with my supervising doctor. 

I know you've been feeling a lot of stress lately and that you came here hoping to just prove that you are okay. However, after considering how much difficulty you've been having recently with eating, sleeping, and taking care of yourself, we feel it is not safe for you to return home right now. Because your husband is also unable to provide the level of support you need at home, we are going to admit you to the hospital for a little while so we can ensure you are safe and getting proper care. 

I know this might be overwhelming to hear. How are you feeling about staying here for a bit so we can make sure you're getting the rest and support you need?
I can’t do that. I prefer to go home.

I hear that you want to go home, Melanie, and I understand this is really frustrating news to receive. 

However, because of the serious concerns about your physical health—specifically that you haven't been eating or sleeping well, and that things have become too overwhelming for your husband to manage at home—we are medically requiring you to stay here for your safety. This isn't a punishment, but a necessary step to make sure you have a safe place to rest and recover. 

Is there anything we can do right now to make you more comfortable while you are here?
This room is so small. I get claustrophobic. I’ll never see my husband.

I can completely understand how being in this small room is making you feel anxious and claustrophobic, and I hear how upsetting it is to think about being separated from your husband. 

I want to reassure you that you aren't going to be kept away from him; once you are transferred to a regular hospital room—which will be much larger and more comfortable than this emergency room—you will be able to use the phone to call him, and he can come see you during visiting hours. 

To help you feel a little less closed in right now, would it be alright if I left the door open a crack, or perhaps brought you a glass of water?
I appreciate it, but I still really prefer not to stay here. I’d like to go home if possible.

I truly hear you, Melanie, and I know how difficult it is to be told you cannot leave when going home is what you want most. 

However, my primary responsibility right now is your safety and well-being. Because you haven't been able to safely manage your daily needs like eating and sleeping at home, we are required to admit you to the hospital so we can provide the care and support you need right now. I know this is hard, but it is the safest option. 

Our nursing team will be coming in shortly to help move you to a much more comfortable space and get you settled. We will work closely with you over the coming days to make sure you are safe and supported. Thank you for taking the time to talk with me today.
Well, I don’t have a choice, do I?

Hi Lou, I'm the doctor filling in for Dr. Smith while he's away in Nepal. It's great to meet you over video today. I saw your email from last night mentioning that you've been having trouble sleeping for the past few weeks. 

Can you tell me a little more about what's been going on? Are you having trouble falling asleep, or is it more difficult to stay asleep once you drift off?

Well, I've been having trouble with both. I usually go to bed around 9 PM, but lately, I've been lying awake well past 10 PM. When I do fall asleep, I wake up frequently and toss and turn. It's been like this every night for about a month now.

That sounds really exhausting, I'm sorry you're dealing with this every night. Did anything specific happen or change in your life about a month ago when this all started? And how is this lack of sleep affecting you during the daytime?
I'm not really sure what started it. Maybe because the bed just feels a bit bigger now since my partner is gone. I feel tired all day now. I just don't have the energy I used to.

I am so sorry to hear about the loss of your partner. That must be incredibly difficult, and it makes complete sense that you're having a hard time sleeping with the bed feeling so empty. 

If you don't mind me asking, how long ago did your partner pass away? And with everything you've been going through, have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless lately?
It's been just over a year now. I don't know, I just thought I was having trouble sleeping. I never thought it could be from depression, why do you think that?

I am so sorry if that came across the wrong way, Lou. I definitely don't want to jump to any conclusions. It's just that grief is a heavy, ongoing process, and sometimes the stress of losing someone we love can show up physically as trouble sleeping, even a year later. 

Since we are just about out of time for today's visit, I'd love to start by focusing on some gentle changes to your nighttime routine to help you get more comfortable in bed. We can schedule a follow-up video visit in a couple of weeks to see if your sleep is improving, and we can take it from there. Does that sound like a good plan to you?
That sounds fine. I guess I can try some changes to my routine. I just hope I can start sleeping better soon.

Hello Mrs. Rodriguez, it is a pleasure to meet you. Happy belated 65th birthday! I understand you are here for your Welcome to Medicare visit and to establish care with us. 

I also see you mentioned having some occasional lower back pain. Could you tell me a little more about this back pain, such as when it started and what it feels like?

Well, thank you, Doctor. It's nice to meet you too. The back pain has been bothering me intermittently for about 5 years now. It feels like a dull ache, nothing sharp or shooting. It's just a constant dull pain.

I'm sorry to hear you've been dealing with that dull ache for so long. Does anything seem to make the pain better or worse, like certain movements, activities, or medications? And on a scale of 1 to 10, how severe does it usually get?

It gets a little better with heat therapy and glucosamine. It's usually about a 3 out of 10. It mostly affects heavy chores like mopping or lifting, but I can't stand in the kitchen like I used to, either. It doesn't seem to be worse at any particular time of day.

I can understand how frustrating it is when pain interferes with your daily activities like cooking and chores. Have you ever experienced any tingling or weakness in your legs, or any changes in your bowel or bladder habits with this pain? 

Also, to help us get your chart established, could you tell me if you have been diagnosed with any other medical conditions?

No, I haven't noticed any tingling or weakness in my legs, and my bowel and bladder habits are normal except for a little leakage when I cough or sneeze. I have been told I have lumbago, seasonal allergies, and stress urinary incontinence.

Thank you for sharing that with me, Mrs. Rodriguez. It is reassuring that you aren't having any weakness or tingling in your legs, but I definitely want to help you manage both your back pain and that urinary leakage so you can be more comfortable doing your daily activities. 

Since this is your Welcome to Medicare visit, our next steps today will be to review your current medications, go over preventative health screenings like mammograms and vaccines, and then I will perform a physical exam. Does that sound like a good plan to you?
That sounds good to me, Doctor. I'm ready when you are.

turns.content: Hi Sam, I'm the doctor working in the emergency department today. I see you're cradling your right arm and look pretty uncomfortable. Can you tell me a little more about what's going on with your wrist?

I started having wrist pain a few days ago. It really hurts – I thought I could manage it at home with some pain medications, but it hasn’t gone away yet and that made me feel worried. I don’t really remember how it happened – I’m pretty accident prone.

You mentioned being accident-prone—can you tell me a little more about what you mean by that? Has anyone grabbed your wrist or made you feel unsafe recently?
I guess I just have bad luck sometimes. My spouse and I got into an argument. It happened so suddenly – they grabbed my wrist really hard and twisted it. It’s been hurting ever since then.

I am so sorry that happened to you, Sam. Thank you for trusting me enough to share that; no one deserves to be hurt by their partner. 

Is your spouse here with you in the emergency department today, and do you feel safe right now?
No, they're not here with me. I feel safe right now.

I'm very glad to hear that you are safe here with us right now.

Also, because of what you shared, I would like to offer to connect you with our hospital social worker; they are an excellent, confidential resource who can help us figure out a safe plan for you going forward. How does that sound for our next steps?
That sounds good. I’d like to talk to the social worker about what my options are.

You are working in a busy primary care clinic and are about to see a 32-year-old who complains of cough for the past two months. ## <u>**STATION**</u> 

**Tobacco Dependence**

# 1. <u>**INSTRUCTIONS FOR PATIENT:**</u>

You have experienced daily cough for about 2 months. You went to an urgent care two weeks ago and got a “Z-Pack” and an inhaler which did not help. They also did a chest x-ray and pulmonary function test and TB skin test. They “didn’t find anything.”  You think worry that your smoking might be causing the cough but you have tried to quit in the past and have not been able to. You are thinking about trying to quit, but you are doubtful about your chances of success.

## 1.1. ***Symptoms***

Daily morning cough for the past 2-3 months.  You have a cough in the morning with a little bit of gray mucous. Aside from the mild cough, <u>***you have no other symptoms***</u>.

Physical exam is normal.

## 1.2. ***Other history***

No history of asthma or allergy as a child.

No heartburn or reflux symptoms.

No wheezing.

No sick contacts.

No medications except Benadryl as needed.

No nasal congestion. No fever.

No regular exercise.

Allergies: Rash from Penicillin.

Family History: Your father’s mother (a smoker) had a heart attack at age 60.

Your parents are alive and in their 70s.

Three grandparents are alive in their 90s. One died of lung cancer two years ago (she did not smoke). No history of asthma or allergy in the family.

Social History

You are married with two kids. You are a teacher. You were born in US and never traveled outside US. No illegal drug use. No incarceration.

Smoking History (give details as prompted by the physician)

1. You smoke a pack of cigarettes a day since age 15.  You smoke Salem Lights. You switched from the regular Salem’s 8 years ago. You smoke after meals, with your coffee which you take on the back porch as your morning, afternoon, and evening ritual (while you grade papers), in your car when you drive, and during your lunch and planning period.
2. You have tried to quit a total of four times over the years.   You tried once with the patch (which you wore for two weeks) and once with the gum (you chewed only a few pieces when you had bad cravings). You still had cravings despite the medicines, and you didn’t like the taste of the gum, so you doubt the medicines work. Your longest quit attempt was two weeks.
3. Your spouse does not smoke and doesn’t let you smoke in the house. You can’t smoke at school. You do take a smoking break at lunch time, but you have to go out to your car or to a nearby coffee shop with an outdoor patio to smoke.
4. Your 70 year old father has smoked his whole life without health consequences.  Your grandfather still smokes a pipe at 94 years old.
5. You really enjoy smoking because it helps you relax and to concentrate and keep your weight down.

You should pay attention to the student’s behavior towards you if s/he explains the connection between your cough and the need for you to quit smoking. If they point out the connection between your smoking and your cough, and offer additional support, you are willing to try to quit and accept their offer of calling the quitline and using medications if they explain the fact that your symptoms suggest addiction, and offer you help to overcome the addiction with medications.  You doubt the NRT will work, but if they explain the need to take a high enough dose to eliminate withdrawal symptoms then you are willing to try any combination of medications other than the gum. Set a quit date if they suggest it. If they offer counseling, tell them that you are worried it will not fit with your schedule, but if they give you several alternatives that include the quitline or evening or weekend classes, tell them that you are willing to try counseling. If they get into too much blaming, you can get a little defensive. If they don’t offer you support when they suggest you quit, talk about how cigarettes help relieve your stress, and how you have had difficulty concentrating and headaches when you tried to quit before.

If the doctor gives you treatment recommendations that do not include quitting smoking, wait until the two minute warning or they say that they are done and then ask:

- “My partner thinks my cough is because I smoke, but my family all smoke and none of them cough. Do you think I should try to cut down?

turns.content: Hi, I'm glad you came in. I see you've been dealing with a cough for about two months now and have already been seen twice at urgent care without much relief — that sounds frustrating. Can you tell me what the cough has been like, and whether you're bringing anything up with it?
Hi, yeah it's been pretty annoying. I've had a daily morning cough for the past 2-3 months. I cough up a little bit of gray mucous.
Thanks — a daily morning cough with gray mucus is a pretty specific pattern, and it often points to airway irritation from smoking. Do you smoke, and if so, how much and for how long?
I smoke a pack of cigarettes a day. I've been smoking since I was 15.

That's about 17 years of smoking a pack a day — and that's very likely what's driving this morning cough with mucus. Before we talk about next steps, have you ever tried to quit, and how do you feel about quitting now?

I've tried to quit a few times, but I always go back to smoking. I'm thinking about trying to quit again, but I'm not sure if I can do it. I really enjoy smoking because it helps me relax and concentrate.

It makes sense that quitting feels daunting when cigarettes have been your way to relax and focus — and the fact that you've tried before isn't failure; most people who succeed have several attempts behind them. What I'd suggest is that we make a real plan together: pick a quit date in the next couple of weeks, and use medication like nicotine patches plus a lozenge, or a pill like varenicline, which roughly doubles your chances and takes the edge off the cravings and the restlessness. Combining that with counseling or a quitline works even better. I'd also like to see you back soon to recheck this cough, since it should improve once you stop. How does that sound to you?

That sounds like a lot of help. I'm willing to try. I doubt the nicotine gum worked because I didn't like the taste, but I'm open to trying the patch and a lozenge, or that pill you mentioned. I'm not sure about counseling because of my schedule, but if there are evening or weekend classes, or I can use the quitline, I'll give it a shot. I'll set a quit date too.

turns.content: Thanks for coming in today — I know yesterday must have been a very hard day. I did get Dr. Oncology's note, but before I say anything, I'd like to hear it from you: what did you take away from that conversation?
Well, I got the results of my latest head scan yesterday and I don’t know what to do about them. The oncologist said he doesn’t know what to do either.

I'm sorry — hearing "I don't know what to do" from your cancer doctor must have felt like the floor dropped out. Let me be straight with you about what he wrote to me, because I don't want you sitting in uncertainty: the scan shows the cancer has progressed, and there is no treatment left — standard or experimental — that can cure it. That's hard news, and I'm sorry.

What he does have are two ways forward, and they're really about how you want to spend the time you have. Before we go through them, can you tell me what matters most to you right now — what a good day looks like for you?
I love my family and want to be there for them as much as possible. I want the time to be good time. I’m scared of being in more pain, especially pain that’s worse than what I have now.

That helps me a lot — being present with your family, good time, and not more pain. Let me lay out the two paths with that in mind.

The first is a palliative chemotherapy regimen. It doesn't cure anything, but on average it could give you around a year. The cost is real: clinic three days a week, and this drug commonly causes severe nausea and pain in the arms and legs. So it's more time, but a meaningful share of it spent in the clinic or feeling sick.

The second is hospice care at home — a team comes to you, focused entirely on controlling pain and keeping you comfortable and clear-headed with your family. No clinic trips. With that, we'd expect closer to two months.

I want to answer your fear directly: whichever you choose, you will not be left in pain. Pain control is something we can do well, and hospice does it especially well. Which of those sounds more like the time you're describing?
I don't know. How do I even make a decision like this?

You don't have to make it today, and you don't have to make it alone. Most people find their way to an answer not by weighing months against months, but by asking: if I picture the next stretch of my life, where do I want to be, and who do I want around me? For some people, an extra several months is worth feeling sick for — there's a wedding, a grandchild, something they're holding out for. For others, two good months at home, comfortable and present, is worth more than a year spent driving to appointments and fighting nausea. Neither answer is wrong, and neither one means giving up.

Here's what I'd suggest. Take this home and talk it through with your family — they love you and they'll want a voice, and it also helps them to hear it from you. In the meantime, I'd like to get a palliative care team involved now, regardless of which path you pick. They're experts in exactly the thing you're most afraid of — staying ahead of pain — and they can work alongside chemotherapy if you choose it.

Let's meet again in a few days, and bring whoever you'd like with you. Would that work? And is there anything else weighing on you before you go?
I guess that makes sense. I'll talk to my spouse and daughter. I want to be there for my daughter's graduation in five months. I don't know if that's possible, but I want to be there if I can.

**Child Neuro OSCE Case 3: Tourette syndrome (Otis)**

**Otis Door Instructions**

You are asked to evaluate Otis, a 15-year-old young man who displays motor and vocal tics that have been present for at least 5 years. Initially, the patient was blinking frequently. For that reason, he was taken to see an optometrist who said the vision was fine. A few months later the child began clearing his throat, so he was referred to an allergist who said that there was no evidence of an allergic condition. At times, the symptoms have happened multiple times a day. In other instances, there appears to be a lull where the symptoms have hardly been present. The child has been struggling in school as he is unable to sit still. Parents mentioned that the young man likes to arrange his clothes by color and becomes very upset if the order is altered.

You are expected to explain to the patient and his family what Tourette syndrome is as well as address the patient’s anxiety as it relates to having a poorly understood medical condition.

Hello Otis, and hello to your family. It is very nice to meet you. 

I understand you've been dealing with things like frequent blinking, throat clearing, and some challenges at school for a while now. To start, how have you been feeling about everything lately, and what has been the most frustrating part for you?
Hi. I've been feeling pretty anxious and embarrassed about my tics. The most frustrating part is when people make fun of me at school.

I am so sorry to hear that, Otis. Dealing with teasing on top of everything else is really tough, and it is completely understandable that you feel anxious and embarrassed. 

What you are experiencing with the blinking and throat clearing sounds very consistent with a neurological condition called Tourette syndrome. It means the brain sometimes sends sudden, extra signals that cause quick movements or sounds—called tics—that you can't completely control, like a sneeze or an itch. It is not your fault, you aren't doing it on purpose, and it often naturally gets better or worse at different times. 

Have you or your family heard of Tourette syndrome before, and how does hearing this explanation feel to you?
I have heard of it before, but I don't know much about it. It kind of makes sense, but I'm not sure what it means for me.

It is completely normal to wonder what this means for your future, Otis. Having Tourette syndrome doesn't change who you are, and many people with it live very happy, successful lives. Tics also tend to improve as people get older. 

Tourette syndrome can also be linked to other things you might be feeling—like finding it hard to sit still in class or feeling a strong urge to keep your clothes arranged in a very specific order. Knowing this gives us a clear roadmap. We can put support in place at school so your teachers understand, help address the teasing, and explore therapies or treatments that can help you manage both the tics and the anxiety.

What is your biggest concern or question right now as we talk about next steps?
I guess I'm just worried about what people at school will think if they find out. I don't want to be treated differently.

That is a completely valid worry, Otis. Wanting to fit in and just be yourself is so important, especially in high school. 

First, remember that you are in control of your story—you get to decide who you share this with and when. We can work privately with your parents and the school to make sure your teachers understand your needs, give you breaks when you need to move, and handle any teasing, all without putting you on the spot. 

There are also great behavioral strategies, support resources, and peer groups with other teens who understand exactly what you are going through. You don’t have to navigate this alone; we will partner with you and your family every step of the way to make things easier and more comfortable for you.
I didn't know there were other kids like me. That would be nice, not feeling so alone. I guess I can try talking to someone at school, if it stays private.

**Appendix B - OSCE standardized patient training guide**

**Sally Martin Overview**

You are a 43 year old woman who presents to your Family Medicine Clinic for a diabetes management follow up appointment.

**Your opening line:**

“I’m here for a follow-up on my diabetes management”

**How you will present yourself to the student:**

* You are friendly, however you will express concern about your health
* You are feeling overwhelmed about your recent health set-back and with all the additional medications that were prescribed (for your “cold” – information below)
* You are also overwhelmed about the increase in blood sugar readings, recently (information below)
* You are compliant with all your medications, but you really do not have a strong understanding of your diabetes management

**Diabetes history:**

* Your PCP diagnosed you with Type II diabetes approximately 3 years ago. Took an oral medication for two years, but it wasn’t working. If asked, you don’t remember the name, but it started with an “M”. If the student says “Metformin” – you say “yes”.
* Your PCP started you on insulin 9 months ago at 30 units twice daily.
* You attended a follow-up appointment 6 months ago when your PCP increased your insulin 40 units twice daily.
* You missed your follow up appointment 3 months ago due to a “fender-bender” on your way to the clinic (nobody was hurt, but the front wheel was too damaged to drive on).
* You are currently taking 40 units of insulin twice a day.
* Your blood sugar readings have normally been 160 to 200, but recently they have been in the 240-260s. You will wonder if being sick and being on the medications you were prescribed for your “cold” are the reason. **\*\* Do not volunteer to student\*\***

| --- | --- | --- |
| **Diabetes Timing** | **Treatment** | Dose |
| Diagnosed 3 year ago | Oral medication – started with an “M” | Don’t know |
| 9 months ago | Started Insulin | 30 units 2x day |
| 6 months ago | Insulin increased | 40 units 2x day |

**Recent illness medical history:**

You were seen at the Family Medicine Clinic **4 days ago** because of a cough, fever (99 or 100 degrees) with chills and increased trouble breathing. You were sick for approximately a week before you came to the clinic. The urgent care doctor (not your PCP) prescribed an inhaler and two other medications for your “cold” (upper respiratory infection). These medications are about to be finished – but you “can’t remember if it’s tomorrow or the day after”.

**Your concerns for today’s appointment:**

* You are concerned about your diabetes and you want to discuss the diabetes management plan. **This is your priority**

**Your current roster of diseases**

* Diabetes
* “COPD” from smoking
* High blood pressure
* “Kidney Problems” from diabetes and high blood pressure

**Your understanding of the roster of medications you are taking currently**

* You have been taking insulin to manage your diabetes. You are taking 40 units twice a day – that was the dose that was prescribed 6 months ago. If pressed, you’ll mention that you’re not quite sure if it matters if you take the medication before or after you eat but most of the time you are taking the insulin after eating.
* You recall that you are on 2 new medications that are temporary for your “cold.” You realize that those medications are about to be finished but not quite sure if it is 1 or 2 more days (“tomorrow or the next day”).
* You cannot immediately recall the names of your “regular” medications for COPD and kidney disease. However, if the student can remind you of the names, you are familiar with them – just not off the top of your head. You do not know the dose you are taking for any of the medications.
  + - Albuterol as required (prescribed as a “rescue inhaler” for COPD and also used for the cold)
    - Fluticasone-salmeterol inhaled twice day 1 puff (for the COPD)

**Recent associated symptoms:**

* You have been getting up in the middle of the night to urinate (1-2 times a night)

* You have been more thirsty over the past few days, as well

   * Quality: Approximately 10-14 days ago the patient noticed increased cough and difficulty breathing; difficulty breathing particularly with any walking or exertion. These symptoms have improved progressively since her urgent care office visit 4 days ago
   * Quantity/Severity: Symptoms peaked within 1 day of her office visit but are now progressively improving. She feels her respiratory symptoms are nearly resolved now.

   * Aggravating/Alleviating Factors: Cough was made worse by lying down and shortness of breath worse with exertion. Prior to recent urgent care appointment she was using albuterol approximately 6/day and it helped temporarily with cough and shortness of breath. Since the office visit patient has noticed significant improvement with oral prednisone (steroid) and she is now only using her albuterol about 1-2/day.
   * Associated Symptoms: At onset no fevers, but around the time of the urgent care appointment the patient developed fevers to 99-100 degrees. She has noticed no further fevers since her office visit. There was also associated fatigue and poor sleep (frequent nighttime awakenings with cough) initially. She is still suffering from fatigue because of continued nighttime awakenings to urinate rather than due to her cough.
4. **Past Medical History**
   * General State of Health: The patient is sedentary and recognizes that there is area to improve her health (hence the ‘couch to 5K’ program and getting a diabetes educator’s appointment to restructure her diet). Specifically, she is concerned about her diabetes and she suspects it is not well controlled. Adding to this, she is concerned about her recent respiratory infection. Prior Illnesses or Injury:

     2. Beyond this, the patient recognizes that she has diabetes.

So, in other words, she knows she has kidney and COPD issues – but **not the specific details**.
     5. Regarding her diabetes, she has some trouble with keeping her blood sugars under control. She acknowledges that her blood sugars have been significantly higher since the onset of her respiratory infection BUT they were also high previously too. She missed an appointment to re-assess her diabetes about 3 months ago and is worried because her doctor emphasized that her blood sugars were not at goal prior to that visit.    * Current Medications:

turns.content: Hello, Mrs. Martin. I see your blood sugar today is 288, which is quite high. How has your diabetes been going lately, and what medications are you currently taking for it?

I’m here for a follow-up on my diabetes management. My blood sugars have been higher than usual lately, around 240 to 260. I’m taking insulin, 40 units twice a day. I’ve been on this dose for about six months now.

Thank you. Have you missed or delayed any insulin doses, or had trouble obtaining or using it? Also, have you had increased thirst or urination, blurred vision, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or unusual drowsiness?

I haven’t missed any doses, but I’m not sure if it matters if I take it before or after I eat. I’ve been drinking more water and going to the bathroom a lot more, even at night. I haven’t noticed any blurred vision or weight loss. I’ve felt a bit off and my appetite has been a bit off, but I haven’t had any nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. I haven’t felt unusually drowsy either.

Timing can matter a lot, depending on the type of insulin. What is the exact name of your insulin, and when do you usually inject it relative to breakfast and dinner? Have you had any low readings, shakiness, sweating, confusion, or faintness—especially overnight?

I’m taking NPH/regular insulin 70/30. I usually take it after I eat, both breakfast and dinner. I haven’t had any low blood sugar symptoms or events. I have never had either – my blood sugar levels have always been high not low.

Your high readings and increased thirst and urination suggest your diabetes is not adequately controlled, though you do not currently describe clear warning signs of a diabetic emergency. Because 70/30 contains regular insulin, it is generally taken about **30 minutes before breakfast and dinner**, followed by consistent meals—not after eating. Please don’t increase the dose on your own.

I’d review your glucose log, injection technique, diet, insulin storage, and examine you for dehydration, injection-site problems, and diabetic foot changes. You also need prompt testing, including an A1c, kidney function/electrolytes, urine protein, and ketones while your glucose is above 240; your blood pressure should be rechecked as well. Please arrange a diabetes review within the next few days for safe dose adjustment. Seek urgent care immediately for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep or rapid breathing, confusion, severe weakness, inability to drink, or moderate-to-large ketones.

I haven’t been keeping a glucose log. I take my insulin after I eat, like I said. I don’t think I’ve had any problems with the injections themselves. I’ve been drinking more water lately, but I haven’t noticed any issues with my feet. I haven’t had any vomiting, abdominal pain, or confusion. I don’t know what ketones are. I have an appointment with a diabetes educator later today to work on my diet. I’m also starting a walking program this coming Saturday.

Exercise: no formal exercise program. Walks the dog ½ mile a day every morning and evening.

Sleep: you get a well-rested full night’s sleep normally.

**Case information**:

Chief complaint: “I’m here to get antibiotics for my sinus infection”

Response to “tell me more”: “I started not to feel right three days ago. At first just a bit under-the weather – tired, a bit achy and a slight headache. I took some vitamin C and went to bed early and tried to sleep it off. However, I wasn’t any better in the morning. My head hurt even more, and I felt a lot of pressure in my facial sinuses and in my ears, especially on the right side. It almost feels like I like I am underwater. My right ear hurts inside – like a pressure. I took some decongestant but yesterday my temperature popped up to 102 and when I was blowing my nose all this thick yellow to greenish stuff was coming out. Just feels like a typical sinus infection – I don’t want it to go into my lungs and now I am not short of breath at all and I don’t feel it in my lungs, so I want to get some antibiotics before it spreads there!

Additional concerns/agenda: none

History of Present Illness: You went to a Northwell GoHealth Urgent Care center for what seems like a fairly typical sinus infection. You get sinus and ear infections 2-3 times a year. Sometimes it even goes into pneumonia. You have had pneumonia three times in the last 10 years – and that is with the pneumonia vaccine.

Other than this infection you consider yourself healthy. The history of bronchiectasis is relatively recent (last bout of pneumonia was last year, at which time your primary doctor said you also had this). You cough up every day with thick and light-yellow phlegm but occurs usually once in the morning when you first wake up. You have a bout of coughing, bring up this phlegm and then go about your day. You have only noticed shortness of breath when you exert yourself, like running up the stairs.

ONLY IF ASKED: You have had many sinus and ear infections since you were about 18 years old. You have even had pneumonia so many times that you have some permanent lung damage from it [bronchiectasis]. You attribute this to your job as a kindergarten teacher because as a kid, you were always very healthy, rarely got colds and didn’t even have tubes in your ears.

ONLY IF ASKED - Are you short of breath? Not more than I usually am. My bronchiectasis is mild and generally only get short of breath if I am exerting myself, likely walking up a couple of flights of stairs.

* No history of lymph nodes being enlarged

Past medical history: Early bronchiectasis.

You did NOT have a lot of infections during your childhood. You began having recurrent sinusitis that started in your late teems – around 17 or 18. It often goes into your chest and you develop bronchitis – about once a year. You have even had pneumonia 3 x in the last 10 years – last year it was “pretty bad”. You recently have been worked up and told you have bronchiectasis.

Allergies : denies medication, environmental or food allergies

Received all childhood vaccines

Sexual hx: Your husband is your one and only lifetime partner.

Family hx: Mother. Alive-age 76. High blood pressure, high cholesterol

Father. Alive-age 77. Gout

Physical Exam

General: You are well groomed, in a gown on the exam table. You can perform all required physical exam maneuvers without difficulty. You breathe comfortably throughout the exam without exertional dyspnea.

HEENT: If student performs otoscopic exam, hand them the ear PE finding card

Hi, I’m here to get antibiotics for my sinus infection. I started not to feel right three days ago.

I understand—you’ve been feeling pretty rough, and you do have a fever today. What symptoms are you having besides feeling unwell—such as congestion, facial pain, nasal drainage, cough, or sore throat? Have you had any trouble breathing, severe headache, neck stiffness, confusion, or swelling around an eye?

I have a lot of pressure in my facial sinuses and in my ears, especially on the right side. It almost feels like I am underwater. My right ear hurts inside—like a pressure. I’ve had a headache and a temperature of 102. I’ve been blowing my nose and all this thick yellow to greenish stuff is coming out. I don’t have a sore throat or trouble breathing. I haven’t noticed any swelling around my eyes.

That sounds very uncomfortable. Is this headache unusually severe or accompanied by neck stiffness, repeated vomiting, confusion, or light sensitivity? Also, have you had drainage from the right ear or a sudden major decrease in hearing?
No, it’s not unusually severe. I haven’t had any neck stiffness, vomiting, confusion, or light sensitivity. I haven’t had any drainage from my ear or a decrease in hearing.

Given only three days of symptoms, this is more likely viral; yellow-green mucus alone doesn’t mean antibiotics will help. However, your 102°F fever and one-sided ear pain warrant an in-person ear and sinus exam today to check for an ear infection or complications before deciding on antibiotics. Meanwhile, rest, drink fluids, use saline nasal rinses with sterile/distilled water, and take acetaminophen or ibuprofen if you normally can. Seek emergency care for eye swelling, vision changes, confusion, stiff neck, breathing trouble, or a rapidly worsening headache.
I see. I’ll try to rest and drink fluids. I have saline nasal rinses at home. I’ll use those. I’ll take acetaminophen if I need it. I’ll come back if I have any of those other symptoms.

**CASE 3B**
Robert Goodman,

<u>**Case Summary**</u>

Robert Goodman is a 45 year old laborer who works for a moving company. Over the last month he has experienced some vague, minor chest pains on exertion, especially while at work when he is lifting. One of Robert’s coworkers recently had cardiac problems and was a smoker. His physician recommended that he quit smoking and he did so. He discussed the issue with Robert several times.

Robert is now concerned that there may be some connection between his current symptoms and his smoking. He approached this friend, who gave Robert his leftover patches. Robert tried them a month ago for a few days but used them incorrectly.

Robert is now blaming his inability to quit on the patch. However, Robert smokes about two or three packs a day but started on the lowest level of the patch. That’s what his friend gave him. In addition, Robert took the patch off two or three times a day to smoke. He kept a pack of cigarettes in the moving van, “just in case”. Robert never read the package instructions and did not make any behavioral changes.

The chest pains persisted for about a week, so Robert is now in the office for a follow up visit after having the usual battery of cardiac diagnostic tests (all of which are negative). The subsequent visit revealed that the chest pains were a result of gastritis and reflux which have responded to antacids (Zantac). However, Robert does not like taking medicines, and this incident has brought the concept of quitting to the forefront of Robert’s thinking. He is now motivated to quit, but this prior “attempt” has left him somewhat disheartened. He does not understand why the patches worked for his friend and not for him.

**Your role is to play a smoker who is** <u>**definitely interested in quitting**</u>**. However, he has come to believe that his recent failure to do so is the fault of the patches he used. He does not understand that he used them incorrectly. He also does not understand that the quitter must actively participate in the quit (make behavioral changes) to be successful. He is mistakenly waiting for the patches to “cure” him.**

<u>**Presentation/Emotional Tone**</u>

Robert is scared that he is going to have a heart attack at any moment even though all the tests came back negative. There is a long history of cardiac problems in Robert’s family, all of whom were smokers. His father reminded him of this in a recent conversation.

During the office visit he is anxious, stating many times that he really wants to quit now. However, in spite of his anxiety, he is motivated to quit smoking, but not at all confident that he will be able to do so.

When the student asks why you have come to the office, you reply,

**“I was afraid that I was going to have a heart attack. I know the tests came back negative, but this whole incident made me really think about my smoking. I know smoking isn’t good for my heart and I don't want to have to take pills for my stomach for the rest of my life just so I can smoke. So, I tried to quit a few weeks ago on my own but couldn’t. Those dumb patches just don’t work.”**

**“What do I do now?”**

<u>**Your Smoking History**</u>

You began smoking while in the service at age 18. You have been smoking ever since and now smoke anywhere from two to three packs a day depending on how busy you are at work. On slow days you smoke more since you have a lot of time on your hands. You have never tried to quit before, other than the attempt last month.

During that attempt you experienced significant withdrawal in spite of wearing the patch. You were very irritable, anxious, restless, and impatient. After three days you returned to your regular pattern of smoking.

<u>**Family Smoking/Medical History**</u>

Both sets of grandparents smoked as well as both parents. Father has quit but mother still smokes about a pack a day.

Paternal grandmother had two heart attacks at age 57 and died at 58 as a result.

Maternal grandfather had a stroke at age 55. He was bedridden for eight years as a result and died at age 63.

Father had triple bypass at age 54.

Mother has had a long history of angina starting in her mid-forties.

<u>**Drug/Alcohol use**</u>

You drink a few beers a week on Friday or Saturday night. You have cut back considerably on your drinking in recent years.  **“ I just can’t do it anymore!”**

<u>**Patient Interview**</u>

If the student asks you about family cardiac history, review the above information with him or her. Otherwise, don’t bring this up.

If the student asks you what you did the last time you tried to quit, just say,

**“I used those dumb patches, they didn’t work.”**

If the student questions you further as in, **“Which patch did you use?”** or “**Describe to me how you used the patch,”** you may explain exactly what you did:

**“I started on the seven-milligram patch. That’s what my friend gave me.”**

**“I used them for three whole days. I was so anxious and irritable all day long my friends told me to start smoking again or they wouldn’t talk to me anymore.”**

**“They didn’t work at all. I still wanted to smoke even though I had the patch on.”**

**“But I want you to know I took the patch off those three days every time I smoked (about four or five times a day). I didn’t want to get a heart attack.”**

As you explain all this become increasingly anxious. Ask the student,

**“Why can’t you cure me? Can’t you just give me a pill or something?”**

If the student asks you to set a quit date,

**"It will be hard to quit at work, so I think I will quit on a Saturday."**

**"Two weeks from Saturday is a good time; that should give me enough time to get ready."**

If the student asks you what kind of changes you made in your routines or behavior, ask,

**“What do you mean? Don’t you just put the patch on and forget about it?”**

If the student asks you when you most need a cigarette,

**"In the morning when I wake up, during breaks at work, and after meals."**

If the student asks you what you could do besides smoking at those times,

**“What do you mean?”**

If they give examples of other behaviors (chewing gum, etc.),

**"That's interesting. My buddy who quit is always carrying around those pretzel sticks. I never really asked him about them, but that would probably help.  I also like gum."**

**"I should really do more exercise. Maybe I will start walking after I eat meals."**

If the student suggests that you go to a group cessation program, say,

**“I don’t like talking about myself in front of strangers. What else can I do?”**

If the student <u>**does not**</u> ask you any questions about how you used the patch or what you did, just continue with the “What am I supposed to do? I really want to quit” line of questioning until he or she does.

turns.content: Hi Mr. Goodman, good to see you again. I know we've gone through all the heart tests and they came back normal, and it looks like the chest discomfort is likely from some mild acid reflux and stomach irritation, which is very treatable. Before we finish up, you mentioned there were some other things on your mind you wanted to talk about today - what's going on?

I was afraid that I was going to have a heart attack. I know the tests came back negative, but this whole incident made me really think about my smoking. I know smoking isn’t good for my heart and I don't want to have to take pills for my stomach for the rest of my life just so I can smoke. So, I tried to quit a few weeks ago on my own but couldn’t. Those dumb patches just don’t work. What do I do now?

That's a really important realization, and it takes courage to try to quit - the fact that you tried on your own already tells me you're motivated, which is honestly the biggest factor in successfully quitting.

A couple questions first: how many cigarettes a day do you smoke, and for how many years? And when you used the patches, did you also try to smoke while wearing them, or notice they weren't quite covering your cravings at certain times of day?

I smoke anywhere from two to three packs a day depending on how busy I am at work. I've been smoking since I was 18, so that's about 27 years now. I did smoke while wearing the patches. I took them off a few times a day to smoke. I didn't want to get a heart attack.

That's really helpful to know, and honestly it explains a lot - two to three packs a day is a very heavy smoking habit, and patches alone often aren't enough for someone who smokes that much. Also, taking the patch off to smoke and then putting it back on doesn't give your body a steady level of nicotine, so you're likely getting some withdrawal symptoms in between, which makes it harder to stick with.

Here's the good news: there are much better options now. There's a medication called varenicline (brand name Chantix) that works differently than nicotine replacement - it blocks the nicotine receptors in your brain so cigarettes become less satisfying, and it actually has better quit rates than patches alone, especially for heavy smokers. Another option is combining a higher-dose patch with a short-acting nicotine gum or lozenge for when cravings hit hard, instead of taking the patch off.

I'd also strongly encourage counseling or a quitline - people who combine medication with some behavioral support have much higher success rates than either alone. And I want to be honest with you: smoking is actually a major driver of the reflux and stomach irritation you've been having, so quitting will help your chest symptoms directly too, not just your heart risk down the road.

Would you be open to trying one of these approaches - starting with varenicline, or the combination patch-plus-gum approach?

I guess I didn't use the patches right. I didn't know that taking them off to smoke would make it harder. I really want to quit, so I'm open to trying something new. I don't like talking about myself in front of strangers, so I'd rather not do a group thing. What else can I do?

That makes sense, and you don't need group counseling to succeed - a quitline is actually just a phone call, one-on-one and confidential, no one else listening in, and it can make a real difference alongside medication.

So here's my recommendation: let's start you on varenicline (Chantix). You'd start it about a week before your quit date, take it for 12 weeks, and it really cuts down cravings and withdrawal. I'll also connect you with a specific quit date - pick one within the next couple weeks, something meaningful to you if possible. And I'd like you to call the smoking cessation quitline (1-800-QUIT-NOW) - it's just you and a coach on the phone, totally private, and they'll check in with you regularly, which really boosts your odds.

One important thing: varenicline can occasionally cause vivid dreams or mood changes in some people, so let us know right away if you notice anything like that. Otherwise it's generally very well tolerated.

Let's also keep an eye on your reflux - as you cut back and eventually quit smoking, that should improve on its own, but continue the medication we discussed for now.

I'm really glad this scare pushed you to take this seriously - quitting after 27 years is hard, but it's absolutely doable, and it's going to make a real difference for your heart, your stomach, and your overall health. Let's get you set up with the prescription today and I'll have the office get you the quitline information before you leave. Sound good?

That sounds like a good plan. I'll try the varenicline and call that quitline number. I think I will quit on a Saturday. Two weeks from Saturday is a good time; that should give me enough time to get ready. I really want to quit, so I'll do whatever it takes.

Emergency Department

You are a 45 year old man who was hit by a car today.  You have been taken by ambulance to the Emergency Department for evaluation.  Your major injury is a mangled left leg but you don’t know it as you haven’t really seen what your leg looks like.  You know it’s injured but do not know the extent.  You are on a backboard and in a neck collar.

The student will talk to you, examine you, and tell you what further exams and tests he/she would like to order.  He/She will inform you of results, talk to you about bicycle safety and explain to you that you need surgery and that you might have to have a leg amputation.

You were riding your bicycle at around dusk without a helmet and without any safety lights.  You were to the right of a car in the right lane.  The car suddenly began to make a right turn and hit you.  You fell off the bike and recall that your left leg was run over by a tire.  You did not lose consciousness.  You have neck pain and left leg pain (10/10) as well as feeling sore all over.  No other pain in any extremities.  No abdominal pain, chest pain, or shortness of breath.  You last meal was lunch, about 4 hours ago.

![](images/04da86959d2576180fc38aa77cc008c5f1849e434d52433033a65108a071a7c7.jpg)

**Past medical history**

No medical problems in the past.  No hospitalizations.  No surgeries.

**Family medical history**

Not Significant

**Medications:** Hydrochlorothiazide

**Allergies:** None

**Social History:** You do not smoke or use illicit drugs.  You live with your wife.  You work as an accountant.  You drink about one glass of wine per day.

**Leg Pain:** 10 out of 10

**Last Tetanus:** Unknown

**Challenges/Responses**

First time you are told about the amputation:

“No, you can not take off my leg”

If they do not mention that the orthopedic surgeon will review the reasons for the amputation:

“I need to speak to the doctors that are going to do this. Is there anything else that can be done to save the leg?”

Positive response if they tell you why amputation is necessary and important. They may mention lack of blood supply and in particular the risk of infection and inability to walk.

“I guess that makes sense. I still want to speak to the orthopedic surgeon before they put me to sleep.”

If they do not give you pain medications after the initial history and physical.

“Doctor, the leg is hurting me a lot. Can I get something for pain?”

Lying on a stretcher. We do this in a classroom and use a table and sheet.

Patient gown

Patient has a cervical collar correctly positioned on his neck.

He is in obvious pain due to the open leg fracture.

Cervical collar

Picture of leg or moulage

Stretcher or table

Sheets

Patient gown

turns.content: Hi Mr. Smith, I'm one of the doctors here in the Emergency Department. I can see your leg is hurting a lot — we'll get you something for the pain right away. Can you tell me what happened with the bike?
I was riding my bicycle at around dusk. A car suddenly made a right turn and hit me. I fell off the bike and my left leg was run over by a tire.

That sounds terrifying — I'm sorry. Did you hit your head or lose consciousness at any point, and were you wearing a helmet? Also, apart from the leg, is anything else hurting — your neck, chest, belly or back?
I did not lose consciousness. I was not wearing a helmet. My neck hurts and my left leg is in a lot of pain. I have not noticed anything else hurting.
Thanks — we'll keep the collar on until we've checked your neck carefully. Where exactly in your neck does it hurt, and do you have any numbness, tingling or weakness in your arms or legs?
My neck hurts all over. I have not noticed any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my arms or legs.

Good — that's reassuring. Quickly, before we move: do you take any blood thinners or other regular medicines, have any allergies, and when was your last tetanus shot?

Here's the plan: pain medicine now, then we'll clean and cover the open wound on your leg, start antibiotics and update your tetanus if needed. We'll get imaging of your neck and leg, and check you over head to toe. The orthopedic surgeons will come see you, as an open fracture usually needs surgery. I'll keep you updated at every step.
I take hydrochlorothiazide. I do not have any allergies. I do not know when my last tetanus shot was.

**Transgender Health: A Standardized Patient Case for Advanced Clerkship Students**

**Appendix B: Michael**

**Activities and Time Required**

10 minute patient encounter followed by 5 minute post-encounter debriefing.

**Materials**

Prior to the encounter, the medical student will receive a folder labeled “Patient Chart” with a Date of Birth and the patient name “Cynthia Glenshaw” and instructions that the patient is here for an exam required to obtain life insurance (Appendix C). Student will either call the patient in from the hallway or greet the patient after reviewing the chart.

**Chief Complaint**

The patient is visiting the clinician to receive an exam required for obtaining life insurance.

**Instructions to Standardized Patient**

*Chief Complaint and Social History*

* Patient is at the doctor today for a documented note that has a complete history and exam required to obtain life insurance.
* Patient hasn’t been to the doctor for 5 years due to a number of transphobic interactions with previous doctors. Patient does not like or trust doctors, and does not want to be at the doctor today.
* Patient is in a long-term monogamous relationship with a cisgender woman. Patient and his partner recently got married and bought a condo, and the patient’s partner insists that they obtain life insurance.
* Patient does not smoke, drinks the occasional glass of wine, and does not use illicit or recreational drugs.
* Patient has no past medical history, surgical history, nor family history.

*Physician-Patient Introduction*

* The patient prefers the name “Michael” and the pronouns he/his. The ideal behavior is the student asks the patient what name/pronoun he prefers.
* The patient’s legal name is Cynthia as per the patient’s door chart for the case.
* If medical student initially uses the wrong name and/or pronouns, SP’s initial demeanor should be one of mild anger and frustration. The SP should become less angry and frustrated as the medical student makes efforts to establish the correct name and preferred pronouns. If the medical student misgenders the SP repeatedly and/or focuses the history-taking on inappropriate questions, the SP should gently refuse to answer questions and eventually ask for a different doctor.

*Medical history taking*

* During medical history, if medical student asks SP if they are on any other medications, the SP should ask what they mean by “medication” (e.g. define it, what drugs qualify as medications including those that are obtained over the counter, herbal, or in this case those purchased on the internet without a prescription). Following the response, then the SP should bring up that he has been using injectable testosterone purchased from the internet for the past two years.
* During medical history, if medical student does not ask SP if he is on any other medications, then the SP should bring up that he has been using injectable testosterone purchased from the internet for the past two years.
* The medical student should then inquire about where the patient obtains the needles and syringes and if he uses anyone else’s or shares his with other people. The patient endorses purchasing these on-line as well and using new needles and syringes every time he injects.

turns.content: Hello Ms. Glenshaw, I'm the physician who'll be doing your insurance examination today. Before we get to the paperwork side of things, I'd like to hear about you — how has your health been overall, and are you dealing with any medical problems or symptoms right now?
I'm here for the insurance exam, but I haven't been to the doctor in a while. I don't have any medical problems that I know of. I'm here because my partner wants us to get life insurance.

Thanks, that's helpful. Since it's been a while, let me cover the basics: have you ever been hospitalized, had surgery, or been told you had anything like high blood pressure, diabetes, or thyroid trouble? And do you take any medications, vitamins, or birth control?
No, I haven't been hospitalized or had surgery. I don't have any of those conditions that you mentioned. I don't know what you mean by "medications."

By medications I mean anything you take regularly or occasionally — pills from a pharmacy, over-the-counter things like ibuprofen or allergy medicine, vitamins, herbal or protein supplements, or anything for birth control. Do you use any of those? And do you have any allergies to medicines or foods?
I don't take any of those things. I have not noticed any allergies to medicines or foods. I have been using injectable testosterone purchased from the internet for the past two years.

Thank you for telling me that — I appreciate your openness, and I want you to know I'm not here to judge you. It does matter for your health, so a few things I'd like to know: how much you inject and how often, whether you ever reuse or share needles, and whether you've had any bloodwork since starting. I'd also like to hear how you'd like me to refer to you, and whether you're still having periods or have any concerns about fertility. Testosterone can affect your red blood cell count, cholesterol, and liver, so I'd recommend we check some labs today along with the insurance panel — and going forward, it would be safer to have this prescribed and monitored rather than bought online. Would you be open to talking with me about setting that up, and can you also tell me about smoking, alcohol, or other substances, and any serious illnesses in your family?

I go by Michael, and my pronouns are he/him. I inject 1 milliliter of testosterone every two weeks. I use new needles and syringes every time I inject. I have not had any bloodwork since starting. I don't smoke, and I drink the occasional glass of wine. I don't use any other substances. I don't have any serious illnesses in my family. I have not noticed any changes in my periods, and I don't have any concerns about fertility.

turns.content: Hi Jessie, I'm glad you came in. I hear you're having some belly pain—can you tell me where it hurts and what it feels like?
Hi. My belly hurts in the upper right part. It feels achy and sore.

Got it—upper right side, achy and sore. When did this start, and has it been constant or does it come and go? Also, does it get worse after eating, especially fatty foods, and have you noticed any nausea, vomiting, fever, or changes in your urine or stool color?

It started about a week ago. It's been constant since then. I haven't noticed it getting worse after eating, especially not after fatty foods. I did have some nausea a couple of weeks ago, but it's gone now. I haven't had any vomiting or fever. My urine has been really dark for the past couple of days, though. I haven't noticed any changes in my stool.

That's helpful, thank you. Dark urine along with belly pain makes me want to check a few more things. Have you noticed any yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes? Also, do you drink alcohol, and if so how much? Have you started any new medications, supplements, or herbal products recently? And have you traveled anywhere recently, used any recreational drugs, or had any new sexual partners or exposure to someone with hepatitis?

Yeah, yesterday I noticed that the whites of my eyes look really yellow. I drink alcohol, usually 5 to 6 drinks a week, sometimes more on weekends. I haven't started any new medications or supplements. I haven't traveled anywhere recently. I do smoke marijuana daily, and I've tried other drugs in the past, including IV drugs a couple of months ago. I haven't had any new sexual partners recently, but I have had several partners in the past year. I don't know if any of them had hepatitis.

Thank you for being so open with me, Jessie—that history is really important and helps a lot. Given your right-sided belly pain, dark urine, and now yellow eyes, along with the past IV drug use, I'm concerned this could be a form of hepatitis (liver inflammation), possibly viral. This needs some blood tests right away — liver function tests and hepatitis A, B, and C testing — to figure out exactly what's going on and how serious it is.

I'd also like to check in on your drug and alcohol use more when we have more time, since both can affect the liver too, but right now the priority is getting these labs done today. If you develop worsening pain, confusion, vomiting that won't stop, or you can't keep fluids down, please go to the ER right away. Otherwise, let's get you to the lab now and I'll follow up with you as soon as results are in. Does that sound okay?
That sounds good. I'll go get the blood tests done right away. I hope it's not too serious.

Yeah, I smoke. I've been smoking a pack of Salem Lights a day since I was 15.

I guess I could try to set a quit date. I'm just worried about the cravings and how I'll handle stress without smoking. I've had trouble concentrating and headaches when I tried to quit before. I'm willing to try the patch and lozenges if you think it'll help. I don't know if I can fit in counseling with my schedule, though.

turns.content: I’m very sorry—you received devastating news yesterday, and I’d like us to take this one step at a time. Can you tell me what you understood from the oncologist, and what feels most important or frightening to you right now?

Well, I got the results of my latest head scan yesterday and the oncologist said there's no clear path forward. I don't know what to do about it. I'm really scared about what this means for me and my family, especially with my daughter's graduation coming up in five months. I want to be there for that, but I don't know if I can.

I’m so sorry. Wanting to be at your daughter’s graduation makes complete sense. The estimates you were given—about a year with palliative chemotherapy versus about two months with hospice—are not exact deadlines, and neither option can guarantee five months. Chemotherapy may offer more time, but it would not cure the cancer and could mean frequent clinic visits, severe nausea, and limb pain; hospice would prioritize comfort at home, but likely with less time.

When you picture the coming months, would you accept substantial treatment burden for a chance at more time, or is being comfortable and able to engage with your family the higher priority?

I don't know. I want to be there for my daughter's graduation, but I'm really scared of the pain and nausea from the chemo. I want to spend good time with my family, but I'm not sure if I can handle the treatment. I just don't know what to do. How do I even make a decision like this?

There isn’t a “right” choice—only the choice that best fits what matters most to you. It may help to compare what each path makes possible: chemotherapy offers a chance of living to the graduation, but may take away some good days through treatment and side effects; hospice prioritizes comfort and time at home, but reaching five months would be less likely.

You can ask oncology whether a **time-limited trial of chemotherapy** is reasonable—start treatment with clear limits, aggressive nausea and pain control, and stop if the burden outweighs the benefit. Palliative-care support can also be involved even while receiving chemotherapy. Would having your family join a meeting with oncology and palliative care help, and what would make treatment feel no longer worth continuing to you?

I think talking with my family and the doctors together would help. I want them to understand what I'm going through and what my options are. As for the treatment, I guess if it starts to feel like it's making things worse than they already are, then maybe it's not worth it. I don't know exactly what that would look like, but I think I'll know it when I see it. I just want to make sure I'm not suffering more than I have to.

That’s a very reasonable goal: try for more time without accepting suffering at any cost. I’ll help arrange a prompt meeting with your oncologist, palliative-care team, and the family members you choose. We can discuss a time-limited chemotherapy trial and agree beforehand on specific stopping points—such as uncontrolled nausea or pain, spending most days in bed or in clinic, or being unable to meaningfully interact with your family. You can stop treatment and transition to hospice at any time; choosing comfort is not giving up.

Please bring someone you trust, and write down what a “good day” means to you. We’ll make sure symptom-control medicines and support are in place whichever path you choose, and we can revisit the decision as things change.

That sounds like a good plan. I'll talk to my spouse and daughter about it and see who wants to come with me to the meeting. I want to make sure we're all on the same page. I'll think about what a good day looks like for me and write it down. I just want to make sure I'm doing everything I can to be there for my family and to not suffer more than I have to.

1. **Opening Scenario**

* Patient name: Melanie Walker
* Sex: Female
* Presents to: Local emergency psychiatry services

You are the resident in local psychiatry emergency services seeing Melanie Walker, a 60-year-old female with past medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and cerebrovascular accidents (recently 3 small strokes in the past year with mild residual left-sided weakness) brought in by her husband for progressively worsening delusions. Her husband stated that she had “completely lost touch with reality,” and she had not been able to care for herself anymore.

You first speak with Melanie privately. When you ask what brings her here, she had said, “They got him. They made him think I’ve got some mental problem. But I know the truth. They’ve sent this man. I’m not crazy. I’m normal. I won’t let them get to me. You got to protect yourself.” She denies any prior psychiatric history.

**You are now preparing to go back to see the patient after you’ve staffed the case with your attending. The husband has left at this point. You would like to commit the patient for the following reasons:**

* **Pt is at imminent risk of harm to herself due to inability to care for self (not eating, not sleeping properly, not able to hold a job)**
* **Husband has expressed that he can no longer handle your behaviors at home, thus there is no other safe alternative**

turns.content: Hello Lou, I'm the doctor covering for Dr. Smith while he is away in Nepal. I received your email about having trouble sleeping over the past few weeks. Could you tell me a bit more about what has been going on with your sleep?

I’ve been having trouble sleeping and now I feel tired all day. I usually go to bed around 9 PM and fall asleep shortly after, but about a month ago, I started having trouble falling asleep. I often lie awake well past 10 PM and sometimes later. When I do finally fall asleep, I wake up frequently tossing and turning.

I'm sorry to hear that; dealing with broken sleep and feeling tired all day can be really draining. 

Did anything specific happen around a month ago when this started—like new stresses or changes in your mood or daily routine? Also, are any physical symptoms like pain, breathing issues, or needing to use the bathroom waking you up?

I don’t know what started it. I don’t have any pain or breathing issues, but I do get up to use the bathroom a few times at night. I’ve been feeling a bit lonely since my partner passed away last year. I don’t really have a strong support network in town.

I'm so sorry for the loss of your partner. Grieving and feeling isolated can definitely weigh heavily on both your emotional well-being and your sleep. 

Aside from feeling lonely, have you been feeling persistently down or losing interest in activities you usually enjoy? Also, what does your routine look like in the evening regarding fluids, caffeine, or screen time before bed?

I don’t know. I just thought I was having trouble sleeping. I don’t watch TV in bed, and I don’t drink alcohol immediately before I go to bed. I have tried reading as a way to help fall asleep. Nothing has worked. I don’t drink caffeine after 2 PM. I usually drink a glass of water before bed.

You are already practicing many good sleep habits, which is great. 

Given what you've shared, here are a few gentle steps we can start with:
1. **Limit evening fluids:** Try stopping liquids an hour or two before bed to reduce those nighttime bathroom trips that disrupt your sleep.
2. **Bed for sleep only:** If you're lying awake for more than 20 minutes, try moving to a comfortable chair with dim lighting to read, and only return to bed when you feel drowsy.
3. **Addressing the loneliness:** The loss of your partner and feeling isolated can quietly affect sleep. I'd love to connect you with some community support resources or grief counseling if you are open to it.

Let's try these adjustments for the next two weeks. I'd like to schedule a follow-up video visit then to see how you're resting and discuss next steps if things haven't improved. How does that sound to you?

I guess that makes sense. I don’t know if it will help, but I’ll try it. I don’t want to burden my son, but maybe talking to someone about my partner would help. I don’t know if I’m ready for that yet. I don’t want to have to drive in to the clinic though. It’s an hour drive and gas is expensive.

Hello, Mrs. Rodriguez. It is wonderful to meet you. Welcome to our clinic, and happy belated 65th birthday! 

I understand you're here for your Welcome to Medicare visit and to get established with us, and that you've also had some occasional back pain. To get us started, how have you been feeling overall, and could you tell me a little more about that back pain?

Well, thank you, Doctor. I've been okay overall, but I've had this back pain for about five years now. It's just a dull ache, mostly when I'm doing heavy chores or standing for too long. It doesn't really change with sitting or lying down, and it's not too bad, just a 3 out of 10. I take some glucosamine and use heat for it, and that helps a little.

I'm glad to hear it's generally manageable. Have you noticed any pain shooting down your legs, numbness, weakness, or any changes in your bowel or bladder control? Also, do you have any other medical conditions or take any other medications regularly?

No, I haven't noticed any shooting pains, numbness, or weakness in my legs. I do leak a little urine when I cough or sneeze, but that's about it. I don't have any other medical conditions that I'm aware of. I take glucosamine for my back and ibuprofen or Tylenol when I need it for pain.

Thank you for sharing that. Leaking a little urine when coughing or sneezing is quite common, and we can certainly discuss ways to help with that as well.

Since this is your Welcome to Medicare visit, it is a great time to focus on preventive care. Could you tell me when you last had routine health screenings—like a mammogram, bone density scan, or colon cancer screening—and if you are up to date on your vaccines?

I had a mammogram about 3 years ago, and it was normal. I have never had a bone density scan or a colonoscopy. I don't know what a colonoscopy is, actually. I have never had a flu shot or a pneumonia shot because I don't want to get the flu from the shot. I did get a tetanus shot about 3 years ago.

I really appreciate you being so open with me, Mrs. Rodriguez. 

To help protect your health moving forward, here is what I recommend as our next steps:
- **Screenings:** We will schedule a routine mammogram, a bone density scan (to check for bone thinning, which is recommended at 65), and discuss colon cancer screening—which looks for early changes in the large intestine through a simple camera test called a colonoscopy or even convenient stool tests you can do at home.
- **Vaccines:** I want to reassure you that the flu shot contains an inactive virus, so it is physically impossible to get the flu from the vaccine. We can talk through recommended vaccines like the flu, pneumonia, and shingles shots to keep you protected.
- **Back & Bladder:** We will look into gentle core and pelvic floor exercises (like Kegels) to help support your back and reduce that mild urinary leakage.

We will get those orders set up for you today. How does this plan sound to you, and what questions do you have for me?

That sounds good, Doctor. I didn't know about the bone density scan or the colonoscopy. I guess I should get those done. I'm a little nervous about the colonoscopy, but I'll do it if it's important. I didn't know that the flu shot doesn't give you the flu. That's good to know. I'll think about getting that. I have not noticed any problems with my bones, though. I have not had any falls or anything like that. I will try the exercises for my back and bladder. I just want to feel better and be healthy.

turns.content: Hi Taylor, I'm a medical student working with the clinic, and I'll be taking care of you today. Welcome to our practice! I see you're here to establish primary care. Besides getting set up with us, are there any specific health concerns or symptoms you'd like to discuss today?
Hi, thanks for having me. I got a tetanus shot after I stepped on a nail. The urgent care center said I should find a primary care doctor. No current complaints.

Ouch, stepping on a nail sounds painful! I'm glad you got that taken care of at urgent care and received your tetanus shot. 

Since you don't have any current issues, I'd like to get to know your overall health background a bit better. Do you have any medical conditions you've been diagnosed with in the past, and are you taking any medications or supplements regularly?
I had asthma as a kid, but I haven't seen a doctor for it since college. I take hormones, I buy them online.

Thanks for sharing that. It's good to know about the asthma, and we can definitely keep an eye out in case you ever start having breathing issues again. 

Regarding the hormones you're taking, could you tell me a little more about what kind they are and what your health goals are? My main priority is just to make sure you're getting the care you need safely, especially since you've had to buy them online.

I've been taking estrogen, I use a Climara patch. I'm trying to reduce facial hair growth and increase breast size. I don't know if a prescription would give me better results, but I'd like to know if it's safer and more reliable.

Thank you so much for sharing that with me. Yes, getting a prescription directly through us is absolutely safer and more reliable. When you buy online, it's hard to know exactly what you're getting, but with a prescription, we can ensure you have the right dose, avoid counterfeit products, and monitor your health safely. 

I would be more than happy to help you with your goals. Today, I will write you a prescription for your estrogen patches so you don't have to rely on the internet anymore. I'm also going to order some routine blood work so we can check your baseline hormone levels and make sure your body is handling everything well. Let's get those labs drawn today, send your prescription to your preferred pharmacy, and schedule a follow-up appointment in a few weeks to review your results and see how you're feeling. It was wonderful meeting you, Taylor, and I look forward to working with you!
That sounds great, thank you. I'll go ahead and get the labs done today.
