Hi Jane, it's good to see you again. I know you're here today to talk about your pain management and getting refills for your medications since your previous doctor retired. 

Before we discuss the next steps, I need to go over the results of the urine test you provided last week. The results came back and were concerning because they didn't match the medications you are prescribed. Can you help me understand how you've been taking your pain medications lately, or if there's anything else you've been taking?
I need another prescription for my pain medicine. I only have enough for one more week. I've been taking my morphine and Vicodin as prescribed. I haven't taken anything else.

Jane, I want to help you manage your pain, but I need us to be completely open with each other. The lab results from your urine test actually showed no trace of the morphine or Vicodin in your system. If you were taking them daily as prescribed, they would have shown up on the screen. 

I know dealing with chronic pain is incredibly difficult, and I see in your chart that you've worked really hard on your recovery in the past. Can you tell me honestly what is going on with your medications? Have you run out early, or been taking something else?

I'm sorry. I don't know why the Vicodin didn't show up. I've been taking it as prescribed. I did use some marijuana a few nights ago to help with the pain and sleep. I really don't want to go back to using heroin.

I appreciate your honesty about the marijuana, and I want you to know I am fully committed to helping you avoid a relapse. Your five years of recovery is a huge accomplishment, and protecting that is my top priority. 

However, because the morphine and Vicodin were not in your system, this violates the pain management agreement you signed with your previous doctor. Because of these results and the safety risks involved, I cannot continue to prescribe these narcotic medications for you. I know you are in pain, though, so I want to work with you on safer alternatives. Can we discuss some non-opioid medications and other therapies to help manage your back pain?

That sounds very scary to me. I can’t live normally with the pain from my back and I’m afraid I won’t be able to work. I will lose my job. I just can’t afford to have that happen. Please can’t you continue the medication because it works, and besides then I can keep my job.

I completely hear how scared you are, Jane, and I know how crucial it is for you to be able to work and keep your job. Please know that my primary responsibility is your health and safety. Because the medications weren't in your system, prescribing opioids right now is simply too dangerous and violates the safety agreement, so I cannot refill them. 

However, I am not abandoning you. We can use the week of medication you have left to help safely taper you so you don't go into withdrawal. At the same time, we will start safer, non-addictive pain medications and look into physical therapy to treat your back. I also want to connect you with a specialist who can help manage your pain while protecting your hard-won recovery. You've worked too hard these last five years, and we are going to work together to keep you safe and moving forward.

I don’t know what I’m going to do. I can’t live with the pain. I’m afraid I will lose my job. I will try the other medications and physical therapy. I just hope it helps. I don’t want to go back to using heroin.

If on the other hand the trainee is calm, professional, gentle, sensitive, then you should act visibly more relaxed.

Within seconds after speculum is placed, you should become very nervous, whispering to yourself “Oh no, Oh no, Oh no” (or something similar), legs start to tremble. Then say, “I don’t know if I can do this. Is there anything I should be doing?”

If the trainee tries any stress reduction techniques (any of the below or other similar interventions), state that you feel a little better, but are still really nervous – is there anything else you can try to bring down the stress level? After a second stress reduction technique, state that you’re feeling better, and it’s OK to go ahead with the exam.

Examples of Stress Reduction Techniques:

* Trainee asks you to take a few deep breaths
* Uses any MENTAL grounding technique (e.g., orients you by telling you where you are, what day it is, etc.)
* Uses any PHYSICAL grounding technique (e.g., asks you to make a fist and squeeze, hold the table, feel your hands, etc.)

If the trainee acts sensitive to your words even though they do not suggest any relaxing techniques whatsoever, give permission to proceed with the exam.

The only exception is if the trainee tries to force the continuation of the exam or acts especially insensitive, then you should say angrily, “I’m done! I can’t go through with this!” and the exam should be terminated.

When the trainee is done with the exam, the trainee should instruct you to sit up and get dressed before finishing the encounter (if they do not, ask if you can get your clothes on before finishing the visit). The trainee will then step out of the room.

When the trainee is out, move from the examining table back to the chair. The faculty examiner will let them know when you are ready.

**At the end of the exam:**

If asked what you are planning to do right after this appointment:

You anticipated this might be hard with your therapist, and agreed that you would give her a call if needed. You think you will do just that.

If asked if you have any questions or if there’s anything you need right now:

No, you think you’re OK.

# Station 3 – Shared Decision Making

Scenario:

You are a third year student rotating through a longitudinal ambulatory rotation. You are seeing a patient, Joanna Mills, for the second time. Ms. Mills is a 45-year old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. When you saw her for the first time last week, she had not been receiving medical care or medication refills for 6 months due to the loss of her medical insurance. Last week, she came to clinic to re-establish care and receive refills of her medications for diabetes mellitus. Last week, you agreed to refill her medications and ordered blood work. Ms. Mills has come in to clinic today to discuss the lab results with you.

You discussed this with your attending preceptor prior to seeing Ms. Mills. Your attending physician instructs you to discuss the results with Ms. Mills and encourages you to engage in shared decision making with your patient.
private_patient_context:
**Station 3 – Shared Decision Making**

**Training Materials:**

# 3. <u>Scenario for Standardized Patient</u>

You are Joanna Mills, a 45-year old woman. Last week, you came to a new hospital-based clinic to establish a primary care doctor and get refills of your medications, since you ran out of medications for diabetes mellitus. You haven’t been to see a doctor in over six months, and you’ve been rationing your medications during that time, but you ran out of medications last week.  The medical student whom you met last week gave you a one month supply of your medications (metformin and glyburide) but asked you to get blood work done so that s/he could “get a sense of how well controlled your diabetes was” and to make changes in medications, if necessary. You went to the laboratory last week after your visit and are now here for your scheduled follow up visit to go over the results of the blood test. You feel fine and have refilled your medications and do not have any new problems to report to the medical student today; but you are curious to learn about the results of your blood tests and hope to hear that your diabetes is well controlled.

<u>Medical History:</u>

You were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus four years ago by your primary care doctor at the time, Dr. Alvarez. You were not surprised when you received this diagnosis because you have a strong family history of diabetes. You know that the A1C blood test shows whether or not your diabetes is controlled, and you also know that anything less than 7 is good and anything higher than 7 means that the sugars are too high. You remember that when you were first diagnosed with diabetes, your A1C was 7.6. The doctor had you on Metformin first, but the following year, she added glyburide because the A1C was not at goal. Your doctor slowly increased the doses of these medications; and as of one year ago, had you at your current dose of metformin and glyburide.

You have not had any complications related to diabetes mellitus, and you have been taking your medications as prescribed. However, 6 months ago, you lost your job and your medical insurance. You could not afford to continue seeing your primary care doctor so you stopped going at that time. The doctor gave you last refills of your medications and encouraged you to come to the hospital-based clinic since they had a sliding scale fee service for patients. Six months ago at your last visit with Dr. Alvarez, you also had a blood test. You received a letter from Dr. Alvarez stating that your A1C was 8.8 and that you needed to follow up on this, but you were unable to see her or any other doctor until now.

You have been busy for the past few months so you did not come to the hospital clinic.

You have admittedly stretched out your remaining pills, sometimes skipping doses to make the prescription last a little longer. Last week, you were completely without medications; and you were scared about your sugars getting too high, so you came to the clinic.

<u>Family History:</u>

As noted above, you were not surprised when you were diagnosed with diabetes four years ago. Both of your parents suffered from it, and you know that it is an illness that can run in the family. However, you were still frightened when you were first given the diagnosis. You have seen both of your parents suffer from medical problems related to diabetes. Your father had high blood pressure and kidney problems, which his doctor said was due to diabetes. He passed away suddenly from a heart attack when he was 66 years old. Your mother, who is now 64, is alive but has many medical problems. Prior to her recent stroke 3 months ago, she had very poorly controlled high blood pressure and diabetes.  She has been in and out of the hospital several times a year for the past few years, either for chest pain or “fluid in the lungs” or skin infections and infected foot ulcers.

Besides diabetes, you do not have any other medical problems.

<u>Social History:</u>

You were laid off from your job as a clothing buyer for a large department store. Since then, you have been looking for a new job and have been trying to keep your spirits up. You were busy caring for your mother in another state for the past few months because she had a recent stroke. Between your mother’s illness and your search for a job, the past six months have been extraordinarily stressful for you; and you have not really had time to take care of yourself. But you have always wanted to stay in good health to avoid illness, and you know that it’s important to focus on your health right now.  You have been without health insurance since losing your job as you could not afford COBRA and you postponed looking into applying for Obama care in hopes that you would soon have a new job.  You have been unable to afford to refill your medications, and therefore, rationing the pills until you ran out of them last week.

You do not have any history of tobacco, alcohol, or drug use.

You are divorced and have a 20 year-old daughter, who is in college and no longer living at home

<u>Emotional Tone:</u>

You are very concerned about your health condition although it has been difficult for you to focus on your own health for the past six months, between your economic hardship and your mother’s acute illness. When you had insurance, you were always good about following up with your primary care doctor and taking all of your medications. Even though you have had diabetes for four years, you were told that you could be “in control” of your illness and maybe avoid complications of diabetes. You have been happy to take your pills, as long as it meant controlling your illness and avoiding complications of the disease.  You know that you have not taken your pills as prescribed, mostly because of financial concerns and the cost of medications.  You are very reluctant to start insulin. You know that being on insulin means needing to prick yourself several times a day to check your blood sugar and give yourself the insulin shots and you hate the thought of pricking yourself so frequently with needles.  Also, you know that the diabetic supplies (insulin and more lancets and paper strips for frequent sugar checks) are expensive and another cost that you feel would be really hard to absorb now.

**Your role is to portray a patient who is very concerned about your health. You want to know how to keep yourself healthy. Yet, you are upset and worried when you learn that your diabetes is not well controlled.  You are reluctant to start insulin therapy because you dislike the thought of using the needles to give yourself medication and the extra cost of medications and supplies feels like a financial burden that you feel unable to take at this time. In addition, although you know it is not rational you feel that using insulin means you are more likely to develop the complications you saw your parents go through because they were on insulin.  However, you normally always follow your doctor’s advice and are unsure about going against his advice by not starting insulin.**

<u>Scenario:</u> 

The student will enter the clinic room, where you are waiting to be seen. You are seated next to the desk, appearing comfortable but a little anxious. You met this student last week and are happy to see the same person again.

The student may ask, “I wanted to talk to you about your blood test results that we did last week. Do you know what an A1C test signifies?”

**“Yes, I remember my last doctor telling me that it was a blood test that the doctors took to show whether the diabetes was controlled or not. I know that it’s supposed to be below 7.”**

The student will inform you that your A1C level was elevated, at 11.

You are surprised and concerned.

**“Oh no, that’s really high isn’t it?”**

The student should inform you that this A1C is very elevated and indicates that the diabetes is very poorly controlled at this time. You are upset and very worried by this news.

**“It’s never been so high like this. You know I was worried about my sugars but I never thought it could get up to this level.” What does this mean I have to do now?”**

The student should describe treatment options. Since you are on high doses of your current medications, there is no way to simply go up on the current dose of medications. The student will recommend starting insulin therapy as a way to rapidly bring down the A1C level and control the diabetes.

You interrupt the student when s/he mentions insulin and get visibly upset.

**“Wait, insulin? Oh, I don’t want to do that.”**

The student should ask you why you do not want to start insulin. S/He should give you a chance to state what your concerns are. You state many reasons why you don’t want to start insulin therapy now. After you give each reason, you should give the student a chance to discuss it with you.

**“I know that there are a lot of reasons why my sugars got uncontrolled like this. I wasn’t doing all the things that I know I should have been doing about my health. I wasn’t eating right, I wasn’t consistently taking my pills every day. I wasn’t really focusing on my health. I think that there are a lot of things besides insulin that I can do to get my health back in order.”**

**“I know that when you start insulin, you have to check your sugars many times throughout the day. And those extra supplies, those strips and lancets, they all cost a lot of money that I don’t think I’d be able to afford right now.”**

**“To tell you the truth, I’m really afraid of pricking myself with a needle to give myself insulin.  I don’t think that I could do that. I hate needles and the thought of giving myself shots every day is really scary to me.”**

**“I am so afraid of insulin.  I know it isn’t rational but I feel like insulin means I have diabetes with a capital D.  Do you know what I mean – it seems more serious.  I saw my dad go through so much, and now my mom with her stroke.  They were both on insulin.”**

The student should respond to all of your concerns and reasons for not wanting to start insulin. If he does not acknowledge or validate your concerns then you should remain resistant to starting insulin.

The student should ask you about what your desires regarding the management of your illness are. S/He might ask, “Ms. Mills, can you tell me a little bit about how diabetes is affecting your life, and what you are hoping to do to manage your illness? What would you like to see for yourself regarding your diabetes?

**“I really don’t want to be sick from diabetes like my mother was. I know all about the complications, the foot ulcers, the amputations, dialysis, strokes… I’m just really scared about my diabetes being out of control because I never want to go through what she’s been going though with her health. I want to be healthy for my daughter and for myself. So I want to do what you think is best. I’ve always listened to doctors in the past. But right now, I am just really scared of this insulin for a lot of reasons too. I am just hoping for a way that I can get back into good health again without going down the insulin road.”**

The student should try to engage you in deciding what the best treatment for your diabetes is. If he only recommends insulin and says that nothing else will work right now, but you don’t feel that he/she acknowledges the reasons why you do not want to start insulin, you will be more resistant to starting insulin now. However, if the student shares information with you about insulin treatment that addresses your concerns, you might consider changing your mind. Here are some examples of effective statements:

“The insulin that I would recommend starting you on is a once daily insulin that works slowly over 24 hours. You do not have to give yourself multiple injections of insulin each day. Rather, you could give yourself one injection a day.”

“The benefit of starting insulin is that it is more likely to successfully bring your A1C level down to signify good control of your diabetes. The better we control your diabetes, the less likely it is that you would ever get the complications of diabetes (such as kidney problems or eye problems.)

“One concern that I have in continuing with oral medicines rather than insulin, is that the oral medications do not bring down the A1C level as effectively as insulin does. I can tell that it is really important for you to get in control of your diabetes, and I think that this is the most successful way that we can do it.”

“Insulin is one part of the plan that we can create to control your diabetes. You are right that diet and exercise and taking your medications every day are equally important in controlling your diabetes. I think that we can work together on each of these issues, and perhaps insulin can be a component of this plan.”

If you feel that the student has engaged you as a partner in making the decision and has given you a chance to address your beliefs and concerns about your illness, then you should agree to work with the student to come up with a plan together; and you can agree to try the insulin.

**“Okay, I see what you are saying. I think that if you feel the insulin may really help me get my diabetes under control and keep me healthy, then I will try it for a while and see how my sugars improve.”**

If you feel that the student has not given you a chance to speak about your concerns and has not enlisted you as a partner in decision making, but rather unilaterally recommended insulin without building a consensus with you, then you should not agree to start insulin. You are calmer at the end but are very resolute about not starting insulin today.

**“You know, I don’t think I am able to get over my fear of starting insulin right now. I’d really rather try getting back on my pills every day and see how I do for a while before I switch my medicines.”**

If at any time the student asks a question that you do not understand or is at all unclear, then you should ask them to clarify. You can say:

**“What do you mean by that?”**

Hi, I've been feeling okay since we last talked. I've been taking my medications regularly again since I got the refill, so that's been going fine.

I'm glad the medications are going smoothly. So let's go over the lab results from last week. You are a 45 year old man who was hit by a car today.  You have been taken by ambulance to the Emergency Department for evaluation.  Your major injury is a mangled left leg but you don’t know it as you haven’t really seen what your leg looks like.  You know it’s injured but do not know the extent.  You are on a backboard and in a neck collar.

The student will talk to you, examine you, and tell you what further exams and tests he/she would like to order.  He/She will inform you of results, talk to you about bicycle safety and explain to you that you need surgery and that you might have to have a leg amputation.

You were riding your bicycle at around dusk without a helmet and without any safety lights.  You were to the right of a car in the right lane.  The car suddenly began to make a right turn and hit you.  You fell off the bike and recall that your left leg was run over by a tire.  You did not lose consciousness.  You have neck pain and left leg pain (10/10) as well as feeling sore all over.  No other pain in any extremities.  No abdominal pain, chest pain, or shortness of breath.  You last meal was lunch, about 4 hours ago.

**Past medical history**

No medical problems in the past.  No hospitalizations.  No surgeries.

Not Significant

**Medications:** Hydrochlorothiazide

**Allergies:** None

**Social History:** You do not smoke or use illicit drugs.  You live with your wife.  You work as an accountant.  You drink about one glass of wine per day.

**Leg Pain:** 10 out of 10

**Last Tetanus:** Unknown

First time you are told about the amputation:

“No, you can not take off my leg”

If they do not give you pain medications after the initial history and physical.

“Doctor, the leg is hurting me a lot. Can I get something for pain?”

Lying on a stretcher. We do this in a classroom and use a table and sheet.

Patient gown

Patient has a cervical collar correctly positioned on his neck.

Cervical collar

Picture of leg or moulage

Stretcher or table

Sheets

Patient gown

**Transgender Health: A Standardized Patient Case for Advanced Clerkship Students**

**Appendix B: Michael**

**Activities and Time Required**

10 minute patient encounter followed by 5 minute post-encounter debriefing.

**Materials**

Prior to the encounter, the medical student will receive a folder labeled “Patient Chart” with a Date of Birth and the patient name “Cynthia Glenshaw” and instructions that the patient is here for an exam required to obtain life insurance (Appendix C). Student will either call the patient in from the hallway or greet the patient after reviewing the chart.

**Chief Complaint**

The patient is visiting the clinician to receive an exam required for obtaining life insurance.

**Instructions to Standardized Patient**

*Chief Complaint and Social History*

* Patient is at the doctor today for a documented note that has a complete history and exam required to obtain life insurance.
* Patient hasn’t been to the doctor for 5 years due to a number of transphobic interactions with previous doctors. Patient does not like or trust doctors, and does not want to be at the doctor today.
* Patient is in a long-term monogamous relationship with a cisgender woman. Patient and his partner recently got married and bought a condo, and the patient’s partner insists that they obtain life insurance.
* Patient does not smoke, drinks the occasional glass of wine, and does not use illicit or recreational drugs.
* Patient has no past medical history, surgical history, nor family history.

*Physician-Patient Introduction*

* The patient prefers the name “Michael” and the pronouns he/his. The ideal behavior is the student asks the patient what name/pronoun he prefers.
* The patient’s legal name is Cynthia as per the patient’s door chart for the case.
* If medical student initially uses the wrong name and/or pronouns, SP’s initial demeanor should be one of mild anger and frustration. The SP should become less angry and frustrated as the medical student makes efforts to establish the correct name and preferred pronouns. If the medical student misgenders the SP repeatedly and/or focuses the history-taking on inappropriate questions, the SP should gently refuse to answer questions and eventually ask for a different doctor.

*Medical history taking*

* During medical history, if medical student asks SP if they are on any other medications, the SP should ask what they mean by “medication” (e.g. define it, what drugs qualify as medications including those that are obtained over the counter, herbal, or in this case those purchased on the internet without a prescription). Following the response, then the SP should bring up that he has been using injectable testosterone purchased from the internet for the past two years.
* During medical history, if medical student does not ask SP if he is on any other medications, then the SP should bring up that he has been using injectable testosterone purchased from the internet for the past two years.
* The medical student should then inquire about where the patient obtains the needles and syringes and if he uses anyone else’s or shares his with other people. The patient endorses purchasing these on-line as well and using new needles and syringes every time he injects.

turns.content: Hi Morgan, I'm Dr. [Name]. I can see you're really uncomfortable — I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Can you tell me what's going on with your right arm, and when it started?
Hi, yeah, it's been pretty bad. My right arm has been hurting, red, and swollen for about four days now. It started as a little cat bite, but it's gotten a lot worse since then.

That sounds really painful, and four days of it getting worse is concerning. A couple of important things I want to ask - have you noticed any red streaking going up your arm, pus or drainage from the wound, or any chills, confusion, or feeling like your heart is racing? Also, can you tell me how the bite happened - was this your own cat or another animal?

Yeah, I've noticed some red streaks going up my arm. There's some pus coming out too. I've been feeling really warm and shivery, and my heart's been racing. It was my own cat that bit me. I was trying to play with him, and he got a bit aggressive.

That's really helpful, thank you for sharing all that - the red streaking and fever with a fast heart rate tell me this infection may be spreading, so I want to make sure we take this seriously. A few more quick things: do you have any medical conditions like diabetes, or any issues with your immune system? Are you on any medications, and do you know if you're up to date on your tetanus shot? Also, have you tried cleaning the wound or taking any antibiotics already?

No, I don't have any medical conditions like diabetes or immune system problems. I'm not on any medications right now. I don't know if my tetanus shot is up to date. I tried cleaning the wound at home, but I haven't taken any antibiotics.

Okay, thank you for all that information, Morgan - it's really helpful. Here's where things stand: given the redness spreading up your arm, the fever, chills, and fast heart rate, this looks like a worsening infection from the cat bite, called cellulitis, and cat bites can carry bacteria that get serious quickly. I'm going to have my attending come examine your arm right away, and we'll likely need to start IV antibiotics and check some blood work to see how far this has spread - you may need to be monitored closely, possibly even admitted, depending on what we find. We'll also make sure you get a tetanus booster if you need one. I know this is scary, but you did the right thing coming in today, and we're going to take good care of you. Do you have any questions before I bring my attending in?
I guess I'm just wondering how bad this can get if it's not treated right away. I've had infections before, but nothing like this. I'm just really worried about what's going to happen next.

turns.content: Hi María, it's nice to meet you. I'm the clinician who will be seeing you today. What brings you into the clinic?
Hi, nice to meet you too. I haven’t had my period in 3 months.
Thank you for letting me know. To start, is there any chance that you might be pregnant? Have you taken any home pregnancy tests recently?
I don't think so. I use oral contraception. I haven't taken any pregnancy tests.

Even with birth control, pregnancy is still a possibility, especially if a pill is missed or taken late. Have you missed any of your pills recently, or noticed any other new symptoms like nausea or breast tenderness?
I haven't missed any pills. I have noticed some breast changes, but no tenderness. I have had some milk secretion from my breasts. I haven't noticed any nausea.

Thank you for sharing that. The milk secretion along with the missed periods gives us a very helpful clue. Have you been experiencing any frequent headaches or changes in your vision recently? 

Since we are wrapping up our initial chat, I want to share our next steps. We will start with a quick urine pregnancy test today just to be absolutely sure, and then we'll draw some blood to check your thyroid and a hormone called prolactin, which can commonly cause both missed periods and breast discharge.

**Appendix B - OSCE standardized patient training guide**

**Sally Martin Overview**

You are a 43 year old woman who presents to your Family Medicine Clinic for a diabetes management follow up appointment.

**Your opening line:**

“I’m here for a follow-up on my diabetes management”

**How you will present yourself to the student:**

* You are friendly, however you will express concern about your health
* You are feeling overwhelmed about your recent health set-back and with all the additional medications that were prescribed (for your “cold” – information below)
* You are also overwhelmed about the increase in blood sugar readings, recently (information below)
* You are compliant with all your medications, but you really do not have a strong understanding of your diabetes management

**Diabetes history:**

* Your PCP diagnosed you with Type II diabetes approximately 3 years ago. Took an oral medication for two years, but it wasn’t working. If asked, you don’t remember the name, but it started with an “M”. If the student says “Metformin” – you say “yes”.
* Your PCP started you on insulin 9 months ago at 30 units twice daily.
* You attended a follow-up appointment 6 months ago when your PCP increased your insulin 40 units twice daily.
* You missed your follow up appointment 3 months ago due to a “fender-bender” on your way to the clinic (nobody was hurt, but the front wheel was too damaged to drive on).
* You are currently taking 40 units of insulin twice a day.
* Your blood sugar readings have normally been 160 to 200, but recently they have been in the 240-260s. You will wonder if being sick and being on the medications you were prescribed for your “cold” are the reason. **\*\* Do not volunteer to student\*\***

* You are concerned about your diabetes and you want to discuss the diabetes management plan. **This is your priority**

**Your current roster of diseases**

* Diabetes
* “COPD” from smoking
* High blood pressure
* “Kidney Problems” from diabetes and high blood pressure

**Your understanding of the roster of medications you are taking currently**

* You have been taking insulin to manage your diabetes. You are taking 40 units twice a day – that was the dose that was prescribed 6 months ago. If pressed, you’ll mention that you’re not quite sure if it matters if you take the medication before or after you eat but most of the time you are taking the insulin after eating.
* You recall that you are on 2 new medications that are temporary for your “cold.” You realize that those medications are about to be finished but not quite sure if it is 1 or 2 more days (“tomorrow or the next day”).
* You cannot immediately recall the names of your “regular” medications for COPD and kidney disease. However, if the student can remind you of the names, you are familiar with them – just not off the top of your head. You do not know the dose you are taking for any of the medications.
  + - Albuterol as required (prescribed as a “rescue inhaler” for COPD and also used for the cold)

    - NPH/regular insulin 70/30, 40 units twice a day with breakfast and dinner (Diabetes)
    - Losartan (kidney problems and high blood pressure)
    - Simvastatin (cholesterol)
    - Azithromycin antibiotic added at urgent care visit for your “cold” (finishing tomorrow or day after)
    - Prednisone (oral steroid) added at urgent care visit for your “cold” (finishing tomorrow or day after)

**Recent associated symptoms:**

* You have been getting up in the middle of the night to urinate (1-2 times a night)
* You have been urinating every 5-6 hours during the day. **So, yes, you are “peeing more than usual”**
* You have been more thirsty over the past few days, as well

turns.content: Hi Mrs. Martin, it's nice to see you today. I understand you're here for a follow-up on your diabetes. I noticed your blood sugar check in the clinic today was running quite high at 288. How have you been feeling overall, and have you noticed any symptoms lately like increased thirst or needing to urinate more often?

I’m here for a follow-up on my diabetes management. I’ve been feeling a bit off for the past few weeks. I’ve been getting up at night to use the bathroom and I’ve been urinating every 5-6 hours during the day. I’ve also been really thirsty lately.

I'm sorry to hear you've been feeling off and dealing with that extra thirst and frequent urination. To help me figure out what's going on, could you tell me what medications you are currently taking for your diabetes and how it's been going with taking them every day?

I’ve been taking insulin for my diabetes. I take 40 units twice a day. I usually take it after I eat. I’ve been taking it like this for the past 6 months. I don’t really know if it matters if I take it before or after I eat.

Thank you for sharing that. The timing of your insulin actually does make a big difference; we usually recommend taking it before your meals so it's ready to work right when your body digests the food. Have you happened to miss any doses of your insulin recently, and have there been any recent changes to what you typically eat in a day?

I don’t think I’ve missed any doses. I’ve been trying to take it every day. I’ve been eating more snack foods like crackers and chips. I’ve skipped lunch a couple of times. I’ve been drinking mostly water but occasionally Coke (Regular Coke) and unsweetened tea. I don’t know exactly how much I’ve been drinking, but I know it’s more than usual.

Thank you for sharing that. It sounds like taking the insulin after meals instead of before, along with the extra carbohydrate snacks and regular soda, is causing your blood sugar to run high. This perfectly explains your recent symptoms of increased thirst and frequent urination. 

Today, I would like to do a physical exam, particularly to listen to your heart and check your feet for any loss of sensation or sores, which is important for diabetes care. 

Going forward, my main recommendations are to start taking your insulin 15 to 30 minutes *before* your meals and to try swapping the regular Coke and snacks for sugar-free options. I also noticed your blood pressure was a bit elevated today, so we will need to keep a close eye on that as well. What questions do you have about this plan?

Appendix B:  *SP Training Notes*

**Patient Name:** Robin Samuels

Setting: Outpatient/ Ambulatory Urgi-Center

Chief Complaint: “I’m here to get antibiotics for my sinus infection”

**Patient Profile**

SP recruitment profile: 20-40 years old, adaptable to any sex, race and age

Appearance: well-groomed, hospital gown

Moulage: petechiae, lower extremities

Affect: Pleasant and cooperative, normally a high energy person

Employment: Full time kindergarten teacher in Elmhurst, NY. You love your job and cannot think of any other job that you would want to have.

Education: You graduated high school and college – you were working on your masters but couldn’t keep up with it between your children, work and getting sick so often…. You decided to hold off on it for a few years until your children are a bit older.

Lifestyle: You lead a simple yet busy life, particularly as you balance working full time at a school and taking care of your three young children. They are involved in many after school activities and you love taking them to all of them. Your husband works in his own business (restaurant) and so is not around that much – weekends and evenings are his busy times and so you must do most of the child care.

Relationships: You have been married to your high school sweetheart for 15 years. You have a strong relationship. You have never been unfaithful to him, nor do you believe he has to you.

Habits: Smoking: you never smoked

Coffee/Caffeine: you drink a coffee in the morning – and 1-2 teas in the afternoon. In the summer you drink ice tea. You occasionally have a coke – but not often

Alcohol/Drugs: You have a glass of wine only on the weekends if you go out to dinner. No drugs.

Nutrition: You try to eat a well-balanced and healthy diet.

Exercise: no formal exercise program. Walks the dog ½ mile a day every morning and evening.

Sleep: you get a well-rested full night’s sleep normally.

Religion: You are protestant and attend service regularly

**Case information**:

Chief complaint: “I’m here to get antibiotics for my sinus infection”

Response to “tell me more”: “I started not to feel right three days ago. At first just a bit under-the weather – tired, a bit achy and a slight headache. I took some vitamin C and went to bed early and tried to sleep it off. However, I wasn’t any better in the morning. My head hurt even more, and I felt a lot of pressure in my facial sinuses and in my ears, especially on the right side. It almost feels like I like I am underwater. My right ear hurts inside – like a pressure. I took some decongestant but yesterday my temperature popped up to 102 and when I was blowing my nose all this thick yellow to greenish stuff was coming out. Just feels like a typical sinus infection – I don’t want it to go into my lungs and now I am not short of breath at all and I don’t feel it in my lungs, so I want to get some antibiotics before it spreads there!

Additional concerns/agenda: none

History of Present Illness: You went to a Northwell GoHealth Urgent Care center for what seems like a fairly typical sinus infection. You get sinus and ear infections 2-3 times a year. Sometimes it even goes into pneumonia. You have had pneumonia three times in the last 10 years – and that is with the pneumonia vaccine.

Other than this infection you consider yourself healthy. The history of bronchiectasis is relatively recent (last bout of pneumonia was last year, at which time your primary doctor said you also had this). You cough up every day with thick and light-yellow phlegm but occurs usually once in the morning when you first wake up. You have a bout of coughing, bring up this phlegm and then go about your day. You have only noticed shortness of breath when you exert yourself, like running up the stairs.

ONLY IF ASKED: You have had many sinus and ear infections since you were about 18 years old. You have even had pneumonia so many times that you have some permanent lung damage from it [bronchiectasis]. You attribute this to your job as a kindergarten teacher because as a kid, you were always very healthy, rarely got colds and didn’t even have tubes in your ears.

ONLY IF ASKED - Are you short of breath? Not more than I usually am. My bronchiectasis is mild and generally only get short of breath if I am exerting myself, likely walking up a couple of flights of stairs.

ONLY IF ASKED- Are you coughing more? My cough is generally mild but daily. It is not worse than it has been.

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have chest pain? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have cough up blood? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Is your nasal discharge bloody? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Have you had weight loss? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Are you bringing up more phlegm than usual? no

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have any kidney problems? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have any rashes? Lately you notice these little red dots on your legs and arms where you were holding some groceries. They don’t itch, they don’t hurt, they don’t seem to be getting worse and they fade. You weren’t that concerned about them. during the PE if the student is examining it – say “isn’t that weird – it is so flat you can’t feel it.

Impact on Life: “if I get my antibiotics I do fine and there is no impact. If I don’t get my antibiotics, then I get sick really fast.”

Concern: “you are concerned that if you don’t get antibiotics quickly you will get really sick”

Explanatory model: “You are constantly exposed to sniffly, sick kids at work.”

Review of systems: Do not volunteer these symptoms – only disclose them if asked

Pertinent Positives:

* With the bronchiectasis you have a chronic cough with mucous production – there has been no change in this with this infection.
* You have chronic diarrhea – with watery stools daily – no hx of gi infections like salmonella, campylobacter or giardia. You attribute this to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
* Lately you seem to be bruising a bit more easily- you seem to get them out of nowhere – they are mostly on your legs, but you also noticed them on your arm where you were holding a bag of milk.

Pertinent Negatives:

* No weight loss
* No history of cancers or lymphomas
* No history of lymph nodes being enlarged

Past medical history: Early bronchiectasis.

You did NOT have a lot of infections during your childhood. You began having recurrent sinusitis that started in your late teems – around 17 or 18. It often goes into your chest and you develop bronchitis – about once a year. You have even had pneumonia 3 x in the last 10 years – last year it was “pretty bad”. You recently have been worked up and told you have bronchiectasis.

Medications: no prescription, over the counter or herbal medications.

Allergies : denies medication, environmental or food allergies

Vaccinations: Flu shot yearly in November

Received all childhood vaccines

Pneumonia vaccine several years ago at PMD – “was supposed to help with my sinus issues and prevent me from having pneumonia again, but apparently it didn’t work out too well”

Sexual hx: Your husband is your one and only lifetime partner.

Family hx: Mother. Alive-age 76. High blood pressure, high cholesterol

Father. Alive-age 77. Gout

Physical Exam

General: You are well groomed, in a gown on the exam table. You can perform all required physical exam maneuvers without difficulty. You breathe comfortably throughout the exam without exertional dyspnea.

Vital Signs:

HEENT: If student performs otoscopic exam, hand them the ear PE finding card

Skin: Moulage will be applied to your lower legs. It will be a diffuse small scattered erythematous macule. As the student examines your rash, say “isn’t that weird, it’s so flat that you can’t even feel it!”

Lungs You will have SimScope patches placed on your front and back lung fields (rhonchi in lower fields)

Heart You will have SimScope patches placed over your heart (normal)

Abdomen: You will have a SimScope patch on your belly (normal)

Extremities: If student examines the nailbeds, hand them the finger PE finding card

turns.content: Hi Robin, I'm the clinician seeing you today. I noticed your temperature is quite high at 102 degrees. Can you tell me what's been going on and how you're feeling?

I’m here to get antibiotics for my sinus infection. I started not to feel right three days ago. At first, I was just a bit under the weather—tired, a bit achy, and a slight headache. I took some vitamin C and went to bed early, but I wasn’t any better in the morning. My head hurt even more, and I felt a lot of pressure in my facial sinuses and in my ears, especially on the right side. It almost feels like I'm underwater. My right ear hurts inside—like a pressure. I took some decongestant but yesterday my temperature popped up to 102 and when I was blowing my nose all this thick yellow to greenish stuff was coming out.

That sounds miserable, I'm sorry you're dealing with all that pressure and the high fever. To help me get a better picture of what's going on, have you had a cough, sore throat, or any trouble breathing? And have you noticed any changes in your ability to taste or smell?

I haven't had a sore throat or trouble breathing. I do have a cough, but it's been the same as usual—just a bit of phlegm in the morning. I haven't noticed any changes in my ability to taste or smell.
You mentioned having your usual cough with some morning phlegm—do you currently smoke or vape? And have you taken anything like Tylenol or ibuprofen to help bring that fever down?
I don't smoke or vape. I haven't taken anything for the fever.

Thank you for letting me know. Since you're only on day three of these symptoms, it's highly likely that this is a viral infection, which means antibiotics won't actually help right now and could cause unwanted side effects. I would highly recommend taking some Tylenol or ibuprofen to help bring your fever down and relieve that facial and ear pain. Normally, my next step would be to do a physical exam to look inside your ears, nose, and throat to rule out a bacterial ear infection, and then we could finalize the best plan to keep you comfortable while you recover.

private_patient_context:
**Case summary**

Name: Jonny Spencer

Chief complaint: pelvic examination for the purpose of cervical cancer screening

Profile: Jonny is a 45 year-old self-identified lesbian who established primary care with you 3 weeks ago and returns by mutual agreement to discuss and possibly undergo a pelvic examination. Her last Pap test was 20 years ago, and she admits that she has avoided gynecological care for years because of a history of incest and a “terrible experience” during her last pelvic examination.

**Standardized Patient Instructions**

Name:JONNY SPENCER

Setting: outpatient clinic

Dress: clean, casual clothes appropriate for a female in her 40s

Affect: cautious, nervous

**Background for appointment:** You are a 45 year-old self-identified lesbian who established primary care with this trainee 3 weeks ago and now return by mutual agreement to discuss and possibly undergo a pelvic exam/Pap test. Last time you came to clinic you had a good experience with this trainee. You already addressed the rationale for and the process of the pelvic exam and agreed to come back to do it today.

**General guidelines:** You have been dreading the visit, which is part of the reason that you couldn’t go through with it a month ago. Your one and only prior Pap test was 20 years ago, and you’ve avoided gynecological care ever since because it was such a terrible experience. You’ve been seeing a therapist for the past year because of PTSD related to childhood incest, and she’s been working with you to get back on track with health screenings.

Purpose for the visit: You are here for your pelvic exam and Pap test. If the trainee asks for more details: You have no symptoms. You’re feeling pretty anxious, but you feel like things went well at the last visit, and that’s given you the confidence to be here today.

**Review of systems:**

If asked about your periods: You started menstruating at age 13. Your periods are regular and don’t bother you in any way. You think the amount of bleeding is normal. Your last period was 2 weeks ago.

If asked about vaginal discharge: You haven’t noticed anything like that.

If asked about other symptoms or diseases: No, I’ve never experienced anything like that.

If asked what happened during your last pelvic exam: You can’t remember all the details, because you think you blocked some of it out. You just remember experiencing searing pain when the doctor put something in your vagina. It seemed to go on and on. Afterwards you worried that something was wrong because you noticed blood staining your underwear for a few days. You never called the doctor to ask because you were afraid she hurt you during the exam and didn’t feel safe having any more contact.

If asked what you know about the reasons for doing a pelvic exam: You know it’s done to look for cancer and STDs.

If asked if you think it would be helpful to learn more about the pelvic exam: No, you heard the trainee loud and clear last time and you have no further questions.

If asked whether you have any concerns, say, “I’m just nervous that I will freak out or that this will be painful. I just don’t want to experience what happened last time.”

If the trainee asks whether you would be willing to try doing the pelvic exam today: “Yes, I think that would be okay.”

If asked if you would like to have a support person or a chaperone present during the exam:

Yes, you think that might be a good idea. You’d like to try to get it over with today and your partner couldn’t make it. It’s OK with you to have the medical assistant be the chaperone.

Past history:

If asked about any medical problems you've had: Except for the PTSD, you’ve always thought you were pretty healthy.

If asked about your medications: You do not use any prescription or over the counter medications.

If asked about drug allergies: You are not aware of any drug allergies.

Sexual history:

If asked about your current sexual activity:

You are a ‘non-practicing lesbian’. You have zero libido these days, do not masturbate, and you have not been sexually active with your partner since the early days of your relationship 15 years ago.

If asked about prior sexual partners:

Before Ann, you had 2 girlfriends. You were infrequently sexually active with them also. Your stepfather made you give him blow jobs when you were in middle school. You have never had sexual contact with any other men.

If asked about use of barriers:

You’ve never used dental dams or Saran Wrap when you’ve been sexual with women. Condoms have never been an issue because you don’t use sex toys and aren’t sexual with men.

If asked about contraception use:

You’ve never used contraception because you haven’t needed it.

If asked about STD/HIV testing/treatment:

You were tested for everything a few years ago and all the tests were negative. There isn’t any need to test you again now because you aren’t sexual.

Information about safety and intimate partner violence:

If asked about any history of physical or sexual abuse/assault:

Your stepfather made you give him blow jobs when you were in grade school.

If asked if your current partner insults or talks down to you, screams or curses at you, makes you feel threatened or has ever made you feel unsafe or afraid, has ever physically hurt (pushed, grabbed, slapped, choked, or kicked) you:

No, Ann is very calm and supportive.

If asked if you’ve ever been coerced into having sex or pushed into doing things sexually you didn’t want to do:

No, Ann has a history of sexual abuse too, and sex has always been infrequent. In the past when you were more sexual together, it was always consensual and loving.

If asked if you or your partner own a gun or other weapon:

No.

If asked if you have ever attempted suicide:

No. You used to have suicidal thoughts, but not for a very long time. You never tried anything and don’t think you ever could.

If asked if you are having suicidal thoughts now:

You used to have suicidal thoughts, but that’s passed. The work you’ve been doing with your therapist has given you a lot of hope.

Information about coping and self-care:

If asked about support systems, safe places, personal strengths, how you’ve coped with hard things in the past and might use those skills to cope now:

Your partner is a huge support, and you have a lot of friends.

You see your therapist every week, and can call her if you need to between sessions.

You’ve developed a toolbox of coping strategies, including writing thoughts down so you can set them aside, playing the piano, and taking a walk.

Your personal history:

If asked about smoking: You smoked occasional cigarettes when you were a teenager.

If asked about alcohol use: You binged a lot in your 20s, but only have a few drinks weekly now.

If asked about drug use: You tried marijuana once or twice, but haven’t used any other drugs.

If asked about your job/school: You’re a tax accountant.

If asked about your living situation: You live with your partner and 2 cats.

Family history: Your father died suddenly when you were 10. There was no autopsy and you don’t know why.

**During the exam:**

The trainee will step out of the room at the examiner’s instructions. At this point, move to the exam table, sit in a cross-legged position, and with the examiner’s help place the pelvic model at the end of the exam table. Cover your lap and model with a paper drape.

If asked if you would like to try inserting the speculum yourself, rather than having the trainee insert it: No, you’d rather just get on with it and let them do their thing.

If asked if you would feel more comfortable with your feet in a different position other than in the footrests (stirrups): That’s OK. It doesn’t really make a difference to you what position you’re in. It’s tough no matter what.

**General Guidelines during exam:**

From the start of the exam, you should adjust your level of anxiety based on how sensitive or gentle the trainee is. For example, if the trainee is abrupt, not talking through all the steps, or not recognizing your baseline anxiety, you should have increased anxiety. If on the other hand the trainee is calm, professional, gentle, sensitive, then you should act visibly more relaxed.

Within seconds after speculum is placed, you should become very nervous, whispering to yourself “Oh no, Oh no, Oh no” (or something similar), legs start to tremble. Then say, “I don’t know if I can do this. Is there anything I should be doing?”

If the trainee tries any stress reduction techniques (any of the below or other similar interventions), state that you feel a little better, but are still really nervous – is there anything else you can try to bring down the stress level? After a second stress reduction technique, state that you’re feeling better, and it’s OK to go ahead with the exam.

Examples of Stress Reduction Techniques:

* Trainee asks you to take a few deep breaths
* Uses any MENTAL grounding technique (e.g., orients you by telling you where you are, what day it is, etc.)
* Uses any PHYSICAL grounding technique (e.g., asks you to make a fist and squeeze, hold the table, feel your hands, etc.)

If the trainee acts sensitive to your words even though they do not suggest any relaxing techniques whatsoever, give permission to proceed with the exam.

The only exception is if the trainee tries to force the continuation of the exam or acts especially insensitive, then you should say angrily, “I’m done! I can’t go through with this!” and the exam should be terminated.

When the trainee is done with the exam, the trainee should instruct you to sit up and get dressed before finishing the encounter (if they do not, ask if you can get your clothes on before finishing the visit). The trainee will then step out of the room.

When the trainee is out, move from the examining table back to the chair. The faculty examiner will let them know when you are ready.

**At the end of the exam:**

If asked what you are planning to do right after this appointment:

You anticipated this might be hard with your therapist, and agreed that you would give her a call if needed. You think you will do just that.

If asked if you have any questions or if there’s anything you need right now:

No, you think you’re OK.

turns.content: Hi there, how are you feeling right now? I wanted to come by and walk you through what happened yesterday and last night—especially why it took some time before we figured out you had a perforated ulcer that needed surgery. Before I explain, can you tell me how your pain and breathing feel at this moment?

Hi doc, I'm feeling a bit tired and sore from the surgery, but the pain is under control right now. My breathing is okay, nothing unusual there. I'm just glad to be feeling better than I was last night.

I'm really glad to hear the pain is better controlled and you're breathing comfortably now. I know yesterday was a rough ride, so let me explain what happened.

When you first came to the ER, your symptoms—stomach pain, some nausea—looked a lot like a common condition called dyspepsia, basically bad indigestion or ulcer irritation, which is very common and usually doesn't require surgery. Your vital signs were stable, and your exam at that point didn't show the classic signs we look for with a perforation, like a rigid, board-like abdomen. So the initial plan was reasonably to send you home with medication and outpatient follow-up.

But then your pain got worse over the next few hours, which was an important signal that something more was going on. That's when the team appropriately changed course and admitted you for observation rather than sending you home. When I examined you around 9pm, you were uncomfortable, but the picture still wasn't fully clear yet.

What ended up happening after that is that further evaluation—imaging and repeat exams—showed that you actually had a small perforation, a hole, in your duodenum (the first part of the intestine right after the stomach), which needed surgical repair. This is a known complication of ulcers, and sometimes the signs are subtle early on, especially if the leak is small or partially sealed off by nearby tissue, which is often why it doesn't look like a classic "surgical abdomen" right away.

Do you have questions about that timeline, or about how the perforation was ultimately found?

I don't understand... how could something like this happen? I was in agony... how could you have left me that way... I could have died. I thought I was getting good care... I don't know how to feel about this... this is why I don’t like going to doctors.

I hear you, and I'm really sorry you went through that — being in that much pain and feeling like you weren't being taken seriously is frightening, and it makes complete sense that you're upset and questioning things. You deserve an honest answer, not excuses.

The truth is, perforated ulcers can be genuinely difficult to catch early. In many cases, the initial presentation looks almost identical to ordinary stomach pain or bad indigestion — same location, similar quality of pain — especially if the perforation is small or the body starts to wall it off. Your vital signs were stable early on, and the exam didn't show the more obvious red flags we typically rely on, like a rigid abdomen or signs of shock. That's not an excuse for what you experienced — it's the reality of why this diagnosis is sometimes missed on a first pass, even with careful evaluation.

What matters most is that when your pain escalated, the team didn't dismiss it — they changed the plan, kept you in the hospital, and continued to reassess you, which is exactly what needed to happen. And ultimately, the perforation was identified and surgically repaired, and you're now on the other side of that surgery, awake, talking, with your pain controlled.

I want to be transparent with you: this wasn't a case of anyone ignoring you or being careless — it was a diagnosis that unfolded over hours because the symptoms evolved. But I also want to acknowledge that "explainable" doesn't take away how frightening and painful that experience was for you, and your feelings about it are completely valid.

Is there anything specific about the timeline or the decision-making that's still bothering you, that I can try to clarify further?

I appreciate you being honest with me. I guess I just don't understand how the X-ray at 10 pm didn't show the problem right away. I was in so much pain, and it feels like it took forever for someone to figure out what was wrong. I'm just glad I'm going to be okay, but it's still scary to think about what could have happened. I thought I was getting good care, and now I'm not sure what to think. I don't know how to feel about this.

That's a really fair question, and I understand why that's confusing and scary to sit with. I have to be honest with you — I wasn't directly involved in reading that particular imaging or in the details of exactly what it showed at that time, so I don't want to guess or give you inaccurate information about that specific study. What I can tell you in general is that early imaging for a perforation can sometimes look normal or subtle, especially if the leak is small or sealed off temporarily by surrounding tissue — free air or other signs can take time to become visible, or may be easy to miss on a first read. This is a real and recognized challenge in diagnosing these injuries, not unique to your case.

What I'd really encourage is that you ask the surgical team taking care of you now — they'll have the full picture of your imaging and can walk you through exactly what was seen and when, which will give you much clearer answers than I can from where I sit. You deserve that clarity, and you deserve to have your questions fully answered.

For what it's worth, I know today has been overwhelming, but you got through the surgery, your pain is controlled, and you're recovering. It's okay to feel shaken and unsure — that reaction makes total sense given what you went through. Please don't hesitate to keep asking questions, of the surgical team, of the nurses, of anyone — you have every right to understand your own care. Is there anything I can help arrange right now, like getting a message to your surgical team so they can come speak with you about the imaging specifically?

I guess that makes sense, but it's still hard to wrap my head around. I'll make sure to ask the surgical team about the X-ray when they come by. I just want to understand what happened. I appreciate you being so open with me. It's a lot to take in, but I'm just glad I'm going to be okay. I think I just need some time to process everything. Thank you for coming by and explaining things to me.

## <u>**STATION**</u> 

**Tobacco Dependence**

# 1. <u>**INSTRUCTIONS FOR PATIENT:**</u>

You have experienced daily cough for about 2 months. You went to an urgent care two weeks ago and got a “Z-Pack” and an inhaler which did not help. They also did a chest x-ray and pulmonary function test and TB skin test. They “didn’t find anything.”  You think worry that your smoking might be causing the cough but you have tried to quit in the past and have not been able to. You are thinking about trying to quit, but you are doubtful about your chances of success.

## 1.1. ***Symptoms***

Daily morning cough for the past 2-3 months.  You have a cough in the morning with a little bit of gray mucous. Aside from the mild cough, <u>***you have no other symptoms***</u>.

Physical exam is normal.

## 1.2. ***Other history***

No history of asthma or allergy as a child.

No heartburn or reflux symptoms.

No wheezing.

No sick contacts.

No medications except Benadryl as needed.

No nasal congestion. No fever.

No regular exercise.

Your parents are alive and in their 70s.

You are married with two kids. You are a teacher. You were born in US and never traveled outside US. No illegal drug use. No incarceration.

1. You smoke a pack of cigarettes a day since age 15.  You smoke Salem Lights. You switched from the regular Salem’s 8 years ago. You smoke after meals, with your coffee which you take on the back porch as your morning, afternoon, and evening ritual (while you grade papers), in your car when you drive, and during your lunch and planning period.
2. You have tried to quit a total of four times over the years.   You tried once with the patch (which you wore for two weeks) and once with the gum (you chewed only a few pieces when you had bad cravings). You still had cravings despite the medicines, and you didn’t like the taste of the gum, so you doubt the medicines work. Your longest quit attempt was two weeks.
3. Your spouse does not smoke and doesn’t let you smoke in the house. You can’t smoke at school. You do take a smoking break at lunch time, but you have to go out to your car or to a nearby coffee shop with an outdoor patio to smoke.
4. Your 70 year old father has smoked his whole life without health consequences.  Your grandfather still smokes a pipe at 94 years old.
5. You really enjoy smoking because it helps you relax and to concentrate and keep your weight down.

You doubt the NRT will work, but if they explain the need to take a high enough dose to eliminate withdrawal symptoms then you are willing to try any combination of medications other than the gum. If they offer counseling, tell them that you are worried it will not fit with your schedule, but if they give you several alternatives that include the quitline or evening or weekend classes, tell them that you are willing to try counseling. If they don’t offer you support when they suggest you quit, talk about how cigarettes help relieve your stress, and how you have had difficulty concentrating and headaches when you tried to quit before.

If the doctor gives you treatment recommendations that do not include quitting smoking, wait until the two minute warning or they say that they are done and then ask:

- “My partner thinks my cough is because I smoke, but my family all smoke and none of them cough. Do you think I should try to cut down?

turns.content: Hello. I'm glad you could come in today. I know you saw your oncologist yesterday to go over your MRI results, and I received their notes. It sounded like a very difficult conversation. How are you holding up, and what did they tell you about where things stand?
Well, I got the results of my latest head scan yesterday and I don’t know what to do about them. The oncologist said he doesn’t know what to do either. I'm really struggling with this.

I am so sorry. Hearing that news must be incredibly overwhelming, and I can completely understand why you are struggling right now. My understanding from the oncologist's note is that while there is no longer a path to cure the cancer, there are two different options for how we focus your care moving forward. Did they discuss those options with you, or would it be helpful if we walk through them together?
They did mention two options, but I didn't really understand them. I think I need to hear them again. I want to make sure I understand what I'm choosing.

It is completely understandable that it was hard to take everything in yesterday. Let's go through them together. 

The first option is a new chemotherapy regimen. While it wouldn't cure the cancer, it could give you about a year of life. However, it is very intensive—it requires coming to the clinic three days a week and is known to cause severe nausea and pain in your arms and legs. 

The second option is to focus entirely on your comfort and quality of life through home hospice. This means stopping cancer treatments and focusing strictly on medications and therapies that keep you comfortable and pain-free at home. With this path, the expected time you have left is about two months. 

I know this is incredibly heavy to process. What are your initial thoughts or fears when you hear these two paths?

I don't know what to do. I want to be there for my daughter's graduation in five months, but I'm scared of being in more pain. I don't want to spend my time feeling sick and in agony. I want the time I have left to be good time. I'm really afraid of dying. I don't want to leave my family.

I hear you, and it is completely normal to be terrified right now. Wanting to be there for your daughter's graduation is a beautiful and deeply important goal, and I can't imagine how heartbreaking it is to weigh that against the fear of spending your remaining time feeling sick and in pain. 

It is an agonizing choice between trying to push for more time to reach that milestone, and focusing purely on having the best possible quality of life at home with your family. You do not have to make this decision today. I recommend we take a little time to let this settle, and perhaps we can bring your family in to talk through this together if you are comfortable with that. Whatever you decide, I am here for you and will support you every step of the way.
I think I need to talk to my family about this. I don't want to make this decision alone. I want to be there for my daughter, but I don't want to be in pain. I need some time to think about this.

turns.content: Hi there, thanks for reaching out even though you're feeling so rough. I'm sorry you've been dealing with this for 4 days now. Can you tell me more about the cough — is it dry or are you bringing up any mucus, and what color is it if so? Also, are you having any fever, chills, or trouble breathing?
I've been coughing up some clear or yellowish mucus, but not a lot. I haven't had a fever, no chills, and no trouble breathing. It's just this nagging cough and runny nose that won't go away.

Okay, that's helpful to know — no fever or breathing trouble is reassuring. A couple more questions: Is the runny nose clear or thicker/discolored, and do you have any sinus pressure, sore throat, headache, or ear pain? Also, any body aches, fatigue, or issues with your sense of taste/smell? And do you have any history of asthma, COPD, or other lung/heart problems?

The runny nose is clear or yellowish. I've had a bit of a sore throat in the morning, but it gets better throughout the day. I've been feeling achy, and I'm pretty tired. Once we have those results, we'll discuss the best plan moving forward. Do you have any questions before we get started with those tests?
No, I don't have any questions. I'm ready for the tests.

turns.content: Hello Mrs. Martin, it's good to see you today. I see we're following up on your diabetes management. How have you been feeling lately, and how have your blood sugar levels been running at home?

I’m here for a follow-up on my diabetes management. I’ve been feeling a bit overwhelmed lately. My blood sugar readings have been higher than usual, in the 240-260 range, especially since I had that cold.

I understand how frustrating and overwhelming that can be, especially after dealing with an illness. To help me get a clearer picture, what medications are you currently taking for your diabetes, and have you been able to take them as prescribed?

I'm taking insulin for my diabetes. I take 40 units twice a day, usually after breakfast and dinner. I've been taking it as prescribed, but I'm not sure if it matters if I take it before or after I eat. I've been compliant with all my medications.

The timing of insulin around meals can definitely make a difference in your numbers. Are you experiencing any symptoms like increased thirst, frequent urination, blurry vision, or any numbness or tingling in your hands and feet?

I've been getting up at night to urinate and I've been urinating every 5-6 hours during the day. I've also been more thirsty over the past few days. I've noticed some numbness in the bottom of my feet and burning. It seems to be stable since I started insulin. I haven't noticed any blurry vision.

Thank you for sharing those details, Mrs. Martin. Your blood sugar is elevated today at 288, and those home readings along with your increased thirst and nighttime urination indicate your diabetes is currently not well-controlled. Recent illness and taking your insulin after meals rather than before can certainly contribute to these high numbers. 

Here is what I recommend for our plan today:
1. **Physical Examination:** We will perform a physical exam today, focusing particularly on checking your heart, blood pressure, and a thorough foot exam to evaluate the numbness and burning you've felt.
2. **Insulin & Medication Adjustments:** We will clarify your specific insulin type and adjust the timing so you take it before meals, and possibly adjust the dosage to bring your blood sugars down safely.
3. **Lab Work & Referrals:** We will check your A1c to see your 3-month average, check your kidney function and urine, and arrange for an annual dilated eye exam.
4. **Blood Pressure:** Your blood pressure is also a bit high today (152/85), so we will monitor that closely and discuss treatment if it stays elevated.

We will also connect you with our diabetes educator to provide extra support. If you ever feel severely nauseous, confused, or have shortness of breath, please seek emergency care right away. How does this plan sound to you, and what questions do you have?

That sounds good. I'm just worried about my blood sugars being so high. I want to make sure I'm doing everything right. I'm glad I'll be seeing the diabetes educator later today. I don't have any other questions right now.

Appendix B:  *SP Training Notes*

**Patient Name:** Robin Samuels

Education: You graduated high school and college – you were working on your masters but couldn’t keep up with it between your children, work and getting sick so often…. You decided to hold off on it for a few years until your children are a bit older.

Lifestyle: You lead a simple yet busy life, particularly as you balance working full time at a school and taking care of your three young children. They are involved in many after school activities and you love taking them to all of them. Your husband works in his own business (restaurant) and so is not around that much – weekends and evenings are his busy times and so you must do most of the child care.

Relationships: You have been married to your high school sweetheart for 15 years. You have a strong relationship. You have never been unfaithful to him, nor do you believe he has to you.

Habits: Smoking: you never smoked

Coffee/Caffeine: you drink a coffee in the morning – and 1-2 teas in the afternoon. In the summer you drink ice tea. You occasionally have a coke – but not often

Alcohol/Drugs: You have a glass of wine only on the weekends if you go out to dinner. No drugs.

Nutrition: You try to eat a well-balanced and healthy diet.

Exercise: no formal exercise program. Walks the dog ½ mile a day every morning and evening.

Sleep: you get a well-rested full night’s sleep normally.

Religion: You are protestant and attend service regularly

**Case information**:

Chief complaint: “I’m here to get antibiotics for my sinus infection”

Response to “tell me more”: “I started not to feel right three days ago. At first just a bit under-the weather – tired, a bit achy and a slight headache. I took some vitamin C and went to bed early and tried to sleep it off. However, I wasn’t any better in the morning. My head hurt even more, and I felt a lot of pressure in my facial sinuses and in my ears, especially on the right side. It almost feels like I like I am underwater. My right ear hurts inside – like a pressure. I took some decongestant but yesterday my temperature popped up to 102 and when I was blowing my nose all this thick yellow to greenish stuff was coming out. Just feels like a typical sinus infection – I don’t want it to go into my lungs and now I am not short of breath at all and I don’t feel it in my lungs, so I want to get some antibiotics before it spreads there!

Additional concerns/agenda: none

History of Present Illness: You went to a Northwell GoHealth Urgent Care center for what seems like a fairly typical sinus infection. You get sinus and ear infections 2-3 times a year. Sometimes it even goes into pneumonia. You have had pneumonia three times in the last 10 years – and that is with the pneumonia vaccine.

Other than this infection you consider yourself healthy. The history of bronchiectasis is relatively recent (last bout of pneumonia was last year, at which time your primary doctor said you also had this). You cough up every day with thick and light-yellow phlegm but occurs usually once in the morning when you first wake up. You have a bout of coughing, bring up this phlegm and then go about your day. You have only noticed shortness of breath when you exert yourself, like running up the stairs.

ONLY IF ASKED: You have had many sinus and ear infections since you were about 18 years old. You have even had pneumonia so many times that you have some permanent lung damage from it [bronchiectasis]. You attribute this to your job as a kindergarten teacher because as a kid, you were always very healthy, rarely got colds and didn’t even have tubes in your ears.

ONLY IF ASKED - Are you short of breath? Not more than I usually am. My bronchiectasis is mild and generally only get short of breath if I am exerting myself, likely walking up a couple of flights of stairs.

ONLY IF ASKED- Are you coughing more? My cough is generally mild but daily. It is not worse than it has been.

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have chest pain? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have cough up blood? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Is your nasal discharge bloody? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Have you had weight loss? No

ONLY IF ASKED- Are you bringing up more phlegm than usual? no

ONLY IF ASKED- Do you have any rashes? Lately you notice these little red dots on your legs and arms where you were holding some groceries. You weren’t that concerned about them. during the PE if the student is examining it – say “isn’t that weird – it is so flat you can’t feel it.

Impact on Life: “if I get my antibiotics I do fine and there is no impact. If I don’t get my antibiotics, then I get sick really fast.”

Concern: “you are concerned that if you don’t get antibiotics quickly you will get really sick”

Explanatory model: “You are constantly exposed to sniffly, sick kids at work.”

Review of systems: Do not volunteer these symptoms – only disclose them if asked

Pertinent Positives:

* Lately you seem to be bruising a bit more easily- you seem to get them out of nowhere – they are mostly on your legs, but you also noticed them on your arm where you were holding a bag of milk.

* No history of cancers or lymphomas
* No history of lymph nodes being enlarged

Past medical history: Early bronchiectasis.

You did NOT have a lot of infections during your childhood. You began having recurrent sinusitis that started in your late teems – around 17 or 18.
